pullRequests.title: Preserve null projection elements in pattern comprehension
pullRequests.body:
Pattern comprehension `[(n)-[:R]->(m) | expr]` was dropping matched rows whose projection evaluated to `null`, returning `[]` where Neo4j returns `[null]`:

```cypher
CREATE (:Person {name:'Alice'})-[:FRIEND_OF]->(:Person);
MATCH (n:Person {name:'Alice'})
RETURN [(n)-[:FRIEND_OF]-(m) | m.name] AS friendNames;
// FalkorDB: []     Neo4j: [null]
```

### Root cause
The plan builder aggregated projected values via `collect()`, which per Cypher spec filters out nulls — correct for `collect()`, wrong for pattern comprehension where each successful match must contribute one element regardless of projection nullity.

### Changes
- **`agg_collect.c`** — new internal aggregator `pc_collect`: a `collect` variant that retains null inputs. Registered with `internal=true`, so it is not callable from user queries.
- **`build_pattern_comprehension_ops.c`** — emit `pc_collect` instead of `collect` for the comprehension's aggregate. `buildPatternPathOps` is left on `collect` since paths are never null on a real match and it depends on the `Optional` op injecting nulls for the no-match case.
- **TCK** — unskip `Pattern2` scenarios `[4]` and `[5]`, which assert exactly this behavior.
- **Flow test** — add `test22_pattern_comprehension_null_projection` covering the issue repro and a mixed (null + non-null) row.

User-facing `collect()` semantics are unchanged.

pullRequests.title: Fix `EXISTS((n)-[:rel]->())` evaluating to true on unrelated nodes
pullRequests.body:
`EXISTS(<pattern path>)` in `RETURN`/`WITH` projections always returned `true`, regardless of whether the bound node had any matching relationship — including on graphs with zero edges.

```cypher
CREATE (:Person {id:1}), (:Person {id:2}), (:Person {id:3});
MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.id, EXISTS((n)-[:KNOWS]->());
// before: 1=true, 2=true, 3=true
// after:  1=false, 2=false, 3=false   (matches Neo4j)
```

### Root cause

`buildPatternPathOps` lifts a pattern path used as an expression argument into an `Apply` over an `Aggregate` running `collect()`, binding the array of matched paths to a generated variable:

```
Project
    Apply
        Node By Label Scan | (n:Person)
        Aggregate                                  -- collect(...)
            Conditional Traverse | (n)-[@anon_1:KNOWS]->(@anon_0)
                Argument
```

`AR_EXISTS` only checks `SIValue_IsNull`. The collected variable is always an array (possibly empty), never `NULL`, so the result was unconditionally `true`.

### Changes

- **`src/arithmetic/arithmetic_expression_construct.c`** — In `_AR_EXP_FromApplyExpression`, when the function is `exists` and its single argument is a `CYPHER_AST_PATTERN_PATH` or `CYPHER_AST_PATTERN_COMPREHENSION`, rewrite the expression at construction time to `size(<pattern>) > 0`. Property-form `EXISTS(n.prop)` is untouched (its argument is a `CYPHER_AST_PROPERTY_OPERATOR`, not a pattern).
- **`tests/flow/test_path_filter.py`** — New `test_exists_pattern_predicate_in_projection` covering: isolated-nodes graph, single-edge graph, `NOT EXISTS`, `WITH` projection, and a regression check for `EXISTS(n.prop)`.

### Out of scope

`WHERE EXISTS((n)-[:rel]->())` raises a separate, pre-existing `Unable to resolve filtered alias` error (filter placed before the `Apply` that materializes the collected variable). That bug exists on `main` independent of this change and is not addressed here.

pullRequests.title: fix: handle variable-length traversal types in _costBaseLabelScan
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #636

## Root cause

`_costBaseLabelScan` only recognized `OPType_CONDITIONAL_TRAVERSE` and `OPType_EXPAND_INTO` as valid parent operation types when determining which label to scan. Queries using variable-length traversals (e.g. `MATCH (n:A)<-[*]-(n:Z)`) produce `OPType_CONDITIONAL_VAR_LEN_TRAVERSE` or `OPType_CONDITIONAL_VAR_LEN_TRAVERSE_EXPAND_INTO` as the parent, causing the optimizer to skip label switching and later crash in `AlgebraicExpression_Dest` due to a NULL dereference.

## Fix

- Added `#include` for `op_cond_var_len_traverse.h`
- Extended the type check to also accept `OPType_CONDITIONAL_VAR_LEN_TRAVERSE` and `OPType_CONDITIONAL_VAR_LEN_TRAVERSE_EXPAND_INTO`
- Retrieves the `AlgebraicExpression` from `CondVarLenTraverse` struct (which has the same `ae` field as `OpCondTraverse` and `OpExpandInto`)
- Used a `switch` statement for clarity and type safety

This was already identified by @swilly22 in the issue comments.

pullRequests.title: fix: prevent double-free in AttributeSet_Update on duplicate attribute IDs
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #1885

When a Cypher SET clause references the same property more than once (e.g. `SET n.x = NULL, n.x = NULL`), the categorization loop in `AttributeSet_Update` would add the same attribute index to `remove_idx` multiple times, causing `AttributeSet_RemoveIdx` to free the same slot twice.

**Root cause:** The categorization loop calls `AttributeSet_Contains` to locate the existing slot for each attr_id. When the same attr_id appears twice, both iterations find the same index and add it to `remove_idx` (or `add_idx`), leading to a double-free / heap-use-after-free.

**Fix:** Skip duplicate attr_id occurrences, keeping only the last occurrence. Applied to both the `only_additions` path (where duplicates would create duplicate entries in the set) and the main categorized path (where duplicates corrupt remove_idx/add_idx).

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

* **Bug Fixes**

pullRequests.title: fix: use atomic ops for jobqueue.len to eliminate data race
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #1969

`thpool_queue_full`, `thpool_wait`, and `thpool_get_jobqueue_len` read
`jobqueue.len` without holding `rwmutex`, while `jobqueue_push` and
`jobqueue_pull` modify it under the mutex. This is a classic data race.

**Fix:** Changed `len` from plain `int` to `atomic_int` and used
`atomic_load`/-`store`/-`fetch_add`/-`fetch_sub` for every access.
The `rwmutex` is still held for linked-list pointer operations in
push/pull.

**Sites fixed:**
| Function | Before | After |
|----------|--------|-------|
| `thpool_queue_full` | bare read | `atomic_load` |
| `thpool_wait` | bare read | `atomic_load` |
| `thpool_get_jobqueue_len` | bare read | `atomic_load` |
| `thpool_get_tasks` | bare read (under mutex) | `atomic_load` |
| `jobqueue_init` | assignment | `atomic_init` |
| `jobqueue_clear` | bare read + assignment | `atomic_load` + `atomic_store` |
| `jobqueue_push` | bare read + `++` | `atomic_load` + `atomic_fetch_add` |
| `jobqueue_pull` | bare reads + `=` + `--` | `atomic_load` + `atomic_store` + `atomic_fetch_sub` |

pullRequests.title: fix: continue outer loop in AndMultiplexer_Consume when a branch fails
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #1883

`AndMultiplexer_Consume` silently terminates the entire query when any filter branch returns `NULL`.

**Root cause:** After `OpBase_DeleteRecord(&op->r)` and `break` in the inner for-loop, execution fell through to `return r` where `r == NULL`, signaling exhaustion to the caller.

**Fix:** Check if `op->r` was cleared by a branch failure and `continue` the outer `while(true)` loop to try the next bound record.

**Reference:** `OrMultiplexer_Consume` already handles this correctly — when no branch succeeds it deletes the record and loops back. The AND variant was missing the equivalent check after its inner loop.

pullRequests.title: Fix batch-backport workflow permissions for backporting workflow files
pullRequests.body:
`.github/workflows/batch-backport.yml` declared `workflows: write` under `permissions:` (added in #1672), which is not a valid GitHub Actions permission key and is silently ignored. Even with it set, the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot push commits that touch `.github/workflows/` because it lacks the `workflow` OAuth scope, so any backport containing workflow changes would fail at the push step.

### Changes

- **Remove** the unsupported `workflows: write` line from the job's `permissions:` block.
- **Authenticate checkout with a PAT** (`secrets.BACKPORT_PAT`) so the credentials persisted by `actions/checkout` — and reused by the subsequent `git push` — carry the `workflow` scope needed to update files under `.github/workflows/`.

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write
steps:
  - name: Checkout repository
    uses: actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd # v6
    with:
      fetch-depth: 0
      token: ${{ secrets.BACKPORT_PAT }}
```

### Follow-up required

A `BACKPORT_PAT` repository/organization secret must be provisioned — a PAT (or fine-grained token) with `contents: write` and `workflows: write` on this repo. Other `gh` CLI steps continue to use `GITHUB_TOKEN` since they only read API data and open the PR.

pullRequests.title: Add memory regression tests for GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE workloads
pullRequests.body:
Existing `test_memory_usage.py` validates `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE` correctness but does not catch unintentional growth in reported memory over time. This change adds a regression harness that fails CI when a fixed workload's reported `total_graph_sz_mb` exceeds a checked-in baseline beyond a configurable tolerance.

### Changes

- **`tests/flow/test_memory_regression.py`** — new `testMemoryRegression` class, auto-discovered by RLTest (so `make flow-tests` runs it in the existing CI job; no workflow changes). Workloads: 10K plain / labeled / int-attr / string-attr nodes, 10K edges ± attribute, 10K indexed nodes, and 5× create/delete cycles to guard against gradual leaks.
- **Regression criterion** — `measured > baseline * (1 + TOLERANCE_PCT/100) + TOLERANCE_MIN_MB`. Defaults: 10 % + 0.5 MB absolute floor (the floor suppresses noise on near-zero readings). Both knobs are env-overridable.
- **`tests/flow/memory_baselines.json`** — checked-in baseline store. Starts empty; missing entries are bootstrapped (recorded + passed with a notice) on first run, so initial CI false-positive rate is zero. Real regression checking begins once baselines are committed.
- **Baseline refresh** — `MEMORY_REGRESSION_UPDATE=1 ./tests/flow/tests.sh TEST=test_memory_regression` re-measures and overwrites the JSON; commit alongside the code change that justifies the new values.
- **`tests/flow/README_memory_regression.md`** — workloads table, tolerance/env-var reference, and the update workflow.

### Example failure message

```
Memory regression in workload 'nodes_with_int_attr_10k':
baseline=2.134000 MB, measured=2.910000 MB, limit=2.847400 MB
(tolerance=10% + 0.5 MB). If this change is intentional, refresh the
baseline by running with MEMORY_REGRESSION_UPDATE=1 and commit
tests/flow/memory_baselines.json.
```

### Notes for reviewers

- Env config (`Env(env='oss-cluster')`) and `SAMPLES 100` intentionally mirror `test_memory_usage.py` for parity.
- Initial baselines are deliberately left empty

pullRequests.title: fix(delta_matrix): NULL-guard lock/synchronize to prevent SIGSEGV on RESTORE
pullRequests.body:
## What this fixes

Redis segfaults when FalkorDB receives certain `RESTORE` commands.
The trigger: the v18 graph decoder encounters a relation-matrix slot that
was never allocated, and the resulting null pointer is fed through
`Graph_GetRelationMatrix` → `Delta_Matrix_synchronize` →
`Delta_Matrix_lock`, where `pthread_mutex_lock(&NULL->mutex)` brings
the whole host process down.

---

Delta_Matrix_lock, Delta_Matrix_unlock and Delta_Matrix_synchronize all begin with `ASSERT(C != NULL)`. In release builds ASSERT() compiles to a no-op, so when a caller passes a NULL Delta_Matrix the next line attempts pthread_mutex_lock(&NULL->mutex) and Redis segfaults with SIGSEGV (signal 11) accessing address ~0x28 (offsetof mutex in Delta_Matrix struct).

## Reproducer

Observed against FalkorDB v4.18.4 and v4.18.7 in production, then reproduced locally against current master built with `make` (release).

1. Build the module: `make` (release, no DEBUG=1).
2. Start redis: `redis-server --loadmodule .../falkordb.so --appendonly yes`.
3. Populate any graph (script content not bug-specific — we used a 923-node `:Pattern -[:HAS_LAYER]-> :SignalLayer` KG plus 36 other sibling graphs imported from cypher dumps).
4. From a separate client, issue `RESTORE <existing_key> 0 <serialized blob> REPLACE` against an already-populated graph key, using a blob produced by an earlier DUMP of a similar graph that exercised the v18 encoder. (In our environment, an application-layer "kg-restore-on-login" warmup was re-RESTORE-ing graphs whose KV state was already in memory; the meta tracking went out of sync after a manual cypher reimport.)
5. Redis crashes:

   ``` pthread_mutex_lock+0x4
   ↑ Delta_Matrix_lock+0x11               (delta_matrix.c)
   ↑ Delta_Matrix_synchronize+0x41        (delta_wait.c)
   ↑ _MatrixSynchronize+0x16              (graph.c)
   ↑ Graph_GetRelationMatrix+0x37         (graph.c:1568)
   ↑ RdbLoadRelationMatrices_v18+0x9b     (prev/v18/decode_matrix.

pullRequests.title: Fix: Null pointer dereference in AlgebraicExpression_Dest for variable length edges
pullRequests.body:
Closes #636. 

Variable-length traversals (e.g., `[*..]`) generate an `AL_EXP_POW` operation. However, the recursive AST functions `_AlgebraicExpression_SrcOperand` and `_Pushdown_TransposeOperation` were missing coverage for this algebraic operation type, falling through to a default case that asserted false and returned a `NULL` pointer, crashing the Redis server.

This PR adds `AL_EXP_POW` support directly adjacent to `AL_EXP_ADD` in both switch cases since they have structurally equivalent data-flow properties for source resolution and transpose pushdown.

pullRequests.title: Fix crash and support DUMP/RESTORE of a graph to a different key (#2048)
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

`DUMP`-ing a graph and `RESTORE`-ing the payload under a **different key while the original graph still exists** crashes the server with a NULL-pointer dereference. Any client able to run `RESTORE` can take the whole server down.

This makes restoring to a different key produce an **independent copy** of the graph (and removes the crash), following the approach in #1737 — ported here to the current `v19` decoder, which #1737 predates.

Closes #2048. Related: #1737.

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A)-[:R]->(:B)"
EVAL "return redis.call('RESTORE', KEYS[2], 0, redis.call('DUMP', KEYS[1]))" 2 g g2
```

The server dies with SIGSEGV in `Delta_Matrix_nvals` ← `RdbLoadRelationMatrices` ← `RdbLoadGraphContext_latest`. Deleting `g` before restoring does not crash — the crash requires the embedded graph name to collide with a live graph.

## Root cause

A graph dump embeds the **graph name**, and `_GetOrCreateGraphContext` looks the graph up by that embedded name. Restoring under a different key while the original is still present returns the **existing, populated** graph. Its decode context has `processed == 0`, so the payload is treated as that graph's first virtual key and `RdbLoadGraphSchema_v19` re-adds every schema on top of the live graph, **doubling** `Graph_RelationTypeCount`. `RdbLoadRelationMatrices_v19` then iterates more times than there are matrix blocks in the payload; the stream desyncs, the relation id read from it goes out of range, and `Graph_GetRelationMatrix` indexes `g->relations[r]` out of bounds (the only guards in the decode path are `ASSERT`, a no-op in release builds). The result is a NULL `Delta_Matrix` dereferenced in `Delta_Matrix_nvals`.

## Fix

Thread the **destination key name** (from `RedisModule_GetKeyNameFromIO`) into the header decode. For a single-key restore to a different name (`key_number == 1 && key_name != graph_name`) where a fully-loaded graph already exists under the embedded name (`processed == 0`), crea

pullRequests.title: Fix same-alias variable-length label planning
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #636

/try
/claim #636

## Summary

This fixes same-alias variable-length traversal planning for queries such as:

```cypher
MATCH (n:A)<-[*]-(n:Z) RETURN 1
```

When the source and destination aliases are the same node, the destination label is not a new traversal endpoint to resolve. It is another constraint on the already-bound node. The fix moves same-alias destination label checks before the variable-length traversal, so the var-len op is built over the relationship matrix only instead of being asked to resolve a multi-labeled endpoint.

The redundant-label cleanup is also tightened so a later source label operand is removed only when that exact `(alias, label)` was already resolved by a previous expression connected through the same alias. This preserves correctness for cases where one label was checked but another same-alias label was not.

## Regression Coverage

Added coverage for:

- the original issue-style multi-label query, with and without the `WHERE` clause
- the simplified maintainer repro: `MATCH (n:A)<-[*]-(n:Z) RETURN 1`
- an `A`-only self-loop, which must not match `(n:A)<-[*]-(n:Z)`
- an `A:Z` self-loop, which should still match

pullRequests.title: Fix value operator precedence before predicates
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #751

/claim #751

## Summary
- rotate parser-produced value/predicate binary expression trees so value operators bind before CONTAINS, STARTS WITH, ENDS WITH, and IN
- preserve explicit parenthesized predicate operands by checking the original query source ranges before rotating
- add flow coverage for string predicates, list append/concat before IN, chained right-hand value expressions, explicit parenthesized predicates, and the exact issue #751 reproduction
- unskip the two relevant Precedence3 TCK scenarios now that they pass

## Root cause
libcypher can produce left-to-right binary ASTs for value operators mixed with predicate operators. For example, an expression like `(n.k)+'1' CONTAINS '1'` can become a value-expression root instead of a predicate-expression root, so WHERE receives a string and raises `Type mismatch: expected Boolean but was String`.

pullRequests.title: ci: notify rust-port repo when a flow-test PR is merged
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Adds `.github/workflows/notify-rust-port.yml` that fires on `pull_request.closed` against `master` when:
- The PR was **merged** (not just closed), and
- It touched `tests/flow/**`.

It then POSTs a `repository_dispatch` event (`event_type: upstream-flow-test-merge`) to `FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen` with a JSON payload containing:
- `upstream_pr_number`
- `upstream_pr_title`
- `upstream_pr_url`
- `upstream_merge_sha`
- `changed_flow_files[]`

## Why

The rust-port repo (`falkordb-rs-next-gen`) needs to mirror new/changed flow tests from this repo as it catches up on parity. Previously it polled via a cron job, which is laggy and noisy. With this notify workflow, the rust-port `flow-tests-migration` agentic workflow opens **one** downstream draft PR per upstream PR within seconds of merge, with the upstream PR linked in the body. If the downstream CI fails, an RCA agent gets the full upstream PR context (title, body, C-side diff) automatically.

Cron-based polling stays in place on the rust-port side as a backstop, so if this dispatch is ever missed/throttled the work still gets picked up within the hour.

## Required secret

Add a repository (or org) secret named **`RUST_PORT_DISPATCH_TOKEN`** containing a fine-grained PAT with:
- **Repository access:** only `FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen`
- **Permissions:** `Contents: Write` (only)

The PAT does **not** need any access to this repo — the upstream PR diff is read via the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.

## Security notes

- All attacker-controllable fields (PR title, PR URL) are passed through `jq -n --arg` rather than shell interpolation, so titles cannot escape into the shell or the JSON.
- Workflow runs with `pull_request_target`-equivalent privileges only because it triggers on `pull_request` (closed) which runs against the base branch; no untrusted code from the head ref is checked out or executed.
- Only fires when `github.event.pull_request.merged == true`, so closed-without-merge PRs (including spam)

pullRequests.title: ci(build): decouple promote-toolchain from the app build (fix unpublished stable images)
pullRequests.body:
## Problem

After #2101 merged, every master build / PR that doesn't touch a builder Dockerfile fails with `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:<os>: not found` — the **stable** toolchain images were never published.

## Root cause

`promote-toolchain` depended on the `build` job and gated on `needs.build.result == 'success'`. `build` transitively depends on the **PR-only** `build-rc-toolchain`, which is **skipped** on the master push. GitHub propagates a skipped state down the `needs` chain, and a downstream job whose `if` lacks a status function is skipped **before its conditions are evaluated**. So promote was skipped on the #2101 merge despite every condition being satisfied, and the stable `:<os>` images were never published.

## Fix

Converge `promote-toolchain` onto the proven pattern in [FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen](https://github.com/FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen)'s `rust-push.yml`:

- **Depend only on `check-builder-changes`** — an entry job that always runs on push and is never skipped. No skipped dependency to propagate ⇒ no `always()`/status function needed.
- **Drop the `build` gate.** A toolchain image's validity is independent of whether the FalkorDB app compiles, and the RC was already exercised end-to-end in the PR's CI. Promotion is a pure byte-identical retag (`imagetools create`) of `:<os>-pr-<N>` → `:<os>`.

This **structurally** cannot hit the skip-propagation footgun, rather than papering over it with `always()`.

The current breakage was recovered by republishing the 7 stable images via `build-toolchain.yml` `workflow_dispatch`.

pullRequests.title: fix: prevent SIGSEGV in self-referential variable-length algebraic expressions
pullRequests.body:
## fix: prevent SIGSEGV in self-referential variable-length algebraic expressions

### Abstract

Self-referential variable-length path patterns `(n:A)<-[*..]->(n:B)` with differing labels on the same alias trigger a NULL pointer dereference in `AlgebraicExpression_Dest()`. The fix implements atomic operand extraction to ensure source and destination label operands are captured before any AST mutations, preventing intermediate NULL states that caused the crash.

### Root Cause

In `_AlgebraicExpression_IsolateVariableLenExps()`, label extraction was performed sequentially: first `AlgebraicExpression_RemoveSource()` modified the expression tree, then `AlgebraicExpression_Dest(exp)` was called on the partially-stripped expression. For self-referential traversals with different labels, this second call returned NULL because the expression's operand source/destination pointers had been cleared. The subsequent `exp->operand.dest` access in `AlgebraicExpression_Dest()` at `algebraic_expression_operand.c:151` then dereferenced this NULL, producing SIGSEGV.

### Architectural Correction

**Atomic Operand Extraction:** Both source and destination label operands are now extracted BEFORE any AST mutations. For self-referential paths, destination labels are merged into source via `_AlgebraicExpression_MultiplyToTheRight()` applied pre-traversal.

**Defensive NULL Guard:** Added NULL check in `_AlgebraicExpression_RemoveRedundentOperands()` to survive edge cases.

### Verification

All three fuzzer queries from Issue #636 now execute cleanly:

- `MERGE (:label8) MERGE (:label2{})<-[:reltype5]-(node_0{})<-[:reltype7]-({})`
- `MATCH (node_0:label8{})<-[*..]-(node_0:label9) WHERE node_0.prop7 = [ FALSE ] RETURN *`
- `MATCH (node_0:label8{})<-[*..]-(node_0:label9) RETURN *`

Fixes #636

pullRequests.title: fix: raise runtime error when Path/List used as aggregate grouping key (closes #2127)
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Fixes #2127 — server SIGSEGV crash when `allShortestPaths` is used with endpoint variables that are **not pre-bound** in a preceding clause.

## Root Cause

`ExecutionPlan_ProcessPattern` correctly detected the unbound-endpoint condition and called `ErrorCtx_SetError`, but then **continued building and executing the plan** with the invalid traversal op. `AllPathsCtx_New` asserts `src != NULL`, so when the record produced a NULL node pointer the server crashed with SIGSEGV.

## Fix

Add an early `return NULL` immediately after `ErrorCtx_SetError` for the unbound-endpoint case. The caller already checks `ErrorCtx_EncounteredError()` and aborts plan compilation when the return value is NULL — the error is delivered to the client as a compile-time validation message:

> **Source and destination must already be resolved to call allShortestPaths**

## Reproducer

```cypher
GRAPH.QUERY my_graph "CREATE (:Paper)-[:REL]->(:Paper)"
GRAPH.QUERY my_graph "MATCH p = allShortestPaths((a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper)) WITH *, count(a) AS count_a RETURN p"
```

The second query now returns the compile-time error instead of crashing the server.

## What changed

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `build_match_op_tree.c` | `return NULL` after setting the unbound-endpoint error |
| `op_aggregate.c` | Removed overly-broad T_PATH/T_ARRAY rejection that broke TCK |
| `error_msgs.h` | Removed unused `EMSG_INVALID_GROUP_KEY_TYPE` |
| `test_all_shortest_paths.py` | Updated test08 to assert the correct validation error message |

The T_PATH/T_ARRAY restriction was an incorrect diagnosis — the crash was never in the aggregate hashing logic, and Cypher requires paths and lists to be valid grouping keys (TCK Return5, With6, Pattern2, Quantifier1-4 all cover this).

pullRequests.title: Fix #622: Crash
pullRequests.body:
Closes #622

## Summary

The crash occurs when a property access expression (like `x.n1`) is used within a pattern node inside a CALL subquery that references an outer variable. The issue is in the expression resolution where the outer variable reference is not properly handled during pattern matching in subqueries.

## Changes

## Fix: Crash when using property access on outer variable in CALL subquery pattern

### Issue
The database crashes when executing queries that use property access on outer-scope variables within node patterns inside CALL subqueries. 

Example crash query:
```cypher
WITH 1 AS x
CALL {
    WITH x
    MATCH ({v:x.n1}), ()
    RETURN 0
}
RETURN 0
```

### Root Cause
When processing a node pattern that contains a property map with a property access expression (like `x.n1`) referencing a variable from an outer CALL scope, the expression resolution fails to properly handle the outer variable reference during the pattern matching phase. This results in a null pointer dereference.

### Fix
Added defensive null checks in the expression construction and filter tree application paths to gracefully handle cases where outer-scope variable references cannot be immediately resolved during pattern compilation.

### Testing
- Added test case for the reported query
- Verified fix doesn't break existing subquery functionality

pullRequests.title: Fix variable-length traversal under-returning bounded ranges (convergent diamond)
pullRequests.body:
## Problem

A bounded variable-length pattern like `-[:F*1..2]->` could return a **strict subset** of the exact-length pattern `-[:F*2..2]->`, silently dropping reachable endpoints. Since `*1..2` must contain every endpoint of `*2..2`, this is a clear correctness bug.

It only affected the **optimized** variable-length traversal path (`AllNeighborsCtx`), selected for a single relationship type with no filter, edge unreferenced, and a directed traversal. The untyped / multi-type path uses `AllPathsCtx` and was always correct — which is why removing the edge type made the bug disappear.

Closes #2157.

## Root cause

`AllNeighborsCtx` runs an iterative DFS and tracks the nodes on the current path in two structures that must stay in sync:

- `visited` — the path stack
- `visited_nodes` — a hash set mirroring the stack, for O(1) cycle checks

`visited_nodes` was updated **unconditionally** (via the side effect of `HashTableAdd`), but a node was only pushed onto the `visited` stack — and therefore only ever removed from `visited_nodes` on backtrack — when it was expanded (`current_level < maxLen`). A node returned at `maxLen` (a leaf) was added to the set but never removed, **leaking** it.

Once leaked, that node was treated as "already on the path" when later reached at a shallower depth on another path, so it was not expanded and all of its descendants were dropped. In the convergent diamond, `4349` is first reached as a depth-2 leaf (`5→8798→4349`) and leaks; the later depth-1 visit (`5→4349`) is then not expanded, dropping `765` and `775`.

## Fix

Keep `visited_nodes` a faithful mirror of the `visited` stack: add to the set exactly where we push onto the stack, and test membership with `HashTableFind` instead of relying on `HashTableAdd`'s side effect. Leaf nodes are added to neither structure, so they no longer leak.

## Testing

- Reproduced the drop and confirmed the fix restores correct results across ranges `*1..1 … *1..5`, including cycles; typed and untyped t

pullRequests.title: fix(defrag): don't stall or orphan writes under active defrag
pullRequests.body:
## Problem

Reports of very slow / unusable write performance on the edge docker image (built from `master`) under active defrag — following #2175 (Defrag locking).

## Root cause — two distinct bugs, both from #2175

Active defrag runs on the Redis **main thread** and takes the graph write election before scanning.

1. **Main-thread freeze.** The defrag callback waited up to **50ms per lock** — write election *and* rwlock = up to **100ms** — blocking the event loop, and the wait was not counted against any budget.

2. **Orphaned write / permanent hang (the "unusable writes").** A write query is delegated to the write queue by its worker, which then trusts the current writer to drain the queue. When defrag *transiently owns the election*, it does **not** drain the queue (it's on the main thread), so a write delegated during defrag's hold is left **orphaned** — the blocked client never gets a reply and hangs forever, while the server stays responsive. With a single in-flight client, nothing else ever elects a writer.

## Fix

- **Shared budget instead of per-lock timeouts.** A single `DEFRAG_BUDGET_MS` (50ms) is shared across the election wait, the rwlock wait, and the scan, so a defrag step never blocks the main thread longer than the budget while still making progress. (A non-blocking `timeout=0` was considered and rejected — it starves defrag under read load.) The election wait now polls a monotonic deadline instead of decrementing an assumed sleep, so the timeout stays honest if `nanosleep` wakes on a signal.
- **Defrag hands the queue back.** After releasing the election, defrag calls `Graph_DrainWriteQueue`, which dispatches a worker to elect a writer and drain the queue. **The writer path is unchanged / defrag-oblivious** — the coupling is one-directional. The drain runs strictly after defrag releases the election + rwlock, so a writer never overlaps defrag's memory relocation (preserves the #2175 UAF protection).

- Reproduced the permanent han

pullRequests.title: Fix vector-indexed nodes disappearing from KNN after update/delete
pullRequests.body:
## Problem

A node indexed by a vector index "disappears" from `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` (KNN) after **any** update to it, and after a node is deleted a new node inserted at the same coordinates is unfindable. With the default `k=1` the query returns 0 results even though the property is present.

## Root cause

Vector removal from the HNSW graph was never happening for indexes created through the RediSearch low-level C API (which is how FalkorDB creates them):

1. **Update:** every write re-indexes the node as a RediSearch REPLACE, which mints a new docId and appends a new vector — the old vector must be removed, but that removal is gated on the spec flag `Index_HasVecSim`, which `RediSearch_CreateField(RSFLDTYPE_VECTOR)` never set (only the textual `FT.CREATE … VECTOR` parser did).
2. **Delete:** the LLAPI `RediSearch_DeleteDocument` only removed the doc-table entry and never removed the vector at all (unlike the command-layer `IndexSpec_DeleteDoc`).

Either way the old vectors linger as orphans (docIds that no longer resolve to a document) and shadow live entries in KNN, so fewer than `k` results come back.

## Fix

Vendored RediSearch bump to **FalkorDB/RediSearch#23**, which:
- sets `Index_HasVecSim` in the vector branch of `RediSearch_CreateField`, and
- removes the document's vectors in `RediSearch_DeleteDocument` (guarded by `Index_HasVecSim`, mirroring `IndexSpec_DeleteDoc`).

## Tests

`tests/flow/test_vecsim.py`:
- **test08** — re-SET (same value, different value, unrelated property) keeps the node findable at `k=1`.
- **test09** — deleting a node removes its vector, so a new node at the same coordinates is found (not shadowed).

Both **fail against the pre-fix submodule** (`test08`: `0 == 1`; `test09`: `[] == ['B']`) and **pass with the bump**; the existing `test01`–`test07` are unaffected.

## Merge order

Depends on FalkorDB/RediSearch#23. This bumps the submodule to the fix branch commit; once #23 merges into `vector-low-level-api`, re-point the subm

The `release` job failed at the "Verify tag matches version.h" step because `grep FALKOR_VERSION_MAJOR` matched two lines in `src/version.h` — the actual `#define` and the `FALKOR_MODULE_VERSION` macro that references it — yielding a garbage `FILE_VERSION` (`v4` + junk) and a false tag mismatch.

```
##[error]Tag 'v4.20.0' does not match version.h 'v4
FALKOR_SEMANTIC_VERSION(FALKOR_VERSION_MAJOR,.20
```

### Changes

- **`.github/workflows/release-image.yml`** — anchor the grep to the definition lines only:
  ```bash
  # before
  grep FALKOR_VERSION_MAJOR
  # after
  grep '^#define FALKOR_VERSION_MAJOR '

pullRequests.title: Fix GRAPH.CONSTRAINT crash-loop on AOF replay (blocks fake client during load) (FalkorDB/private#178)
pullRequests.body:
## Crash issue
FalkorDB/private#178 — production instance `instance-e4rtnu93m` (pod `node-s-0`) crash-loops on restart.
Signature: `aof.c:1692 '(fakeClient->flags & CLIENT_BLOCKED) == 0'` → `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile` → `loadAppendOnlyFiles` → `loadDataFromDisk`, exit **139**, `blocked_clients:1`.

## Root cause
`Graph_Constraint` (`src/commands/cmd_constraint.c`) **unconditionally** blocks the client and defers the work to a worker thread:
```c
cmd_ctx->bc = RedisModule_BlockClient(ctx, NULL, NULL, NULL, 0);
ThreadPool_AddWork(_Graph_Constraint, cmd_ctx, true);
```
During AOF replay, Redis executes each command on a synthetic `fakeClient` and asserts it is never left blocked (`aof.c:1692`). Because any `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT` command persisted in the incremental AOF is replayed on load, `RedisModule_BlockClient` sets `CLIENT_BLOCKED` on the fake client → the assertion aborts the process mid-load → the server can never finish loading to rewrite the AOF → **CrashLoopBackoff**.

`GRAPH.QUERY` already avoids this (`src/commands/cmd_dispatcher.c`): it inspects the context flags and runs synchronously on the main thread when loading / replicated / MULTI / Lua / deny-blocking. `Graph_Constraint` was missing exactly this guard.

## Fix
Mirror the `GRAPH.QUERY` dispatch and the existing `CommandCtx_ThreadSafeContextLock` convention (acquire the GIL only when running off the main thread):
- Add a `main_thread` parameter to `_Constraint_Create` / `_Constraint_Drop` and guard `RedisModule_ThreadSafeContextLock/Unlock` with `if (!main_thread)` (on the main thread the GIL is already held).
- Extract the operation into `_Graph_Constraint_Exec(rm_ctx, ctx, main_thread)`.
- In `Graph_Constraint`, when `REDISMODULE_CTX_FLAGS_{REPLICATED,MULTI,LUA,DENY_BLOCKING,LOADING}` is set, run synchronously on the main thread without `RedisModule_BlockClient`; otherwise keep the original block-and-dispatch path.

## Reproduction
1. `redis-server --appendonly yes` (FalkorDB module).
2. Create 500 `:Cl

pullRequests.title: ci: require every PR to close an issue
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2243

Adds `.github/workflows/pr-linked-issue.yml`, which fails a PR that does not close an issue — intended to become a **required status check** in branch protection.

## Detection

Queries GraphQL `closingIssuesReferences`, the only source that covers **both** a `Closes #N` keyword in the PR body **and** an issue attached through the PR's "Development" sidebar. REST exposes neither.

Verified against real PRs before writing the workflow:

| PR | `totalCount` | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `falkordb-rs-next-gen#743` (`fix(#726): ...`) | 1 | pass |
| `falkordb-rs-next-gen#734` | 0 | fail |

## Design choices worth reviewing

- **No `paths:` filter** — a required check that never reports blocks the PR indefinitely, so it must run on every PR to a covered branch.
- **`edited` in the trigger list** — editing the body is how a PR gains or loses its link; without it the verdict goes stale.
- **Branch filter mirrors `rust-pr.yml`**: `main`, `main-rs`, `[0-9]*.[0-9]*`.
- **Read-only permissions** (`contents: read`, `pull-requests: read`).
- **No exemptions** — bot PRs must close an issue too (deliberate policy).

## Before making it required

1. Let it report once on a PR, so the check name exists in branch protection.
2. Be aware it will block the next Dependabot PR (weekly `cargo` / `github-actions`) and any `batch-backport` PR, since there are no exemptions.

## Contributor gotcha (documented in the failure output)

Linking via the **Development sidebar does not fire a `pull_request` event**, so the check will not re-evaluate on its own. `Closes #N` in the body is the happy path.

Two triggers that `master` relies on are delivered **only from the repository's default branch**. When the default branch moves from `master` to `main` for the Rust engine, anything depending on them stops firing — **silently**, with no failing check to notice.

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2258

## Why

The perf CI depends on infrastructure this repository does not have:

- it publishes dashboards and flame graphs to a **`gh-pages` branch** — this repo has only `master` and `main-rs`;
- it provisions **ephemeral GCE runners** from `vars.BENCHMARK_*` / `vars.PROFILE_*` / `GCP_ZONES_ARM`, none of which are configured here (unlike `GCP_SA_KEY` / `GCP_PROJECT_ID` / `GH_SA_TOKEN`, which C's own workflows already use);
- it is driven by PR labels and `/benchmark` slash commands that only make sense in the repo it grew up in.

Left in place it fails or silently no-ops, and it kept `contents: write` on the post-merge workflow for no reason.

## Why it all comes out together

The pieces are hard-coupled:

- `profile.yml` sparse-checkouts `.github/scripts/benchmark` and calls `profile.sh`, `view-slug.sh`, `gh-pages-push.sh`;
- `shellcheck.yml` only ever linted those scripts — its `paths:` filter is `.github/scripts/benchmark/**`, so it would never fire again once they were gone.

## Deleted

`benchmark.yml`, `_benchmark.yml`, `profile.yml`, `shellcheck.yml`, and the 16 files under `.github/scripts/benchmark/`.

## Edited

- **`rust-push.yml`** — drop the `benchmark-edge` job (the canonical-trend feed), and reduce top-level `permissions` from `deployments: write` + `contents: write` to `contents: read`. **Audited before changing:** those grants existed solely for gh-pages publishing; `find-pr`, `docker` and `promote-edge` declare their own permissions, and every remaining job needs read only. ## Summary

- treat negative equality and upper bounds as empty, and negative lower bounds as unconstrained
- cover negative, contradictory, and zero-boundary predicates across labeled and unlabeled ID scans

`evaluate_id_filter` cast signed integer bounds to `u64` before comparison. Negative predicates therefore wrapped to very large positive IDs, producing incorrect ranges and potentially enormous allocations.

pullRequests.title: fix(algo): bound algo.SPpaths memory with a per-node search
pullRequests.body:
## What

`algo.SPpaths` / `algo.SSpaths` searched over **paths** rather than nodes. Every heap entry owned a cloned visited-set and edge-list, so the frontier held one state per partial path and grew exponentially with hop count.

Reported as an OOM in the [benchmark](https://github.com/FalkorDB/benchmark) suite against `falkordb/falkordb:edge-rs`: `ExitCode=137`, `OOM=true`, `used_memory_dataset` ≈ 100% of `used_memory`. Not a leak — memory returns to baseline after every query. It is a single unbounded query.

Reproduced on pokec-small (10k nodes / 121,716 `Friend` edges, **12 MB** in FalkorDB), one connection, running the benchmark's own `shortest_path` query:

```
[0] from=1825 to=410     877.2ms  peak=2249.0MiB  rows=1
[1] from=4507 to=4013   1550.0ms  peak=2994.7MiB  ERR Query timed out
[2] from=3658 to=2287   -> OOMKilled=true ExitCode=137
```

Pair `3658 → 2287` has no path; alone it climbed to 4.9 GiB in 21 s and killed the server. `falkordb/falkordb:edge` (C) answers `rows=0` in 4.0 ms.

The regression dates to `78f54ffae` (2026-03-29), when `algo.SPpaths` was first implemented in Rust — `algo_procedures.rs` did not exist before it, and the search has not been touched since. It sat unexposed for four months because nothing called the procedure; the benchmark switched its `shortest_path` queries from the `shortestPath()` clause to `algo.SPpaths` on 2026-07-28, two days before the report.

## How

Ports the three mechanisms `Proc_SPpathsInvoke` uses in the C engine, in place of the best-first search:

| | |
|---|---|
| `dijkstra_single_path` | Unconstrained single-shortest-path shape. One `DijkstraLabel { parent, edge, weight }` per node, 16-byte heap items, lazy deletion. Guarded on the same five conditions C uses. |
| `bfs_find_bound` | Per-node BFS. Unreachable target → return empty after one linear sweep; otherwise its weight seeds the pruning bound (for `pathCount` 0 and 1 only — the k-th path can legitimately be heavier). |
| `enumerate_paths` | DFS wi

pullRequests.title: feat(cow_btree): point lookups, memory accounting, tuple cursor + narrowable doc width
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2380

## What

Adds six enhancements to the always-compiled CoW B⁺-tree substrate (`graph/src/index/falkordb/data_structures/cow_btree/`), harvested from the tensor-decouple work:

1. **`first_doc(key)` / `contains_key(key)`** — allocation-free reference-descent point lookup. Unlike `point()→RangeIter` it clones no page `Arc`s and allocates no cursor stack, so it's the cheap primitive for equality filters / `EXISTS` / "one representative doc" probes. Handles the child-boundary case (a key whose entries begin at a separator) via a recorded `right_sep`.
2. **`heap_bytes()`** — approximate resident-memory accounting (leaf blob bytes + branch vec sizes), the primitive `GRAPH.MEMORY` needs. `O(pages)`; call off hot paths.
3. **`insert` / `remove` return a `#[must_use]` changed-`bool`** — lets a caller maintain an exact live cardinality in `O(1)` instead of an `O(n)` page walk, and cleanly detects idempotent-insert / absent-remove no-ops. (The change signal is distinct from `remove`'s internal underflow flag.)
4. **`DOC_BYTES` const generic** (`CowBTree<LEAF_MAX, BRANCH_MAX, const DOC_BYTES = 8>`) — narrows the fixed-stride AoS doc field (16→12 B/entry for a 4-byte doc), capturing the per-entry saving the compaction gate forfeits on high-entropy keys. **Defaults to 8** (byte-for-byte identical to today); a narrower width `assert!`s loudly on an over-width doc — no silent truncation. Nothing is instantiated below 8 in this PR.
5. **`Extract` / `TupleExtract` + `range_tuples`** — a zero-cost cursor generalization (`const NEEDS_KEY`) so a scan can also yield the encoded key for covered / index-only reads. The doc-only fast path is unchanged.
6. **`for_each_tuple`** — a bulk full-scan that matches each leaf's format once and runs a tight inner loop (for eager whole-tree consumers: memory/stats/serialize), faster than the lazy cursor.

## Why now / no call sites yet

These enhance the **substrate ahead of its consumers**: the native numeric index that uses `CowBTree` i

Replaces this branch's tree wholesale with the **Rust implementation of FalkorDB**. `main` becomes the development line for 6.0 and later; the **C engine continues on `master`** with its own CI, releases and maintenance.

## How to review this — don't read 7,000 files

The commit was built by plumbing, not by hand: its tree is **byte-identical** to `main-rs`, the branch carrying the Rust engine's full history. One command proves it:

```bash
gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/commits/$(gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/ref/heads/rust-migration --jq .object.sha) --jq .tree.sha
gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/commits/$(gh api repos/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/git/ref/heads/main-rs        --jq .object.sha) --jq .tree.sha
# both → 50390330b99856ca2d970fd14cd3203e7abf622c
```

So the review question isn't "is every line right?" — it's **"is `main-rs` the tree we want `main` to have?"** The Rust tree has been under CI on `main-rs` throughout.

## Shape of the commit

```
main            …─ C history ─● 9d49fcd3
                               └─● cc48e5ab   ← this commit: tree = main-rs, ONE parent
main-rs   (orphan) ●─●─●─ … ─● d975d677       ← 2,873 Rust commits, NOT an ancestor
```

Single parent on `master`'s lineage, so **`git log main` stays linear** — C's history followed by one migration commit.

pullRequests.title: ci: require every PR to close an issue
pullRequests.body:
Re-creation of #2245 against `main`. Same two commits, same single file — see the note at the bottom on why a base change wasn't possible.

Part of #2280.

## What it does

Adds `.github/workflows/pr-linked-issue.yml`, which fails a PR that doesn't close an issue — intended to become a **required status check** in branch protection.

### Detection

Queries GraphQL `closingIssuesReferences`, the only source that covers **both** a `Closes #N` keyword in the PR body **and** an issue attached through the PR's "Development" sidebar. REST exposes neither.

### Design choices worth reviewing

- **No `paths:` filter** — a required check that never reports blocks the PR indefinitely, so it must run on every PR to a covered branch.
- **`edited` in the trigger list** — re-titling or re-describing a PR re-evaluates the verdict instead of leaving a stale one.
- **Branch filter** mirrors `rust-pr.yml`: `main`, `main-rs`, `[0-9]*.[0-9]*`.
- **Read-only permissions** (`contents: read`, `pull-requests: read`).
- **No exemptions** — bot PRs must close an issue too. Deliberate policy; see the consequence below.

## How linking actually works here (verified)

**On a non-default base, the Development sidebar is the only mechanism that works.** GitHub registers a closing link from a body keyword *only* when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**.

Measured on #2245 (base `main-rs`, default `master`):

| state | `closingIssuesReferences` |
| --- | --- |
| `Closes #2243` as the first body line | **0** |
| issue attached via the Development sidebar | **1** |

Corroborated: GitHub search reported that PR as `-linked:issue`, and its timeline held no `CONNECTED_EVENT` / `CROSS_REFERENCED_EVENT`. The link genuinely doesn't exist, so no API can report it.

The failure message therefore points at the sidebar, and notes that a sidebar link emits no `pull_request` event — so the check must be **re-run** after linking. Observed live on #2245: failed at creation, passed on re-run once lin

**Step 1 of 2** for #2290. This one must merge **first** — see Ordering.

`main` (Rust engine) is now the default branch, so the plain `:edge` channel should serve the Rust image. This gives the C engine its own rolling channel rather than taking it away.

## Change

`build.yml`'s `publish-edge` job dispatches `release-image.yml` with `-f tag=edge` → **`-f tag=edge-c`**.

Because `release-image.yml` derives **every** tag it pushes from `env.TAG_NAME`, that single value renames the whole family:

```
edge-c            edge-c-x64            edge-c-arm64v8
edge-c-alpine     edge-c-alpine-x64     edge-c-alpine-arm64v8
edge-c-rhel8-x64  edge-c-rhel9-x64      edge-c-amazonlinux2023-x64
```
…plus the `falkordb-server` equivalents — 15 tags in total, all still rolling for C.

Also renames the **unreachable** `TAG_NAME="edge"` in `release-image.yml`'s `workflow_run` arm (that trigger was removed when `publish-edge` took over the hand-off). Keeping it in step means re-adding the trigger can't resurrect a C-side publisher for the plain `:edge` channel and race the Rust one.

## Why rename rather than delete

- C is maintained through 5.x and benefits from a rolling image for testing `master` before a release.
- Reverting the whole channel swap becomes a **one-line change**.
- Nothing is deleted, so no consumer loses an image outright — they just move to an explicitly-named channel.

## Ordering — this PR first

The two halves live on **different branches** and cannot be atomic. If the Rust side starts publishing `:edge` while C still does, `:edge` **flip-flops per push** depending on which branch was touched last — worse than either steady state.

Merging this first leaves `:edge` frozen-but-stable during the gap, then step 2 (on `main`) picks it up.

## Behaviour

No change beyond the tag names. The `Verify tag matches version.h` step is gated on `startsWith(env.TAG_NAME, 'v')`, which is false for `edge-c` exactly as it was for `edge`, so it still skips. `actionlint`: **28 fi

  - Threaded a recursion-depth counter through the `parse_array`/`parse_value` call chain.
  - Added a fixed maximum nesting threshold (low-hundreds scale) appropriate for real query usage.
  - Return a parse error instead of recursing further when the threshold is reached.

- **Behavioral impact**
  - Normal parameter parsing behavior remains unchanged for valid, practical nesting.
  - Pathological deeply nested array payloads now terminate in controlled parse failure rather than stack overflow.

    - fails deterministically at/over the limit

static bool parse_value(const char **head, SIValue *v, uint32_t depth);

    if (depth >= PARAM_MAX_NESTING) return false; // parse error path

fix(bulk): index rows appended by GRAPH.BULK into an existing graph
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2294.

## The bug

`GRAPH.BULK` creates a graph only when the batch carries a `BEGIN` token; a batch without one appends to the existing graph. On that append path the loaded rows were never indexed.

It is not a partial miss — the index returns **zero** rows for data that is plainly there, so any index-served query on that graph silently returns nothing:

| | index count | scan count |
|---|---|---|
| before | **0** | 100 |
| after | 100 | 100 |

## Root cause

Two separate causes, one per entity type.

**Nodes — right logic, wrong order.** `set_nodes_labels_bulk` already decides which nodes need (re)indexing:

```rust
if self.node_indexer.has_index(label) && self.node_attrs.has_attributes(id) {
    index_add_docs.entry(label_id).or_default().insert(id);
}
```

but it ran *before* `import_node_attrs_resolved`, so `has_attributes(id)` was always false and it collected nothing. The map it filled was then dropped without ever being committed. Fixed by importing the attributes first, then collecting, then publishing with `commit_index`.

**Edges — no maintenance at all.** `import_relationship_attrs_resolved` did none, unlike its `import_relationship_attrs` sibling. It now tracks the imported edges, and the caller publishes them with `commit_edge_index`. Tracking runs *before* the import because `import_attrs_resolved` drains its input. `track_edge_index_updates` now takes an iterator so both the map-shaped and `Vec`-shaped callers can use it.

Nothing repaired this afterwards: `GRAPH.BULK` does not run the post-load `populate_indexes_sync` rebuild — that belongs to the RDB and replica load paths.

## Reachability

The official `falkordb-bulk-loader` **cannot** trigger this. It always sends `BEGIN` against a fresh graph, and creates its own `-i` indexes *after* the load ("Add in Graph Indices after graph creation"), so no index can pre-exist. That is presumably why this went unnoticed.

pullRequests.title: Adaptive fold policy: bound MVCC delta growth on every write path
pullRequests.body:
Port of [falkordb-rs-next-gen#767](https://github.com/FalkorDB/falkordb-rs-next-gen/pull/767) onto this repo's `main`, plus one fix for a regression that only shows up against `main`'s newer test suite (see *What is new versus #767*).

## Summary

Outside `GRAPH.BULK`, deltas were never folded into the base matrix: `flush()` was only called from `flush_for_bulk`, so a long-lived graph accumulated unbounded `dp`/`dm` deltas and every read paid an `O(|delta|)` materialization/merge forever (measured: after the bench setup, the entire 10k-edge adjacency still lived in `dp` — `m=0, dp=10103`).

This PR makes every mutation path fold, governed by a cost model whose constants are measured rather than estimated:

- `should_fold(delta, tx_added, base_nvals)` / `should_fold_read(...)`: fold when `2·delta ≥ base_nvals`, or at the sqrt balance point `delta² ≥ K · tx_added`. `K = 2·F/w` is measured per path — read `K = 82_000` (fold at `287·sqrt(tx_added)`), write `K = 20_500_000` (fold at `4528·sqrt(tx_added)`).
- Delta sizes come from approximate atomic counters maintained by the mutation methods — `GrB_Matrix_nvals` on a delta forces its pending tuples to merge (+35% instr on single-node creates when measured).
- Decisions latch in `dup()` (version creation) and `wait()` (read path); execution happens in `flush()` before the next mutation, replacing the COW dup of both delta and base. `wait` deliberately does not schedule the fold mid-tx (a create+delete tx folding its own pending adds measured 18–63x slower small creates after `write 1m`).
- Shared-base folds build into a fresh matrix + `Cow::replace` instead of deep-copy-then-rewrite.
- Same mechanism applied to `Tensor`'s forward layers.
- `build_adjacency_matrix` gains a single-relationship-type fast path.
- `set_all_new`: an unchecked bulk delta insert for entries guaranteed absent from the committed base, plumbed as an `all_new` flag through `set_nodes_labels_bulk` (true for `GRAPH.BULK` and effect-replay creates, fals

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2354

Brings the native numeric index into the engine. Everything is
behind the `index-falkordb` feature, **off by default** — with the flag off the graph crate's
tests are unchanged (109 pass); with it on, 137.

## What this adds

A numeric index column per indexed `(label, attr)`, built on the CoW B-tree, with the read and
write paths wired to it.

- **Folded-roots MVCC.** The index is a `Graph` field, so `new_version()` CoW-clones it and
  publishing an index change *is* publishing a version — no separate index versioning. Cloning
  is O(1) per column (a root-`Arc` bump), so a fork shares pages with the prior version until a
  writer touches that particular column.
- **Node and edge columns are separate maps.** A node label and a relationship type can share a
  name, so one keyspace would collide. Edge columns store `edge_id`s; the read path recovers
  `(src, dst)` from the graph's own reverse index, so no endpoints are duplicated.
- **`CREATE INDEX` builds synchronously**, on the write thread, so the create returns with a
  column that already serves reads. (Making it a background build is #2351 — that is the entire
  content of the next PR.)
- **Write maintenance** removes each changed entity's old values and adds its new ones, as one
  batched merge per column per write call, removes before adds so a tuple removed and re-added
  nets to present. The delete paths run *before* the graph tears down types and attributes, so
  an edge's type is still resolvable when its removal is recorded. The replica's own write
  paths (`set_nodes_attributes_rows_of_labels`, `set_relationships_attributes_of_type`,
  `set_node_labels_product`) are maintained the same way.
- **Reads** route a numeric `Equal`/`Range` predicate to the native column and fall through to
  RediSearch for anything else — a Range index also holds strings and geo, which RediSearch
  still owns.

pullRequests.title: feat(index): online (background) index build
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2355

`CREATE INDEX` on the native numeric index now returns immediately, and the column is built in
batches while the server keeps serving, the way C populates an index (`src/index/index_construct.c`).

## Online build

`graph_writes::create_index` creates each Range column empty, in the `Building` state, and returns.
While a column is `Building`, reads on it fall back to the existing path, and writes maintain it as
usual.

The entities that already exist are indexed by `graph_writes::build_step`. Each step indexes the
next batch of the label's entities (10,000 nodes or 1,000 edges, as in C) at the values they hold
at that moment, adds them to the column, and moves the column's cursor (`BuildCursor`) past them.
The step that reaches the end flips the column `Ready`. An edge step finishes the multi-edge pair
it stops in, and the next step resumes inside the same row.

Each step is a unit of work of its own: it runs on a fresh version and is committed when it
returns, so it sees every write committed before it. Nothing written during the build has to be
remembered for later. A write to an entity no step has reached yet updates the column directly; the
step that reaches the entity reads its current value; and adding a tuple the column already holds,
or removing one it never held, changes nothing.

`DROP INDEX` mid-build removes the column and its cursor, and a re-created column starts from the
first entity. The RDB-load path (`graph_writes::populate`) still builds synchronously.

## Scheduling (`graph/src/index/falkordb/online_build.rs`)

Build steps run on a pool of their own in the graph crate: `INDEX_BUILD_THREAD_COUNT` workers (a
load-time module config, default 1), which never serve queries. The workers share one queue,
ordered by when each graph's next turn may start. After a turn a graph is queued again, not before
as long as the turn took, so its writers get the slot and the GIL between its turns while the
worker moves on to another graph. A graph is e

pullRequests.title: Stream cartesian-product branches instead of materializing their product
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2367

## Problem

A `CartesianProduct` with more than one right child cross-multiplied every right branch into a single flat batch before joining it with the left rows. For `MATCH (a), (b), (c), (d)` over 1001 nodes that is 1001³ ≈ 10⁹ rows — built inside **one** `next()` call. The timeout and memory-capacity guards run at the top of `BatchOp::next()`, so neither could fire until that call returned.

Reproduced on 1001 nodes with `MATCH (a), (b), (c), (d) RETURN *` and a 1 ms timeout:

| | reply | elapsed | RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | none (killed at 2m39s) | >159 s | 33 MB → **20.8 GB** |
| after | `Query timed out` | 25 ms | 27 MB → 28.9 MB |
| C reference | `Query timed out` | 27 ms | 23.5 MB → 25.2 MB |

## Fix

Materialize each right branch on its own (one dense batch per branch) and walk the branches as an odometer, emitting `BATCH_SIZE` rows per `next()`. Memory held is the **sum** of branch sizes instead of their product, and the deadline is checked between batches.

`BatchBuilder::push_merged_many` performs the N-way row merge directly from the N cursors, so no intermediate batch is built. `push_merged` keeps its own two-batch loop, and the operator retains the original tight scan for the single-right-branch case.

## Performance

Measured with all builds running simultaneously and measurements alternating, since sequential runs on this machine drift ~10%:

- 2-way `MATCH (a),(b)` over 1001×1001: **62.26 ms → 62.28 ms** — parity.
- 3-way: **557.5 ms → 573.1 ms (+2.8%)** — the odometer costs slightly more per row than reading a pre-flattened batch, traded for O(N) instead of O(N²) memory. C takes **45.8 s** on the same query.

## Tests

Added `test07_multi_branch_cartesian_product_is_streamed` to `tests/flow/test_multi_pattern.py`, covering both the deadline and a no-timeout `LIMIT 1`. Verified it fails on the unfixed operator (124 s / 116 s / 113 s against the 10 s bound) and passes after.

pullRequests.title: Match GRAPH.QUERY arguments case-insensitively
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2368

## Problem

`GRAPH.QUERY key "<query>" TIMEOUT 1` — the documented spelling — was **silently ignored**. The handlers compared each argument with `arg == "timeout"`, so anything but lower case fell through the `if`/`else if` chain and the query ran with **no deadline at all**:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a),(b),(c),(d) RETURN *" TIMEOUT 1
(runs forever)
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a),(b),(c),(d) RETURN *" timeout 1
(error) Query timed out
```

The C dispatcher (`cmd_dispatcher.c`) compares these with `strcasecmp`. `--compact`, `--track-memory` and `version` had the same problem.

The existing timeout tests never caught this because they all go through falkordb-py, which only ever sends `timeout` in lower case (`command.extend(["timeout", timeout])`). Any client using the documented uppercase form got no timeout enforcement.

## Fix

`eq_ignore_ascii_case` in all three handlers — `GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.RO_QUERY`, `GRAPH.PROFILE`.

## Tests

Added `test12_timeout_argument_is_case_insensitive` to `tests/flow/test_timeout.py`, issuing raw commands with `TIMEOUT` / `timeout` / `TimeOut` and asserting each both times out at 1 ms and succeeds at 5000 ms. Verified it fails without the fix on exactly the two non-lowercase spellings and passes after.

pullRequests.title: perf: reclaim entity ids with one ordered walk, not a rank lookup per id
pullRequests.body:
## What

`reserve_nodes` / `reserve_relationships` called `RoaringTreemap::select(i)` once per id being reclaimed from the deleted-id pool. `select` restarts at the first container on every call, summing cardinalities until it reaches rank `i` and then scanning words inside that container — so reclaiming N ids costs O(N × position) rather than O(pool).

This replaces the loop with a single ordered walk, `iter().skip(base).take(reclaimed)`. The ids are identical: `select(i)` is by definition the i-th smallest value, which is exactly what the skipped iterator yields.

## Why

`RoaringTreemap::select` was the hottest single leaf inside the module on a create-after-delete profile — 1,057 samples, 65% of all roaring time, ahead of GraphBLAS's `GB_quicksort_2_32_32` (738).

## Measured

Node capacity pinned at 200,000 in every graph so only the deleted-id pool varies. Query: `UNWIND range(1, 10000) AS i CREATE (:T {x: i})`. Instructions per node created, from `proc_pid_rusage` deltas:

| deleted-id pool | before | after | |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0 | 7,757 | 7,823 | unchanged |
| 10,000 | 8,070 | 7,854 | −2.7% |
| 100,000 | 11,266 | **5,408** | **2.08× faster** |
| 200,000 | 10,968 | **4,974** | **2.20× faster** |

The +45% penalty for creating into a large reclaim pool is gone, and reclaiming is now *cheaper* than allocating fresh ids, since it avoids capacity growth.

Standard bench rows (`bench measure --n 200`), before → after:

| row | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| write 10k | 317,320,239 | 294,056,053 | −7.3% |
| create 10k | 103,794,591 | 99,686,111 | −4.0% |
| write 1 / 100 / 1k | | | flat |
| delete node / 100 / 10k | | | flat |
| traversal + count, label scan, RETURN 1 | | | flat |

Nothing regressed.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p graph` — 114 passed
- `pytest tests/test_mvcc.py tests/test_concurrency.py tests/test_e2e.py` — 103 passed
- flow: `test_graph_deletion` 30, `test_access_del_entity` 18, `test_graph_create` 10, `test_index_delete` 14 — all pas

pullRequests.title: perf: make node deletion O(deleted) instead of O(graph)
pullRequests.body:
## What

`delete_nodes` cost O(graph) for a delete of *any* size. Two separate terms did it:

1. It iterated **every** entry of `node_labels_matrix` and filtered by delete-set membership, to find which labels the deleted nodes carry.
2. It built diagonal mask matrices and handed them to `remove_mask`, whose `element_wise_multiply` takes `m` as an operand — so GraphBLAS walks the base matrix's vectors.

The second was the dominant one. This PR replaces both:

- **Label lookup** uses `seek` (→ `GxB_rowIterator_seekRow`, a row jump) on a single re-seeked iterator, rather than scanning everything or constructing one iterator per node.
- **Removal** uses `VersionedMatrix::remove` per entity — `dm[i,j] = true` when `m` holds the pair, else drop it from `dp` — which is what `remove_nodes_labels` already does. Three mask matrices per delete go away with it.

Both paths are now O(|deleted|) for every input, so **there is no size threshold and no fast/slow path** — nothing about the input shape makes the old whole-matrix scan preferable.

### Why the per-entity removal is equivalent

`dp ∩ m = ∅` holds for `VersionedMatrix<bool>`: its `set` clears the `dm` tombstone when `m` already holds the pair, rather than writing a shadowing `dp` entry, and asserts as much. So `remove_mask`'s two effects — tombstone `mask ∩ m`, drop `mask ∩ dp` — can never both apply to one entry, which is exactly the per-entry choice `remove` makes. The valued matrices *do* allow `dp` to shadow `m`; `remove` is defined only on the boolean ones, and all three matrices here are boolean.

## Measured

One node created and deleted, per transaction — with the C reference for scale:

| other resident nodes | main | this PR | | C reference |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 0 | 1,199,818 | **766,741** | −36% | 827,548 |
| 50,000 | 64,748,827 | **1,049,311** | **61.7× faster** | 588,825 |
| 200,000 | 240,431,307 | **3,128,144** | **76.9× faster** | 563,827 |

pullRequests.title: feat(index): serve `IN [...]` natively as a union of point lookups
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2381

**Based on #2351** — review that first; the diff here is only this layer.

## What it does

`n.a IN [...]` used to reach the index as `Or(Equal, ..)` — the scan ops expanded the list before
calling the index — and `query_numeric` declined every `Or`, so the whole query went to
RediSearch. The native numeric index now serves it.

**`IN` reaches the index as one `InList`.** The scan ops keep the same members as before
(Int/Float/String/Bool) but hand them over as `InList { key, list }` rather than an `Or` of
`Equal`s, so the index sees one attribute and a list of values. RediSearch's query builder already
turns an `InList` into the same union it built from the `Or`, and the scan op's check gives an
`InList` the rule its members got as an `Or`: non-empty, every value indexable.

**A lazy chain of point lookups.** The union walks the distinct values in turn, and only descends
the tree for a value when the previous one runs out — nothing until the first row is pulled. So
`IN $list` with many values does no work up front, and a `LIMIT` stops it early.

**Not merged into id order.** Cypher promises no order without `ORDER BY`, and nothing on the read
path relies on one: a single range lookup already yields rows in value order, not id order.

**One snapshot for the whole union.** The union keeps its own copy of the tree root (an `Arc`
clone) taken when it is created, and answers every value from it. A write that lands mid-scan is
invisible to values whose lookup had not started yet.

**Each entity once.** Values are deduplicated by encoded key. That is sufficient: an entity is
indexed under one key per column (lists are not encoded, so an array-valued property is not in the
numeric column), so two distinct keys cannot hold the same entity.

**All values, or none.** An `IN` list is served only when every value encodes to a numeric key;
otherwise the index returns `None` and the query falls back whole. Serving just the numeric values
would drop rows another kind

pullRequests.title: feat(index): no fallback under the flag, plus the xfail ledger and its CI gate
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2382
Closes #2357

**Based on #2383** — review that first; the diff here is only this layer.

Under `--features index-falkordb` the native index becomes the *only* Range index. A predicate it cannot serve raises an error instead of quietly reaching RediSearch, and the flow tests that fail because of this are recorded in a ledger that a CI job checks in both directions. With the flag off, nothing changes.

## No fallback under the flag

`NodeByIndexScan` and `EdgeByIndexScan` used to send any predicate the native index declined on to RediSearch. Under the flag they now raise:

```
native index cannot serve this predicate on node :L — equality on `x` with a non-numeric value. The `index-falkordb` build has no RediSearch fallback; this index kind or predicate shape is not implemented natively yet.
```

An error rather than an empty result, because an empty result is indistinguishable from "nothing matched" and passes any test that happens to expect few rows. A loud failure is the only way a missing index kind can be counted.

The message names the shape that was declined (`graph/src/index/falkordb/mod.rs`, `describe_predicate`), because the shapes need different work:

* equality or range with a non-numeric value or bound — says "non-numeric" only when `encode_numeric` actually rejects the value;
* a union that is not all-numeric, vs. a union that spans more than one attribute;
* a conjunction, listing each child;
* array-contains and geo predicates.

## "Still building" is not "cannot serve"

`FalkorDbIndex::query_numeric` now returns a three-way answer:

| answer | meaning | scan op does |
|---|---|---|
| `Some(NumericAnswer::Rows(..))` | served natively | iterates the rows |
| `Some(NumericAnswer::NotReady)` | the column exists, its background build has not installed the base yet | scans the label/type |
| `None` | cannot be served | raises the error above |

Without the split, every query against an index still being built would have become an error.

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): plan an inline property map once, instead of twice
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2389.
Closes #3173.

`MATCH (a {p: 1})` is surface syntax for a predicate. The planner lowered it to an `IR::Filter` but also left it on the `QueryNode`/`QueryRelationship` embedded in the plan, so the same predicate existed in two places. Some passes re-derived it from the copy (`select_scan_node` re-emitted the endpoint Filter, which is #2389's `And(p, p)` that no index can serve), and `CondTraverse` checked an edge predicate a second time, in the operator, against the Filter the planner had already emitted above it. Lowering is now consuming: the predicate is lowered once and stripped from the pattern.

#2389 proposed deduplicating the two copies where stacked Filters merge. This removes the second copy instead, so a planner that starts producing duplicates again cannot look healthy.

## A wrong-answer bug, first

Endpoint lowering was skipped whenever the alias was already bound. `CondTraverse` covered that at runtime by re-checking endpoints per row, but `CondVarLenTraverse` and `AllShortestPaths` only ever check the *edge*'s attrs, so for those two nothing enforced the predicate at all:

```cypher
CREATE (n1:N {x: 1}), (n2:N {x: 2}), (n3:N {x: 3}),
       (n1)-[:R]->(n2), (n2)-[:R]->(n3)

MATCH (a:N) WITH a
MATCH (a {x: 1})-[:R*1..2]->(b)
RETURN b.x ORDER BY b.x
```

returned `2, 3, 3` — the third row starts at `n2`, which does not satisfy `x = 1`. Same for the destination endpoint, and for `allShortestPaths`.

## The consumers of the second copy

Each needed re-expressing against the plan, not just deleting:

- `make_scan_subtree` re-derived the filter from the node it was rebuilding. It now salvages the `Filter`s off the pruned subtree's spine — but only where it rebuilds the *same* endpoint. On the chain-reversal paths those filters constrain the old endpoint, which the reversed traverse binds rather than scans, so they are re-attached above the traverse instead.
- Endpoint scoring needed splitting. `collect_filtered_vars` only looked above the chai

pullRequests.title: fix(parser): chain unary signs so `- -5` parses
pullRequests.body:
## What

`RETURN - -5` failed with `Invalid input Dash`, and so did `--5` and `+ -5`. Valid Cypher was rejected, which bites generated or parameterised query text where the operand's sign is not known up front.

## Why it happened

The unary level consumed at most one `+` followed by at most one `-`, in that order, so a second sign fell through to the primary parser and failed there. `-` is a single-character token, so `--` is two signs rather than a comment, and the spaced form `- -5` failed the same way.

## Fix

Follow Neo4j's two rules rather than counting signs:

```
expression3   : expression2 | (PLUS | MINUS) expression2
numberLiteral : MINUS? ( DECIMAL_DOUBLE | UNSIGNED_DECIMAL_INTEGER | ... )
```

`expression3` does not recurse, so signs do not stack. What makes `- -5` legal is the second rule: the inner minus belongs to the number. So the unary level takes one sign and leaves a minus sitting directly on a number to the primary, which builds a signed literal. `- -x` and `+ +5` stay rejected, since neither operand is a signed number.

This removes the `i64::MIN` special case instead of adding to it. The literal now owns its sign, so `-9223372036854775808` is a literal rather than a negation the parser had to undo, and the out-of-range check moves to where a bare 2^63 token can only mean the literal did not fit.

Closes #2309

## Proof

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN - -5"
Invalid input Dash, errCtx: RETURN - -5, pos 8      # before
5                                                    # after
```

Accepted: `-5`, `+5`, `- -5`, `--5`, `+ -5`, `-x`, `-(-5)`, `1 - -2`, `3 * -2`, `-9223372036854775808`.

Rejected, with the reason rather than a bare token name:

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN - - -5"
Invalid input '-': only one sign is allowed, and only a number may carry a
second one, as in '- -1', errCtx: RETURN - - -5, pos 8
```

Same for `+ +5`, `- +5`, `- -x`. And `- -9223372036854775808` now overflows rather than returning `i64::MIN`.

## Tests

pullRequests.title: fix(aggregation): resolve grouping keys read outside the aggregation
pullRequests.body:
## TLDR

A projection item that aggregates was evaluated against the group's key row. That row carries each grouping key only under the name the clause projects it as, so a key written in any other form was simply absent and resolved to Null, which then collapsed whatever expression contained it

The same data answered two different ways depending on nothing but the projection list:

```text
RETURN paths, paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0    ->  5, true
RETURN paths > 0 AND count(n) > 0           ->  null
```

`RETURN n.a, n.a + count(*)` did not even get that far. The projected key had taken over the slot the bare variable would have used, so it failed with `Type mismatch: expected Map, Node, Edge, ... but was Integer`

This rewrites each such sub-expression to read the key by its projected name, which the key row does carry, and rejects the reads that name a key the clause never projects. openCypher [CIP2021-07-07](https://github.com/opencypher/openCypher/blob/master/cip/1.accepted/CIP2021-07-07-Grouping-keys-and-aggregation-expressions.adoc) requires exactly that: every sub-expression outside the aggregation must be a constant, a parameter, or a grouping key of the same clause. Neo4j reports the rest as "implicit grouping expressions". FalkorDB let them evaluate to Null, which is how the wrong answers got out

Recognized grouping keys are variables and property lookups, matching the CIP. Comprehensions, quantifiers and `reduce` are descended into carrying the variables they bind, so a key they capture resolves while their own variables are left alone. Pattern comprehensions are the one exception and are copied verbatim: the planner lifts them into their own sub-plan, which runs against the row feeding the aggregation rather than the group's key row, so the projected alias does not exist there

## User Flow

Any `WITH` or `RETURN` that aggregates while also reading a variable or property outside the aggregation. The reported shape was a `CASE`, but `CASE` is incidental,

pullRequests.body:
## TLDR

`CREATE (n),(n)` created one node and reported success. A pattern keeps one node per alias, so the second `(n)` was dropped on the way in and the redeclaration was never visible to any check

Neo4j and Memgraph reject it as a redeclaration, and FalkorDB already rejects the same mistake written other ways: `CREATE (n) CREATE (n)` and the relationship form `CREATE ()-[e:R]->()-[e:R]->()` both error with `The bound variable ... can't be redeclared in a CREATE clause`. The inconsistency was confined to this one shape

This reports it the same way, off the value `add_pattern_node` already computes about whether the alias is new to the pattern

Reusing an alias to attach a relationship is a reference rather than a declaration, so `CREATE (a),(b),(a)-[:R]->(b)` stays valid. The check therefore only fires on a path that opens on a bare repeat, decided by peeking for the relationship token the path parser is about to read anyway

Unaliased nodes need no exemption. Each is given a fresh `_anon_<n>` from a per-parse counter, so its alias is unique and it passes the "alias is new" test on its own. An earlier revision exempted the `_anon` prefix by name, which left `CREATE (_anon),(_anon)` creating one node silently, since a query may write that name itself

## User Flow

`GRAPH.QUERY` with a `CREATE` that names the same variable twice as a standalone node pattern

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): cap the row count of a unit CALL subquery
pullRequests.body:
## TLDR

A `CALL {}` with no `RETURN` is a unit subquery: it runs for every input row and contributes no rows of its own. It was planned as `Apply(input, Optional(body))`, and `Optional` guarantees *at least* one row without capping at one, so the body's own fan-out multiplied the outer row count. Three `:S` nodes produced nine rows, and a third level of nesting twenty-seven

This gives it a dedicated operator that drains the body and then emits the input rows unchanged

Draining is the point. The writes are why the body exists, and a body that fans out internally performs them once per row it produced, so capping with a limit would have traded a wrong row count for a wrong write count

## Correcting the issue

The issue also reports the write count as wrong, expecting three `:Tmp` where nine are written. That part is not a bug. Measured against the C engine, which this repo treats as the reference:

| | rows | `:Tmp` written |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C (`falkordb-server:edge-c`) | 3 | 9 |
| Rust, before | 9 | 9 |
| Rust, after | 3 | 9 |

Only the row count ever differed. Nine writes is right: the body runs per input row, and the inner returning subquery yields three rows each time, so the `CREATE` fires nine times while the outer cardinality stays at three

## A body that collapses rows runs per row

Draining the whole input batch through one body instance is safe for the rows it produces, since they are all discarded, but not for its writes. A body that collapses rows applied once across the batch instead of once per input row, so its side effects happened the wrong number of times. Over three input rows:

| `WITH z LIMIT 1` | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| `WITH count(y) AS c` | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| `WITH z SKIP 1` | 3 | 5 | 3 |
| `WITH DISTINCT z` | 3 | 1 | 3 |
