pullRequests.title: fix(eval): stop a simple CASE matching null against null
pullRequests.body:
## What

A simple `CASE` treated `null` as matching `null`, so `CASE null WHEN null THEN 'match' ELSE 'no match' END` answered `'match'`. Neo4j and Memgraph select no branch here

## Why it happened

The value form compared with `==`. `PartialEq for Value` keeps only the ordering half of `compare_value` and drops the flag saying a null took part, and two nulls order equal. `=` reads that flag and answers `null`, so the same pair compared two different ways depending on how the query was written

## Fix

`eval_case` in `graph/src/runtime/eval.rs` now compares on the same terms as `=`: equal ordering *and* no null involved. Covers nulls nested in a list or map too, since `=` is null for those as well

Closes #2208

## Proof

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN CASE null WHEN null THEN 'match' ELSE 'no match' END"
match                       # before
no match                    # after

$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN [1,null] = [1,null], CASE [1,null] WHEN [1,null] THEN 'm' ELSE 'no' END"
(nil)  m                    # before, `=` and CASE disagree
(nil)  no                   # after

pullRequests.title: fix(lexer): accept subnormal float literals
pullRequests.body:
## What

`RETURN 2.2e-308` failed with `Float overflow '2.2e-308'`. Subnormals are finite and representable, and nothing about them overflows. Neo4j and Memgraph accept them

## Why it happened

`str2number_token` in `graph/src/parser/lexer.rs` excluded them by hand, alongside the infinities:

```rust
Ok(f) if f.is_finite() && !f.is_subnormal() => Ok(Token::Float(f)),
Ok(_) => Err(format!("Float overflow '{str}'")),
```

The engine already produces these magnitudes on its own, so the parser and the evaluator disagreed about the same value depending on how it was written

## Fix

Drop the `!f.is_subnormal()` clause. Genuine overflow is still caught by `is_finite`

Closes #2182

## Proof

```
$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 2.2e-308"
Float overflow '2.2e-308'      # before
2.2e-308                       # after

$ redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1.0e-307 / 10 = 1.0e-308"
Float overflow '1.0e-308'      # before, the division alone returned 1e-308
true                           # after, parser and evaluator agree
```

Still rejected: `1e400`, `1.8e308`. Still accepted and unchanged: `1.7976931348623157e308`, `0.0`, `1e-400` (underflows to zero). Values survive a round trip: `CREATE (n {v: 2.2e-308}) RETURN n.v` gives `2.2e-308`

## Tests

Two unit tests in the lexer's own module. `subnormal_float_literals_are_accepted` covers four literals down to the smallest positive subnormal and asserts each lexes to a subnormal; it fails on the base with `2.2e-308 should lex, got Float overflow '2.2e-308'`. `float_literals_beyond_the_representable_range_still_overflow` pins the overflow path so this cannot be loosened into accepting infinities; it passes either way, which is the point

Full flow suite, TCK, `cargo test -p graph` (116), pytest 142, fmt and clippy all clean. The flow suite's usual failures are unchanged and come from a redis-py version mismatch in my local venv

pullRequests.title: fix(udf): bound the JS evaluation that rebuilds a worker's context
pullRequests.body:
## What

Problem 3 in #2401 is present on `main` in a different place than the issue describes, and is worse than filed: a registered UDF can hang every worker thread until no graph query is served at all.

A library's top-level code is evaluated **twice** — by `validate_script` at registration, and again by `rebuild_context` on each worker thread that first calls into it. Only the first was bounded.

## Why it happened

The two evaluations install different globals. `__falkor_registered_names` exists only while validating, `__falkor_current_lib` only at runtime, so a script can read `globalThis` to tell them apart and loop only in the second:

```js
if (typeof globalThis.__falkor_registered_names === 'undefined') {
    while (true) {}
}
falkor.register('spin', function() { return 1; });
```

That passes registration and spins in `rebuild_context`, which had no interrupt handler.

## Fix

`graph/src/udf/js_context.rs`: install the same interrupt handler `validate_script` uses, and clear it after the rebuild so a load-time deadline cannot fire during a later call. The call path already installs its own per invocation.

Two smaller items from the same issue, also on this branch:

- `graph.UDF` gains `deny-oom` in `src/lib.rs`, matching the other mutating commands. It already had `write`.
- `src/redis_type.rs` no longer sizes its allocation from the entry count just read off the RDB.

Closes #2401

## Proof

Registering the script above, then calling it. Before, on the merge base:

```

pullRequests.title: fix(udf): bound JS evaluation, fail RDB load loudly, mark the command a write
pullRequests.body:
## What

The three C-side defects in #2401, confirmed against a local `master` build.

**Nothing capped CPU.** `JS_SetMemoryLimit` caps memory, but the only interrupt handler lived in `AR_UDF` and was installed only when `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` was non-zero, which is not the default. Validation, registration and the per-thread context populate had none at any setting.

**`AUXLoadUDF_latest` validated with `ASSERT`**, which compiles out in release, so a library that failed to load was skipped and the server came up reporting success with it missing. `lib_len--` / `script_len--` were unconditional, underflowing `size_t` to `SIZE_MAX` on a zero-length buffer.

**`graph.UDF` was not a write**, so a read-only replica accepts it and ends up holding libraries the primary does not have.

## Fix

`UDF_ArmJSDeadline` / `UDF_DisarmJSDeadline` in `udf/utils.c`, armed around every JS evaluation: validation, registration, `UDF_RepoPopulateJSContext`, and `AR_UDF` when no timeout is configured. Budget is the query timeout, capped by `UDF_JS_TIMEOUT_CAP_MS` so a "no limit" setting still cannot hold a thread. The populate path is the one worth noting: it evaluates library code on the worker thread that first calls in, separately from the validation done at registration.

`AUXLoadUDF_latest` logs and fails the load, which meant returning `bool` up through `AUXLoad` to `_GraphContextType_AuxLoad`. Zero-length buffers are rejected before the decrement, and a count wider than the `unsigned int` the encoder writes is rejected outright.

`graph.UDF` registered `write deny-oom deny-script`.

Bounding the loop made two adjacent failures visible, both fixed here:

- a library that fails to evaluate into a worker's context now reports why, per library, instead of `Unknown function`. `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` joins the JS heap and stack limits in bumping the repo version, so raising it retries a load the old value interrupted.
- a failed `LOAD REPLACE` whose rollback also fails now says the library is gone,

pullRequests.title: perf: keep edge-property aggregates on the vectorized path (2.3x)
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2415.

## What

`sum(r.prop)` over a relationship classifies as `AggInputKind::Property`, whose bulk materialiser is node-only — `extract_node_ids` returns `Some` only for `Column::NodeIds`, and there is no relationship counterpart. Classification does not consult the variable's type, so edge aggregates took that path, failed on every batch, and fell through to `consume_batch_per_row`, which calls `to_owned_row()` and allocates a `Vec` of every column per row.

`sum(r.prop * 2)` classifies as `Computed`, stays on the vectorized path, and reads through a borrowed `BatchRow`. That is the whole difference, and it is why wrapping a property in an expression was *cheaper* than reading it plainly.

This reads the column per row when it is not a node column, keeping the batch vectorized. One property lookup per row — what the expression path already paid.

## Measured

`main` (`27edbd56`) vs this branch. 176,000 edges over 1,000 nodes, instructions from `proc_pid_rusage` on the server pid, so the driver is not in the numbers.

| query | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN sum(r.k)` | 2,864 | **1,252** | **2.29x** |
| `MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN sum(r.k * 2)` | 1,601 | 1,600 | unchanged |

`sum(r.k)` is now cheaper than `sum(r.k * 2)`, which is the ordering that should always have held.

Against the C implementation on a whole-graph scan, across a multiplicity sweep at fixed `|E|` (instructions/edge; this branch was measured on top of `fold-policy` for the sweep, since that is where the sweep harness lives):

| mu | before | after | C | after vs C |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1.0 | 3,191 | 1,578 | 3,222 | **2.04x better** |
| 1.1 | 3,379 | 1,766 | 3,056 | **1.73x better** |
| 2.0 | 4,138 | 2,525 | 2,315 | 1.09x worse |
| 4.0 | 3,274 | 1,662 | 1,779 | **1.07x better** |
| 16.0 | 2,610 | 997 | 1,376 | **1.38x better** |

The residual loss at mu=2 is a **different** bug, not this one: multi-edge traversal pays per edge where C pays per p
Resolve: #2418

pullRequests.title: fix(bulk): replicate GRAPH.BULK from the background writer
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2347

## What was wrong

`GRAPH.BULK` never reached replicas — silently, with a healthy replication link and no error anywhere. It also corrupted the AOF, which the issue did not cover.

The background-writer path replicated with `RM_ReplicateVerbatim` on a **thread-safe context**. That API propagates `ctx->client->argv`, and the client behind a thread-safe context is a *fake pooled* one carrying no argv. Redis says so inline (`module.c`):

> Even when the context is associated with a blocked client, we can't access it safely from another thread, so we use a fake client here

`alsoPropagate()` with `argc == 0` is **not** a no-op — it emits a zero-element RESP array. Every bulk batch propagated a literal `*0`:

```
*2..$6..SELECT..$1..0..*0..*26..$4..XADD..
                        ^^^^ the propagated zero-arg command
```

Replicas skip that frame, hence the silent divergence. The AOF is less forgiving — `*0` makes it unparseable, so an AOF-enabled server **refused to restart at all** after a bulk load:

```
# Bad file format reading the append only file appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.1.incr.aof at offset 23
```

Both `GRAPH.BULK` paths were affected: the `BEGIN` batch and the append batch.

## The fix

**1. Rebuild the command instead of replicating verbatim.** This is what C does when it replicates off the main thread — `QueryCtx_Replicate` calls `RM_Replicate` (`query_ctx.c`) — and what `graph_core::replicate_effects` already does from this same position. `RM_Replicate` builds its own argv, so the fake client stops mattering.

The arg slice borrows the tokens already copied for the worker, so the payload is not copied a second time. The key is carried as raw bytes because `to_string()` is lossy and would rewrite a non-UTF-8 graph name into replacement characters and address a different key on the replica.

**2. Widen the inline guard to C's dispatcher predicate.** This is *required* to make (1) safe, not optional hardening. Once the command actually reached t

pullRequests.title: perf: skip the edge-id lookup when nothing reads the edge (1.99x)
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2427.

A chain-less `CondTraverse` binds its edge alias to a representative edge id for every row it emits, and finding one costs a tensor lookup per row — `Tensor::get` → `eff_get`, up to three GraphBLAS `extractElement` calls to read the effective value through the `dp`/`dm`/`m` delta layers. On a traversal that never reads the edge, all of it is waste.

### Why `emit_relationship` couldn't already decide this

`emit_relationship` answers row *multiplicity*: false means one row per `(src, dst)` pair instead of one per edge. An anonymous edge inside a named path gets `emit_relationship: false` — one row per pair is correct — and still has to be bound, because `PathBuilder` reads the alias to assemble the path. The runtime comment said exactly that, and resolved it by always doing the lookup.

So the two questions get two answers. `CondTraverse` gains `bind_relationship`, conservatively `true` at planning time and lowered by a new `reduce_bound_edge` pass that walks ancestors looking for a reference to the edge alias. This is the same shape as the existing `emit_path` / `reduce_var_len_path` pair, and reuses its `ir_references_variable`.

The pass runs **last** in the pipeline, after everything that rebuilds a `CondTraverse` or moves its ancestors (including `fuse_optional_traverse`). Every constructor sets `bind_relationship: true`, so a rebuilding pass can only ever be conservative and this pass has the final say.

Dropping the lookup also drops its `found_id` guard, which never fired: `f` is built from these same tensors, so every pair it yields has at least one edge in one of them.

### Measured

1,000 nodes, 88,000 `(src, dst)` pairs, release build, instructions per pair (median of 5, macOS `proc_pid_rusage`):

| query | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `MATCH (a:N)-[:R]->(x:N) RETURN count(x)` | 1,467 | 736 | **1.99x** |
| `MATCH (a:N)-[r:R]->(x:N) RETURN sum(r.k)` | 3,944 | 3,938 | unchanged |

Identical at multiplicity 2 (735/pair) — one row

pullRequests.title: perf: make the multi-edge demote path linear in the batch (26x)
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2429.

Deleting an edge from a 2-edge pair — the *demote* transition that returns the surviving id to the inline cell — was ~95x C's cost and **quadratic in how many pairs one query demotes**.

### Cause

Instrumented per call site inside `Tensor::remove_all`, rather than guessed. At 1,000 demoted pairs the function was 13.18 ms of a 14.35 ms query:

| site | 125 | 250 | 500 | 1000 pairs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `me.iter` right after `me.remove` | 269 µs | 1.76 ms | 3.50 ms | **9.88 ms** |
| `eff_get` right after the `dp` write | 14 µs | 995 µs | 1.54 ms | **2.90 ms** |
| the writes themselves | 28 µs | 104 µs | 167 µs | 0.32 ms |

Read-after-write on an MVCC delta layer *inside* the per-edge loop: each read has to materialise the tuples the previous iteration left pending. The originally suspected `dp`/`wait_fwd` path is only ~22% of it — the dominant term is `me`, where `me.remove` dirties the delta and the very next `me.iter` waits on it. The original evidence (quadratic in batch, flat in `|me|`) could not separate the two, since neither scans `me`'s base.

### Fix

The slow path is split into a read phase and a write phase — the same shape `set_all_from_slices` already uses on the insert side. The read phase touches no layer it also reads: it reads each multi pair's `me` row **once per pair** rather than twice per edge, replays that pair's transitions in a per-pair `PairPlan` (`Multi` → `Single{demoted}` → `Emptied`), and buffers the `me` removals. The write phase applies them, probing only committed bases, with all `dp` erases ordered ahead of all `dp` inserts so no probe can observe another write's pending tuples.

Layer writes, `multi_count`, `mt` and cancel-to-clean make byte-for-byte the same decisions as the old loop, so the documented delta invariants — and the Lean proofs over them — are untouched. pullRequests.title: docs: the relationship tensor's design, mechanised invariants and measured cost
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2432.

Documentation, proofs and the measurement harnesses the paper reports on. **No change to shipped behaviour, CI or Cargo**: the Rust in the diff is `#[cfg(test)]` bench modules plus one test-only hook and two `pub(super)` constants those benches read, so nothing here is compiled into the module. (An earlier revision of this description said "zero changes to Rust" — that was true when the harnesses lived on a separate branch, and is no longer.)

## What lands

**`docs/papers/tensor.tex`** — a 40-page standalone treatment of the relationship tensor: the design space it sits in, the ten-state per-pair automaton, the invariant set, the algorithms with their proof strategies, the fold policy's cost model, and a measured evaluation.

**`proofs/tensor/`** — the Lean 4 mechanisation the paper reports on: ~7,200 lines, ~380 theorems (of which `Tensor/` is ~6,200 and ~320), `lake build` clean, `#print axioms` showing no `sorry`. It has already earned its keep by identifying two unreachable branches that were subsequently removed from the engine, one of which fabricated edge id 0 on a backward read.

## The design, in one paragraph

Three ways to store a multigraph's edge identities inside a GraphBLAS matrix: **(A)** a heap container per multi-edge cell, reached by a tagged pointer — what the C engine does; **(B)** keep the adjacency Boolean and hold every id in a second structure; **(C)** make the adjacency `UINT64`, store a lone id inline, and promote a pair into an overflow matrix only when it gains a second edge, marking the cell with a reserved sentinel. (C) is what this engine does. It buys the common case at the price of a state transition and the invariant discipline that transition requires.

pullRequests.title: refactor: drop bind_relationship, which said nothing emit_relationship did not
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2436. Follow-up to #2428, which I over-built.

### The flag carries no information

#2428 added `bind_relationship` to `IR::CondTraverse` plus a `reduce_bound_edge` pass to lower it. After the passes run:

```
emit_relationship = emit_rel_initial && referenced_by_ancestor
bind_relationship =                     referenced_by_ancestor
```

They differ only when `referenced && !emit_rel_initial` — an anonymous edge that no named path mentions, yet some ancestor references. `_anon…` aliases are synthesised by the binder and unnameable in Cypher, and the only IR that references one is `PathBuilder`, which implies the edge *is* in a path's vars and hence that `emit_rel` already returned true. Unreachable.

Checked rather than argued: over 18 queries spanning named and anonymous edges, named paths, `relationships(p)`, `OPTIONAL MATCH`, `WITH` barriers, `DELETE`, `SET`, multi-hop, cartesian-plus-join and `DISTINCT`, the two agree on every `CondTraverse` — 0 disagreements.

**The justification in #2428 was wrong, not just redundant.** It claimed an anonymous edge inside a named path gets `emit_relationship: false` and still needs binding because `PathBuilder` reads it. In fact `emit_rel` is `!anonymous || appears in a named path's vars`, so that case emits and routes to the per-row path. I asserted a distinction from a closure I hadn't read.

### Which makes the lookup dead, not conditional

`batched_eligible` requires `!emit_relationship`, so the batched path runs only when nothing above reads the alias. The representative-edge-id lookup there was unreachable for *every* query, and so was the `RelIds` column it filled — both are now removed outright rather than gated. The stale comment that justified them ("Required because downstream PathBuilder reads the edge alias even when emit_relationship is false") goes with them, as does the `from_alias` binding the lookup was the only reader of.

Net: −1 IR field, −5 constructor sites, −1 optimizer pass and its registratio

pullRequests.title: refactor: derive the multi-edge pair count instead of maintaining it
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2438. **Stacked on #2431** — that PR restructured `remove_all`, where the counter's decrement lived, so this targets it rather than `main`.

Implements the third and most ambitious of the paper's three repairs for this invariant: rather than police the counter, remove the obligation.

### Why the field can go

`multi_count` exists only to keep the cardinality identity O(1), but promotion completeness makes it the non-empty row count of `me` — a structure already present. It was a hand-maintained cache, and the maintenance is the whole problem: seven call sites add or remove a row of `me`, three touched the counter.

Two things made removal cheaper than expected:

- `has_multi_edge()` never used it — already `me.nvals() != 0`.
- `Decode` never read it from the blob, it derived it from the tensor-section counts. **The on-disk format is untouched.**

Which leaves `edge_count()` as the only consumer, reached from planning, `db.*` procedures and two graph algorithms — never per row.

### The derivation, and its worst case

| state of `me` | cost |
|---|---|
| no multi-edge pair anywhere (dominant case) | `nvals`, O(1) |
| assembled | its vector count — metadata, since a hypersparse matrix stores its non-empty vectors and nothing else |
| live deltas | walk the effective rows: O(multi), never O(\|E\|) |

The third row is the one to worry about, and it is not reached in practice: commit folds `me`, so by the time a query asks for a count the metadata path is taken.

### Measured

| | ratio |
|---|---|
| **full suite, instructions** (two independent pairs) | **0.9961x**, **1.0018x** |
| `write 1m` | 1.002x |
| `create 10k` | 1.000x |
| `multi-edge demote/promote` | 0.995x |
| `untyped edge scan` | 0.987x |

Worst case — a metadata count query over a graph of all-multi-edge pairs — is 1.03–1.12x of the counter build at 10,000 and 100,000 pairs, on a query costing ~0.5M instructions.

Two honesty notes on the measurements. The same microbenchmark is **not trustworthy

pullRequests.title: fix(parser): quadratic parameter parsing (5.8x) and unbounded-nesting server abort
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2443

Two parser defects found while sampling a live `redis-server` during a slow bulk load. Both are pre-existing on `main`.

---

## 1. Parsing an inlined parameter payload was quadratic (5.8x)

A `[` sends the expression parser probing for a list comprehension and then a pattern comprehension before it settles on a plain list literal. Both probes call `parse_ident`, and both **discard** its error — but the error was built first, and `Lexer::format_error` embedded the **entire query text** in every message:

```rust
format!("{}, errCtx: {}, pos {}", err, self.str, self.pos)
```

Bulk loaders inline their rows: `CYPHER batch=[{...},{...}]` payloads run to megabytes, with one list literal per embedding vector. Every `[` then paid two copies of the whole payload.

Sampling put **96% of the busy thread's samples** in `alloc::fmt::format` → `_platform_memmove` under `parse_ident`, with no graph work at all:

```
execute_query → Graph::get_plan → Parser::parse_parameters
  → parse_expr → parse_primary_expr → parse_map        (nested)
    → parse_expr → parse_primary_expr → parse_ident
        → alloc::fmt::format  ...  _platform_memmove   ← 7,100 / 7,393 samples
```

**Fix** — either half removes the quadratic term; together they also stop FalkorDB returning multi-megabyte error strings to clients:

- `format_error` quotes an 80-byte window around the error position instead of the whole query. Cut on char boundaries — slicing a multi-byte character in half would panic.
- `try_parse_ident` returns `Option` and formats nothing, for the seven call sites that were only ever probing.

**Measured** on a 6.7 MB batch of 1477 maps each with a 384-dim embedding — the shape the slow log recorded:

| | time |
|---|---|
| before | 1810 ms |
| after | **310 ms** |
| | **5.8x** |

Parse time is now linear. At a fixed 3.6 MB, splitting across more list literals used to cost 20x more; now flat:

| list literals | 1 | 100 | 1000 | 4000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 154 ms |

pullRequests.title: fix(bulk): bound GRAPH.BULK declared counts and make id reservation fallible
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2426

## What was wrong

`GRAPH.BULK` trusted the client-declared `node_count` / `edge_count` and passed them
straight to `Vec::with_capacity`, so a single command aborted the process:

```console
$ redis-cli GRAPH.BULK g BEGIN 9223372036854775807 0 0 0
Error: Server closed the connection
```

```
# FalkorDB panic: panicked at library/alloc/src/raw_vec/mod.rs:28:5:
capacity overflow
   9: graph::graph::graph::Graph::reserve_nodes
```

Both count fields are affected — `reserve_relationships` has the identical shape. Nothing
validated the declared counts against the payload; the only existing check covered the number
of *tokens*, which is why the repro needs no payload at all: with `node_token_count == 0` the
token-count check passes and nothing is ever parsed.

Still present verbatim on `main` at `cf3ec7a6f`: `graph.rs:1309` and `graph.rs:2030`.

## The fix

**`src/commands/bulk_insert.rs`** — three changes at the trust boundary:

1. `parse_count` replaces the four `str::parse` calls, matching `string2ll`: rejects a leading
   `+`, leading zeros, and any non-digit byte, while keeping Rust's rejection of negatives.
2. A pre-pass bounds each declared count by what the payload can **describe**, not by its byte
   length. `max_records` reuses `parse_header` and the reader's own arithmetic — a record costs
   at least `endpoints_len + P` bytes (`P` = header property count; a property is ≥1 byte
   because `BI_NULL` is just its marker), and a node token with `P == 0` describes zero records
   since the read loop is byte-driven. The sections are positional, so each count is bounded by
   its own section: the first `node_token_count` tokens for nodes, the rest for edges.
3. The graph key is created **after** validation, so a rejected batch leaves the keyspace
   untouched. Key resolution stays first, preserving C's error precedence for
   `"…already exists."` and `"Invalid graph operation on empty key"`.

`parse_header`'s property pre-allocation is also capped by rem

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2421

## What was wrong

**An AOF-enabled server could not restart.** Not a clean failure — `SIGSEGV`, and the server
never came up.

AOF replay drives a fake client that carries `CLIENT_DENY_BLOCKING` but *not* `CLIENT_MASTER`,
so `REPLICATED` is not set for it. Every Rust guard site checked only `MULTI || REPLICATED`, so
that client took the blocking path and was left blocked, which Redis asserts against:

```
# === ASSERTION FAILED ===
# ==> aof.c:1692 '(fakeClient->flags & CLIENT_BLOCKED) == 0' is not true
# Redis 255.255.255 crashed by signal: 11, si_code: 2
```

C's dispatcher (`src/commands/cmd_dispatcher.c` on `master`) treats five flags as "this context
must not block" — `MULTI | LUA | DENY_BLOCKING | LOADING`, plus `is_replicated`. The Rust ports
checked two.

This does not need index or constraint DDL to trigger. `should_use_effects` falls back to
verbatim `GRAPH.QUERY` whenever a write's average per-effect time is under `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`
(default 300µs), so two ordinary `CREATE` statements reach it — which is what the reproduction
below uses.

Same commands, same conditions (`appendonly yes` at startup, RDB removed, no `BGREWRITEAOF`):

| nodes before restart | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| AOF contents | 2 × verbatim `GRAPH.QUERY` | 2 × verbatim `GRAPH.QUERY` | 2 × verbatim `GRAPH.QUERY` |
| survives restart | yes | **no — signal 11** | **yes** |
| nodes after restart | 2 | — | **2** |
| load source | `DB loaded from append only file` | — | `DB loaded from append only file` |
| assertion lines in log | 0 | 4 | **0** |

The issue suggests inlining the widened predicate at each of the five sites. That would have
produced **six** copies once you count the one #2420 already landed in `bulk_insert.rs` — and
five sites each having grown their own narrower copy of C's single predicate is precisely what

pullRequests.title: fix: don't mistake a multi-arg constructor call for the rewritten struct form
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2446. Found by the `fuzz` job while it was running against an unrelated PR.

### The crash

```cypher
WITH localdatetime({year: 1984, month: 10, day: 11, hour: 12, mid: true},
                   {list: [6], fd: 645876123}) AS d
RETURN d
```

kills the server — client sees `Connection closed by server`, then connection refused. Reproduced on a **release** build of `main` at `71c65bbd5`, so this is not a debug-only assertion.

### Cause

`rewrite_struct_constructor` rewrites a constructor call whose **single** argument is a constant-keyed Map into positional children: exactly one child per slot, absent keys as `Constant(Null)`. Anything else it leaves alone.

The evaluator inferred that rewrite from arity alone:

```rust
if let Some(struct_fn) = func.struct_fn
    && node.num_children() > 1
```

`date`, `localtime` and `localdatetime` are declared `var_arg`, so a two-argument call passes arity validation, is mistaken for the rewritten form, and reaches a `struct_fn` expecting `slots.len()` values. `localdatetime_struct_pure` then reads `args[3]` of a 2-element slice — the `debug_assert_eq!(args.len(), 10)` in test builds, an out-of-bounds index that aborts the process in release.

`duration` was never affected: it declares `args: [..]`, so the extra argument is rejected before evaluation.

### Fix

Guard on equality against `struct_slots.len()` — the only arity the rewrite ever produces. Any other arity falls through to the ordinary path.

### Verification

The regression test is in `tests/test_functions.py` and I checked it actually catches the bug: **without** this change it fails with a dropped connection, **with** it passes. It asserts the weaker property deliberately — either a value or an error is fine, a dead server is not — since the arity question below is unsettled.

`cargo test -p graph` 137 passed; `test_functions` + `test_mvcc` + `test_concurrency` pass; TCK green; fmt and clippy clean.

pullRequests.title: fix: re-check pause and role before a write commits, not just at admission
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2371

## What was wrong

A graph write is **admitted** on the Redis main thread — where Redis has already vetted the
pause state and the role — but it **mutates and replicates later, from a background thread**.
Nothing re-checked either condition in between. So a `CLIENT PAUSE` / `FAILOVER` window opening
in that gap, or a demotion to replica, let the write proceed and crash the master:

```
# === ASSERTION FAILED ===
# ==> server.c:3600 '!(isPausedActions(PAUSE_ACTION_REPLICA) &&
#                      (!server.client_pause_in_transaction))'
```

Redis's own comment at `server.c:3613` gives the reason: *"the dataset should be fixed during
replica pause (otherwise data may be lost during a failover)"*. It is a `serverAssert` rather
than an error return because by then the write is already applied — there is nothing to roll
back, and letting it into the replication stream would break the guarantee a failover is
predicated on.

The invariant holds for ordinary Redis commands because admit → apply → propagate happens in one
uninterrupted turn. FalkorDB breaks that atomicity, so it has to re-establish the check itself.

## 1. Query write path

`upgrade_to_write` re-validates **under the GIL, immediately before mutating**. Holding the GIL
is what makes it race-free: `CLIENT PAUSE` and role-change events both run on the main thread,
which needs the GIL we are holding, so neither can move between the check and the commit.

Mirrors C's `QueryCtx_AcquireWriteLock` (`src/query_ctx.c`, PR #2372): bypass on
`LOADING`/`ASYNC_LOADING`, then `AvoidReplicaTraffic`, then `READONLY`.

Two details carried over deliberately:

* **`READONLY`, not `MASTER`** — a replica running `replica-read-only no` accepts writes, and
  rejecting them there would break replica-divergence testing. C corrected this the same way in
  #2372. Confirmed against Redis source: `READONLY` is set only when `SLAVE && repl_slave_ro`
  (`module.c:3999-4002`).
* **No check for a role that flipped away and ba

pullRequests.title: perf(parser): read parameters straight into values, not an expression tree (6.5x)
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2463

> #2442 has merged, so this now targets `main` directly and is a single commit. Rebased onto the squashed merge — which dismissed the earlier approval, so it needs another look.

Follow-up to #2442. After that PR the 6.7 MB bulk-load batch was still **13.7× slower than the C module**, and the whole gap was parameter parsing. This closes most of it.

## The problem

A parameter is a literal — `evaluate_param` accepts constants, lists, maps and negation, and nothing else. But every parameter was parsed into an `ExprIR` tree first and then walked **twice**: once in `get_plan` for the optimizer, once in `graph_core` for the runtime.

For the payloads bulk loaders inline, that tree is one node per literal. A 6.7 MB batch of 1477 maps each with a 384-dim embedding is ~567k literals, and building their nodes *was* the query — profiling put `parse_expr_inner`, `parse_primary_expr` and `parse_map` at the top with `evaluate_param` barely registering.

Decomposition before this change (6.7 MB each):

| | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| params only (`RETURN 1`) | 20.6 ms | **302.3 ms** |
| params + `UNWIND` + count | 22.1 ms | 302.5 ms |
| no params, same bytes | 16.9 ms | **7.0 ms** ← Rust already wins |

Execution cost ~1.5 ms on both. Marginal cost per literal: C ≈ 27 ns, Rust ≈ 335 ns.

## The fix

`parse_param_value` reads the common case straight into a `Value` — no tree, no evaluation pass. `Plan::parameters` now holds values, which removes both walks.

Anything the fast path doesn't recognise, **or that turns out to be an expression rather than a literal** (`p=1+2`, `p=[1,2][0]`), is handed back to `parse_expr` + `evaluate_param`. So non-literal parameters keep their old result *and* their old error message by construction, rather than by me re-deriving them.

## Measured against C

6.7 MB batch, 21 iterations:

| engine | min | median | p95 | vs C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **C (reference)** | 23.9 ms | **26.2 ms** | 34.9 ms | — |
| **this PR** | 52.1 ms | **54.

pullRequests.title: feat(index): index numeric array elements, and serve conjunctions
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2452

**Based on #2386** — review that first; the diff here is only this layer.

Two gaps from the ledger that #2386 introduced, closed here. Both are read-path capability, which
is why they are their own layer rather than part of the no-fallback change.

## Numeric array elements

A numeric array is indexed element-wise into a **separate array tree** on the same column, so
`value IN n.samples` is a point lookup into it. Scalars and array elements never share a key
space — sharing one would make `WHERE n.v = 1` match a node whose `v` is `[1, 2]`, and the
`Equal` plan carries no post-filter to catch that. This mirrors how RediSearch keeps `numeric`
and `numeric:arr` as separate sub-fields.

`EncodedTuples { scalar, array }` is the transport the online build already needed: BASE, DELTA
and TOMB each carry both halves, so a build that starts mid-write stages array elements the same
way it stages scalars. A value changing between scalar and array — and back — re-indexes into
the right tree, which is pinned by a round-trip test.

## Conjunctions

All three shapes are served:

| shape | how |
|---|---|
| the same predicate twice | collapsed before the index sees it |
| several bounds on ONE attribute | folded arithmetically into a single window |
| bounds across TWO attributes | one column per attribute, intersected |

The same-attribute fold happens **in the index, not the planner**: `merge_range_queries` gives up
whenever two conjuncts constrain the same side of the window, because at plan time the bounds may
still be expressions it cannot compare — by the time the index sees them they are concrete values.

The cross-attribute case is a **set probe, not a sorted merge**. `DocIter` yields docs in value
order, not id order, so a merge would need both sides sorted by id; instead the first attribute is
materialised and the rest probe it. Rows match the RediSearch build; order differs, which Cypher
permits without `ORDER BY`. A column still building declines the whol

pullRequests.title: fix: one attribute dictionary per graph, and an RDB the C engine can load
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2457

Two engines that cannot load each other's RDB cannot be swapped by failover, in
either direction. This makes them able to, and the attribute-id fix #2457 asks for
is what made the comparison possible in the first place.

## 1. One attribute dictionary per graph, not one per store

`AttributeStore` owned its own name → id table, so node and relationship
attributes were numbered **independently**. The RDB, however, carries a single flat
`attribute_names` list and seeds *both* stores from it. So a master that had never
been reloaded kept split numbering while a replica seeded by full sync had the
unified one — and property effects put a **bare `u16` id on the wire with no name
to verify against**.

Same id, different attribute on each side:

```
master   {since: 9999}
replica  {a: 9999, since: 2026}
```

The value lands on `a` — a node attribute that should not exist on an edge — and
the intended one stays stale. No error, no log line. **Any resync heals it**, so it
presents as a replica that intermittently disagrees and then fixes itself.

Reachability is counter-intuitive: `should_use_effects` picks effects when *average
per-effect time > `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`* (default 300µs), so a 20 000-edge bulk `SET`
replicates correctly via the verbatim path while a **single-edge `SET` behind an
expensive match** diverges.

### It was a violated invariant, not merely a mismatch

Bare ids are not an oversight — `pending.rs` states the contract above the
`CREATE_NODE` emission:

pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Dependabot on `main` currently tracks only `github-actions` and `cargo`. Three dependency surfaces in the Rust tree receive no updates at all, so vulnerable versions there would go unflagged indefinitely.

This adds one entry per uncovered surface. The three existing entries — including the `target-branch: master` entry that keeps the C engine's Actions bumps alive (#2255) — are untouched.

## Changes

- **`pip` at `/tests`** — `tests/requirements.txt` (`behave`, `pytest`, `redis`, `RLTest`, `hypothesis`, `falkordb`, `textual`)
- **`uv` at `/bench`** — the benchmark harness is its own uv project with `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`; `pip` would not read the lockfile, so it needs the `uv` ecosystem
- **`docker` at `/build`, `/build/runtime`, `/.devcontainer`** — the `debian:trixie-slim`, `node:24-bookworm-slim` and `ubuntu:24.04` base images
- Each entry is **grouped** (`patterns: ["*"]`) so it opens one consolidated PR per week instead of one per dependency

### Two deliberate exclusions

- **`/bench` is not in the docker entry.** `bench/Dockerfile` is `FROM ${C_IMAGE}` — an entirely ARG-driven base that Dependabot cannot resolve to a registry tag. Including it would add a directory that yields nothing.
- **`gitsubmodule` is not added.** `main` has no `.gitmodules`; submodules exist only on `master`, where `submodule-update.yml` already handles them. Enabling it would produce duplicate, conflicting PRs pinned to unreleased upstream commits.

### Note on the `redis<8.1` pin

`tests/requirements.txt` pins `redis<8.1` with a documented reason (falkordb-py 1.6.2 forwards `himport_registry` to the sync constructor). Dependabot honours declared version constraints and will not widen them, so this pin holds until someone edits it by hand. The comment in the config records why.

## Testing

- Every configured directory was confirmed to contain a manifest Dependa

pullRequests.body:
## Summary

`RETURN date('2020-01-01','x')` terminates the server process. So do `localtime(1,2)`, `localdatetime(1,2)` and `date(1)`. Any client able to run a query can take the database down with one malformed call, so this fixes that.

Found by the `fuzz` job on #2304, which panicked at `temporal.rs:635` with `left: 2, right: 7`.

## Changes

`date`, `localtime` and `localdatetime` are registered with a var-length signature so their zero-argument "now" form binds. That signature is looser than what they accept, and two separate things relied on it being accurate.

- **`eval.rs`** — the struct-constructor fast path identified the binder's rewritten positional form by testing `node.num_children() > 1`. `rewrite_struct_constructor` always emits exactly one child per slot, so the correct test is equality. For a fixed-arity constructor like `point` the loose test was still safe, because arity validation rejects a second argument before evaluation; for these three nothing did, so a user-written `date(a, b)` entered the fast path and handed `date_struct_pure` a 2-element slice that indexes `args[0..6]`. Match on `func.struct_slots.len()`.
- **`functions/mod.rs`** — `validate_args_type` had `FnArguments::VarLength(_) => {}`, so a var-length signature's declared element type was decorative. The three constructors declare `Map | String | Null` and their pure functions treat anything else as `unreachable!()`, which `date(1)` reached. Validate the declared type. Every other var-length function declares `Type::Any`, and `value_of_type` returns `None` for `Type::Any`, so none of them are affected.
- **`functions/temporal.rs`** — give the three their real arity, `args: [Type::Optional(...)]`. `validate` excludes `Optional` from the minimum count, so this is exactly "0 or 1" and is how `duration` and `point` already express the same thing. Using var-length to mean "may be empty" is what pulled the arity check out.

pullRequests.title: test(var-len): cover fixed-length path multiplicity
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Regression tests for the `fixed-rust` cluster in which a **fixed-length variable-length traversal collapsed distinct paths**, silently behaving as though `DISTINCT` had been applied — and, more confusingly, merely *binding a path variable* changed the result.

@K-Jo's original analysis in #73 explains the mechanism: the traversal was evaluated as a boolean adjacency-matrix product, which records only *whether* the destination is reachable, not *how many* distinct paths reach it. The Rust engine fixed this; nothing in the suite pinned the multiplicity contract.

## Changes

Added `test18_fixed_length_path_multiplicity` to `tests/flow/test_variable_length_traversals.py`, building a diamond with two distinct 2-hop paths and asserting:

- `MATCH (a:A)-[:LIKES*2]->(c)` returns the destination **twice**, with no implicit `DISTINCT` (#73, #1450)
- the result is **identical with and without a bound path variable** (#354, #1450)
- it also matches the equivalent **explicit two-hop** pattern
- the two paths stay **distinguishable** by their intermediate node — `nodes(p)[1]` gives `n00` and `n01`
- a bounded range `[*1..2]` is likewise consistent with and without a path variable

This is a new test rather than an extension: the file's only existing multi-hop fixture (`test13_fanout`) is a *tree*, so no diamond exists in it and path multiplicity cannot be observed. The existing `[*2]` assertions at lines 242/244 only check `length(p)` on a single path.

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_variable_length_traversals ./flow.sh` → **18/18 pass**.

Each assertion fails on the era build and passes on `main`:

| query | `v4.2.2` | `main` | asserted |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:LIKES*2]->(c)` | **1** | 2 | 2 |
| `MATCH p=(a:A)-[:LIKES*2]->(c)` | 2 | 2 | 2 |

The 1-vs-2 split on `v4.2.2` is precisely the "assigning a variable changes query results" symptom of #354.

pullRequests.title: fix(dependabot): stop widening the deliberate redis<8.1 test pin
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #2464. The `pip` entry I added for `/tests` carried no `ignore` rule, on the incorrect assumption — stated in a comment in that PR — that Dependabot treats a `<` ceiling as a hard constraint. It does not: the pip ecosystem defaults to `versioning-strategy: auto`, which widens ranges.

Dependabot then opened #2476, raising `redis<8.1` to `redis<8.2`.

## Why that is a problem

**It re-admits the exact release the pin excludes.** `<8.2` permits redis-py 8.1.0, which adds `himport_registry` to `ConnectionPool.connection_kwargs`; falkordb-py 1.6.2 forwards it to the sync `Redis()` constructor, and every flow test that builds its own pool fails with a `TypeError`.

**It desyncs two pins that must move together.** The identical pin lives at `build/Dockerfile:141`, and the comment above it says "Keep in sync with build/Dockerfile". #2476 touches only `tests/requirements.txt`.

**CI gives false assurance.** `tests/requirements.txt` is installed by *no* workflow — the flow suites run inside `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build`, which bakes its own copy of the pin. So `flow-test-matrix` passes on #2476 without ever exercising the changed file. The breakage surfaces only on local and non-container runs, which is why this needs a config guard rather than a test.

## Changes

- Add `ignore: [dependency-name: "redis"]` to the `/tests` pip entry
- Replace the comment that made the wrong claim, recording why the ignore exists, that CI cannot catch the regression, and the condition for removing it

## Testing

- `.github/dependabot.yml` parses under `yaml.safe_load`; all six update entries verified intact with the `ignore` attached to the `pip` `/tests` entry only
- Confirmed `tests/requirements.txt` matches no reference in `.github/workflows/`
- Confirmed the duplicate pin at `build/Dockerfile:141`
- No change to the other five ecosystems; the `target-branch: master` github-actions entry is untouched

## Memory / Performance Impact

N/A — CI configuration only

pullRequests.title: ci: exempt Dependabot PRs from the "PR closes an issue" check
pullRequests.body:
The required `PR closes an issue` job fails on every Dependabot PR ([run 31624938048](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/31624938048/job/94208797670), PR #2474). The assert is unsatisfiable for Dependabot — the app cannot attach an issue through the Development sidebar, `Closes #N` keywords only register on the default branch (these PRs target `main`), and Dependabot-triggered runs get a read-only Dependabot-scoped token — so `closingIssuesReferences.totalCount` is always `0` and every dependency bump is permanently blocked.

### Changes to `.github/workflows/pr-linked-issue.yml`

- **Exempt Dependabot** — the step exits 0 with an explanatory job summary when `github.event.pull_request.user.login` is `dependabot[bot]` (or legacy `dependabot-preview[bot]`), before the GraphQL query runs.
- **Exemption lives inside the step, not a job-level `if:`** — the check is required in branch protection, so it must always report a conclusion rather than leave the PR waiting on a status that never arrives. This mirrors the workflow's existing "no `paths:` filter" rationale.
- **Header comment updated** — the block previously declared "There are no exemptions: bot PRs (dependabot, batch-backport) must also close an issue"; it now documents the single exemption and why. Every other author, bots included, is unchanged.

```bash
PR_AUTHOR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.user.login }}
...
if [ "${PR_AUTHOR:-}" = "dependabot[bot]" ] || [ "${PR_AUTHOR:-}" = "dependabot-preview[bot]" ]; then
  ...
  exit 0
fi
```

Literal string comparison rather than a `case` glob is deliberate: `[bot]` in a glob pattern is a character class and would match `dependabott` but not the actual login.

### Companion issue

The sandbox has no write-capable GitHub credential (`gh` unauthenticated, MCP GitHub tools read-only), so the issue could not be filed from here. Suggested text:

> **`PR closes an issue` check blocks all Dependabot PRs**
>
> The required `PR closes an issue` job fails on eve

## Summary

Regression tests for two `fixed-rust` crashes in which hostile arguments took the **whole server down** (SIGSEGV/SIGFPE, `ExitCode=139`) instead of producing a query error. Both are fixed by the Rust engine; neither had a test.

## Changes

**Extended `test79_Range`** (#385) — `range()` negated `i64::MIN` while computing its span, which is undefined at the 64-bit boundary:

- `range(0, -9223372036854775808, -1)` — the original report
- `range(0, -9223372036854775807, -1)` — the adjacent value, which used to OOM instead
- `range(-9223372036854775808, 0, 1)` — the same limit as the *start* bound

All must raise `Range too large`. Also pinned the neighbouring `step = 0` error so the two failure modes stay distinct.

**Added `test96_exists_unbound_variables`** (#2264) — `exists()` dereferenced unresolved entities when its traversal pattern referenced unbound variables and reused a relationship variable:

- `RETURN exists( (n0)-[r1]-(n1), (n1)-[r1]-(n0) )` → `'n0' not defined`
- `RETURN exists( (n0)-[r1]-(n1) )` and the bound-source variant → `traversal patterns are not allowed as arguments to exists()`
- a trailing `RETURN 1` asserts the **server is still responsive**, which is the property that actually regressed

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_function_calls ./flow.sh` → **94/94 pass**.

Both crashes were reproduced on the era image before writing the tests:

| issue | query | `v4.20.1` | `main` |

| #385 | `range(0, -9223372036854775808, -1)` | `Server closed the connection` 💥 | `Range too large` |
| #2264 | `exists( (n0)-[r1]-(n1), (n1)-[r1]-(n0) )` | `Server closed the connection` 💥 | `'n0' not defined` |

In both cases the container died and the follow-up `PING` returned `Connection reset by peer`.

N/A — tests only.

pullRequests.title: test(all-shortest-paths): cover aggregating WITH * over unresolved endpoints
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Regression test for #2127, a SIGSEGV: `allShortestPaths()` whose endpoints are declared **inline in its own pattern** correctly raises `Source and destination must already be resolved`, but when the clause was followed by an **aggregating `WITH *`**, raising that error with an aggregation still pending took the whole server down.

## Changes

**Extended `test01_invalid_shortest_paths`** — that test already enumerates the invalid `allShortestPaths` forms and asserts a clean error for each, so this is the same narrative rather than a new test. Added:

- `MATCH p = allShortestPaths((a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper)) WITH *, count(a) AS count_a RETURN p` → `Source and destination must already be resolved to call allShortestPaths`
- a trailing `RETURN 1` asserting the **server is still alive** — the property that actually regressed

## Testing

`RELEASE=1 VERBOSE=0 TEST=tests/flow/test_all_shortest_paths ./flow.sh` → **7/7 pass**.

I bisected the reported query on the era image to isolate what actually crashes, because the issue's own root-cause analysis (hashing `Path`/`Array` as `GROUP BY` keys) turns out not to be the trigger:

| query on `v4.18.10` | result |
|---|---|
| `MATCH p = allShortestPaths((a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper)) RETURN p` | clean error ✅ |
| the same **+ `WITH *, count(a)`** | `Server closed the connection` 💥 |
| `MATCH p = (a:Paper)-[*..2]-(b:Paper) WITH *, count(a) ...` | works ✅ |
| `MATCH (a:Paper) WITH *, [a.x, 1] AS arr, count(a) ...` | works ✅ |

So grouping by a `Path` or an `Array` was never the problem — the crash needs the **error path** and the **pending aggregation** together. The test asserts exactly that combination.

I also checked the case already covered by this test's first assertion (`MATCH (v1),(v4), p = allShortestPaths((v1)-[*]->(v4))`): it errors cleanly on `v4.18.10`, so it never covered this crash and the extension is not duplication.

N/A — tests only.

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): order a reversed traversal chain from its new anchor (78x), and run the most selective hop first
pullRequests.body:
Two commits, both in `select_scan_node`'s chain rewrite.

## 1 · The bottom hop had no bound endpoint (78x)

The pass reverses a `CondTraverse` chain when the better scan endpoint is at the top. It reversed the hop list, then walked that list backwards again while rebuilding — so the hop placed directly on the new scan was the one *furthest* from it, with neither endpoint bound by anything below. The runtime can only answer that by enumerating every edge of the relationship type, once per input row.

The plan stayed *correct* (brute force finds the same rows), so it never showed up as a test failure — only as cost.

10k-node benchmark graph, 300 executions per query, `bench`'s rusage backend:

| query | before | after | | C engine |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `reversed 2hop chain` | 34,365,659 | **439,796** | 78x | 418,834 |
| `reversed chain mid filter` | 35,906,332 | **499,645** | 72x | 413,612 |
| `reverse 3hop` | 40,420,641 | **508,481** | 79x | 450,593 |
| `reverse 1hop` | 370,879 | 378,692 | — | 380,558 |
| `forward 2hop` | 445,173 | 448,374 | — | 409,717 |

Those were the worst two Rust/C ratios in the whole 317-query set (134x and 142x on query work); they now land at ~1.05x of C. p99 for `reversed 2hop chain` was 1.791 ms against C's 0.087 ms. It also fixes their **allocation**: 775,626 B → 2,263 B and 813,275 B → 2,016 B, i.e. down to the per-query floor ([measurement](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/pull/2491#issuecomment-5277173606)).

Dropping the second reversal alone is not enough: once the pattern branches — `(a)-->(b)-->(c), (b)-->(d)` — the hop leaving the branch point still has to run in storage direction, so `transposed` is not a property of the chain. Doing only that made the branching query return **0 rows instead of 2**. Hops are therefore ordered greedily, each oriented to start from an endpoint that is already bound, and the pass leaves the plan alone if no such order exists.

## 2 · The order was pattern order, not a cheap order

Greed

pullRequests.title: fix(bench): read jemalloc stats by column, not by whitespace
pullRequests.body:
## The bug

`jemalloc_totals` splits the `bins:`/`large:` rows of `MEMORY MALLOC-STATS` on whitespace. Those tables are fixed-width and right-aligned, and the `(#/sec)` rate fields are 8 characters wide — so a rate ≥ 10,000,000/sec fills its field exactly and leaves no space before the `nmalloc` next to it:

```text
nmalloc (#/sec)      ndalloc (#/sec)
    1379247  689623      1355704  677852     <- fine, 6-digit rates
21949879 10974939 21947904 10973952          <- fused, 8-digit rates
```

`line.split()` reads that `nmalloc` as one 16-digit number and shifts every later column left, so `ndalloc` picks up a fused value too. The cumulative total jumps ~7e16 bytes when a hot size class crosses 10M allocs/sec and drops back when it cools — and since `measure` reports **deltas** between two snapshots, that lands as per-query allocation in the petabytes, or negative when the fusion clears between snapshots.

## Not hypothetical

Three full 317-query runs on one host, each producing exactly 8 physically impossible rows, consistently:

| query | rep 1 | rep 2 | rep 3 | with this fix |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `MSF nodes yield` | 351,207,481,011,826 | 351,207,097,013,232 | 351,210,249,012,702 | **10,649,197** |
| `write 1m` | −39,655,479,199,115,760 | −39,656,013,599,155,096 | −39,656,194,399,073,920 | — |
| `write 100k` | 320,185,648,034,151 | 320,142,448,020,056 | 320,139,888,012,900 | — |
| `write 1k` | 3,182,176,503,580 | — | — | **485,442** |

`alloc_bytes` is the column the `benchmark-cov` CI comment uses **against the C engine** (callgrind can't measure that engine reliably), so this breaks the one vs-C reading CI has. It needs a full run to trigger — a handful of queries never gets a size class hot enough — which is why it survived.

## The fix

Slice each field by the character range of its own table's header. Overflow in a right-aligned field spills *left*, so a field read up to its own end column stays correct and only its left neighbour (a rate nothing here

| | instr/query |
|---|---:|
| full path | 232,289 |
| without slow_log + telemetry | 149,316 |
| → slow_log alone | ~300 |
| → **telemetry** | **~83,000** |
| …channel send + flusher wakeup + formatting + GIL | 49,154 |

| …replicating the XADD | 2,395 |

pullRequests.title: perf(runtime): answer a label predicate from the label matrix (1.77x)
pullRequests.body:
## What

`n:Label` reaches the runtime as a `hasLabels` call, answered via `Runtime::get_node_labels`, which per row:

1. builds an `OrderSet<LabelId>` from the label matrix,
2. applies pending label changes into it,
3. builds a **second** `OrderSet<Arc<String>>` of label *names*,

and then the predicate compares strings. Two allocations and a name comparison per row, to read what is one bit of the label matrix.

## Measured

Benchmark graph (10k `:Person` plus the `:Doc`/`:Geo` corpus, 15k nodes), 100 executions each, instructions per query:

| query | before | after | | C engine |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person RETURN count(n)` | 48,942,607 | **27,642,373** | 1.77x | 22,369,592 |
| `label predicate` (`… AND n.id < 5`) | 55,573,511 | **34,261,231** | 1.62x | 24,896,439 |

Per row that is 3.3k → 1.8k, against C's 1.5k; the ratio to C goes 2.19 → 1.24 and 2.23 → 1.38.

For contrast, the same scan filtering on a *property* — `MATCH (n) WHERE n.id < 5` — costs 1,987,320 here against 8,985,762 on C. Property access was never the problem; the label test was.

## How

`Runtime::node_has_label(id, name)` is the one place a label test is decided, and it decides it for every node the query can see, in the order `get_node_labels` uses: a node this query deleted answers from the labels captured at the delete, a label this query staged answers from `Pending::node_has_label` (a removal winning over an add, the precedence `update_node_labels` applies), and everything else is one bit of the committed label matrix. Nothing falls back, so a pending node gets the cheap path too, and `hasLabels` no longer carries a second copy that compares label *names* against a materialized `OrderSet`. `NodeByIndexScan`'s extra-label filter was a third copy of the same per-row test; it now runs through the same function.

Resolving the name is per-row too, so `Graph::get_label_id` no longer walks `node_labels`: a `node_labels_index` reverse map makes it O(1), mirroring what th

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): keep path multiplicity when fusing anonymous traversals
pullRequests.body:
fix #2470

## Summary

`MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)` returns **1** where it must return **2** when two distinct 2-hop paths connect the same pair of endpoints. The `fuse_anonymous_traverse` optimizer pass collapses the two hops into one fused `Conditional Traverse`, and the runtime evaluates a fused chain as a **boolean** matrix product — which records whether a destination is *reachable*, never how many paths reach it. Cypher relationship-isomorphism requires one row per distinct relationship pair.

The pass reasoned "the intermediate is anonymous and unreferenced, therefore invisible, therefore safe to collapse". The flaw is that **invisible is not irrelevant**: the intermediate still multiplies rows, and that multiplicity *is* the result-set cardinality feeding `count(*)` and every aggregate.

### Reproduction

```cypher
CREATE (a:A), (b1:B), (b2:B), (c:C),
       (a)-[:R]->(b1), (a)-[:R]->(b2), (b1)-[:R]->(c), (b2)-[:R]->(c)
```

| Query | Before | After | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c:C) RETURN count(*)`  | **1** | 2 | 2 |
| `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(m)-[:R]->(c:C) RETURN count(*)` | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| `MATCH p = (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c:C) RETURN count(*)` | 2 | 2 | 2 |

Only the anonymous-intermediate spelling was wrong — the three forms are semantically identical and now agree.

## Changes

- `graph/src/planner/optimizer/fuse_anonymous_traverse.rs`
  - New helper `feeds_existence_only`, which walks the ancestor chain from a candidate `CondTraverse`, passing through `CondTraverse` and `Filter` nodes, and returns true only when it reaches a `SemiApply`/`AntiSemiApply` **via child index 1**, or an `OrApplyMultiplexer` via **any child index >= 1**.
  - `can_fuse` now requires `feeds_existence_only`.
  - Module docs gained a "Why fusion is restricted to existence tests" section with the diamond counter-example.
- `tests/flow/test_traversal_construction.py` — new regression test.
- Plan-level uni

filter is pushed below `Optional` it lands on the scan branch, which produces no

Started as regression coverage for #2506 (`RESTORE <key> 0 <blob> REPLACE` of an indexed
graph's own `DUMP`, which SIGSEGVs the C engine in `Index_SetLanguage`). The new test then
found a **real bug on our side**: the same sequence aborts the Rust engine on any build with
debug assertions — the coverage and ASAN images — so this PR carries the fix too.

```
FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/graph_core.rs:97:5:
register_graph: name already registered; missing graph_free or placeholder swap
```

`RESTORE ... REPLACE` deserializes the payload *before* it deletes the value currently bound
to the key (deliberately — a corrupt payload must leave the existing key intact). So
`graph_rdb_load` registers the decoded graph while the graph it replaces is still registered
under the same name, which is exactly what `register_graph`'s invariant forbids.

## Changes

**Fix — `src/graph_core.rs`, `src/redis_type.rs`**

- New `register_decoded_graph`, used by the three `graph_rdb_load` registration sites, which
  displaces an existing registration without asserting.
- Displacing is safe there: Redis frees the replaced value moments later and `graph_free`
  unregisters by `data_ptr`, so it only ever removes entries pointing at the graph being
  freed — never the one the loader just installed. A query still holding the replaced graph
  sees `graph_is_registered` go false and aborts its write, which is the intended outcome for
  a key replaced underneath it.
- The strict invariant stays in force for every command path (`GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.COPY`,
  `GRAPH.RESTORE`, bulk insert, effects, constraints), which is where a duplicate registration
  really would mean a leaked Arc. The displaced-Arc background drop is factored into
  `drop_displaced_graph` and shared by both entry points.

**Test — `tests/flow/test_rdb_load.py`**

Extends the existing `testRdbLoad` class rather than adding a file — it is already the home of
the DUMP/RESTORE round-trip coverage:

- `test_restore_replac

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): enforce relationship uniqueness for anonymous edges
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

`MATCH (a)-[:R]-(b)-[:R]-(c)` on a graph holding a **single** `R` edge returned
rows (issue #2441). Cypher's relationship-uniqueness rule forbids binding the
same relationship twice inside one `MATCH`, so the correct answer is no rows.

The planner only listed **named** edges in `sibling_edges`, the list the runtime
uses for its uniqueness check, deliberately excluding anonymous `_anon*` edges
to match the C engine. Named patterns were therefore already correct
(`(a)-[r1:R]-(b)-[r2:R]-(c)` → 0 rows) while anonymous ones were not.

## Changes

- `graph/src/planner/mod.rs`: `sibling_edges` is now computed per relationship
  and includes anonymous edges. Siblings that cannot bind the same physical edge
  are left out — var-length/allShortestPaths patterns (they bind a path) and
  siblings whose relationship-type set cannot overlap. When nothing can collide
  the list stays empty, which keeps the runtime's batched/fused traversal fast
  paths eligible (e.g. `-[:R]->()-[:R2]->`).
- `graph/src/planner/optimizer/reduce_expand_into.rs`: `ir_references_variable`
  now inspects `UNWIND`/`FOREACH` source expressions and `CREATE`/`MERGE`
  patterns. Previously an edge alias was kept alive by accident because its own
  id always appeared in `sibling_edges`; once that list can legitimately be
  empty, queries such as `MATCH ()-[a]->() UNWIND a AS x RETURN id(x)` and
  `MATCH (p)-[e:knows]->() CREATE (:clone {t: TYPE(e)})` failed with
  "Variable not found". Both are covered by existing flow tests.
- `tests/flow/test_bidirectional_traversals.py`: new `test14_relationship_uniqueness`
  and `test15_relationship_uniqueness_disjoint_types`; `test13_multiple_bidirectional_edges`
  updated — it asserted the buggy result (`v1→v1`, `v2→v2`, `v3→v3` obtained by
  walking one edge back and forth).

  his single `act` edge for

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2524.

Bumps the pinned GraphBLAS from `v10.3.1` to `v10.5.0` and brings everything coupled to that pin back into agreement with it.

The pin was first cut against `v10.5.0` and now names the final release. That is a rename, not a rebuild: upstream tagged `v10.5.0` on the same commit as the beta (`ea79e35`, both lightweight tags), so the cloned sources, the headers behind the FFI bindings and the library version the vendored kernels declare are byte-identical to what the verification below was run on.

## PreJIT kernels — regenerated, and this was mandatory

Every one of the 218 vendored kernels declared `v[0]=10; v[1]=3; v[2]=1;` in its `_query` function. GraphBLAS rejects a PreJIT kernel whose version does not match the running library, so left alone they would have been ignored wholesale and every operation would have silently fallen back to a generic kernel — the exact regression PreJIT exists to prevent.

The new set is **224 kernels, all stamped 10.5.0**, harvested by `gen_prejit.sh` inside `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build`. Filenames are not comparable across the bump (the hashes gained a hex digit — `build__e83bbbbb` → `build__1fe83bbbbb`), so the sets were compared by op-shape family instead: **87 families before, the same 87 after**, nothing lost, including the harmonic-centrality HLL `dot4` kernels that `gen_prejit.sh`'s header calls out specifically.

## FFI bindings — were two releases stale

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/mod.rs` was generated against **10.0.2** ("Mar 20, 2025"), not 10.3.1. Regenerated against the installed 10.5.0 headers, preserving the hand-written prelude above the bindgen output.

- **1 symbol removed:** `GxB_GPU_ID`, unused here, superseded by `GxB_GPU_IDS`.
- **68 added:** almost entirely the new memory-arena constructors (`GxB_Matrix_new_arena`, `GxB_Monoid_new_arena_*`, `GxB_arena_init`, …), plus fork-safety hooks (`GxB_atfork_prepare`/`_parent`/`_child`) and lifecycle predicates.

Regeneration now requires `--opaque-type

pullRequests.title: fix: bare GRAPH.INFO, and C-parity for the run-time config surface
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2434.

## 1. Bare `GRAPH.INFO` returned an arity error

On the Rust engine a bare `GRAPH.INFO` returned `ERR wrong number of arguments for 'graph.INFO' command`. The C engine treats "no section given" as "all sections", so the node client's `db.info()` — which sends `GRAPH.INFO` with no section — fails against the Rust engine.

[src/commands/info.rs](src/commands/info.rs): default the three section flags to on when the argument list is empty, instead of returning `WrongArity`. Explicit section lists and the `ERR Unknown section: x` error are untouched, and the command's registered arity was already 1, so nothing changes at the module-registration level. Output for a bare call is now identical to `GRAPH.INFO RunningQueries WaitingQueries ObjectPool`, in that order — matching the C output quoted in the issue.

## 2. Three configs C sets at run-time, refused here

`CMD_INFO`, `MAX_INFO_QUERIES` and `DELAY_INDEXING` are all runtime-settable in C; `GRAPH.CONFIG SET` answered `This configuration parameter cannot be set at run-time` for each. Two of them were worse than read-only:

- `CMD_INFO` was never *read*. Telemetry streamed regardless, so even `CMD_INFO no` at load time did nothing.
- `MAX_INFO_QUERIES` ignored its load-time module argument too — it is not in the `redis_module!` config section and the manual arg loop never looked for it — so the telemetry stream was always trimmed at the 1000 default.

Changes:

- [src/config.rs](src/config.rs): `CONFIGURATION_CMD_INFO` moves from a GIL-guarded `bool` to an `AtomicBool` so the query hot path can read it off the main thread; `MAX_INFO_QUERIES_CAP` names the 1000 cap.
- [src/lib.rs](src/lib.rs): `CMD_INFO` and `DELAY_INDEXING` registered `DEFAULT` instead of `IMMUTABLE`, so `CONFIG SET graph.*` works too. Each shares one storage location with `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`, so the two surfaces cannot drift.
- [src/commands/config_cmd.rs](src/commands/config_cmd.rs): `CMD_INFO` and `DELAY_INDEXING` take `yes|no` (also `1/0/

pullRequests.title: feat(index): the tag and geo kinds, and the xfail ledger closes
pullRequests.body:
**Based on #2453** — review that first; the diff here is only this layer.

Adds the two index kinds that were missing beside the numeric one, so a Range column holds what a
RediSearch Range field holds: NUMERIC, TAG and GEO, co-resident, with a predicate routed by the
type of its operand. **All 17 xfail-ledger entries pass and the ledger is now empty.**

## Tag: interned, not encoded

The tuple tree keys on a `u64` and a string does not fit in one. Every scheme that squeezes it in —
an 8-byte prefix, a hash — answers `n.name = 'Bob'` with a *superset*, and that is not allowed here:
`utilize_index` drops the filter for a plain string equality (the plan is a bare `Node By Index
Scan`), so nothing downstream would reject the extra rows.

So the string is **interned**. A per-column dictionary gives each distinct string a dense id and the
tree holds `(tag id, doc)`. Equality is exact because the id is exact. Lexicographic order lives in
the dictionary rather than the key, so a range resolves in two steps — the dictionary names the ids
inside the window, the tree is scanned once per id.

The dictionary is **shared** (behind an `Arc`) and **append-only**, and both are load-bearing:

* Shared keeps `Clone` O(1), so the MVCC fork on `new_version()` is unchanged — and it is what makes
  the online build work. BASE is encoded off the write thread against the same numbering the live
  column uses, so the ids in BASE, DELTA and TOMB are the same ids and `install_base` merges raw
  tuples exactly as the numeric kind does. `EncodedTuples` never had to learn about strings.
* Append-only means an id, once handed out, means that string forever. Reclaiming one would corrupt
  any older snapshot still holding it. The cost is an entry per string the column has *ever* seen —
  released when the column is dropped. **This is the one deliberate memory trade in the PR.**

Mutating a shared dictionary from a version fork is safe because it is a *name table*, not index
content: an id an older

pullRequests.title: Bound expression tree height in the parser so deep nesting is rejected instead of crashing the server
pullRequests.body:
Deeply nested parenthesized arithmetic (`RETURN ((((1+1)+1)+1)…)`, ~1000 levels) crashed the engine with a raw SIGSEGV — the stack overflows before the panic handler can run, so one small query kills the server for every connected client with no diagnostic in the log.

The parser already had two nesting guards — `MAX_NESTING` for call recursion and `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` for constructs that open a level on the expression stack — but neither sees a construct that **wraps what it has already parsed**. Those shapes built arbitrarily tall trees that the binder, planner and evaluator then walked recursively:

```
RETURN ((1+1)+1)      -- parens that cannot collapse: an operator wraps each level
RETURN 1+(1+(1+…))
RETURN 1+1-1+1-1…     -- only alternating operators nest; same-operator runs flatten
RETURN 1 IS NULL IS NULL IS NULL…
RETURN 1<2<2<2…       -- each step nests another And
```

## Changes

- **`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs`, `graph/src/parser/macro.rs`** — every frame of the parser's expression stack now carries the height of the tree it has built so far. Wrapping an operand adds a level, folding a sub-expression into its parent lifts the parent above it, and the `((x))` collapse gives its level back.
- **`Parser::check_depth`** rejects at `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` (256, unchanged) *the moment* a height crosses it, not on the finished tree: every wrap copies the tree it wraps, so a post-hoc check would let a large query burn quadratic time first (a 20 000-level expression is now refused in ~12 ms instead of building for seconds).
- **`Parser::with_child_height`** carries heights out of the helpers that embed expressions in trees of their own (`parse_primary_expr`, `x[i]`, map projections), so nesting spread over several `parse_expr` calls is still counted as the one tree it becomes. The chained-comparison path measures its cloned middle operand with an iterative `tree_height` walk, which the clone already pays for.
- The existing descent-time `open`/`nested()` guards are untouch

pullRequests.title: fix(index): keep residual filter for i64::MIN index lookups
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

An indexed equality lookup on `i64::MIN` returned neighbouring values as
matches: on a graph where `karma` is indexed,
`MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.karma = -9223372036854775808` also returned nodes
holding `-9223372036854775807`. Ranges were skewed the same way —
`WHERE n.karma > -9223372036854775808` dropped those nodes.

Reported by query fuzzing through a double-negation oracle: the plain form and
`WHERE NOT (NOT (n.karma = ...))` disagreed. The double-negated form was the
correct one; it is planned as a label scan plus filter and never touches the
index.

## Changes

- `graph/src/index/mod.rs`: widen the mask in `int_loses_f64_precision` from
  `0x7FF0_0000_0000_0000` to `0xFFF0_0000_0000_0000`.

  Numeric index entries are stored as `f64`, so distinct `i64` values past 2^53
  share an index key; the optimizer compensates by keeping a residual `Filter`
  above the index scan whenever the literal is in that lossy range.
  `i64::MIN.unsigned_abs()` is `1 << 63`, whose only set bit sits above the old
  mask, so it was classified as lossless and the filter was dropped. The value
  round-trips through `f64` exactly, but everything up to `i64::MIN + 512` maps
  onto the same `f64` and leaked through. `i64::MIN` is the only value with this
  property, which is why the bug was so narrow. The same mask is used by the C
  implementation, so this is long-standing rather than a Rust regression
  (`edge-c` reproduces it identically).

- `tests/flow/test_index_scans.py`: `test_36_int_min_index_scan_retains_filter`
  asserts the filter is retained and checks equality at both ends of the `i64`
  range plus a `>` range query.

## Testing

- New test fails on `main` and passes with the fix:
  ```
  ❌ 'Project\n    Node By Index Scan | (n:K)' should contain 'Filter'
  ❌ [[-9223372036854775808], [-9223372036854775807], [-9223372036854775296]] == [[-9223372036854775808]]
  ❌ [[3]] == [[5]]
  ```

pullRequests.title: fix(telemetry): keep the flusher ahead of the load, stop hanging shutdown, and honour MAX_INFO_QUERIES 0
pullRequests.body:
Follow-up to #2493, from a post-merge review of it. Nine of the fourteen findings held up; each was reproduced first, fixed, then re-measured with the same repro. Two did not hold up and are answered at the bottom.

## Correctness

**The flusher could not keep up, and the queue had no bound.** Every iteration was `recv_timeout` (which returns immediately when a backlog exists) → `sleep(FLUSH_LINGER)` → drain at most `FLUSH_BATCH_MAX`, capping the flusher at 256 entries per 5ms — ~51k/s in theory, 36k measured — while `mpmc::unbounded_blocking` kept accepting at whatever rate the clients managed. 400,000 `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1"` at 140k ops/s (`redis-benchmark -c 16`):

| | drain lag after the load stopped | peak `used_memory` |
|---|---|---|
| before | 8.2s | 53.3MB |
| after | 0.3s | 4.4MB |

The linger is now skipped when a full batch is already queued — a backlog is the signal that there is nothing left to batch for — and the channel has a cap (`QUEUE_MAX`, four batches), past which entries are dropped and the flusher logs how many. That is what C does structurally: its per-graph queries log is a fixed-size circular buffer that overwrites its oldest entry.

The serial path this PR series exists to optimise is unchanged — median of 5 runs of `redis-benchmark -n 20000 -c 1`: **27,624 → 28,288 ops/s**, p50 0.031ms in both.

**`MAX_INFO_QUERIES 0` meant "never trim" rather than "keep nothing".** `if max_len > 0` skipped the trim, and 0 is accepted by both `GRAPH.CONFIG SET` and the module argument, while C passes it to `RedisModule_StreamTrimByLength` unconditionally. Repro: 2000 queries under `MAX_INFO_QUERIES 0` left all 2000 entries in the stream, with no setting left that could bound it. Now 0, covered by `test10_max_info_queries_zero_keeps_nothing`.

**Shutdown deadlocked whenever entries were in flight.** `shutdown_flusher_thread` joins the flusher from the main thread, which holds the module GIL for the whole shutdown event callback; the flusher woke on `Dis

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): anchor a variable-length traverse on an endpoint bound below the scan
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2561

`select_var_len_scan_node` only rewrote when the planner's own scan for `from`
was the traverse's child and nothing below it mattered — the leaf case #2491
addressed. When the other endpoint is already bound by an operator further down
(a `WITH`/`Project` barrier, or an `UNWIND` chain), the pass left the plan alone
and the scan on the free endpoint stayed:

```
Conditional Variable Length Traverse | (p)-[:E*0..INF]->(u)
    Node By Label Scan | (p:P)          <-- spurious
        Limit / Project / Filter
            Node By Index Scan | (u:P)
```

`CondVarLenTraverseOp` then took the non-reversed path and seeded its DFS with
every node carrying `from`'s label, once per input row.

## The change

Look one level deeper for the binding and, when it is provably there, **drop**
the scan instead of replacing it. `to` bound with `from` free is the shape the
runtime already handles:

```rust
let reversed = from_id.is_none() && to_id.is_some() && !bidirectional;
let dest_labels = if reversed { &rp.from.labels } else { &rp.to.labels };
```

`reversed` walks the relationship backwards from the single bound endpoint and
enforces `from`'s labels as its destination filter, so the label predicate the
scan carried is not lost — the new test asserts exactly that by adding a
non-`:P` node that reaches the same `u` and checking the unlabeled pattern
matches strictly more paths. No runtime change is needed.

`Argument(None)` is opaque about what it binds, so its presence anywhere below
leaves the plan alone.

## Measurements

Engine-internal time, median of 3, same host. Row counts identical across C,
pre-fix and post-fix in every case.

| chain-800, bound target | 1.47 | 98.61 | **0.74** | 0.50x | 134x |
