pullRequests.title: perf: call a scalar function once per batch when all its arguments are constant
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2714.

Sixth in the stack: #2686 → #2690 → #2691 → #2693 → this (#2685 has landed).

Fixes the worst instruction ratio in the benchmark — `split+trim+replace` at **2.83× C**.

## The cause

`VectorEval::eval_function` evaluated every scalar function once per row, even when each argument column was an `ExprColumn::Scalar` — one value already shared by the whole batch. So a constant subexpression cost exactly as much as a row-dependent one, and materialised a `Vec<Value>` of identical results on the way out.

The benchmark row is nothing but constants:

```cypher
UNWIND range(0, 99) AS i
RETURN count(split(replace(trim('  a,b,c  '), ',', ';'), ';'))
```

Marginal cost per row, each function measured against the same query with `count(1)` as the floor:

| function | instructions/row |
|---|---|
| `trim` | 813 |
| `toUpper` | 833 |
| `replace` | 1,107 |
| **`split`** | **3,578** |

`split` alone cost more than C's entire query (3,081/row). The implementation is not the problem — five allocations for three parts is reasonable — it was being called 100 times for one answer.

## Why fold in the evaluator rather than the planner

There is already a constant-folding pass in the optimizer, but it works through `GraphFn::pure_fn`, a `Runtime`-free form that only the temporal and map constructors provide. `trim`/`replace`/`split` have none, so it cannot reach them.

Folding here instead needs no new per-function plumbing and **composes**, which is the point: the literal is a `Scalar`, so `trim` returns one, so `replace` sees a `Scalar` and returns one, and `split` likewise. The chain collapses to three calls per batch from three per row. It also catches arguments that are scalar without being literals — a parameter, or anything upstream that folded.

## Measured

| row | before | after | | vs C before | vs C after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `split+trim+replace` | 871,972 | 227,062 | **3.84×** | 2.83× | **0.74×** |
| `UDF echo scalars` | 2,147,570 | 753,407 | **2.85×**

pullRequests.title: fix: register aof_rewrite for GRAPH_TYPE and GRAPHMETA_TYPE
pullRequests.body:
## Cause

`GRAPH_TYPE` and `GRAPHMETA_TYPE` never registered `aof_rewrite`. With `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes` (default) this is invisible: `BGREWRITEAOF` emits an RDB preamble and never calls it. With `no`, Redis calls `aof_rewrite` unconditionally per key of that type. A null callback dereferences a null pointer, segfaulting the rewrite child. Since `auto-aof-rewrite-percentage` keeps re-triggering a rewrite that can never succeed, the server never recovers.

## Fix

`graph_aof_rewrite` emits one `GRAPH.RESTORE` per key via `RedisModule_EmitAOF`, reusing the byte format `GRAPH.COPY` already replicates (`vec_save_graph` / `graph_restore`). Virtual keys are skipped: they only exist to split one graph's RDB image across multiple keys, and the primary key's `GRAPH.RESTORE` already reconstructs the whole graph. `graphmeta_aof_rewrite` is a no-op, for the same defensive reason `graphmeta_rdb_save` already exists — Rust never creates graphmeta keys, but a loaded C RDB could carry one.

Fork-safety matches `graph_rdb_save`: encoding bypasses the `parking_lot` `RwLock` via `data_ptr()`, since a thread holding the write lock at fork time is gone in the child and a normal lock acquisition would deadlock.

## Verification

Built and tested inside `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build` (clang-22):

- `cargo build` / `cargo build --release`: pass
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: pass
- `CXX=clang++ cargo clippy --all-targets`: pass, no warnings
- New flow test `test02_bgrewriteaof_survives_without_rdb_preamble` plus the existing `test01`: 2/2 pass

`test02` sets `aof-use-rdb-preamble no`, writes two nodes, runs `BGREWRITEAOF`, and checks `aof_last_bgrewrite_status == ok` (no crash). It then runs `DEBUG LOADAOF` and re-queries the graph to confirm the rewritten AOF actually reconstructs it, not just avoids crashing while producing an empty one.

Fixes #2710

pullRequests.title: ci: make PR CI fork-safe and gate main on a merge queue
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Fork PR CI has never worked in this repo, and nothing gates `main`. Both have the same root cause and one fix.

A `pull_request` raised from a fork gets a **read-only** `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so `docker push` of `rc-pr-<N>` is denied and every job consuming that tag skips. The usual workaround — `pull_request_target` behind an approval label — hands a writable token to fork-authored code and then needs a lot of gating to contain it.

A merge queue gets that token natively. A `merge_group` run executes on `gh-readonly-queue/<base>/pr-N-<sha>`, a branch in **this** repo, so `packages: write` is available with no `pull_request_target` anywhere. It also tests the merge candidate, so what is tested is what lands.

But the queue is not what fixes fork CI. **PR CI doesn't need an image at all** — and the image-free shape already existed in `rust-push.yml`, running on every push to a trunk for months. Moving it to `pull_request` is what unblocks contributors.

Closes #2632. Unblocks #2396, which has been stuck since it opened.

## Three tiers

| Tier | Event | What it does | Registry |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PR CI** | `pull_request` | lint, unit + e2e + TCK, the flow matrix, coverage — all against a `.so` shipped as a job artifact | none |
| **Merge queue** | `merge_group` | builds the release RC image, runs the image-based suites against it, on the commit that will land | writes |
| **Post-merge** | `push` | promotion only | writes |

## Measured, not assumed

Sized off `rust-pr.yml` run `33478753375` (green, 484 jobs) and `rust-push.yml` run `33480321390` (246 jobs):

- One full pipeline is **956 runner-minutes** and peaks at **239 of the account's 500** concurrent jobs. That is what pins merge-queue build concurrency at 1.
- 96% of the cost is the flow matrix. The RC image build itself — the thing forks cannot do — is 9 jobs and 10 minutes.
- `rust-push.yml` spends **505 runner-minutes** re-testing a tree the PR just tested. 248 of those go in this PR.

pullRequests.title: refactor(effects/v3): apply models the id space instead of guessing at it
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2739

Stacked on #2570 — **base is `feat/effects-v3`, not `main`.** One commit.

## The problem

Two ad-hoc checks in the apply path stood in for a question the graph cannot
answer: a boundary frozen at buffer entry, and a running set of the ids the
buffer had created so far. Neither is the question. Whether the ids a batch
hands the graph describe a *possible id space* is, and nothing could ask it.

`Graph` tracks node liveness with `node_count` and `deleted_nodes` and no live
set, so the only boundary it can offer is `node_count + deleted_nodes.len()`.
That is the boundary *if the id space is dense*, and `max_node_id` is the same
arithmetic — so an assertion written in terms of them checks one derivation of
the state against another derivation of the same state, and passes on a graph
that is already wrong.

Density holds between batches, not within one. Records are ingested grouped by
shape rather than ordered by id, so a create of 500..600 may precede one of
0..500; between them the graph holds 100 live nodes whose highest id is 599 and
reports its boundary as 100.

## What this adds

`graph::id_space::NodeIdSpace` holds the boundary as it stood before a batch and
every id at or above it the batch has ingested, which states the invariant
directly:

```
ingested == [ entry_bound, entry_bound + ingested.len() )
```

It lives beside the graph rather than in the effects module because that is what
it is about — nothing in it knows about replication, buffers or a peer engine.
It is passed to `create_nodes` and `delete_nodes`, which maintain and consult it
themselves:

```rust
pub fn create_nodes(&mut self, nodes: &RoaringTreemap, id_space: Option<&mut NodeIdSpace>)
pub fn delete_nodes(&mut self, nodes, remove_docs, id_space: Option<&NodeIdSpace>)
```

An argument rather than state on `Graph`, so a caller cannot silently forget to
start a batch, and `None` is visible at the call site. `create_nodes` reads the
entry boundary off the space it is handed, so its `f

pullRequests.title: feat(effects): the v3 wire codec
pullRequests.body:
The effects v3 wire format, with no graph in it. Bytes in, `Record` out, and back — nothing here knows what a node is, only what one looks like on a wire.

Split out of #2570, which was 15k lines and covered the codec, the emitter and the apply path together. This is the wire half; #2570 is now the other half and is stacked on this.

## Why this is a unit

`grep -E '\bGraph\b|\bPending\b'` over `graph/src/effects/` returns **doc comments only**. That is what makes the format reviewable against `docs/effects-v3.md` on its own, and testable byte-for-byte without a database. It is also the only part of the effects work the C implementation needs — C has to match these bytes and nothing else in here.

The module doc has claimed this since it was written. It was not true until now: `v3/mod.rs` said "this module is the codec only, deliberately free of `Pending` and `Graph`" twelve lines above `pub mod apply`.

## What is in it

    reader.rs        a bounds-checked cursor; every read is checked
    writer.rs        the EffectWrite sink
    error.rs         DecodeError
    mod.rs           EffectEncode<V> / EffectDecode<V> / EffectDecodeSized<V>
    v3/value.rs      the SIValue codec — C's type bitmask, not our ordinals
    v3/blocks.rs     RelType, LabelSet, AttrIds, AttrValues
    v3/id_list.rs    the id block: segments, the encoding ladder, the cost model
    v3/records.rs    the records, and reading a whole payload
    v3/fixtures.rs   the conformance corpus and its generator

## It carries its own verification

Merging a codec before its callers is only defensible if the codec is proven, so:

- **~2,900 lines of unit tests**, including byte-pinning assertions at all four id widths. A round trip cannot detect a byte swap — the assertion is symmetric in the bug — and with one deliberately planted, **41 of 42 `id_list` tests passed**. Only the new byte-level assertion caught it.

pullRequests.title: perf: size a scan's first batch to the downstream LIMIT
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2790.

## What

A leaf scan packed a full `BATCH_SIZE` (1024) batch regardless of a downstream
`LIMIT`, so `... LIMIT 10` did roughly 100x the work it needed and discarded the
rest. This sizes the scan's first batch to the downstream `Skip`+`Limit` budget.

The tell was a step function at the batch boundary rather than a curve in the
limit — 10k `:Person` + a 10k `:KNOWS` ring, instructions/query:

| query | instructions |
|---|---:|
| `scan LIMIT 10` | 702,890 |
| `scan LIMIT 1000` | 1,178,868 |
| `scan LIMIT 1024` | 1,188,376 |
| `scan LIMIT 2048` | 2,245,072 |

1.7x more for 100x the rows, then exactly 2x once the limit crosses 1024.

## Why it is a small change

Almost all of the machinery was already there and pointed at this exact case:

- `BatchedResultEmitter::set_pack_ceiling` / `apply_record_cap` already existed,
  and the doc comment already said "an operator fed by a downstream
  `Skip`/`Limit` lowers it ... so a capped query produces a small first batch" —
  but only `UNWIND` ever called it.
- `Runtime::record_cap` already walked `Project`/`Skip`/`CondTraverse`/
  `ExpandInto` to find the budget, and already stopped at row-reducing barriers
  such as `Filter`.

The scan simply never asked for it. This wires it up.

## The one new idea: the budget is a hint, not a bound

At a leaf scan the budget cannot be treated as a bound on the operator's own
output, because something between the scan and the `Limit` may discard rows. A
ceiling pinned at the limit is then a losing bet, and an unbounded one.

Measured, on 100,000 nodes where only the last 200 have an outgoing edge, with
`MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN id(b) LIMIT n`:

| | ceiling pinned | ceiling grows (this PR) |

| `LIMIT 1` | 8,433,461,433 | 91,466,726 |
| `LIMIT 10` | 998,926,139 | 91,442,059 |
| no `LIMIT` | 90,826,764 | 90,793,233 |

Pinning would have been a **92x regression** on `LIMIT 1`. So
`apply_hinted_record_cap` doubles the ceiling back to `BATCH_SIZE` after every

Follow-up to #2757, which wired the downstream row budget into the
label/all-node scan only. The index scans use the same `BatchedResultEmitter`
and had the same defect, so this applies the same hinted (growing) ceiling to
`NodeByIndexScan`, `EdgeByIndexScan` and `NodeByLabelAndIdScan`.

**Stacked on #2757 — review and merge that one first.**

Same step-function signature, on an index-backed plan
(`MATCH (a:Person) WHERE a.id >= 0 RETURN id(a) LIMIT n`, index on
`:Person(id)`):

| query | instructions |
|---|---:|
| `index scan LIMIT 1` | 1,286,488 |
| `index scan LIMIT 1000` | 1,738,712 |
| `index scan LIMIT 1024` | 1,732,327 |

I had assumed the ~1.1M floor on `LIMIT 1` was fixed index-query setup cost.
It was not — `get_indexed_nodes` is already a lazy iterator, and that 1.1M was
batch packing. Hence the win is larger here than for the plain scan.

## Results

| query | before | after | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

pullRequests.title: Fix bundled Browser startup in the Rust runtime image
pullRequests.body:
`BROWSER=1` never brings up the Browser in `falkordb/falkordb:edge-rs`: the entrypoint dies with `su-exec: not found`, and starting node manually fails with `libatomic.so.1: cannot open shared object file`.

The `full` stage copies `/app` and `docker-entrypoint.sh` out of the Alpine-based `falkordb-browser` image into the aggressively trimmed `debian:trixie-slim` server image, but never provides the userland those artifacts assume:

- **`su-exec`** — an Alpine tool with no Debian package. The entrypoint uses it both for its writability probe and to drop privileges, so its absence is what actually produces the misleading `Data directory /app/.data is not writable for nextjs (uid=1001)` and `exit 1`.
- **`libatomic.so.1` / `libstdc++.so.6`** — `node` from `node:26-bookworm-slim` links both; neither is in `debian:trixie-slim`. The C image escapes this with `node:24` on the `redis` base.
- **`nextjs`/`nodejs` uid/gid 1001** — the `server` stage purges `passwd`/`login` for CVE trim, so the account the browser runs as never existed, and the entrypoint's hardcoded `/app/.data` was missing.

## Changes (`build/runtime/Dockerfile` only)

- **`server` stage**: create `nodejs`/`nextjs` (1001) next to the `redis` user — the last point where `useradd`/`groupadd` still exist before `passwd` is purged.
- **`full` stage**: install `gosu`, `libatomic1`, `libstdc++6`; symlink `gosu` under the expected `su-exec` name; `COPY --chown=nextjs:nodejs` the browser tree; pre-create `/app/.data` owned by `nextjs`.
- **Build-time guard**: `su-exec nextjs:nodejs node --version` fails the build if the privilege drop or node's shared libs regress again.

```dockerfile
RUN set -eux; \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gosu libatomic1 libstdc++6; \
    ln -sf "$(command -v gosu)" /usr/local/bin/su-exec; \
    ...
COPY --from=browser --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app ${FALKORDB_BROWSER_PATH}
RUN mkdir -p /app/.data && chown -R nextjs:nodejs /app/.data && \
    su-exec nextjs:nodejs node --vers

pullRequests.body:
## Summary

`AggregateOp` has a columnar path and a per-row fallback, and `analyze()` chooses between them. A grouping key was only accepted as a bare variable or `n.prop`; anything else returned `None` — and `None` doesn't just deoptimize *that key*, it abandons the **whole operator**. The bulk aggregate-input reads and the columnar accumulate loop go down with it, and the operator rebuilds an owned `Row` per input row, re-walking every key and every aggregate tree scalar-wise.

Aggregate **inputs** already had `AggInputKind::Computed`, which evaluates an arbitrary tree a column at a time through `VectorEval`. The doc comment on that variant already spells out this exact argument. Keys just never got the same treatment — so `WITH n.id % 100 AS bucket, count(*)`, ordinary Cypher, was the common shape paying the slowest path.

This routes computed keys through that same evaluator.

## Changes

- `KeyExprKind::Computed(QueryExpr<Variable>)` — new variant mirroring `AggInputKind::Computed`.
- `analyze()` — key arms fall through to `Computed` instead of returning `None`. A key whose subtree contains an aggregate still falls back, for the same reason `analyze_agg_tree` refuses one in an aggregate input. `n.prop` where the child isn't a variable now routes to `Computed` rather than bailing.
- `extract_key_columns()` — a `Computed` arm calling `VectorEval::eval_values`.

pullRequests.title: perf: let an unlabelled point lookup use an index
pullRequests.body:
## What

`MATCH (n) WHERE n.p = $v` could not use an index **at all**. `utilize_index`
only rewrites `NodeByLabelScan`, so an unlabelled pattern degraded to an
all-node scan plus a per-node property fetch:

| same predicate, same index | instructions |
|---|---:|
| `MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n.id = 5000` | 371,140 |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n.id = 5000` | 1,857,542 |

A 5x penalty for omitting a label that, in these graphs, every node carries
anyway.

## Why the obvious fix is wrong

Borrowing *any* label's index for an unlabelled pattern is not merely narrow, it
is **incorrect**: a node can carry `p` without carrying the label, and answering
from that label's index silently drops it. That is why this was left as a design
note rather than patched.

The rewrite *is* valid under one condition: some label is carried by **every**
live node, in which case `MATCH (n)` and `MATCH (n:L)` select the same set, and
borrowing `L` is semantics-preserving by construction.

`Graph::universal_label` looks for such a label, and the check is proof rather
than a heuristic:

- each label matrix is **diagonal**, so a node contributes at most one entry;
  therefore `nvals == node_count` cannot be reached by two labels splitting the
  graph between them;
- `delete_nodes` clears a deleted node's label entries, so a stale entry cannot
  inflate the count into a false positive;
- it is **O(number of labels)** — `nvals` is O(1) per label once pending work is
  applied — so it costs nothing at plan time.

Once a universal label is found, the label is injected into the pattern and the
*existing* index machinery does the rest unchanged: label reordering, the
`extra_labels` post-verification, range-conjunct merging, inline `{attr: value}`
attributes. There is no new operator and no new index type.

## The part that needed real care: a cached plan can outlive its premise

Universality is a property of the **data**, but plans are cached against
`schema_version`, and `CREATE ({p: 1})` does not bump that. So

The failure is coverage-specific, so a release build shows nothing. With

pullRequests.body:
Fixes #1279.

### Root cause

`CREATE p=(n) RETURN p` binds `p` as `Type::Path` in the binder
(`binder.rs:1293`), so the variable resolves — but nothing ever builds the
value, which is why the result comes back as a path containing NULL rather
than a valid path. That matches what @gkorland observed on `edge` in the
2026-08-17 comment: the hard error went away, but the result is malformed.

The gap is in `Planner::plan_clause`. The MERGE branch already wraps its
pattern when it declares named paths:

```rust
if paths.is_empty() { merge } else { tree!(IR::PathBuilder(paths.to_vec()), merge) }
```

The CREATE branch returned `tree!(IR::Create(...))` unconditionally, so no
`PathBuilder` ran over the created entities and the path column was never
written.

### Fix

Wrap CREATE the same way MERGE is wrapped. `PathBuilderOp` reads the
component variable columns out of the batch and writes `Value::Path` back to
`path.var.id`, so it works over `Create`'s output exactly as it does over
`Merge`'s — no changes needed to the operator itself.

The paths are captured *before* `self.visited` is updated: `filter_visited`
drops any path whose var is already visited, and the loop below marks this
clause's own variables.

### Verification — please read

- `cargo check -p graph` passes cleanly with this change.
- **I was not able to verify the runtime behaviour.** Building the native
  dependency chain locally (GraphBLAS + LAGraph + the RediSearch submodule)
  wasn't feasible on this machine, so `cargo test` cannot link and I could
  not run the query against a live server.

So this is a compile-checked fix derived from reading the planner, not a
behaviourally-tested one. I did not add a regression test for the same
reason — I would not have been able to run it. If the approach looks right,
`CREATE p=(n) RETURN p` returning a single-element path is the assertion to
add, and I am happy to write it.

I would rather flag that plainly than let it look more verified than it is,
given how man

Fixes #2769

## Reproduction

A single query kills the entire `redis-server` process on the Rust engine (`edge-rs`):

```
GRAPH.QUERY dg "CREATE (a:A)-[r:R]->(b:B) DELETE r SET a.d = outdegree(a) RETURN a.d"
```

```
# <module> FalkorDB panic: panicked at graph/src/graph/graph.rs:2734:9:
relationship 0 not found
  3: falkordb::module_init::graph_init::{closure#0} at src/module_init.rs:150:13
```

The panic hook at `src/module_init.rs:142-154` calls `std::process::exit(1)`, so this is a remote DoS from one query, not just a failed query. Still reproducible on `origin/main` at the time of writing.

## Root cause

`Pending::deleted_relationships` mixes two populations:

1. edges that exist in the committed graph, and
2. edges created earlier in the **same** query and then deleted by it (`ops/delete.rs` → `Pending::deleted_relationship`).

The type lookup on the next line, `Graph::get_relationship_type_id`, has the same shape (`.expect("relationship must have a type in type_matrix")`).

It keys `(node, type)` and `(node, all types)` buckets holding the created and deleted counts, so a lookup is one hash probe per requested type and never touches an unresolvable edge.

- **Pending-created edges are resolved from pending, never from the graph.** This is load-bearing: relationship ids are recycled, so a reserved id can read as present in the committed graph while its pending create is still live. ## Reproduction

A single synchronous `SAVE` permanently destroyed any graph whose key name started with `__placeholder` or `__vkey_placeholder`, with no error to the client:

```

EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"                                --> 1
BGSAVE                                                       -- harmless
EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"                                --> 1
SAVE                                                         --> OK
EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"                                --> 0   <-- destroyed
GRAPH.QUERY "__placeholder_mydata" "MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)" --> 0

if name.starts_with("__placeholder") || name.starts_with("__vkey_placeholder") {
    stale_keys.push(key_name);   // deleted below

The only evidence used was a prefix the client is free to choose, so a real user graph was indistinguishable from a placeholder the module had created itself.

Placeholder-ness is now a structural property rather than a name-derived guess.

- `ThreadedGraph` carries a `placeholder` flag, set only by the new `ThreadedGraph::new_placeholder` constructor.

pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2777

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY lb "CREATE (:L {v:1})"
GRAPH.QUERY lb "MATCH (n:L) REMOVE n:L SET n:L RETURN labels(n)"
-- []   <-- wrong, the last clause asked for :L
GRAPH.QUERY lb "MATCH (n:L) RETURN count(n)"
-- 0    <-- node is now unreachable by label
GRAPH.QUERY lb "MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)"
-- 1    <-- node survives, but has lost its label permanently
```

This is silent data loss: the label is gone for good, and every label scan and index scan on `:L` stops seeing the node. It is also a **constraint bypass** — see below.

## Root cause

`Pending` stages label adds in `set_labels` and label removals in `remove_labels`, and both appliers — `update_node_labels` and `commit` — apply the adds first and the removals second.

The two mutators were asymmetric:

- `remove_node_labels` cancelled a previously staged add (it stripped the label from `set_labels` as well as recording the removal).
- `set_node_labels` / `set_nodes_labels` did **not** cancel a previously staged removal.

So after `REMOVE n:L SET n:L` the label sat in *both* sets, the removal ran last, and the add was silently discarded. The "removal wins" tie-break was even documented on `node_has_label`, `update_node_labels` and `constraint_node_has_label` as if it were intended.

`remove.rs` only stages a removal for labels the node actually has, which is why the existing `test_30_mix_add_and_remove_same_labels` did not catch this — it runs `REMOVE n:L SET n:L` against an *unlabelled* node, so nothing is ever staged in `remove_labels`.

## Fix

Make the two mutators symmetric: staging an add now strips that label from `remove_labels`, exactly mirroring what staging a removal already did for `set_labels`. The two sets are now **disjoint per node**, which is a real invariant rather than a tie-break, and makes last-writer-wins work in both directions.

Reordering `commit` to apply removals before adds was deliberately *not* chosen — that only flips which direction is broken (`SET n:L REMOVE n

pullRequests.title: Fix Value Hash Join matching join keys that contain NULL
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2775

## The defect

Cypher `=` is three-valued: `[1, null] = [1, null]` is NULL, not TRUE, so it must not produce a row. The `Value Hash Join` operator matched such keys anyway, so an optimised plan returned rows that the semantically identical unoptimised plan correctly rejected — two plans, same data, different answers.

```
GRAPH.QUERY nj "CREATE (:A {v:1}), (:B {v:1})"
GRAPH.QUERY nj "MATCH (a:A), (b:B) WHERE [a.v, a.w] = [b.v, b.w] RETURN a.v, b.v"
```

`a.w`/`b.w` are absent, hence NULL. `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` confirms the plan:

```
1) "Project"
2) "    Value Hash Join"
3) "        Node By Label Scan | (a:A)"
4) "        Node By Label Scan | (b:B)"
```

Before this change that returned **1 row**. Putting a `WITH a, b` barrier between the `MATCH` and the `WHERE` keeps the identical predicate as a `Filter` over a `Cartesian Product`, and that returned **0 rows** — the correct answer. After this change both return 0 rows.

## Root cause

`graph/src/runtime/ops/value_hash_join.rs` compared join keys with plain `PartialEq`:

```rust
bucket.iter().find(|(k, _)| k == key)
```

`Value`'s `PartialEq` is `compare_value(..).0 == Ordering::Equal` — it keeps the `Ordering` and throws the `DisjointOrNull` flag away. But `compare_list` reports `(Ordering::Equal, DisjointOrNull::ComparedNull)` for `[1, null]` vs `[1, null]`: *"equal as far as the non-NULL elements go, but the answer is UNKNOWN"*. Discarding that flag collapses UNKNOWN into TRUE, which is exactly the bug.

## The fix

Keep the flag. `keys_match` calls the same `compare_value` and requires `Ordering::Equal` **and** `DisjointOrNull::None`, so an inconclusive comparison is not a match:

```rust
fn keys_match(a: &Value, b: &Value) -> bool {
    let (ordering, disjoint_or_null) = a.compare_value(b);
    ordering == Ordering::Equal && matches!(disjoint_or_null, DisjointOrNull::None)
}
```

That replaces `==` at the two places join keys are compared — the probe-side bucket scan in `fill_matches`, and build-side buc

pullRequests.title: fix(graph): allocate ids against the set the caller holds, not a count of it
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2796

The id allocator kept a **count** of outstanding reservations and used it as a
*position in the recycle bin*. A count cannot tell a reserved id that came from
the bin from one allocated fresh, and after a cancelled reservation it describes
neither — so the next id can land on top of a node an earlier clause already
made. `CREATE (a), (b), (c) DELETE b CREATE (d), (e)` asks for four nodes and
leaves three, `c` and `d` fused onto one id, with no error raised. The
relationship allocator has the same shape and the same bug, and that one also
diverges a replica. Full repro and mechanism in #2796.

## How often this bites

Not a corner case. Seeded sequences of ordinary creates, pending
create-then-deletes and committed deletes, checking after every step that no two
live entities share an id, collide in **23 of 25 trials within eight steps**
against the allocator before this change, and in 0 of 25 after. A wider run —
2,880 steps over four seeds — is 0 collisions here against 30 and 27 on two seeds
of `origin/main`.

Most of them are on **relationships**, not nodes: `[1, 1]` for two edges returned
under one id, `[0, 2, 2]`, `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 6]`. The three hand-written tests
below were written from the mechanism and are all node-shaped, which is why the
fuzz is here too.

## The fix

The allocator now takes the caller's outstanding **set** instead of a count, and
the arithmetic is stated on sets rather than on ranks:

```rust
let free = pool - held;
out.extend(free.iter().take(count as usize));
```

Reserving does not remove an id from the bin — `max_node_id`, `is_node_deleted`
and the id boundary are all derived from the bin and would go wrong
mid-transaction if it did — so "in the bin" does not mean "free", and the
difference is what does.

`Graph` keeps no reservation state at all, so `new_version` has nothing to
assert about it and a rolled-back write nothing to unwind. `reserve_node` /
`reserve_relationship` — the singular forms, which had no callers

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2798

The shared contract every layer above this one codes against. It is separate so
that the decoder and the encoder could be built from the spec without either
reading the other's source — the split that let a third-party conformance corpus
arbitrate between them instead of one implementation defining correctness for the
other.

4 files, 400 lines.

* `src/effects/effects_v3.{c,h}` — opcodes, the five block kinds, the record
  structures, the decode/apply seam, and the distinction between a record this
  build has not implemented and one that is corrupt.
* `src/effects/effects.{c,h}` — `EFFECTS_VERSION`, the highest version this build
  will **read**, separated from `EFFECTS_VERSION_EMIT`, the version it **writes**.
  Without that split, decode cannot land before the switch is thrown, and both the
  decoder and the encoder need it.

**This changes no behaviour.** Nothing here reads or writes a byte and there is no
new call site.

**Readiness flags.** `EFFECTS_V3_DECODE_READY` and `EFFECTS_V3_ENCODE_READY` are
declared here and defined nowhere in this PR, deliberately: a readiness flag is a
claim about what will *link*, so it belongs in the commit that makes it true. Each
is defined by its own layer.

**Out of scope, on purpose:** the v2 reader's missing bounds checks — 22
`fread_assert` calls in `effects_apply.c`, whose `ASSERT` is empty when `RG_DEBUG`
is off. That is separate work on its own branch.

pullRequests.title: effects v3 in C: decode and apply, so a C replica can follow a Rust master
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2799

The milestone of the C side: a C replica under a Rust master stays in sync through
effects rather than falling back to a full resync. Decode comes before encode
because this is the direction that unblocks migration.

* `src/effects/effects_wire.{c,h}` — `fread_checked`, `fstream_remaining`,
  `ReadWireString`. A wire length is validated before it reaches an allocator or
  sizes a stack array.
* `src/value.c` — `bool SIValue_FromBinary` with an out parameter, so the codec
  reports failure instead of asserting; the array/map/vector decoders follow.
* `src/effects/effects_v3_decode.c` — the reader. Every read is bounds-checked;
  there is not one raw `fread` in the file.
* `src/effects/effects_v3_apply.c` — apply for all 14 records, DDL included.
* Two pre-existing defects fixed on the way: `graphcontext.c` returned a schema for
  an out-of-range id, and `update_node_labels.c` read a label id through `GrB_get`
  into a pointer.

**How it is checked.** Against the conformance corpus — `.hex`/`.json` pairs
written by neither the decoder's author nor the encoder's — and end to end by a
Rust master with a C replica, including the RDB transcode. The corpus lives on
`origin/effects-v3-corpus`, deliberately outside this PR; mount it to reproduce.

## Known gap — this PR should not merge until it is closed

`effects_v3_apply.c` creates the entity locally and then checks the master's id
matches. C pops its freelist most-recently-freed; Rust takes the smallest. So after
any delete the ids differ, the check fails, and the pair falls back to a full
resync — permanently, once per delete-then-create cycle, and every state-only
comparison calls that green because a resync does make the two sides agree.

Apply has to accept the master's id. `DataBlock_AllocateItemOutOfOrder` is the
obvious tool and is unsafe here as written: it does not remove the id from
`deletedIdx`, so the id is handed out a second time.

**This PR does not change what any C node puts on the wire.**

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2800

The bytes and nothing else: given a set of effects, produce a v3 payload identical
to the one the Rust encoder produces from the same effects. No call sites, no
config, nothing that changes what a running node emits. Separating the bytes from
the wiring is what makes byte-identity testable in unit tests rather than only
against a live pair.

* `effects_v3_encode.c` — records and shape blocks
* `effects_v3_group.c` — grouping effects into records
* `effects_v3_id_list.c` — `IdList` as segments of ranges, with the per-variant
  encoding choice
* `effects_v3_run_cost.c` — choosing the cheaper of two encodings
* `effects_bytes.{c,h}` — a growable buffer, so the encoder does not write through
  `FILE *`

**How it is checked.** C and Rust produce byte-identical v3 payloads across five
data shapes, four index shapes and multibyte strings, confirmed against three
separate Rust revisions. The corpus round trip — decode, re-encode, compare byte
for byte — passes on 38 of 39 fixtures, and runs from `origin/effects-v3-corpus`
rather than from this PR.

## `test_effects_v3_roaring.c`, and the guard rail it needs

An Ascending segment carries a roaring64 bitmap verbatim, so the two engines agree
on that segment only if the two roaring implementations serialize identically. This
suite pins C's vendored CRoaring 4.5.1 against the Rust `roaring` crate on 11
shapes and both construction paths.

**Its expected bytes are the Rust crate's output.** If a future failure is "fixed"
by re-capturing them from CRoaring, the test silently becomes CRoaring against
itself and pins nothing — a self-check wearing a cross-check's clothes. The
provenance is a comment at the top of the file and must stay there.

Verified to bite: flipping one byte of one Rust-captured constant fails exactly
`addRangePath` and `optimizeNormative`, 2 of 7, with the other five green — scoped
to the constant rather than knocking the suite over.

**The encoder is not reachable from any command in this PR.**

pullRequests.title: effects v3 in C: emitting v3 on the wire
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2801

The switch. Effects reach the encoder, `EFFECTS_VERSION` becomes settable at run
time, and the four DDL effects route through v3 instead of being dropped.

* `src/effects/effects.c` — the emit path; effects accumulate and are encoded once
  per transaction rather than one at a time
* `src/configuration/config.c` — `EFFECTS_VERSION` as a run-time config
* `create_index_effect.c`, `create_constraint_effect.c` and the two drops route
  through v3
* `proc_fulltext_create_index.c` and `index_fulltext_create.c` — fulltext index
  creation states the options it was given, so the effect can carry them
* `tests/flow/test_effects_v3_emit.py`

## Two things to look at first

**v2's bytes do not move.** The fulltext change had to state options for v3 without
changing what v2 emits, which is why it carries two maps. v2's payload md5 is
unchanged at `f861384d139d57ebca90eaf81049b10c` across the whole stack.

**There is no fallback to replaying the query verbatim.** An effect that cannot be
encoded is a bug, not a case to be handled. Removing the fallback turned one
silently passing test into three honest failures, all since fixed.

## One field that is inert here

`records->flags` carries the payload's flags byte, but the decoder refuses a
compressed payload at `effects_v3_decode.c:1258`, so bit 0 is always clear in this
PR. Ownership of that bit — masked out of the buffer's flags and set only by the
compression step — lands in the compression PR, where re-encoding a
decoded-compressed payload is actually reachable.

**`EFFECTS_VERSION_EMIT` still defaults to 2.** Turning v3 on by default is a
separate change.

pullRequests.title: effects v3 in C: compression
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2802

C vendors zstd so a v3 payload can be compressed on the way out and inflated on
the way in, matching what the Rust side already does. **Off by default** —
`EFFECTS_COMPRESSION` is 0 unless set.

11 commits: 50,409 lines of vendored zstd 1.5.7, 809 lines of our own source, 686
lines of tests.

* `src/util/zstd/` — the amalgamation, pristine headers, a generated symbol list,
  `regenerate.sh` and `PROVENANCE.md`. `regenerate.sh` reproduces the checked-in
  files byte for byte and **fails** if any global survives unprefixed.
* `src/util/crc32.{c,h}` — checksum over the **plaintext**, so it survives two
  encoders framing the same input differently.
* `src/effects/effects_compress.{c,h}`, the `EFFECTS_COMPRESSION` config, and hooks
  on both the write and read paths.
* A sweep of every truncation and single-byte corruption of a compressed payload,
  and a compressed master-to-replica round trip.

## Why a vendored copy rather than GraphBLAS's

`deps/GraphBLAS/Source/zstd_wrapper/GB_zstd.c:18` defines `ZSTD_malloc` as
GraphBLAS's own allocator. Calling `GB_ZSTD_compress` would put every effects
compression buffer inside GraphBLAS's memory accounting, permanently. **That
survives any symbol fix**, which is why it is the argument rather than the symbol
collisions.

The collisions are the secondary reason and are worth stating because the obvious
audit gets them wrong: the rename has **five** gaps, not one, and three of them do
not contain the string "zstd" (`FSE_isError`, `HUF_isError`, `g_debuglevel`), so a
`grep zstd` returns one symbol and looks complete.

## The compressed bit belongs to the compression step

`_WriteHeader` masks `EFFECTS_V3_FLAG_COMPRESSED` out of the buffer's flags and
`EffectsV3_MaybeCompress` is the only thing that sets it.

Without that, re-encoding a payload that arrived compressed writes a header
declaring **compressed** over a **plaintext** body — the decoder having already
inflated it — and the double-compression guard then corre

pullRequests.title: test(cow_btree): eliminate flaky snapshot test failure under thread contention (closes #2795)
pullRequests.body:
## Problem
In `snapshot_is_isolated_from_a_concurrent_writer`, the reader thread looped on `while !done_reader.load(Ordering::Relaxed)`. Under high thread contention (e.g. `--test-threads=16`), the main writer thread could complete all its mutations and set `done = true` before the OS scheduled the spawned reader thread for its first iteration. This resulted in `reads == 0` and triggered a false-positive assertion failure `assert!(reads > 0, "reader thread never completed a read")`.

## Solution
Changed the reader loop structure to execute at least one full read pass unconditionally (`loop { ... reads += 1; if done_reader.load(Ordering::Relaxed) { break; } }`) before exiting. This guarantees deterministic liveness and removes the thread-scheduling timing assumption while fully preserving the concurrent isolation test coverage.

Closes #2795

* **Tests**
  * Updated snapshot isolation test behavior to ensure the reader performs at least one validation before stopping.
  * Improved coverage of concurrent read behavior when the completion signal is already set.

pullRequests.body:
Every image that builds `redis-server`/`redis-cli` from source pinned the upstream tag at `8.6.3`. This moves the pin to `8.10.1`.

### Version pins

- `build/Dockerfile`, `build/runtime/Dockerfile`, `build/runtime/Dockerfile.coverage` — `ARG REDIS_VERSION=8.10.1`
- `build/runtime/Dockerfile.asan` — `ARG REDIS_ASAN_VER=8.10.1`

### Comments

- `build/runtime/Dockerfile` — 8.10 removed `BUILD_WITH_MODULES`; the bundled stack modules are now cloned on demand by `make modules-update`, so a plain tag clone is redis-only by default. The `export BUILD_WITH_MODULES=no` stays (a no-op on 8.10, still meaningful if the pin is ever moved back to an 8.6.x tag) with the comment corrected to say why.
- `build/runtime/Dockerfile.asan` — `redis:8.6.x` → `redis:8.10.x` in the trixie-slim rationale.
- `bench/Dockerfile` — dropped the hardcoded `8.6.3`; that redis comes from the published `:edge-c` image, not from this pin, so naming a version here just goes stale.

### Not touched

`Dockerfile.amazonlinux2023` and `Dockerfile.rhel9` build only `libfalkordb.so`; `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` installs the distro's unpinned `redis-server`. None carry a Redis version on this branch.

### Notes for review

8.10 reworked the top-level Makefile (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := build`, recipes delegating to `scripts/build.sh`), so this is not purely a number change in effect:

- `make all` → `build` → `scripts/build.sh` → `make -C src all`, printing `==> No cloned modules under modules/*/src, Redis-only build`.
- The `protected-mode` sed/grep guard and the jemalloc page-size sed still match 8.10.1's sources; the guard would fail the build loudly if they stopped matching.
- Command-line make variables still reach `src/` through `MAKEFLAGS` despite the shell-script hop, so the ASAN stage's `SANITIZER=address OPTIMIZATION=-O1` continues to produce an instrumented binary that clears the Dockerfile's `__asan_` symbol-count check.

This branch targets `main`; `master` needs its own PR — its Dockerfile set differs

pullRequests.title: ci: bump cargo-fuzz to 0.13.2 so the fuzz job can install it
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2821. Unblocks the red `fuzz` job on every open PR, including #2757 and #2570.

## What is failing

The `fuzz` job never reaches the fuzzing — that step is skipped. Installing the tool is what breaks:

```
error: attributes starting with `rustc` are reserved for use by the `rustc` compiler
28 | #[cfg_attr(rustc_attrs, rustc_layout_scalar_valid_range_start(0xf001))]
error: cannot find attribute `rustc_layout_scalar_valid_range_start` in this scope
error: could not compile `rustix` (lib) due to 4 previous errors
error: failed to compile `cargo-fuzz v0.13.1`
```

## Why

The workflow pairs an **unpinned nightly** with a **pinned old tool**:

```yaml
- run: rustup default nightly
- run: cargo install --root ... --version ${{ env.CARGO_FUZZ_VERSION }} cargo-fuzz   # 0.13.1
```

`cargo-fuzz 0.13.1` resolves **`rustix v0.36.5`**, which declares internal compiler attributes behind `cfg(rustc_attrs)`. Current nightly refuses them, so the dependency cannot build. This is unrelated to the fuzz targets or to any branch's code.

It stayed hidden while the `cargo-fuzz-bin-<version>` cache was warm — a cache hit skips the install entirely. Once that entry was evicted, the rebuild met today's nightly and failed.

Repo-wide, not branch-specific: failing on `perf/limit-aware-scan-batching` and `feat/effects-v3-tests` alike, and **no run in the last 60 has a green `fuzz` job**.

## The fix, verified

`cargo-fuzz 0.13.2` resolves **`rustix v1.1.4`**, which carries no such attributes. Tested against `rustc 1.100.0-nightly (cea272fa3 2026-09-07)`, close to CI's:

```
$ cargo +nightly install --version 0.13.2 cargo-fuzz
   Compiling rustix v1.1.4
   Installed package `cargo-fuzz v0.13.2` (executable `cargo-fuzz`)
```

Against the same toolchain, 0.13.1 fails exactly as CI does. The version is also the cache key, so this cannot reuse the stale entry.

## Left alone deliberately

`rustup default nightly` is unpinned, so this class of breakage recurs whenever nightly moves under a pin

pullRequests.title: fix(docker): restore redis-sentinel / redis-check-rdb / redis-check-aof entry points in the runtime image
pullRequests.body:
`build/runtime/Dockerfile` builds Redis itself and copies only `redis-server` and `redis-cli` out of the `redis-builder` stage. `make install` does create `redis-sentinel`, `redis-check-rdb` and `redis-check-aof` as symlinks to `redis-server` (the binary picks its mode from `argv[0]`), but they never reach the runtime image — so `:edge` images lack entry points every previous FalkorDB image shipped, breaking consumers that exec them (e.g. JFalkorDB's `SentinelIT`: `exec: "redis-sentinel": executable file not found in $PATH`).

Both changes are in the `server` stage, which `full` inherits, so they cover `falkordb/falkordb:edge` and `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge`.

### Changes

- **Recreate the three entry points** after the existing `COPY`s. Recreated rather than `COPY`'d because Docker dereferences symlinks — copying would triple the 4.8 MB binary. As relative symlinks they cost 12 bytes each.

  ```dockerfile
  RUN ln -s redis-server /usr/local/bin/redis-sentinel && \
      ln -s redis-server /usr/local/bin/redis-check-rdb && \
      ln -s redis-server /usr/local/bin/redis-check-aof
  ```

- **Extend the runtime sanity check** so a future COPY-only refactor cannot silently drop them again:

  ```dockerfile
      redis-server --version && \
      redis-cli --version && \
      redis-sentinel --version && \
      redis-check-rdb --version && \
      redis-check-aof --version
  ```

  `redis-check-rdb`/`-aof` otherwise treat their first argument as a filename; both explicitly special-case `-v`/`--version` and exit 0 (`src/redis-check-rdb.c:443`, `src/redis-check-aof.c:527` in 8.10.1), so the check is a valid presence assertion rather than an accidental file-open.

### Out of scope

`redis-benchmark` is a real ~6.5 MB binary, not a symlink; restoring it is a separate size trade-off, as noted in the issue.

pullRequests.title: fix(planner): materialize named paths created by CREATE (#1279)
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #1279.

## Problem Description
Executing `CREATE p=(n) RETURN p` or `CREATE p=(a)-[r:R]->(b) RETURN p` in FalkorDB failed with `'p0' not defined` or produced an unmaterialized path result containing `NULL`.

## Root Cause
In `graph/src/planner/mod.rs`, the `QueryIR::Create` planning branch was emitting `tree!(IR::Create(Box::new(filtered)))` directly without checking for declared paths. Unlike `QueryIR::Merge` (which wraps its plan in `tree!(IR::PathBuilder(paths.to_vec()), merge)`), `CREATE` was omitting `IR::PathBuilder`, leaving the bound `Type::Path` variable unmaterialized in the tuple stream prior to projection.

## Changes Made
1. **Planner (`graph/src/planner/mod.rs`):**
   - Extract declared named paths from `filtered.paths().to_vec()`.
   - Wrap `IR::Create` with `tree!(IR::PathBuilder(paths), create)` whenever paths are present, mirroring the MERGE clause pattern.
   - Using `filtered.paths()` rather than `pattern.paths()` ensures paths visited in earlier clauses are not erroneously overwritten or re-materialized.

2. **Regression Tests (`tests/flow/test_create_clause.py`):**
   - Added `test04_named_path_in_create` testing:
     - Single-node named paths: `CREATE p=(n:Person {name: 'Alice'}) RETURN p`
     - Relationship named paths: `CREATE p=(a:Person {name: 'Bob'})-[r:KNOWS {since: 2026}]->(b:Person {name: 'Charlie'}) RETURN p`
     - Path functions on created paths: `length(p)`, `nodes(p)`
   - Full docstrings meeting code quality and pre-merge review standards.

## Opire Bounty Claim
/claim #1279

pullRequests.title: fix: canonical constraint key encoding for numeric equivalence (#2774)
pullRequests.body:
## Summary
`Graph::build_composite_key` previously used `format!("{v:?}")` with literal `'|'` delimiters to build uniqueness keys for `UNIQUE` constraint validation and enforcement. Because Rust's `Debug` format for `Value` is type-tagged (`Int(1)` vs `Float(1.0)`), `UNIQUE` constraints failed to reject numeric duplicates that differed only by numeric representation, even though Cypher equality considers `1 == 1.0`. In addition, literal pipe delimiters were vulnerable to value collisions.

## Changes
- Implemented `Value::encode_constraint_key(&self, buf: &mut Vec<u8>)` with canonical binary key encoding:
-   - Whole floats within 64-bit integer range normalize to `TAG_INT` (including `-0.0` and `0.0` normalizing to `0i64`), ensuring `Value::Int(1)` and `Value::Float(1.0)` produce byte-for-byte identical keys.
-   - Distinct types (such as `String("1")` and `Int(1)`) are unambiguously tagged.
-   - Other types (`Point`, `VecF32`, `List`, `Map`, `Datetime`, `Date`, etc.) are canonically encoded.
- - Updated `Graph::build_composite_key` to frame each property segment with a length prefix, eliminating delimiter collisions.
- - Added unit tests in `composite_key_tests` verifying numeric equivalence (`1` and `1.0`, `0` and `0.0` / `-0.0`), distinct type non-collision, and delimiter safety.
- - Added regression flow test `test10_unique_constraint_numeric_type_equivalence` in `tests/flow/test_constraint.py`.
Fixes #2774

Previously, only the node-target/map-source branch cleared pending properties staged earlier in the query, while the remaining branches only cleared committed properties from the graph. pullRequests.title: fix(graph): order-insensitive constraint matching and duplicate property validation
pullRequests.body:
Resolves #2792

### Overview
In FalkorDB's Rust graph engine, `Constraint::matches` previously compared property slices position-by-position using `.zip().all()`. Consequently:
1. `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` were treated as distinct constraints in Rust, whereas the C engine canonicalizes/sorts attributes, causing state divergence across replication (e.g. effects-v3 replication where master emits both orders).
2. Dropping a constraint using a different property order (e.g. `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT DROP g MANDATORY NODE P PROPERTIES 2 b a`) failed with `Constraint does not exist`.
3. Creating a constraint with duplicate properties (e.g. `PROPERTIES 2 a a`) was not rejected upfront, whereas C rejects it with `"Properties cannot contain duplicates"`.

Following maintainer recommendation (**Option A** in #2792):
- Updated `Constraint::matches` to compare property sets without regard to order (`p1.sort_unstable(); p2.sort_unstable(); p1 == p2`).
- Added duplicate property validation in `Graph::create_constraint`: checks for duplicates and returns `Err("Properties cannot contain duplicates".into())`, matching C engine behavior.
- Retained caller-defined property ordering in `self.properties` so user-facing inspection via `CALL db.constraints()` preserves the original property order declared at creation.

### Testing
- **Rust unit tests:**
  - `graph/src/graph/constraint.rs`: Verified `Constraint::matches` with identical order, reversed order, 3-element permutations, non-matching properties, different lengths, labels, entity types, and constraint types.
  - `graph/src/graph/graph.rs`: Verified duplicate property rejection (`"Properties cannot contain duplicates"`), order-insensitive duplicate constraint detection (`"Constraint already exists"`), and dropping using reversed property ordering.
- **Python flow tests:**
  - `tests/flow/test_constraint.py`: Added `testOrderInsensitiveConstraintMatching` testing end-to-end node and relationship constraint creation, duplicate

pullRequests.title: fix: identify virtual keys the way the C engine does
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2773. Replaces #2786, which fixed the same issue a different way — see **Why not #2786** below.

## Reproduction

A single synchronous `SAVE` destroyed any graph whose key began with `__placeholder` / `__vkey_placeholder`, with no error to the client. `SHUTDOWN` saves too, so a restart lost it as well.

```
GRAPH.QUERY "__placeholder_mydata" "UNWIND range(1,200) AS i CREATE (:Keep {v:i})"
EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"     --> 1
SAVE                              --> OK
EXISTS "__placeholder_mydata"     --> 0    <-- destroyed
```

## Root cause

The pre-save sweep scanned the keyspace for `graphdata` keys and then had to decide, key by key, which results were real graphs and which were the module's own bookkeeping. It decided by the graph's **name**:

```rust
let name = g.borrow().name().to_string();
if name.starts_with("__placeholder") || name.starts_with("__vkey_placeholder") {
    stale_keys.push(key_name);   // deleted below
}
```

The only evidence was a prefix the client is free to choose.

## How the C engine avoids the question

C never asks whether a key is a real graph or its own bookkeeping — three things make the question unnecessary (`src/module_event_handlers.c` on `master`):

| | C |
|---|---|
| Enumerate graphs to save | `Globals_ScanGraphs` — the module's own registry, no keyspace SCAN |
| Delete virtual keys after **save** | exact names recorded by `GraphEncodeContext_AddMetaKey` |
| Delete virtual keys after **load** | exact names recorded by `GraphDecodeContext_AddMetaKey`, identified at decode time by *"the virtual key name is not equal the graph name"* |

C also keeps that last comparison honest: `GraphContext_Rename` re-points `gc->graph_name` at the new key.

## Fix

Port that structure.

* **`create_virtual_keys` enumerates `GRAPH_REGISTRY`** instead of scanning — Rust's existing analogue of `Globals_ScanGraphs`. Virtual keys are never registered, so no test is needed to exclude them. `scan_and_clean_graphdata_keys` and its prefix match

pullRequests.title: Fix Debian runtime builds masking package upgrade failures
pullRequests.body:
## Problem

In both Debian runtime Dockerfiles, the ungrouped `|| true` after the final optional `apt-get autoremove` applies to the preceding `&&` chain. An earlier `apt-get update`, installation or `dist-upgrade` failure can therefore be hidden, and the image build reports success after cleanup.

Group that fallback so it tolerates only the intended optional cleanup. This targets the supported `4.20` branch; it does not change the image's package selection or scanner policy.

## Validation

- Added a dependency-free regression which executes the actual Dockerfile RUN instructions under `/bin/sh` with inert command stubs. All 16 scenarios pass: required failures propagate, successful installation passes, and explicitly optional cleanup failures remain tolerated. The original Dockerfiles fail all eight required-failure scenarios.
- Run the regression in the existing pre-build CI job: `python3 tests/docker/test_runtime_package_failures.py`.
- Built the patched Debian server runtime locally on Linux amd64 with fresh base image/package metadata and no build cache, reusing the unchanged published v4.20.4 module. Redis/graph create, read, save, container replacement and subsequent writes passed. This validates the runtime image; it is not a fresh engine compilation or an arm64 test.

- Trivy 0.70.0 against the rebuilt server runtime (15 September 2026 database): zero fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings. The unfiltered scan still reports 36 HIGH findings without an available fix; no clean-all-severities claim is made.

The failure-masking bug is reproduced directly; there is no claim that a historical upgrade failure caused the current published image's dependency findings. Published full images also need the separate browser dependency fixes and a rebuild (the Sharp update is already tracked in FalkorDB/falkordb-browser#2091).

pullRequests.title: perf(graph): read narrow label rows by point probe instead of a row iterator
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

`Graph::get_node_label_ids` allocated a fresh GraphBLAS row iterator for **every node it read**. Attaching and freeing a `GxB_Iterator` costs ~1,700 instructions — a number already measured and documented in `matrix.rs` — and that cost is paid per node to read a row that, on the overwhelmingly common narrow-schema graph, contains a single entry. The iterator setup dominates the read it performs.

This is the label-projection path shared by `RETURN n` serialization, `labels(n)`, node delete, `expand_into` and effects emit.

The repo had already applied exactly this fix pattern twice elsewhere but never here: `node_has_label_id` uses a cheap `node_labels_matrix.get(row, col)` point read (documented with measured numbers), and `delete_relationships` reuses one re-seekable iterator. This PR extends the point-read pattern to label projection.

## Changes

- `graph/src/graph/graphblas/versioned_matrix.rs`
  - Add `VersionedMatrix::<bool>::probe_row_into`, which fills a caller-owned `SmallVec` by point-probing a row. It has a fast path that reads the committed base alone when both deltas are empty, and a general path through `self.get` that resolves `dp`/`dm` normally.
- `graph/src/graph/graph.rs`
  - Add `LABEL_PROBE_MAX = 6`, documented with the measured crossover sweep.
  - `get_node_label_ids` now branches on schema width: probe when `node_labels.len() <= LABEL_PROBE_MAX`, otherwise keep the existing iterator. Returns `Either` so neither arm boxes.

The threshold was **measured, not estimated**. An instruction-count estimate predicted a crossover near 32 labels; interleaved A/B measurement put it near 8:

| labels | Δ |
|---|---|
| 1 | **-8.0%** |
| 4 | **-6.7%** |
| 6 | **-7.2%** |
| 8 | break-even |
| 12 | +5.5% |
| 32 | +45% |

Hence 6, with wide schemas explicitly left on the iterator. The doc comment records this sweep so the next person does not have to rediscover it.

fix: give every CALL {} body its entry projection as a record boundary
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #2602
Fixes #2601

Both issues are the same defect, so they're fixed together.

## The bug

C's invariant is narrower than "record indices are per-plan-segment". In `build_call_subquery.c`, `_find_feeding_points` plants an `Argument` **only beneath a childless `Project`**, and `ProjectConsume` allocates a fresh record from its own plan's map, copies only the projected expressions in, and deletes its input. So in C the outer record enters a subquery body *only* through a projection that rebuilds it — **no body operator ever sees the outer record.** For a body that imports nothing there is no such tap, so C plants no `Argument` at all, and its row-at-a-time `ApplyConsume` (`nargs == 0`) resets and re-runs the body per outer record, which is where the cardinality comes from.

Rust already had the first of those two routes, and used it correctly — that is why every `CALL { WITH x ... }` variant was already right on `main`. But it emitted the entry projection only when something was actually imported. Without one, the `Argument` feeds the body's scans and traversals **directly**, so the outer row reaches them — and because a runtime row is a dense array indexed by `Variable.id` alone (`scope_id` never reaches the row) while the body's ids restart at 0 in its fresh scope, the outer row doesn't merely leak in, it occupies the very slots the body is about to write.

That single missing boundary produces both reported symptoms:

**#2602** — the body's predicate is tested against the imported value. `x` (scope 1, id 0) and `n` (body scope, id 0) are the same slot, so `push_filters_down` legitimately concludes the `Argument` provides the conjunct's variable and pushes the filter *under* the scan, leaving `n` unfiltered:

```
        Apply
            Project
                Node By Label Scan | (x:A:B)
            Project
                Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B)
                    Filter                  <-- tested against x
                        Argument
```

pullRequests.title: refactor(graph): make IdSpace the id allocation authority
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2839.

`IdSpace` judged id spaces while `Graph` owned the state it judged: two
counters and two recycle bins, moved by twelve raw writes across six
operations. This makes it the authority instead — it owns `live` and
`recycled`, and every id that changes state changes it through a method here.

### What moved

```rust
pub struct IdSpace {
    live: u64,                 // the entity count
    recycled: RoaringTreemap,  // the free set
    entry_bound: u64,          // where the open batch began
    taken: RoaringTreemap,     // what it has taken since
}
```

`Graph` keeps two of these and no counter or bitmap of its own;
`node_count()` and `recycled_node_ids()` read through. `reserve`, `cancel`,
`create` and `release` are methods on the space, taking no state but the ids.

That is the point rather than a side effect: the boundary is
`live + recycled.len()`, so every operation has to move both halves or
neither. A free-set write that nothing counted was #2797, and the
node-id-liveness bug before it.

### The invariant

```text
live + recycled.len() == entry_bound + taken.len()
```

True at every moment and **returned as an error**, not asserted — a corrupt
id space hands out ids that are already live, and a `debug_assert` says
nothing in the build where that matters. Failing is also the cheap outcome: a
write query holds a private MVCC version, so the damage is discarded rather
than published and replicated.

Making it total required a change of meaning. `taken` counts ids the batch
*took* — created, or reserved and then cancelled — because both move the
boundary. Counting only creates made the equation false for every cancelled
reservation, which is exactly what kept `verify` off the write path:
`CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b) DELETE b` reported
`Miscounted { graph_bound: 2, expected: 1 }` on a legitimate query.

With that fixed, the write path is now held to the same check a replica is
(#2839 step 4). It is the one change here that can fail a user's query.

### Batch

pullRequests.title: fix(effects/v3): end a run when a segment reads against it
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2842.

A run is collapsed into one bitmap and read back in a single direction, so every
segment inside it has to read that way too. Two paths put a segment into a run
going the other way, and both return early, before the `continues_run` check
that would have ended it:

* the lone-`Range` step-down rewrite claimed the run's direction only
  `if self.run.desc.is_none()`, so a run already committed to ascending kept a
  `RangeDescending`;
* the ordinary `Range` extension in the hot path grows a singleton into an
  ascending pair without consulting the run, which is the mirror — an ascending
  pair inside a descending run.

Every id survives the collapse and `len` stays right, so the decoder's
cardinality check passes and the buffer applies. An `IdList` is positional — row
*k* belongs to the *k*-th id as written — so two entities exchange values on the
replica with no error, no log and no resync. A state-only comparison calls it
green.

## Measured end to end

A primary/replica pair, same workload both ways, the replica taking three
`GRAPH.EFFECT` and no verbatim command either time:

```
before   master mispaired 0   replica mispaired 2   [[4, 5], [5, 4]]
after    master mispaired 0   replica mispaired 0
```

## The fix

One rule: a segment may take a direction only inside a run reading the same way,
and where it cannot, the run ends at that segment.

It is applied where a segment *acquires* a direction rather than where it is
charged. The charge point does observe the mirror case — but it cannot act
before the collapse, which is the actual argument for the earlier placement.

`restart` clears the direction, so the new run's direction is set at the same
moment; leaving it for the next push to decide reproduces the same bug one
segment further along.

## Cross-engine

C carried an independently written version of the same rule. A differential run
found the two designs diverged on a restarted run whose head is a two-id range —
order preserved on both sides, byte

pullRequests.title: fix(stats): count Labels-added per assignment, not per new label type (#2655)
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Fixes #2655 — the Rust engine's `Labels added` query statistic was computed as the delta in the schema's registered label count, i.e. the number of new label *types*, not the number of label *assignments* to nodes. The two happen to agree only when a query introduces each label type exactly once, so at any scale the value drifts far below the real count and, in the common `SET` on an already-known label, is dropped entirely (implicit `0`). The issue's four reproductions all fail on `edge-rs` today.

The C engine and Neo4j both count assignments; this PR aligns the Rust counter with that.

## Changes

- **`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs`** — remove the schema-delta increment at the end of `Runtime::query` that produced the bug.
- **`graph/src/runtime/ops/create.rs`** — after `pending.set_nodes_labels(...)`, increment by `node_ids.len() * node.labels.len()`. Every node reserved in a CREATE is fresh, so each label in the pattern is a new assignment on each of them. `MergeOp` routes through the same `Runtime::create_batch`, so MERGE's create path is covered too.
- **`graph/src/runtime/ops/set.rs`** — in the `SetItem::Label` arm, count only labels the node does not already carry, consulting `Runtime::node_has_label_id` (which reads pending before the committed matrix). A repeated `SET n:L` in one query therefore counts once, and `SET n:L:L` (whose `OrderSet` dedups to a single label) counts once.

## Tests

New `tests/flow/test_labels_added_stat.py` pins:

- the four cases from #2655's report;
- a `SET` of an already-present label (must be `0`);
- the same `(node, label)` touched twice within one query (must be `1`).

## Test plan

- [ ] `cargo test -p graph`
- [ ] `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/flow/test_labels_added_stat.py -vv`
- [ ] Full flow-test suite

pullRequests.title: CCH path index: DDL syntax, incremental maintenance, full RDB seriali…
pullRequests.body:
Resolve: #3151
…zation

Convert Customizable Contraction Hierarchies from a pair of graph-mutating procedures into a first-class, graph-level index.

Index model
- CCHIndex keyed by the full (sorted+deduped relationship-type set, weight attribute); the hierarchy (ranks, shortcuts, up/down adjacency) is internal and never materialized as SHORTCUT edges / rank properties in the user graph.
- db.idx.cch.query performs rank-pruned bidirectional Dijkstra over the index.

DDL
- CREATE / DROP CCH INDEX FOR ()-[e:A|B]->() ON (e.w), sharing a single consolidated create-index grammar rule; index type is parsed as a plain string, multi-relationship-type patterns supported, multi-label nodes in CREATE INDEX rejected. db.idx.cch.create / .drop procedures removed.

Incremental maintenance
- Commit-coalesced dirty tracking (CLEAN < RECUSTOMIZE < REBUILD) with a scoped recustomize kernel (per-edge seed + scoped customize over lower common neighbours) for weight/edge changes, and a staleness valve; topology changes that add/remove hierarchy adjacency escalate to a full rebuild.

Effects & replication
- Dedicated create/drop CCH effects keyed by the full set; missing relationship types / weight attribute are created via GraphHub so they replicate before the CCH effect. Verified across GRAPH.EFFECT replication and a fresh replica FULLRESYNC.

Persistence (RDB v20, edited in place)
- The entire hierarchy is serialized into / restored from the RDB in a dedicated ENCODE_STATE_CCH_INDICES payload; no rebuild on load. Phase-1 triangulation scratch (xadj/adjncy/parent) is freed after build (~113 MB on se_vag). v19 decoder moved under decoders/prev; encoder/decoder bumped v19 -> v20.

Tests
- test_cch.py flow coverage: create/query/drop, key exactness (rel-type set + weight attr, order-agnostic, deduped), scoped recustomize vs SPpaths oracle, edge/node add/delete, memory report, single- and multi-index RDB reload, replica full-sync, AOF replay.

pullRequests.title: feat(effects): let v3 index records name several schema entities
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2866

## What changed

`CREATE_INDEX` and `DROP_INDEX` now name *n* schema entities instead of one. In the record head, straight after the `u32` schema tag:

```
was:  u32 label_id · string label
now:  u16 n · (u32 id, string name) × n      // n >= 1, sorted ascending by id
```

Everything from `u32 field_type` onward is byte-identical, and the position in the record is unchanged.

Id *and* name per entry, never a bare id, for the reason the attribute refs already work that way: the replica verifies the id against the name rather than trusting it. The count is guarded before allocating, as `IndexFields` already was.

Both records, symmetrically — a create that can name several entities and a drop that cannot would leave such an index undroppable over the wire.

**Attributes needed no change.** `fields` has been a list since the codec landed, per statement rather than per field; issue section 2 records what was verified and why it must stay that way.

## Unknown `field_type` bits are now refused

Previously ignored, which was not inert: the bits gate conditional sections of the options block, so a bit this build did not know meant the block was read one section short and the *next* record was parsed from inside this one. Where it did not — a drop carries no options — `index_type_of` called the unknown type a range index. Either way, a future C emitting CCH at a replica that predates it produced a misparse or a silently wrong index; it is now a clean refusal and a resync.

Known mask is `INDEX_FLD_KNOWN = 0x1F`, pinned by a test so widening it is a deliberate edit rather than a side effect. The writer is held to the same rule: this build will not emit a bit it could not read back.

## Ordering contract

Stated in both directions, because it is the one property a conformance fixture cannot arbitrate — a generated fixture is already in some order, so a corpus run passes whether the decoder enforces or tolerates.

> An encoder **MUST** sort ascending by id, so tw

Thirteen single-dependency Dependabot PRs are open (8 on `main`, 5 on `master`), each burning a full CI matrix run and a separate review. Three of the six entries in `.github/dependabot.yml` still lacked `groups`; the `pip`, `uv` and `docker` entries were already aggregating.

## Changes

- **`github-actions` at `/`** → group `github-actions` (currently #2854, #2855, #2861)
- **`cargo` at `/`** → group `cargo-deps` (currently #2856–#2860)
- **`github-actions` at `/` with `target-branch: master`** → group `github-actions-master` (currently #2478, #2611, #2613, #2614, #2615)
- Refreshed the `master` entry's comment, which claimed it mirrored master's own config "verbatim" — it now carries a group that master's copy does not.

```yaml
- directory: /
  package-ecosystem: cargo
  schedule:
    interval: weekly
  groups:
    cargo-deps:
      patterns:
        - "*"
```

## Notes for review

- **Group names are unique across entries on purpose.** The two `github-actions` entries otherwise differ only by the branch segment of the generated group branch name.
- **One PR against `main` covers both engines.** Dependabot reads `dependabot.yml` from the default branch only; `master`'s copy is dead config, and C's bumps already flow through the `target-branch: master` entry that lives here (see #2255). Grouping `master`'s orphaned copy would need its own PR and only matters if the default branch is ever flipped back.
- **Majors are inside the groups** (`patterns: ["*"]`), consistent with the pre-existing entries, so one bad major blocks its group's PR. Splitting them out via a second group keyed on `update-types: ["version-update:semver-major"]` is a one-line follow-up if preferred.
- **The existing PRs are untouched.** Closing a Dependabot PR by hand tells it not to recreate that specific version, so the safer sequence is to let the first grouped run land before cleaning up whatever remains.

pullRequests.title: Seek by id: accept compound value expressions opposite ID(n)
pullRequests.body:
Resolve: #2871

The seek-by-id optimizer recognized the ID(n) side of a filter by AST node type (AR_EXP_OP vs AR_EXP_OPERAND), so it only reduced a scan+filter to a NodeByIdSeek when the value compared against ID(n) was a bare operand (constant, parameter, or variable). A compound expression such as x + 1 is itself an AR_EXP_OP, so both sides were operations and the filter was not recognized, leaving a full scan + filter, e.g.:

  UNWIND range(0,10) AS x MATCH (a) WHERE ID(a) = x + 1 RETURN a

Recognize the ID(n) side by the scanned alias instead: the scanned node must be referenced on exactly one side, that side must be exactly ID(n), and the other side is taken as the value expression - which is then guaranteed to be independent of the scanned node and hence resolvable from the incoming record. The NodeByIdSeek op already evaluates its range expression per record, so no runtime changes are needed.

This enables the optimization for value expressions over upstream variables (ID(a) = x + 1), previously resolved nodes (WITH a MATCH (b) WHERE ID(b) = ID(a) + 1), reversed operands, inequalities and multi-bound ranges, and the label-scan variant, while still rejecting self-referential filters such as ID(a) = a.v.

Add flow-test coverage in test_node_by_id.py.

pullRequests.title: ci(asan): get llvm-symbolizer from the builder, not apt.llvm.org
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

The ASAN image installed LLVM from **apt.llvm.org** at build time, which fails
intermittently and ejects PRs from the merge queue. **3 of the last 18 `Rust PR`
runs** hit it; PR #2469 was kicked out three times, never for anything in its own
diff. Full diagnosis in #2872.

The whole step existed to obtain one file — `/usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22` — that
the toolchain image **already has**. This copies it across the stage boundary
instead, so the runtime stage talks to `deb.debian.org` only.

## Why the builder already has it

`llvm.sh` runs `apt-get install -y clang-22 …` *without* `--no-install-recommends`;
`clang-22` Recommends `llvm-22-dev`, which Depends on `llvm-22` — the package that
ships the symbolizer, and the `llvm-objcopy-22` the builder stage already uses:

```
$ docker run --rm ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build:latest \
    sh -c 'dpkg -S /usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22'
llvm-22: /usr/bin/llvm-symbolizer-22
```

The runtime stage couldn't see it only because it's a separate stage
(`FROM debian:trixie-slim`).

## Changes

- Drop `wget`/`gnupg`/`lsb-release`, the `llvm.sh` fetch, the `apt.llvm.org` repo
  and `llvm-22` — **four round-trips to one third-party host, gone**.
- `COPY --from=builder` the symbolizer (101 KB) and the `libLLVM.so.22.1` it links
  (143 MB), preserving the `/usr/lib/llvm-22/{bin,lib}` layout. Its `RUNPATH` is
  `$ORIGIN/../lib`, so it is self-locating — no `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, no `ldconfig`,
  no multiarch path to get wrong.
- Add the libLLVM runtime closure explicitly from Debian: `libcurl4` for the binary,
  `libedit2 libffi8 libxml2 libz3-4 libzstd1 zlib1g` for the library.
- `RUN llvm-symbolizer --version` as a build-time smoke test. `apt` used to resolve
  that closure for us; this makes a stale list fail the build loudly instead of
  silently degrading ASAN output to raw addresses at test time.
- Point `ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH` at `/usr/lib/llvm-22/bin/llvm-symbolizer`.

## Testing

Built a probe image with the new `apt` list

pullRequests.title: fix: pattern comprehensions everywhere — no crashes, nested plans for loop variables (#2308)
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2308

## Problem

The planner turns a pattern comprehension into its own sub-plan only in `WHERE`, projections, `UNWIND` and `FOREACH`. Anywhere else, the comprehension reaches `unreachable!("PatternComprehension should be handled by the planner")` in `eval.rs` and panics the module, which takes the whole server down. The issue reports one position (inline relationship properties). A sweep on `main` found more, plus two positions that gave wrong results or errors rather than crashing:

| Position | Example | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inline properties: node, relationship, var-length, CREATE, MERGE | `MATCH ()-[{k:size([(a)-->()\|1])}]-() RETURN 1` | crash | error, same as C |
| `SET` (`=`, `+=`, map) | `MATCH (n) SET n.p = size([(n)-->() \| 1])` | crash | correct result |
| `DELETE` | `MATCH (n) DELETE [(n)-->(y) \| y][0]` | crash | correct result |
| `REMOVE` | `MATCH (n) REMOVE head([(n)-->(y) \| y]).k` | crash | correct result |
| `ORDER BY` | `RETURN n.name ORDER BY size([(n)<--() \| 1])` | `Variable ? not found` | correct result |
| Reads a list-comprehension / quantifier / `reduce` variable | `[x IN ns \| size([(x)-->() \| 1])]` | silently wrong (`[1,1]`) | correct result (`[1,0]`) |
| Procedure arguments | `CALL db.idx.fulltext.queryNodes('A', head([(n)-->(y) \| y.name]))` | crash | correct result |
| `YIELD … WHERE` | `CALL db.labels() YIELD label WHERE size([(a)-->() \| 1]) > 0` | crash | correct result |
| `LOAD CSV FROM` | `LOAD CSV FROM head([(f)-->(x) \| x.file]) AS row` | crash | correct result |
| `MERGE … ON CREATE / ON MATCH SET` | `MERGE (n:A) ON MATCH SET n.p = size([(n)-->() \| 1])` | crash | error (C errors too) |
| Index `OPTIONS` | `CREATE VECTOR INDEX … OPTIONS {dimension: size([(a)-->() \| 1]) + 1, …}` | crash | error |

C rejects every crashing shape above with an error, and errors on `ORDER BY` too. For the loop-variable row, C is silently wrong the same way when the variable is in the pattern, and errors when it isn't

pullRequests.title: ci(release): move Docker Hub :latest to the Rust image on release
pullRequests.body:
Closes #2881

## Problem
When a release is the highest semver, the retag job in `release-image.yml` tags GHCR `:latest`, but on Docker Hub it tags only `:latest-rs`. `release-tag.yml` takes this path on a `v6.*` tag push. So tagging `v6.0.0` would leave `docker.io/falkordb/{falkordb,falkordb-server}:latest` on the C v4.20.6 image.

## Change
- The retag path now also tags `falkordb/${REPO}:latest` on Docker Hub. That matches the rebuild path (`_build-flavour.yml`), which already moves bare `:latest` on both registries.
- `:latest-rs` is dropped. Bare `:latest` replaces it, and it was never published on Docker Hub (`docker.io/falkordb/falkordb:latest-rs` returns not found), so nothing is pinned to it.
- The `:latest` decision itself is unchanged. It still requires the release to be the highest non-draft, non-prerelease semver, so a backport patch on an old version branch doesn't move it.

## Not in this PR
C's `release-image.yml` on `4.20` and `master` sets `IS_LATEST=1` on every release event. That means the next C 4.20.x release would move Docker Hub `:latest` back to C. It needs its own fix on those branches.

## Backport
This goes to `6.0` through the merge queue before `v6.0.0` is tagged. That queue run also builds the `rc-mg-<sha>` image the release retag needs, which `f0f23ead` doesn't have.

## Verification
- `actionlint`: no new findings. The one SC2086 on the deliberately unquoted `$EXTRA_TAGS` is already on `main`.
- Not exercised end to end: this path only runs on a release.
