| before | *(empty)* | 5 keys of graph `b` | preserved |
| after | `a b` | none | preserved |

The same before-result reproduces with the published images (`falkordb/falkordb:6.0.1` → `:v4.20.7`). Also checked:
- C → fixed Rust → fixed Rust: `GRAPH.LIST`, node ids and counts preserved, no leftover keys.

pullRequests.title: fix(restore): return an error for malformed GRAPH.RESTORE payloads
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3168

## What

`GRAPH.RESTORE` crashes the server when the payload is empty or cut short. This PR makes it return an error instead.

## Why it happens

`GRAPH.RESTORE` decodes with `BufferedReader::from_slice`, which sets `rdb` to null. When the reader runs out of bytes, `ensure_available` calls `load_chunk`, and that calls `raw::load_string_buffer(self.rdb)` with the null pointer. Redis dereferences it. The `TYPE_BLOB` branch in `read_buffer` already checks for a null handle, `load_chunk` didn't.

Simplest way to hit it:

```
GRAPH.RESTORE x ""
```

While I was in there I also noticed the header, schema and payload directory decoders do `Vec::with_capacity(count as usize)` with counts read from the payload. A small payload with a huge count makes the process abort on the allocation. `GRAPH.BULK` already caps this kind of thing, so I did the same here.

## Changes

- `load_chunk` returns an error if there is no IO handle
- added `decode_capacity()` and used it for the pre-allocations in the header, schema and payload directory decoding
- new flow test `tests/flow/test_graph_restore.py` (empty payload, truncated payload, wrong tag, huge counts), added to `flow_tests_done.txt`

The RDB load path is not affected by the first change since it always has a real handle.

## Testing

I don't have the full build set up locally (GraphBLAS / RediSearch), so I haven't run the flow tests myself and I'm relying on CI for that. Happy to fix anything it turns up.

On macOS with Homebrew LLVM 23, RediSearch fails to build. pullRequests.body:
Closes #3171

## Problem

The Lean 4 models and proofs of the Rust engine lived outside version control. They found the bugs fixed by many recent PRs, but nobody else could build, extend or review them. They also drifted whenever main moved, unless someone re-targeted them by hand.

## What this adds

- **`proofs/`**: 35 standalone Lake projects, one per engine area. Lean 4.35, core only, no Mathlib; each project pins its toolchain in `lean-toolchain`.

  - Review projects (`pr<N>_review/`) model a PR's merged code while it is under review; once the PR merges, their theorems are folded into the owning projects and the review project is deleted (as done for #2845 and #2917).

- **`proofs/coverage.sh`**: reads every project's `COVERAGE.tsv` (one row per Rust function: PROVEN / CONDITIONAL / AXIOMATISED / MODELLED / NOT COVERED; CONDITIONAL means the proof rests on an undischarged hypothesis about other Rust code), checks the rows against the functions actually in `graph/src` and `src`, and prints coverage per file and in total. pullRequests.title: build(docker): run redis-server as the falkordb user
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3180

Runs `redis-server` in the Docker image as the unprivileged `falkordb` user instead of root, following the official redis image's entrypoint.

### `build/runtime/run.sh`

The container starts as root, as before. When it is root, has `CAP_SETUID` and `CAP_SETGID`, and `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS` is unset, `run.sh`:

1. hands the data directory to `falkordb` (`chown` of whatever it does not already own), but only when the directory holds nothing except `*.rdb`, `nodes*.conf` and `appendonlydir`, and prints a notice otherwise;
2. after `gen-certs.sh` (with `TLS=1`), hands `falkordb` the certificate and key files that script generates, and only those;
3. sets `umask 0077` when the umask is the default `0022`;
4. execs `redis-server` through `gosu falkordb`, so `redis-server` stays PID 1.

`SKIP_FIX_PERMS=1` skips steps 1 and 2. Started with `--user`, without those capabilities, or with `SKIP_DROP_PRIVS=1`, it runs `redis-server` as the current user. The variable names and the data-directory check follow the official image; `nodes*.conf` is added for cluster nodes.

The browser still starts first and drops to `nextjs` through its own entrypoint.

### `build/runtime/Dockerfile`

- creates `falkordb` (uid/gid 999) in place of the `redis` account at the same ids;
- installs `gosu` in the `server` stage (the `full` stage installed it for the browser; it now inherits it);
- owns `/var/lib/falkordb/data` and `/var/lib/falkordb/tls` as `root:falkordb`, mode 0775, so `falkordb` writes through the group and root remains the owner.

pullRequests.body:
Fixes #3226

## What this PR does

Two fixes for lock hazards around the indexes that RediSearch backs.

- Before a query takes the GIL to commit, it reads every RediSearch query that it still has open to the end and frees it. The scan then yields the buffered rest as before. `LIMIT` also drops its input once the limit is met, so a `LIMIT k` write frees its scan before the commit and buffers nothing.
- `Index::pending_count` reads an atomic copy of the current-generation pending count. A BGSAVE child then never takes the pending-slots mutex.

This applies to the default build. Queries that hold no open index scan at commit time do not change. Of the pending-slot functions, only the readers of `pending_count` change: the RDB encoder, `CALL db.indexes()` and the planner's index checks.

## Why we need this

On `main`, a write query whose index scan is still open at commit time stops the server or aborts it. Two common shapes keep a scan open: an index scan below `LIMIT`, and an index scan that feeds a `CALL {}` subquery.

- The server stops answering when another client runs a command that needs the RediSearch write lock under the GIL. `RESTORE` of a graph with indexes is one such command. The writer holds the RediSearch read locks and waits for the GIL. The GIL holder waits for the RediSearch write lock.
- The server aborts when the query writes the property that its scan reads. The index write fails the assertion `attempted to upgrade a spec read lock to a write lock`.

A BGSAVE child can also block forever on the pending-slots mutex of an index. BGSAVE then never finishes, and a replica that needs a full sync waits for it. Each later BGSAVE fails with `Background save already in progress`. The window is short, so the hang is rare. When it occurs, nothing recovers from it without a restart.

## Root cause: open index scans at commit

## What this PR does

`Index::pending_count` now reads an atomic copy of the current-generation pending count. Every change of that count under the pending-slots mutex also stores it in the atomic. The other pending-slot functions do not change.

This applies to every build. Only the readers of `pending_count` change: the RDB encoder, `CALL db.indexes()` and the planner's index checks.

## Why we need this

A BGSAVE child can block forever on the pending-slots mutex of an index. BGSAVE then never finishes, and a replica that needs a full sync waits for it. Each later BGSAVE fails with `Background save already in progress`.

The hang needs a fork while another thread holds the mutex. That window is short, so the hang is rare. When it occurs, nothing recovers from it without a restart.

## Root cause

Line numbers are for `main` at `ec2448f`.

- The RDB encoder runs in the BGSAVE child. `Schema::from_graph` (`src/serializers/mod.rs:708`) calls `Indexer::index_info` (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:793`), which reads `pending_count` of every index (`:805`).
- `Index::pending_count` locks `pending_slots`, a `parking_lot::Mutex` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:2164`).

- `Index` gets `current_pending: Arc<AtomicI32>`. Clones of the `Index` share it, as they share `pending_slots`.

pullRequests.title: perf(constraint): look UNIQUE keys up in the supporting index
pullRequests.body:
## What this PR does

UNIQUE enforcement looks the keys of a commit up in the constraint's supporting range index. It no longer scans the label once per affected entity. The second commit checks only the entities whose key or membership the commit can change.

This applies to every commit that touches an entity under a UNIQUE constraint. MANDATORY constraints do not change.

Fixes #2995. It is an alternative to #2997, and keeps the one-pass check of #2997 as its fallback.

## Why we need this

On `main`, a UNIQUE check costs one pass over the whole label per affected entity (#2995). A write of one entity costs O(label size). A batch of k rows costs O(k x label size).

- One `CREATE` takes 20.9 ms at 100,000 nodes and 0.76 ms at 1,000 nodes.
- A `SET` of an unconstrained property costs the same, because every touched entity is checked.
- Loading 30,000 nodes in three 10,000-row queries takes 111 s.

## Merge order

The index lookup is exact only while the index holds every entity with its current values. Two open bugs break that on `main`, so this PR depends on #3086 and #3098:

- #3069, fixed by #3086: a field added to an index during its population stays empty while the index reports OPERATIONAL.
- #3095, fixed by #3098: a population batch can overwrite a newer document or add a deleted entity back.

Without them, a lookup can miss an existing key, and a duplicate gets in. `test_effects_ddl.py::testEffects_06_ConstraintSettlingRaces::test01` shows it: it fails on this PR alone and passes with #3086 and #3098 under it. Merge this PR after both.

## Root cause

Line numbers are for `main` at `ec2448f`.

- `Pending::enforce_constraints` (`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs:1258`) calls `check_node_constraint` (`:1355`) and `check_edge_constraint` (`:1425`).
- For each affected entity, `check_node_constraint` builds a map of the composite keys of the whole label (`:1397`, loop at `:1400`). `check_edge_constraint` does the same per relationship type (`:1470`, loop at `:1473`)

pullRequests.title: fix(runtime): keep grouping keys bound after accumulator unbind (#3150)
pullRequests.body:
In `AggregateOp::next`, internal aggregate accumulator variables are unbound so they don't leak to downstream operators. The binder can assign an accumulator the same slot ID as a grouping key or an aggregate output (slot ID reuse across scopes). When that slot held a NULL grouping key, unbinding it left the column unbound, `BatchBuilder::finish` emitted `Column::Unbound`, and `src/reply.rs` panicked on `value_at().unwrap()`.

## Changes

- `graph/src/runtime/ops/aggregate.rs`: unbind accumulator slots right after the aggregate outputs are evaluated, then write the pre-projection values, the grouping keys (`acc.merge(&key)`) and the aggregate outputs, in that order. Every slot an accumulator shares is written after the unbind, so NULL keys survive. Accumulators that collide with nothing stay unbound as before.
- This also fixes a key-ordering bug in an earlier revision of this PR, where a per-key re-bind loop mixed input-scope and output-scope slot IDs (`WITH 1 AS a, 2 AS b RETURN b AS x, a AS y, count(*)` returned `x=1`).
- `src/reply.rs`: `value_at().unwrap_or(Value::Null)` as defense in depth, so one bad column can't take down the server.

## Tests

- `test10_null_preceding_aggregate`: the #3150 cases (`RETURN null AS x, count(1)`, `collect`, missing property before an aggregate).
- `test11_null_key_after_aggregate`: NULL key after an aggregate through a `WITH ... AS hops` slot (plain, variable-length path, `algo.SSpaths`), cases that already passed, grouping-key ordering, and the OPTIONAL MATCH + `collect()` shape from the issue thread.
- `TEST="tests/flow/test_null_handling" ./flow.sh`: 11/11 pass locally. test11 fails on the previous revision of this branch.
- Aggregation, WITH and OPTIONAL MATCH flow files pass; `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy` are clean.

Fixes #3150

pullRequests.title: fix: slow log no longer panics on a multi-byte character at byte 2048
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3233

## Problem

The slow log sliced the query and parameter text at byte 2048 (`entry_hash` and `truncate` in `src/slow_log.rs`). Slicing a `&str` inside a multi-byte character panics, so a query (or `CYPHER` parameter string) longer than 2048 bytes that ran past the 10 ms threshold, with a character straddling byte 2048, killed the server:

```
FalkorDB panic: panicked at src/slow_log.rs:49:10:
end byte index 2048 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 2047..2049 of string)
```

## Fix

A `prefix` helper returns the longest prefix of at most 2048 bytes that ends on a char boundary (`str::floor_char_boundary`, already used in the lexer). `entry_hash` hashes that prefix and `truncate` stores it plus `...`. Nothing else in `src/` slices text by a byte limit unsafely: `telemetry.rs` cuts by `char_indices`, `divergence_guard.rs::clip` walks to a boundary, and the `graph_core.rs` slices are at NUL / params offsets.

Query: 2050 bytes, `é` at bytes 2047..2049, `UNWIND range(1, 2000000) …` so it is logged.

| | `main` | This PR | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| query answers | no, server panics and exits | yes | yes |
| `GRAPH.SLOWLOG` query text | — | 2047 bytes + `...` (2050 bytes, valid UTF-8) | 2048 bytes + `...` (2051 bytes, ends `\xc3...`: half of `é`, invalid UTF-8) |
| same with the character in a `CYPHER p='…'` prefix | panics at `slow_log.rs:32` | params 2047 bytes + `...` | 2048 bytes + `...`, invalid UTF-8 |

The stored text differs from C only where C stores a broken character; we drop the whole character (up to 3 bytes fewer) and keep the reply valid UTF-8. Matching C byte for byte would mean storing and returning non-UTF-8 bytes. Unchanged: C also appends `...` to text that is exactly 2048 bytes long, which Rust did not do before and still does not.

## Tests

- New flow test `test_slowlog.py::test07_truncate_on_char_boundary`: for `é`, `€` and `😀` straddling byte 2048, in the query text and in the parameters, it checks the server answers and `GR

pullRequests.title: fix: a refused GRAPH.EFFECT buffer no longer keeps its index DDL
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3023

## Problem

When `GRAPH.EFFECT` refuses a buffer, `MvccGraph::rollback` drops the private version. Index DDL survived that rollback. The `Indexer` map is shared by every MVCC version, so a `CREATE_INDEX` or `DROP_INDEX` that ran before the refusing record stayed applied, while everything else in the buffer was rolled back.

## Fix

This implements option 1 from the issue. `apply_effects` still verifies each `CREATE_INDEX` / `DROP_INDEX` record in place: schema and attribute ids, label, index type. It then queues the statement instead of running it. The queue runs in record order after all records have applied and `Graph::validate` has passed, before `commit_index`. If a data record refuses the buffer, no DDL has run yet.

Deferring the DDL created a problem with population. `docs` only collects documents for indexes that already exist, so an entity the buffer writes now has to reach a newly created index through population. Population reads the **committed** graph, and that graph lacks the buffer's writes until `MvccGraph::commit` publishes the version. To handle this, `populate_index` takes an optional `published_at` version, and the first batch reschedules until the committed graph reaches it. This uses the same 1 ms reschedule as the existing "graph not yet committed" path. The apply path uses the new `Graph::create_index_populated_at` / `drop_index_populated_at`, which pass `Some(g.version)`. `create_index` / `drop_index` pass `None`, so the primary's `CREATE INDEX` / `DROP INDEX` behave as before. Without the gate, a 50k-node buffer had 0 of its nodes in the index. The same race already exists on `main` when an entity comes before its `CREATE_INDEX` in a buffer, and the new test hits it.

| Case (client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT`) | `main` | This PR | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[CREATE_INDEX A(zz), CREATE_NODE 0]`, node 0 live → refused | `db.indexes()` lists `A [zz]` | `db.indexes()` empty | n/a: C cannot read v3 (logs `GRAPH.EFFECT version mismatch expec

## Problem

An attribute keeps one RediSearch field per index type, in creation order. Every query-node builder in `graph/src/index/mod.rs` (numeric/string range, numeric/string equality, point, array-contains) took the attribute's first field, whatever its type. After `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.s)` then `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.s)`, the numeric/tag/geo nodes targeted the fulltext field, so every range-index lookup on `n.s` returned no rows (nodes and relationships alike).

|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s = 'foo' RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `foo` | `foo` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.s > 'c' RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `dog`, `foo` | `dog`, `foo` |
| `MATCH (n:L {s:'bar'}) RETURN n.s` | `[]` | `bar` | `bar` |

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3246

## Problem

`Tensor::resize` to smaller dimensions resized `m`, `dp`, `dm` and `mt`, but not `me`. `me` is keyed by `compound_key(src, dst)` and is `ME_DIM` rows whatever the node count, so a resize never reaches it. A multi-edge pair outside the new bounds lost its `MULTI_EDGE` sentinel but kept its ids: `iter_edges` still returned them and `edge_count` still counted them.

Latent: the only caller that can shrink (`rebuild_derived_matrices` after an RDB load) resizes to `node_cap`, which covers every node id, so Cypher cannot reach it today.

## Fix

In the shrink branch, collect the `me` entries whose `compound_key_inverse` falls outside `nrows x ncols` and remove them. One pass over `me`, on a shrink only; the grow path is unchanged.

`Tensor::new(8, 8)` with multi pairs (0,1) and (5,6) and single pair (1,2), then `resize(4, 4)`:

| | Rust before | Rust after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `iter_edges()` | `(0,1,10) (0,1,11) (1,2,12) (5,6,20) (5,6,21) (5,6,22)` | `(0,1,10) (0,1,11) (1,2,12)` | n/a (no shrink path) |
| `edge_count()` | 5 | 3 | n/a |
| `multi_pairs()` | 2 | 1 | n/a |

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3236

## Problem

`replace_agg_subtrees` binds an ORDER BY aggregate to a projected aggregate when `raw_exprs_structurally_equal` says the two trees match. Its node comparison `expr_ir_eq` compared constant values only for same-type pairs. Every other pair fell back to comparing the `ExprIR` variant, so `Constant(Int(3))` equalled `Constant(Float(4.0))`, `Constant(String("3"))` and `Constant(Null)`. The same fallback ignored the payloads of `Quantifier`, `ListComprehension`, `Reduce`, `Case`, `ShortestPath` and `CompiledRegex`. `RETURN … max(n.v % 3) AS m ORDER BY max(n.v % 4.0)` therefore sorted by `m` instead of failing as it does in C.

Open PR #3011 reuses `raw_exprs_structurally_equal` for non-aggregate ORDER BY expressions, where the same bug would bind `ORDER BY n.v % 4.0` to a projected `n.v % 3`. This fix covers that path too.

## Fix

`expr_ir_eq` compares constants with `Value`'s `==` (Cypher equality). This is what C's `AR_EXP_Equals` does with `SIValue_Compare`: `3` still matches `3.0`, as in C. It also compares the payload of every variant that has one. Graph-pattern variants (`Pattern`, `PatternComprehension`, `NestedPlan`) keep the variant-only comparison: their anonymous elements get a fresh name per occurrence, so comparing the patterns would reject identical copies that C accepts.

| `<x>` | Rust before | Rust after | C |

| `max(n.v % '3')` | rows, sorted by `m` | error | error |
| `max(coalesce(n.x, null))` vs projected `max(coalesce(n.x, 7))` | rows | error | error |
| `max(n.v % 3.0)` | rows `[0,2],[1,2]` | same | same |
| `max(n.v % 3)` | rows `[0,2],[1,2]` | same | same |

pullRequests.title: fix: NOT over a pattern predicate drops rows where the predicate is null
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3241

## Problem

`Planner::expr_to_plan` planned `NOT (complex)` as `AntiSemiApply(input, plan(inner))`. The inner plan passes a row only when the inner predicate is `true`, so `AntiSemiApply` passed every row where it was not `true`, including the rows where it is `null`. `NOT null` is `null` and should drop the row.

## Fix

When `NOT` wraps an `AND`, `OR` or `NOT` (under any parentheses), push it down with De Morgan before planning (`push_not_down`, `graph/src/planner/mod.rs`). These identities hold in three-valued logic. The leaves become `NOT pattern`, planned as `AntiSemiApply` (a pattern is never `null`), or `NOT scalar`, planned as an ordinary `Filter`. Other operators (`XOR`) keep the existing path.

Graph: `CREATE (:N {v: 0}), (:N), (:N {v: 5}), (:N)-[:R]->(:M)`, query `MATCH (a:N) WHERE <predicate> RETURN count(a)`:

| predicate | Rust before | Rust after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NOT (a.v > 1 OR (a)-->())` | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| `NOT (a.v > 1 AND (a)-->())` | 4 | 3 | 3 |
| `NOT (NOT (a.v > 1 OR (a)-->()))` | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| `NOT (a.v = 0 OR NOT (a)-->())` | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| `NOT ((a)-->() OR NOT (a.v < 3 AND (a)<--()))` | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Refs #2972. This is the variable-length shape of that bug. #3099 fixes the fixed-length `CondTraverse` shape and closes the issue. This PR fixes the separate `CondVarLenTraverse` code path, so it does not close #2972.

## Problem

`MATCH (a) WHERE a.v=1 MATCH (a)-[*1..2]->(b:B {w:2})` returned rows for every `a`, not only for `a.v = 1`. `plan_query` stitches the first clause, `Filter(AllNodeScan a)`, under the second clause's `CondVarLenTraverse`. `select_var_len_scan_node` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/select_scan_node.rs`) reverses a leaf traverse when `to` is the more selective end. `planner_scan_alias` looks through `Filter` wrappers, so the stitched clause was taken for the planner's own scan of `from`. The leaf rewrite then pruned it and pushed a bare scan of `b`, keeping only an `Argument` leaf. The non-leaf branch above it already refused a `Filter` wrapper; the leaf branch did not. Anything planned below the scan was dropped too, such as an earlier `UNWIND`.

```
Project
    Conditional Variable Length Traverse | (a)-[_anon_0*1..2]->(b)
        Filter
            Node By Label Scan | (b:B)        <- a.v = 1 is gone
```

## Fix

The leaf rewrite now runs only when the subtree is the planner's own scan: no `Filter` wrapper, and nothing under the scan except an `Argument` leaf, which is the only thing it carries over. Otherwise the planner's direction is kept. `IncludePending` (MERGE) is still rebuilt as before.

pullRequests.title: fix: nested lists in an effects payload can no longer reserve memory quadratic in its size
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3266

## Problem

The v3 `SIValue` decoder checks a nested `T_ARRAY`'s child count only against the bytes left after it, and ignores the siblings that its ancestor frames still owe. Every level of `[[[…` can therefore claim the whole remainder, and each level then calls `ThinVec::with_capacity` for that claim. The reservations add up to the square of the payload. Any client can send `GRAPH.EFFECT`, and a 1 MB payload pushed `redis-server` to a 2.3 GB peak RSS before the decode failed at the end of the buffer.

## Fix

`Value::decode` keeps `owed`, the number of children the open frames still need beyond the one being read now (`Σ (left − 1)`). A new list must fit `n + owed` values in the remaining bytes. Its own children and the siblings it would otherwise take bytes from are disjoint byte ranges, so the total capacity reserved across the stack stays at or below `remaining / 4`, which is linear in the payload. Legitimate values are unaffected, because their claims are always backed by real bytes.

Peak RSS of `redis-server` after one hostile `GRAPH.EFFECT` (repro script in #3266, fresh server per row, `/usr/bin/time -l`):

| payload | Rust `main` | this PR | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| none (idle) | 23.6 MB | 23.6 MB | – |
| 256 KB | 566 MB, fails at EOF | 24.7 MB, refused at once (`ImplausibleCount`) | no v3 decoder |
| 1 MB | 2.31 GB, 1.34 s | 25.5 MB, under 10 ms | no v3 decoder |

## Tests

- New unit test `effects::v3::value::tests::nested_lists_cannot_each_claim_the_whole_remaining_buffer`, which uses 1,000 levels, each claiming the most its trailing bytes allow.
  - Before the fix: `FAILED … expected the claim to be refused up front, got UnexpectedEof { want: 4, have: 0 }`
  - After: `ok`. The payload is refused at the second level.
- `cargo test -p graph --lib effects`: 197 passed, including the 5,000-deep round trip and the nested-list round trip.
- `cargo test -p graph --lib`: all pass except the known `cap_at_or_above_batch_size_is_ignored` (#2922). `

## Problem

Closes #3244

## Problem

`Graph::get_type_id_mut` registered a relationship type and its tensor but did not call `resize()`, so `relationship_type_matrix` (edges x types) stayed one column short. `get_relationship_matrix_mut` and `get_label_id_mut` both resize for this reason. Its callers that register a type with no edge are `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE ... RELATIONSHIP <new type>` on the primary and `ADD_SCHEMA` in effects apply on a replica.

After that, edge deletes (`delete_relationships`, `delete_implicit_edges`) built a removal mask `relationship_cap x relationship_types.len()` that the narrower matrix refused with `GrB_DIMENSION_MISMATCH`. Only a `debug_assert` checks it, so in release the deleted edge kept its type, and the edge that reused its id read back with the old type.

## Fix

Call `self.resize()` in `get_type_id_mut` after registering the type. `resize` costs a few comparisons when nothing changed, and this runs once per type ever. The one change covers both the primary and the replica path.

```
CREATE (:N)-[:A]->(:N)
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g MANDATORY RELATIONSHIP B PROPERTIES 1 x
MATCH ()-[r]->() DELETE r
MATCH (a), (b) WHERE id(a) = 0 AND id(b) = 1 CREATE (a)-[:C]->(b)
MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r), type(r)
```

pullRequests.title: fix: effects payloads of 4 GiB or more ship uncompressed instead of with a truncated length
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3276

## Problem

`maybe_compress` wrote the frame's `plain_len` and `comp_len` with `as u32`. With `EFFECTS_COMPRESSION` enabled, a payload of 4 GiB or more declared a truncated length, for example 5 for 4 GiB + 5. The replica uses that length as the ceiling for `zstd::bulk::decompress`, so it rejected the frame, never applied the write, and looped on forced resyncs.

## Fix

The 12-byte prefix is now built by `frame_prefix`, which narrows both lengths with `u32::try_from` and returns `None` when either does not fit. `maybe_compress` then leaves the payload uncompressed, and an uncompressed payload has no length field to overflow. It also returns early when the plaintext alone is already too long, so a 4 GiB payload is not compressed only to be discarded. Payloads under 4 GiB produce the same bytes as before.

|---|---|---|---|
| < 4 GiB | compressed, `plain_len` exact | same bytes | no v3 / compression |

pullRequests.body:
Closes #2728

## Problem

`MATCH (x:A:B) CALL { OPTIONAL MATCH (n:A:B {id:3}) RETURN n.id AS nid } RETURN x.id, nid` fails with `Variable n not found`. C returns `[1,3],[2,3],[3,3]`. The query in #2728 (`Variable n1 not found`) fails for the same reason.

`push_filters_down` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/push_filters_down.rs:214-242`) handles a filter in the right branch of an `Apply` by walking up to the nearest `Apply` and adding its left branch's variables to the set the filter may be pushed under. The walk stepped over `Optional`, so the filter on `n` in the CALL body's `Optional` reached the outer `Apply` and inherited the outer query's variables (`x`). Variable sets here are ids only, and ids are per scope, so the body's `n` and the outer `x` share an id. The filter was then pushed below `n`'s scan onto its `Argument`, where `n` is unbound:

```
Optional
    Project
        Argument
    Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B)
        Filter                        <- n.id = 3, below the scan of n
            Argument
```

## Fix

The walk stops at the nearest `Apply` or `Optional`, since both feed their left branch's rows to the right branch through `Argument`. When that left branch is a `Project`/`Aggregate`, such as a CALL body's import, it inherits only the variables that operator names (`branch_output_variables`). The filter now stays above the scan:

```
Optional
    Project
        Argument
    Filter
        Node By Label Scan | (n:A:B)
            Argument
```

Setup: `UNWIND range(1,3) AS i CREATE (:A:B {id: i})`

pullRequests.title: fix: CowBTree remove_batch never leaves a one-child non-root branch
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3237

## Problem

`CowBTree::remove_batch` repairs under-full children one level at a time (`merge_underfull`). A branch that ends with a single child cannot repair it — it has no sibling — so it reports its own underflow to its parent. If the parent also ends with one child, the grandparent merges it with a neighbour via `Node::combine`, which concatenates the two child lists; the one-child branch lands in the merged node and nothing re-examines it. A later `remove` that drains its lone leaf leaves an empty non-root leaf, and the next `insert_batch` panics in `Node::min`. Any `BRANCH_MAX >= 4`. Since #2350 the numeric index calls `remove_batch` on commit, but at the production fan-out (256/256) the shape needs a height-3 tree, so this was reproduced as a unit test, not a live query. Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897; found by the Lean model of #2278 (`BugsBatch.lean`).

## Fix

`merge_underfull` (batch path only) now, after each combine, re-runs itself over the children of the node(s) the combine produced (`Node::merge_underfull_below`, a no-op unless one of them is under-full) and re-checks the produced node. The single-key `rebalance` path is unchanged.

| `CowBTree::<2, 4>`: 96 keys, `remove_batch(33..64)`, `remove(32)`, `insert_batch([(0,1),(95,1)])` | Result |
|---|---|
| Rust before | `check_invariants`: "branch must have >= 2 children: 1"; then `insert_batch` panics: `range end index 8 out of range for slice of length 0` (`mod.rs:83`) |
| Rust after | well-formed after every step, contents correct |
| C | n/a (no equivalent structure) |

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3238

## Problem

`CowBTree`'s const assert accepted `DOC_BYTES ∈ 1..=8`, but the doc field is read back with `read_width`, which loads only 1/2/4/8 bytes and treats any other width as 8. `CowBTree::<256, 256, 3>` compiled and panicked on its second insert. Latent: the only production instantiation (numeric index) uses `DOC_BYTES = 8`. Different from the two CowBTree bugs in #2893 / #2897; found by the Lean model of #2278 (`LeafAosD.docBytes3_*`).

## Fix

The smaller of the two options in the issue: a `const fn is_read_width(width) -> bool { matches!(width, 1 | 2 | 4 | 8) }` next to `read_width`, used by the three const asserts (`Default`, `new`, `from_sorted`), so the accepted set is defined by the reader. pullRequests.title: fix: virtual keys of one graph can no longer share a name
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3284

## Problem

`uuid_v4` names the virtual keys that a large graph is split into during an RDB save. It mixed the clock and a per-process counter as `a = t ^ seq` and derived every printed field from `a`. Two calls whose clock and counter changed in the same bits got the same name (`4 ^ 2 == 5 ^ 3`). The second `vkey_map.insert` then replaced the first virtual key, and that slice of the graph was missing from the save.

## Fix

The mixing now lives in `const fn uuid_fields(t, seq)`, and the clock and the counter go in separate fields. The first three fields come from `t`, and the last 48 bits come from `seq * K + C` with `K` odd, which is a bijection modulo 2^48. Two calls in one process therefore always get different names, whatever the clock does, and the clock still separates names across restarts. The name keeps its UUID shape and its `{graph}graph_<uuid>` key format.

| calls | Rust `main` | this PR | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `t=4, seq=2` vs `t=5, seq=3` | same name | different names | random UUID (`UUID_New`), no collision |
| same `t`, consecutive `seq` | different | different | different |

## Tests

This crate's unit tests cannot run outside Redis, because its global allocator is Redis's (`cargo test -p falkordb-rs` aborts with "the Redis Allocator isn't available"). The regression check is therefore a compile-time `const` assertion next to the function, and it runs in every build:

- Before the fix, with the old `t ^ seq` mixing extracted unchanged into `uuid_fields`: `error[E0080]: evaluation panicked: virtual key names collide for (t=4, seq=2) and (t=5, seq=3)`
- After: the build succeeds.

The collision was not reproduced live because it depends on timing. On macOS the clock has microsecond resolution, so consecutive calls cannot collide there. On Linux, two calls exactly 1 ns apart can.

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3245

## Problem

The project rule for Rust is that a node deleted by a query keeps all its details for the rest of the query. `DeleteOp` snapshotted a committed node's labels with `g.get_node_label_ids(id)`, which reads the committed label matrix. The attributes beside them already came from the pending view. So labels the same query set or removed before the `DELETE` were lost, and `labels(n)` / `n:L` answered from the committed labels. Both snapshot sites had this: `delete_nodes_bulk` (`DELETE n`) and `delete_entity` (`DELETE <expression>`, e.g. `coalesce(n)` or a path).

## Fix

A new `staged_label_ids` overlays the query's staged adds/removes (`Pending::staged_node_labels`, which `update_node_labels` now uses too) on the committed label ids, and both snapshot sites use it. The snapshot is still collected straight into the `HashSet` that `DeletedNode` holds, so there is no extra allocation per node.

|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:A) SET n:C DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:C` | `[A], false` | `[A, C], true` | `[], false` |
| `MATCH (n:A) REMOVE n:A DELETE n RETURN labels(n), n:A` | `[A], true` | `[], false` | `[], false` |
| same two with `DELETE coalesce(n)` | `[A], false` / `[A], true` | `[A, C], true` / `[], false` | `[], false` |

pullRequests.title: fix: an inline write no longer fails while a queued write is matching
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3093

## Problem

A queued write claimed `MvccGraph`'s write slot (a CAS) as soon as it started, while it was still a reader matching without the GIL. An inline writer that ran in that window (`MULTI/EXEC`, Lua, `GRAPH.EFFECT`, anything on the main thread) took the GIL and the write lock, found the slot taken, and failed with `another write is in progress, retry the query`. Its write was lost. It could not wait instead, because the queued writer cannot escalate until the inline writer releases the GIL. C commits the inline write.

## Fix

This is option A from the issue: claim the slot at escalation.

- `MvccGraph::fork` makes a private version without claiming the slot. `MvccGraph::claim(fork)` claims it and checks that the fork still extends the committed version (`Claim::Busy` / `Claim::Stale`). `write()` is unchanged (claim + fork) for writers that already hold the write lock.
- `QuerySession::write_version` hands a reader session an unclaimed fork. A writer session claims immediately. `upgrade_to_write` claims the fork right after escalating, under the GIL and the write lock. So the slot is only ever held by a thread that holds the write lock, and an inline writer never finds it taken.
- If an inline writer committed while the query was matching, the claim reports `Stale`. At that point nothing has been mutated in shared state, no index document has been published, and nothing has been replied, so the query is dropped and run again from the start:
  - `execute_query_write` (GRAPH.QUERY / GRAPH.PROFILE) loops on a fresh session.
  - `GRAPH.BULK` rebuilds its fork.
  - `GRAPH.RECORD` (debug) reports the error.
- `abandon_write` and `finish_write` release the slot only if this session claimed it (`QuerySession::release_slot`).

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3271

## Problem

`QueryIR::inner_validate` (`graph/src/parser/ast.rs`) handled `With` in the same arm as `Return`, so it accepted `WITH` as the last clause of a query or of a `CALL { … }` body. `MATCH (n) WITH n` returned the projection as the result set, and `CREATE (a) WITH a` ran its write.

## Fix

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3292

## Problem

When an `AND`/`OR`/`XOR` operand was not a boolean at runtime, the error printed the value in Rust's `Debug` form (`Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)`) and not its type. C, and Rust's own `NOT`, name the type.

## Fix

The four messages (the `And`/`Or`/`Xor` arms in `eval.rs` and the vectorized connective in `vector_expr.rs`) now use `Value::name()` and C's wording for projections.

| query | Rust `main` | this PR | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x AND true` | `Type mismatch: expected Bool but was Int(3)` | `Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` | same as this PR |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x OR false` | `… Bool but was Int(3)` | `… Boolean or Null but was Integer` | same as this PR |
| `UNWIND [3] AS x RETURN x XOR true` | `… Bool but was Int(3)` | `… Boolean or Null but was Integer` | same as this PR |
| `UNWIND ['a'] AS x RETURN x AND true` | `… Bool but was String("a")` | `… Boolean or Null but was String` | same as this PR |

In a `WHERE` filter, C says `expected Boolean but was Integer` without "or Null". The evaluator does not know whether it is running a filter or a projection, so it uses the projection wording that `NOT` already uses. Whether `AND`/`OR` should short-circuit at all is a separate question, tracked in #3293 (needs decision), and this PR does not change it.

## Tests

- New e2e test `test_boolean_operator_type_mismatch_names_the_type` covering the four queries above.

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3279

## Problem

The `Call` arm of `QueryIR::inner_validate` (`graph/src/parser/ast.rs`) checked the procedure's own arguments and then returned `Ok(())`. It never validated the clauses after the `CALL`, so none of the usual checks ran there. A trailing `MATCH` reached the planner as the plan root and panicked in `utilize_node_by_id` (`parent().unwrap()` on `None`), which took the server down.

End the `Call` arm with `iter.next().map_or(Ok(()), |first| first.inner_validate(iter))`, as every other clause arm does.

Closes #3247

## Problem

`apply_record` for `CREATE_NODE` turned the record's `IdList` into a `RoaringTreemap` and created that set. A repeated id was merged before anything could see it, so a client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT` whose record names ids `[0, 0]` (count 2) created one node and replied `OK`. The label and attribute writes after it walk the list, not the set. `CREATE_EDGE` has refused the same shape since #2846 (`create_relationships_bulk`).

Before creating, compare the set's size with the record's id count. On a mismatch, refuse with the same wording as the edge path: `bulk node create got N ids of which only M are distinct; an id names one node`. The buffer is rejected and nothing is applied.

Closes #3299

## Problem

The parser accepted, and ran, shapes that C rejects as syntax errors:

- a parenthesized `SET`/`REMOVE` target that does not open a property lookup: `SET (n.x) = 5` set `n.x`, `SET (n) = {..}` replaced the map, and `SET (n):L` / `REMOVE (n):L` changed labels;
- relationship types joined by a bare `:`: `[:A:B]` was read as `[:A|B]`. The same happened inside `shortestPath(...)`.

## Fix

- `parse_set_items` and `parse_remove_items` call a new `expect_property_after_paren` after the `)` of a parenthesized target. Only `(expr).prop...` gets through.

|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) SET (n.x) = 5` | sets `n.x = 5` | `Invalid input '=': expected '.'` | `Invalid input '=': expected '.'` |
| `MATCH (n) SET (n) = {a:1}` | replaces the map | `Invalid input '=': expected '.'` | `Invalid input '=': expected '<', '-' or '.'` |
| `MATCH (n) SET (n):L` / `REMOVE (n):L` | adds / removes label | `Invalid input ':': expected '.'` | `Invalid input ':': expected '<', '-' or '.'` |

| `shortestPath((a)-[:A:B*]->(b))` | runs | `Invalid input ':'` | `Invalid input ':'` |
| `SET (n).x = 6`, `REMOVE (n).x`, `[:A\|B]`, `[:A\|:B]` | ok | ok | ok |

pullRequests.title: fix: name unnamed pattern entities @anon_N so a query variable can't collide with them
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3302

## Problem

Unnamed nodes and relationships were named `_anon_<n>`, which is a plain identifier a query can write. A user variable `_anon_0` and the unnamed `(:B)` in `MATCH (_anon_0:A), (:B)` became one node. About 15 `starts_with("_anon")` checks in the binder, planner, optimizer and runtime also treated any variable starting with `_anon` as anonymous. For example, `count(_anonymous)` got a fresh variable instead of the one `MATCH` bound.

## Fix

- `parser::ast` gets `ANON_PREFIX = "@anon_"` (C's spelling) and `is_anon()`. The parser builds names from the prefix, and every `starts_with("_anon")` check is now `is_anon(..)`. An unquoted identifier cannot start with `@`, so a query can only collide by backquoting the name, which is also true in C.
- `RETURN *` used to skip `_`-prefixed names, which covered the old anonymous prefix. It now also skips `is_anon` names, so its output is unchanged.
- `EXPLAIN` shows `@anon_N` where it showed `_anon_N`, as C does. The one flow assertion that quoted the old name is updated.

| Query | Rust before | Rust after | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (_anon_0:A), (:B) RETURN count(*)` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| `MATCH (_anonymous:A) RETURN count(_anonymous)` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| `GRAPH.EXPLAIN ... (n)-->()` | `(n)->(_anon_1)` | `(n)->(@anon_1)` | `(n)->(@anon_0)` |

Not in this PR: the other internal names (`_slot_`, `_lc_`, `_quant_`, ...) are still writable. `RETURN *` still drops user variables that start with `_`, so `MATCH (_x:A) RETURN *` errors where C returns `_x`. The issue lists this separately.

## Tests

- New `tests/test_e2e.py::test_variable_named_like_an_anonymous_entity`: against the `main` module it fails with `assert [[0]] == [[2]]`. With this PR it passes. The expected values were checked against C.
- The full flow suite (`flow_tests_done.txt`, 126 files) passes with this PR. `test_execution_plan_print` now expects `@anon_0`.
- `RELEASE=1 pytest tests/test_e2e.py tests/test_functions.py tests/test_mvcc.py`: 136 pas

pullRequests.title: fix: run long clause chains (5000 UNWINDs, 1000 OPTIONAL MATCHes) instead of overflowing the stack
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3304

## Problem

Each clause puts its operator on top of the previous clause's, so a long query produces a tall plan. Four places recurse once per plan level: the optimizer passes, the runtime's operator build, every `next()` pull, and the operator tree's drop. On a 2 MiB pool worker, 2000 chained `UNWIND`s crashed the server with a SIGSEGV, and so did about 285 `OPTIONAL MATCH ... WHERE` or `CALL {}` clauses. C runs these queries. Parsing, binding and planning were fine up to 100 000 clauses.

## Fix

- New `planner::with_plan_stack(plan, f)`. If the plan is tall, it runs `f` on a stack segment sized from the plan's height: 16 KiB per level, about twice the costliest level measured, plus 1 MiB. It uses `stacker::grow`, which stays on the same thread, so thread-locals, the Redis context, the GIL state and inline (MULTI) execution are unaffected. The segment is address space only: it is mapped for the call and unmapped after it, and only the pages the query touches get committed.
- It wraps the two recursive stages: `optimize` in `Graph::get_plan` (both the cached and the uncached path), and `Runtime::query`, which builds, pulls and drops the operator tree. That covers GRAPH.QUERY / RO_QUERY / PROFILE / RECORD and EXPLAIN.
- Shallow queries pay one O(1) `plan.len() <= 128` check. 128 levels of the costliest kind fit easily in the existing 2 MiB worker stack.
- As a last resort, `Planner::check_depth` rejects plans taller than 10 000 levels, twice C's 5000 `UNWIND`s, with the existing `Query nesting exceeds the maximum depth of …` error, so a pathological query cannot ask for an unbounded stack.
- New dependency: `stacker` (with `psm`), the crate rustc uses for the same purpose.

Clause counts per shape: `main` crash point (bisected), and whether each count runs. "Rust after" was run on both the pool and inline (MULTI):

| Shape (per clause) | count | Rust before | Rust after | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `UNWIND [1] AS xN` | 5000 | crash (~1600) | ok, 0.74 s

pullRequests.body:
Closes #3306

The native index is now updated once per unit of work instead of once per graph write call.

## One index update per unit of work

The graph's write paths no longer change the native index themselves. Each records its changes in a `PendingIndexWrites` buffer carried in the unit of work's `IndexDocs`, the struct that already holds its RediSearch documents. The owner applies it once:

- a Cypher query at the end of each `Commit` segment (`Pending::commit`), so a later operator in the same query reads the writes, as it does through RediSearch;
- a replicated effects buffer once per buffer (`effects::v3::apply`);
- `GRAPH.BULK` once per token.

The 14 graph write methods take `&mut IndexDocs` in place of the single RediSearch map they took, and fill the same map as before plus, with the `index-falkordb` feature, `docs.native`. The buffer keeps changes in the order they were made and applies only the last change to each `(value, id)`, because one write step can add an entry and then remove it: `SET n.v = 5 DELETE n` stages the SET's add before the DELETE's remove. `FalkorDbIndex::merge` is replaced by `apply_writes`.

pullRequests.title: Separate map equality from ordering and check every join candidate
pullRequests.body:
> Draft. Opened for review of the approach.

Fixes #3311

## Root cause

`Map_Compare` answered two questions with one integer. Sorting and binary search asked for an order and passed `disjointOrNull = NULL`. Equality operators asked whether two maps are equal and passed a pointer. The two modes gave different results for the same pair:

- With `NULL` it returned the first non-zero value comparison (for `{x: 1.0}` vs `{x: 'x'}`, the type difference).
- With a pointer it returned `0` as soon as one value pair was disjoint or null, with `DISJOINT` or `COMPARED_NULL` set.

`ValueHashJoin` sorts and binary-searches its cache with `NULL`, then confirmed the leftmost candidate with a pointer and rejected only `COMPARED_NULL`. A disjoint map pair passed that check, the rightmost search (with the `NULL` order) found nothing, `number_of_intersections` became 0, and `OpBase_CloneRecord` was called on a NULL record.

The join had a second, independent problem. It assumed that every cached record that sorts the same as the probe value is equal to it under `=`. That is not true for NaN (it compares as `0` to every number), for null inside lists and maps, or for values of disjoint types inside lists. A NaN in the cache also breaks the sort order the binary search relies on, so a scalar join on `a.v = b.v` could both miss real matches and return false ones.

Equality callers that treat a `0` order as equal returned wrong answers without crashing:

- `[{x: 1.0}] = [{x: 'x'}]`, `{x: 1.0} IN [{x: 'x'}]` and `{x: [{y: 1.0}]} = {x: [{y: 'x'}]}` were `true`
- `{a: null, b: 0.0/0.0} = {a: null, b: 1}` was `null`, because the null pair hid the unequal NaN pair
- `(0.0/0.0) IN [1]` and `[0.0/0.0] = [1]` were `true`, because the NaN flag was dropped on the way through `SIArray_Compare` and `SIArray_ContainsValue`
- the result depended on key order: `{a: null, b: 1} = {a: 1, b: 2}` was `null` while `{a: 1, b: null} = {a: 2, b: 1}` was `false`

## Fix

Equality and ordering are now separate

pullRequests.title: Add the CCH path index contract skeleton
pullRequests.body:
Adds the types, signatures and reserved fields for the Customizable Contraction Hierarchies path
index (`index::cch`), with every body unimplemented, so the implementation changes can be written
and reviewed against a fixed contract. Nothing in the engine calls into it: a graph with no CCH
index behaves exactly as before (`Graph::cch_indexes` is an empty `Vec`; `Pending::cch_dirty` stays
`Default`).

- `new_version` clones one `Arc<Cch>` per index, so MVCC versions share the hierarchy.
- `check_size` enforces two limits: `MAX_NODES` (`i32::MAX` nodes) and `MAX_SKELETON_ENTRIES`
  (`i32::MAX` skeleton entries).
- `CchError` derives `thiserror::Error` like the crate's other errors; `InvalidWeight` covers negative,
  infinite and NaN.

Tested: 8 unit tests, including `check_size` at both ceilings and one past (no huge allocation),
`Csr::row`, and `new_version_shares_the_hierarchy` (fails if `cch_indexes` is dropped or the hierarchy is
deep-copied).

Known limits: the entry limit is the one a large graph reaches first. The skeleton is symmetric, so
it allows at most 1,073,741,823 connected node pairs (parallel and bidirectional edges count once;

pullRequests.title: Add CCH Phase 1: elimination ordering and chordal triangulation
pullRequests.body:
Phase 1 reads the undirected skeleton of a `CchInput`, never a weight, and builds the
metric-independent half of the hierarchy that every later customization reuses: a nested-dissection
elimination order (pure-Rust `feral-metis`, new dependency, behind an `Ordering` trait), the elimination
tree by union-find, and the chordal supergraph as one flat upward CSR with a mirrored downward CSR in
rank space. Ported from `CCH_EliminationOrder` / `CCH_ChordalTriangulation` (`src/algorithms/cch.c` on
`master`). An ordering-backend failure is a hard error, not a fallback to the identity order.

Connected components are split before the backend is called. `feral-metis` 0.3.0 splits components itself but
scans all n vertices per component, so ordering is O(n x components), and the skeleton is sized by `node_cap`:
every unused id slot is an isolated component. On the California road network (1,246,102 live nodes, ~294k
padding components at node_cap 1,540,096) the whole-graph call went 3.29 s -> 178 s as padding grew; split, it
stays 3.4-3.5 s with an identical permutation and chordal arc count (5,932,138). The output is byte-identical
to one call on the whole skeleton (tests assert it).

up/down rows, up and down as exact inverses, every skeleton edge present) on grids, random,
disconnected, star, path, parallel-edge and self-loop graphs, with the Metis and identity orders; and a
test that a skeleton with self-loops and duplicates gives the same permutation and hierarchy as a clean
one, and the same permutation on a second run. A backend failure and a non-permutation are `CchError::Internal`

Linux CI

pullRequests.title: Add CCH Phase 2: customization and WeightArr
pullRequests.body:
Phase 2 writes one concrete metric into the structure Phase 1 built. `Cch` now holds the shared `Topology` and a
`Metric` of four per-arc arrays (upward/downward weight and the apex rank each routes through); `Cch::build` runs
Phase 1 then Phase 2, and `Cch::customize` recomputes the metric on the same structure (nothing is written on
error). `seed` scatters the original edges into infinity-filled arrays, so each edge is touched once; `relax` is one
forward sweep over the lower triangles in increasing rank order, which suffices because the chordal supergraph holds
every top arc and the two lower arcs are final when read. Negative, infinite and NaN weights are `InvalidWeight`, and
the layout (id spaces, arc ids, the four arrays, why one sweep is enough) is documented at the top of `customize.rs`.
`WeightArr` hides the storage behind the surface a copy-on-write array would need.

`customize` refuses weights shaped for another graph (a different node count, offsets that do not start at zero or decrease, or an edge the hierarchy has no arc for) with `Internal` instead of silently dropping them or panicking; self-loops in the weights are ignored. pullRequests.title: Add CCH Phase 3: bidirectional upward query and path unpacking
pullRequests.body:
`Cch::query(src, dst)` returns the cheapest weight and the node sequence. Both halves of the search only climb rank
over the upward graph (forward reading the upward weights, backward the downward ones) and meet at the rank minimising
the two distances; the shortcut arcs on the route are expanded through their recorded mids into original edges. It is
stateless, so queries run in parallel against one hierarchy. `None` for an unreachable target or a node outside the
hierarchy; `src == dst` is the single-node path of weight 0; ties break on the lowest meeting rank, so results are
deterministic. A path that repeats a node (possible only with a zero-weight cycle) has its cycles cut, which leaves the
weight unchanged.

Stacked on #3209 (customization) and the PRs below it.

Tested: 119 `index::cch` tests: every pair on grids, random, parallel-edge, self-loop, zero-weight, disconnected and
isolated-node graphs against the oracle's weight, with a path validity check (each hop is a real edge, the sum matches)
and a check that the path is simple; 40 random graphs with half their edges at weight 0 (these fail without the cycle
cut). Full `cargo test -p graph`: 618 pass, plus the macOS-only failure noted on #3321.

Known limits: weights must be finite and `>= 0`, so zero-weight cycles are legal and are what the cycle cut handles.
No benchmark against the C module or `algo.SPpaths` yet.

Part of #3134. Closes #3210

pullRequests.title: fix: parse module-load arguments like C (case-insensitive, validated, refused on bad input)
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3268

## Problem

Module-load arguments (`--loadmodule falkordb.so NAME VALUE ...`) were read by two parsers. redismodule-rs's `module_args_as_configuration` handled the fields registered in `redis_module!`, with case-sensitive names and `value == "yes"` for booleans. An ad-hoc loop in `graph_init` handled the rest, with no `ASYNC_DELETE` arm, plain `parse::<i64>()` and no rejection of unknown names or a trailing odd argument. So `CMD_INFO YES` turned telemetry off, `cache_size 10` and `ASYNC_DELETE no` were ignored, and invalid or unknown arguments loaded where C refuses to start.

## Fix

There is now one parser, as in C's `Config_Init` (option (a) in the issue, plus Dvir's points):

- `module_args_as_configuration` is off. `apply_module_args` (`src/commands/config_cmd.rs`) parses every pair in `graph_init`. Names are ASCII case-insensitive.
- Run-time fields go through the same `validate_config_set` + `apply_config_set` as `GRAPH.CONFIG SET`, one pair at a time like C, with the same timeout cross-checks.
- Load-only fields get C's `Config_Option_set` rules:
  - `CACHE_SIZE`, `THREAD_COUNT`, `OMP_THREAD_COUNT`: positive integer.
  - `NODE_CREATION_BUFFER`: non-negative integer.
  - `INDEX_WORKER_THREADS` (Rust-only): non-negative integer.
  - `IMPORT_FOLDER`: any string.
  - `TEMP_FOLDER`: must exist, be a directory and be writable, with C's messages.
- A bad argument refuses the load. The reason is logged at `warning` level using C's texts:
  - `Encountered unknown configuration field 'FOO'`
  - `FalkorDB received N arguments, all configurations should be key-value pairs`
  - `Failed setting field 'X' with error: ...`
  - `The TIMEOUT configuration parameter should be removed when specifying TIMEOUT_DEFAULT and/or TIMEOUT_MAX`
- **Deprecated but accepted.** The engine has no behaviour yet for these C configs: `ASYNC_DELETE`, `DELAY_INDEXING`, `DELTA_MAX_PENDING_CHANGES`, `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`. They are validated, stored and reported by `GRAPH.CONFIG GET`. T

pullRequests.title: fix: enforce unique constraints by index lookup, not a label scan per entity (#3330)
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #3330.

## Cause

`Pending::check_node_constraint` / `check_edge_constraint` rebuilt a hash of every key in the label **once per written entity**, so a commit cost O(written × label size). A single `CREATE` cost O(label), and a bulk insert was quadratic.

## Fix

The check now looks each written entity's values up in the constraint's supporting index, as C's `EnforceUniqueEntity` does:

- Each `Commit` publishes its index documents before the next one runs (`commit_deferred_indexes`), so the index lags only the commit being checked.
- Written entities are compared among themselves through a key set.
- Index hits are re-verified against the private graph. An entity that was deleted, lost the label, or was re-valued in this commit does not count. Hits that are themselves written in this commit are skipped, since the key set already covers them.
- Without an operational index, or for a value the index can't match exactly (arrays, ints that lose f64 precision, NaN, empty strings), the label is scanned **once for the whole commit**, not once per entity.

Semantics are unchanged: the key is still `build_composite_key`, and NULL or absent properties still opt out.

## Numbers

These are local release builds on Apple M-series, against the C module (`master`). The first table is the issue's repro.

pullRequests.title: fix: a parenthesised WHERE uses the index and NodeByIdSeek again
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3331
Closes #3187

## Problem

Parentheses around a `WHERE` predicate, or around one of its conjuncts, turn off index and id lookups. Results are correct; only the plan is worse:

- `WHERE (n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1)` and `WHERE (n.k = 7) AND n.s = 1` use **Node By Label Scan** instead of **Node By Index Scan** (#3331), with literals or parameters.
- `WHERE (id(n) = 42)` uses **All Node Scan + Filter** instead of **NodeByIdSeek**, and `MATCH (a), (b) WHERE ((id(a) = 1) AND (id(b) = 2))` becomes a **Cartesian Product of two All Node Scans** (#3187).

The parser keeps an `ExprIR::Paren` node for `( ... )`, which it needs while parsing (`(a < b) < c` is not a chain, `SET (n).x` must open with `(`, `((x))` collapses). The binder copied that node into the bound tree. The optimizer passes (`utilize_index`, `utilize_node_by_id`, filter push-down, Cartesian-to-hash-join) match on the filter root and on the children of a top-level `And`, so a `Paren` hid the predicate from all of them.

## Fix

Fixed once in the binder (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs`), so no optimizer pass has to know about parentheses:

- The binder drops the `Paren` wrapper. The tree shape already carries the grouping, so `(x)` binds to the same IR as `x`.
- The binder merges a nested `And`/`Or` into a parent of the same operator. Both are associative, and operand order is kept, so `(a AND b) AND c` splits into all three conjuncts.

Unchanged: column names (they come from the source text, so `RETURN (1 + 2)` is still named `(1 + 2)`), chained comparisons (the parser decides those), `NOT (NOT x)`, and `(a - b) - c` vs `a - (b - c)`. These were checked live against C and match.

| `WHERE n.k = 7 AND n.s = 1` | Node By Index Scan | Node By Index Scan | Node By Index Scan |

pullRequests.title: fix: bound the nesting depth of UDF value conversion
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3337

Fixes uncontrolled recursion in UDF value conversion (GHSA-frmf-ffvc-mxx5).

## Problem

`js_to_value` (UDF result → engine value) and `value_to_js` (engine value → UDF argument) recursed once per nesting level with no limit. A UDF can build an arbitrarily deep array or object in a loop, or an array that contains itself. Converting it exhausted the query thread's stack and the server aborted with SIGSEGV. A UDF returning a 300,000-level array kills the server on `main`.

## Fix

Both conversions now carry a depth and return a query error past `MAX_UDF_VALUE_NESTING`:

```
UDF value nesting exceeds the maximum depth of 1024
```

The check covers arrays, plain objects (maps) and the path members in `js_to_value`, and lists and maps in `value_to_js`. A self-containing array hits the limit and errors instead of recursing forever.

**Why 1,024, and why the stack also grows:** 1,024 is far beyond any nesting real data uses. The cap alone does not keep every build within a 2 MiB worker stack, because each level holds QuickJS handles and an `rquickjs` frame. Measured on a 2 MiB thread with the cap lifted:

| Build | Deepest JS → engine | Deepest engine → JS | Stack per level |
|---|---|---|---|
| release | 2,344 | 3,984 | ~0.9 KB |
| ASAN (CI's debug profile, `opt-level = 2`) | 354 | 354 | ~6 KB |

So each conversion level also runs through `stacker::maybe_grow`, which moves onto a fresh 1 MiB heap segment when less than 128 KB of stack is left. The cap bounds the work; the stack growth means no build's frame size can turn the cap into an overflow.


| Query | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| UDF returning a 300,000-level array | server crashes | query error, server up |
| UDF returning a 300,000-level object | server crashes | query error, server up |
| UDF returning a self-containing array | server crashes | query error, server up |
| UDF returning a 1,024-level array | works | works |

## Tests

- New unit tests in `udf::type_convert::nesting_tests`, run

pullRequests.title: fix: bound value nesting on RDB/RESTORE decode, property writes and bulk insert
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3338

## Problem

`GRAPH.RESTORE` decodes nested `T_ARRAY` values recursively (`Value::decode` in `graph/src/runtime/value.rs`) with no depth limit. A crafted payload with ~60,000 nested arrays exhausts the stack and aborts the server (SIGSEGV). Reproduced on a release build of `main` (8a66c01e5): depth 1,000 restores, depth 60,000 kills the server.

## Fix

A shared constant `MAX_VALUE_NESTING = 4096` (plus `value_nesting_error()`) in `graph/src/runtime/value.rs`, enforced where a nested value enters storage:

- **RDB / GRAPH.RESTORE decode**: `decode_value(r, depth)` counts depth and, on entry, returns a decode error for a value inside more than 4,096 arrays. Nothing recurses past 4,097 frames.
- **Property writes** (`validate_list_property` in `pending.rs`): a list property nested past the cap is refused with `Property values can only be nested up to 4096 levels deep`. Lists can be built arbitrarily deep at runtime (e.g. `reduce(a = 1, i IN range(1, n) | [a])`), so this is checked when a value is stored, not at parse time. Every stored value can therefore always be saved and loaded back. This also covers the stored-value side of public issue #2722.
- **GRAPH.BULK INSERT** (`read_property`): the iterative array reader refuses arrays past the cap. The values it built were otherwise walked recursively everywhere else.

The effects (replication) decoder stays iterative and uncapped, as its comment explains. Its 5,000-level unit test is unchanged and passes.

**Known trade-off:** an existing RDB that already holds a list property nested deeper than 4,096 levels will be refused on load.

## Choosing the cap

On a release build, building and then freeing a nested list on a 2 MiB thread (the query pool's stack) survives about 25,900 levels (measured). 4,096 is a wide margin below that and far beyond any nesting real data uses. The new tests run the decoder, encoder, property validation and drop at exactly 4,096 levels on a thread spawned with a 2 MiB stack.

## T

pullRequests.title: fix: start a correlated multi-hop OPTIONAL MATCH / pattern predicate from the bound node
pullRequests.body:
Closes #3332

## Problem

`MATCH (p:P {id: 7}) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:F]->()-[:M]->(o:O) RETURN count(o)` was planned from the labelled far end:

```
Optional
    Conditional Traverse | (_anon_1)<-(p:P)        Records produced: 1
        Conditional Traverse | (o)<-(_anon_1)     Records produced: 20000
            Argument
```

The planner tapped the outer row into the OPTIONAL MATCH sub-plan with an opaque `Argument(None)` (`add_argument_to_leaves(&mut match_plan, None)`). `select_scan_node` only scores an endpoint as *bound* (score 3) when the child operator says it binds it, and `Argument(None)` says nothing, so `p` scored 0 and the labelled `o:O` (score 1) won. Without the label the two tied and `p` won only on the position tiebreak, which is why the issue's table shows the label as the trigger. Pattern predicates (`WHERE (p)-[:F]->()-[:M]->(:O)`, SemiApply) and pattern comprehensions had the same opaque `Argument` and the same plan; `CALL { WITH p OPTIONAL MATCH ... }` hits it through the inner OPTIONAL MATCH.

## Fix

Pass the variables visited so far (read before the pattern is planned) to the `Argument` for OPTIONAL MATCH, pattern predicates (SemiApply/AntiSemiApply) and pattern comprehensions, the same way MERGE already does (`Argument(Some(bound))`). `select_scan_node` then sees `p` as bound and starts the chain there, so the existing scoring rule (bound endpoint beats any label) applies inside correlated branches too. No optimizer change; no other pass looks at the `Argument` payload (runtime, `push_filters_down`, `references`, `fuse_optional_traverse` all match `Argument(_)`).

When nothing in the pattern is bound by the outer row, the `Argument` is now provably "transparent" and the branch still starts from the best label scan, as before (covered by the test).

pullRequests.title: CCH: make Csr generic over its offset and index widths; the input uses u32 offsets
pullRequests.body:
`Csr

` now takes its offset type `P` and its column-id type `I` as parameters, each bounded by its own trait: `CsrOffset` for `p` and `CsrIndex` for `i` (both implemented for `u32` and `u64`; each provides a lossless `to_usize`). The defaults are the widths that always fit, so a plain `Csr` means what it meant before. `CchInput` (the skeleton and the weights) now stores `Csr`. Both matrices hold at most `MAX_SKELETON_ENTRIES` (below 2^31) entries, so 32-bit offsets always fit; that halves the input's two offset arrays, which live through the whole hierarchy build. The chordal supergraph built from it keeps 64-bit offsets: fill-in is not bounded by the skeleton, and expander-like graphs pass 2^32 arcs on skeletons far below the ceiling. With offsets and ids both `u32`, a connected skeleton no longer gets a copy made for the ordering backend: `csc_view` hands `feral-metis` `bytemuck::cast_slice` views of the same `u32` arrays (safe: same size and alignment, every bit pattern valid). A skeleton of several components is ordered per component (see the Phase 1 change), and those patterns are `i32` copies of each component's rows because each component renames its nodes, so the view saves memory only for a connected skeleton. `bytemuck` becomes a direct dependency of `graph`; it was already in the lock file through `roaring`. The values of a valid skeleton are all below 2^31 (checked before this runs). A malformed skeleton carrying a larger value reads back negative; `MetisOrdering::order` checks the pattern with `CscPattern::new` before anything else reads it, so it is reported rather than ordered as a different graph or indexed out of bounds. Stacked on #3324 (query). Only `index::cch` changes, plus the dependency line. Tested: new: `a_skeleton_value_past_i32_is_refused_not_misread` (an id of 2^31 reads back as `i32::MIN` through the view and is refused; so is an offset of 2^31). pullRequests.title: GraphBLAS wrappers: CSR export, storage settings, FP64, copy-on-write effective matrix
pullRequests.body:
General-purpose safe wrappers over GraphBLAS calls that so far had to be made raw. Only `graph/src/graph/graphblas/`
changes, and nothing here uses or names the path index. Split out of #3360 (Build CchInput from a Graph),
which uses all of them.

- `grb!`: check a `GrB_Info` and panic with the call's text on anything but success. It makes the crate's
  convention explicit: an unexpected `GrB_Info` is a bug or out of memory, not a `Result` (in the module GraphBLAS
  allocates through `RedisModule_Alloc`, which handles out of memory before GraphBLAS sees it).
- Typed storage settings on `Matrix<T>`: `set_sparsity` / `sparsity`, `set_orientation` / `orientation`,
  `set_offset_width` / `set_col_index_width` / `set_row_index_width` and their getters, `set_iso` / `is_iso`.
- A strict CSR export, `to_csr_pattern::<P, I>()` / `to_csr_f64::<P, I>()` → `Result<CsrExport<P, I>,
  CsrExportError>`. It changes no setting and converts nothing: the caller sets the matrix up (sparse, row-major,
  offset and index widths `P` and `I`, `u32` or `u64`, not iso) and anything else is refused before the unload, each
  case with its own variant. The arrays are copied bit for bit out of GraphBLAS's container and handed straight back.
- `Matrix<f64>`: `new` / `set` / `get`; `build` with no `dup` operator (a repeat panics); `min_value` / `max_value`
  (monoid reductions, no allocation; NaN skipped as `fmin`/`fmax` do); `EWiseAdd` for `f64` is `MIN`.
- `Matrix::drop_diagonal`; `Matrix<bool>::pattern_union(a, b, desc)` (`GxB_eWiseUnion` with `GrB_ONEB_BOOL`, so a
  stored 0 is never typecast to `false`; overwrites; iso result); `Vector<T>::nvals`; `Vector<f64>`: `new`, `ptr`,
  `extract_tuples`.
- `VersionedMatrix::effective` / `Tensor::effective_fwd` → `Effective`, the effective matrix `(m ∖ dm) ∪ dp`. The
  `dm` mask is structural (`GrB_DESC_RSC`): a pair in `dm` is deleted whatever value it stores.

**Where it lives.** Two parts get their own modules so `matrix.rs` stays about the `Matrix`

pullRequests.title: Build CchInput from a Graph
pullRequests.body:
`CchInput::build(&Graph, &CchIndexDef)` turns a graph's relationship tensors into the symmetric, self-loop-free
skeleton and the directed weight CSR the hierarchy builder consumes, in GraphBLAS. Per relationship type:

- one `IndexUnaryOp` apply scores every entry of the effective forward matrix (`Tensor::effective_fwd`, the base
  itself when there are no deltas) straight into the weight matrix through a `MIN` accumulator. A `MULTI_EDGE`
  pair is scored `+inf`, the identity of `MIN`, so the forward structure is used as it is;
- one `mxv` per `me` block, `v = me ⊕.⊗ c` over a `MIN` semiring whose multiply is an index-binary operator that
  reads the edge id from the column index, against a full iso vector `c` carrying the context. It scores every
  parallel edge and keeps each pair's cheapest in one call, walking only `me`'s entries.

The operators map a negative, NaN or infinite weight to `-inf`, which wins every `MIN` merge, so one `min`
reduction of the merged weights finds a bad weight wherever it was (behind a cheaper parallel edge, on a second
type, on a self-loop): `InvalidWeight`. A `max` reduction finds a `+inf` the multi-edge pass left behind, a broken
tensor invariant (`Internal`). Neither allocates. Self-loops are then dropped (`Matrix::drop_diagonal`) and the
skeleton is `pattern_union(W, Wᵀ)` (`GxB_eWiseUnion` with `GrB_ONEB_BOOL`). A missing or non-numeric attribute
weighs 1.0, as in C.

The operators take typed arguments (`InlineWeightFn`, `MeWeightFn`). Where they are registered, each is converted
with one `transmute` straight into the bindings' function type (`GxB_index_unary_function`,
`GxB_index_binary_function`), which is an `Option<extern fn>`: that has the layout of a bare fn pointer with `None`
as null, so the result is `Some` of the operator. The typed signature matches what GraphBLAS passes, argument by
argument; only the pointee types differ. They and their context type are created once per process and never freed,
as the C implementation

pullRequests.title: CCH: Graph index API, Cch::new_version and Cch::fits
pullRequests.body:
Fills in the `Graph` methods the contract skeleton declared: `create_cch_index`, `drop_cch_index`, `cch_indexes`,
`cch_index`, `rebuild_cch_indexes`. `create` and `rebuild` build through `CchInput::build`. Every write builds a fresh
`Cch` and replaces or removes an entry on the current version only: a reader holding an older version keeps its
`Arc<Cch>`, and rolling a write back means dropping the new version. Writes are all-or-nothing (`create` checks
`AlreadyExists` before building; `rebuild` builds and re-resolves every definition before replacing any).

Also what a writer needs to choose between recustomizing and rebuilding: `Cch::new_version()` (the `Topology` is shared
by `Arc`, the metric copied) and `Cch::fits(&weights)` (would `customize` accept the shape; no weight value is looked
at). `customize` goes through the same `fits`. Consequences: `customize` looks each entry's arc up twice (O(m) against
an O(sum of triangles) relax), and weights that are both badly shaped and badly valued are now `Internal` (shape)
rather than `InvalidWeight`; a rebuild is unaffected.

Tested on a real `Graph` built through the Graph API: lookup, listing, `AlreadyExists`, `drop`, `NotFound`; an index over
two of three types leaves the third unusable; parallel edges resolve to the cheapest; every ordered pair against the
Dijkstra oracle; MVCC (a create or rebuild on a new version is invisible to the reader's version and keeps its `Arc`;
a rebuild with an unresolvable definition replaces none); a NaN behind a cheaper parallel edge fails `create` with
`InvalidWeight`; 30 seeded zero-heavy graphs with simple paths; every invalid weight refused by `build` and `customize`;
`new_version` leaves the original byte-identical; `fits` agrees with `customize`.

Part of #3134. Closes #3212

pullRequests.title: Rebuild touched CCH indexes after each write
pullRequests.body:
Keeps CCH indexes correct under writes (#3214). A write query records what it touched in a `CchDirty` held by
`Pending` (a node created or deleted: every index; a relationship created or deleted: the indexes spanning its type; an
attribute set or removed on an existing relationship: the indexes spanning its type whose weight it is). Once the whole
query has succeeded, the runtime hands it to `Graph::cch_flush` on the query's private version, which rebuilds each
touched index into a new `Arc<Cch>`, all before any is swapped. A failed rebuild (for example a negative weight on an
indexed type) fails the query naming the index and the cause, and the existing abandon-write path leaves the committed
indexes untouched. Without a CCH index nothing is recorded and the flush is one `is_empty()` check.

**Replayed effects follow the native indexes' `IndexDocs` pattern.** `apply_effects` makes one `CchDirty` for the
buffer, threads it through `apply_record` next to the `IndexDocs`, and flushes it once after `commit_index_docs`, so
`GRAPH.EFFECT` (and everything that applies a buffer) rebuilds only the indexes a record can have changed; unrelated
records stage nothing. Records are marked by the same rules as the query path: nodes created or deleted mark every
index (a deleted node has no edges left, the primary ships each as a `DELETE_EDGE`), edges created or deleted mark the
type the record states, `UPDATE_EDGE` marks (type, weight attribute) when the weight is among its attributes, and
node updates, labels, schema, index and constraint records mark nothing. A stated relationship type id is bounds-checked
like `UPDATE_EDGE`'s; `DELETE_EDGE`'s is read only when an index is held. A failed rebuild fails the buffer, so it takes
the existing rollback and divergence path. `GRAPH.BULK` cannot say what it touched and still rebuilds every index.

random and zero-weight-

pullRequests.title: Add the db.idx.cch.query procedure and the db.indexes CCH listing
pullRequests.body:
Registers `db.idx.cch.query` as a read-only procedure (usable in `GRAPH.RO_QUERY`), yielding `pathWeight` and `path`.
Argument parsing and validation mirror C's `_read_config` (`proc_cch_idx_query.c`) error for error: `sourceNode` /
`targetNode` presence and type, `relTypes` shape, non-emptiness and existence, `weightProp` type and existence.
`db.indexes` lists CCH indexes shaped like C.

The procedure looks the index up, calls `Cch::query`, and resolves the unpacked node-id path into a `Value::Path`.

**Path to edges.** Each hop is turned into the relationship it uses by a `(src, dst)` lookup, not by scanning all of the
hop's source node's outgoing edges: `cheapest_edge` makes one `Tensor::get(src, dst)` per indexed type, which resolves the
delta layers and, for a multi-edge pair, reads only that pair's row of its `me` block. The selection rule matches C's
`_best_road_edge`: the cheapest edge across parallel edges and the indexed types by the weight attribute, a missing or
non-numeric weight counting as 1.0, a tie going to the earlier type and then to the lower edge id. The attribute read is
one function, `edge_weight`, shared with the index build. No per-arc memory is added.

**Inside a write query** the procedure first flushes that query's CCH changes when, and only when, the index it is about
to read was touched by them (`Runtime::flush_cch_before_reading`); otherwise the end-of-query flush is the only one.
Without it, a `SET` earlier in the query was invisible and a `DELETE` failed the whole write with an inconsistent
hierarchy.

missing-attribute hop; `cheapest_edge` against the old scan on every ordered pair of a random three-type graph (parallel

pullRequests.title: Add RDB v20 with a CCH definitions payload
pullRequests.body:
Persists CCH index definitions only, as C's `CCHIndex_RdbSave`/`RdbLoad` do: a new `EncodeState::CchIndices = 10`
(`Final` moves to 11 and is never written), one count-gated payload on key 0, `ENCODING_VERSION` and both `RedisType`
encvers 19 -> 20. The decoder collects definitions in all three decode paths and, after the other indexes are rebuilt,
builds them with `Graph::load_cch_indexes`; a graph without CCH indexes never reaches it. The hierarchy itself is derived
data and is rebuilt on load.

A definition whose hierarchy cannot be built on load (a weight C accepts and this engine refuses, a graph past the size
ceiling, an unknown type, a duplicate definition) is dropped with a warning naming the index and the reason. It never
fails the load or panics the server: the graph must load. This is independent of `CCH_INDEX`, which gates the DDL only.

Tested (`tests/flow/test_rdb_cch_layout.py`, listed in `flow_tests_done.txt`). A Rust-to-Rust reload cannot see a wrong
layout, so the first class reads the bytes of a real saved RDB: the key ends with the payload exactly as C's
`RdbSaveCCH_v20` writes it (index count, then per index the type count, the sorted type ids and the weight attribute id,
each a type tag and 8 LE bytes) for two indexes and for a multi-type index; the directory lists `CchIndices = 10` last
and never `Final`; a graph without an index writes no payload; the graphdata type is encoding version 20. A second class
reloads with `DEBUG RELOAD` and checks that `db.indexes` and `db.idx.cch.query` answers are unchanged, and that a
definition naming an unknown relationship type is dropped with a warning while the graph and its other index load.
