**Note on the reporter's framing:** the report was titled as unauthenticated. That only holds for a server running with no `requirepass` and no ACL. On any instance with authentication configured, this requires a successfully authenticated connection with permission to run `GRAPH.QUERY`. Severity below is our own assessment, not the reporter's.

## Problem

`src/execution_plan/ops/op_aggregate.c` line 126:

static Group *_GetGroup(OpAggregate *op, Record r) {

- Enforce a maximum projection/key count at query-compile time.

issues.title: numeric index - CoW B-tree substrate: point lookups, memory accounting, tuple cursor, narrowable doc width
issues.body:
The CoW B-tree that backs the numeric index needs primitives the index and its build path depend on:

- **point lookups** — `contains_key` and `first_doc`, the cheap existence/first-hit primitives
  (no page `Arc` clones, no cursor stack)
- **tuple cursor** — `range_tuples` and the bulk `for_each_tuple` walk, which the online build's
  install needs to enumerate DELTA and TOMB as `(key, doc)` pairs (the doc-only range cursor
  reads keys at leaf boundaries and cannot supply them)
- **memory accounting** — `heap_bytes`
- **narrowable doc width** — `DOC_BYTES` const generic, so a tree can pack more entries per page
  when the id range allows it
- `insert`/`remove` returning whether anything changed, for callers keeping an exact live count

Closed by #2278.

issues.title: numeric index - serve `IN [...]` as a union of point lookups
issues.body:
`n.a IN [...]` reaches the index as `Or(Equal, ..)` — the scan ops desugar it before the index
sees it — and `query_numeric` declines every `Or`, so the whole shape falls through to RediSearch.

Serve it natively as a lazy chain of point cursors over the deduplicated member keys. No merge:
Cypher guarantees no order without `ORDER BY`, so chaining is O(1) per result, allocates no heap
and stays droppable so a `LIMIT` exits early. Nested unions must flatten — `a IN [..] OR a IN [..]`
arrives as an `Or` of `Or`s.

A member the numeric column cannot represent must decline the **whole** union rather than serving
the numeric subset: a string member may still match entities another kind holds, and answering
without them is a wrong answer, not a slower one. This matches the C core, which drops to a
filtered label scan when a list holds a non-scalar member.

Measured against the six index flow suites with the RediSearch fallback disabled (so nothing can
pass by falling through): 14 failures before, 10 after — the five `IN` entries, node and edge.

issues.title: native index - no fallback: the native index is the only index under the flag
issues.body:
Today `index-falkordb` dark-launches: a predicate the native index cannot serve falls through to
RediSearch, so every gap is invisible and every native regression is silently covered.

Make the flag mean what the design says — native is the *only* index, and an unserviceable
predicate **fails loudly** rather than quietly returning RediSearch's rows.

This cannot land alone: it turns ~10 currently-green gate tests red, which is the point (the gaps
become visible) but only defensible alongside the xfail ledger that records them. Ship the two
together; the CI wiring that enforces the ledger follows in #2357.

Note the failure mode matters. A measurement spike used an empty iterator, which is fine for
counting gaps and wrong to ship — a user would see a query quietly return nothing. It needs to
surface as a diagnosable error.

Parent: #2357

issues.body:
## The class

Three PRs in flight fix the same bug shape: **a write operation whose cost scaled with the resident graph rather than with the work it did.** Each was invisible at test size, each surfaced only under a profile on a large graph, and each turned out to be one line choosing the wrong primitive.

Worth naming as a class because the fixes are unrelated but the *smell* is identical, and because C is flat in graph size on all three — so any residual growth is a Rust-side defect, not a property of the workload.

| PR | Where the graph size leaked in | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #2378 (merged) | `delete_nodes` scanned every `node_labels_matrix` entry, and `remove_mask`'s `element_wise_multiply` takes the base `m` as an operand, so GraphBLAS walks it | Deleting one node from a 200k-node graph: **240.4M → 3.1M instructions**. C: 564k, flat |

> An operation that touches *k* entities costs O(*k*), not O(graph).

Stated that way it is checkable, and the cheap way to check it is the one all three PRs used: **measure the same single-entity operation at several resident graph sizes and require the number to be flat.** A ratio between two sizes is a better regression signal than an absolute number, because it fails loudly when someone reintroduces a whole-matrix operand and does not drift with hardware.

issues.title: Inline property map on a traversal endpoint is planned twice, disabling index utilization
issues.body:
`MATCH (a:L {p: v})-[]->(b)` plans the predicate `a.p = v` **twice**, and both copies survive into the final plan.

### Where the duplicate comes from

Two emissions that are each correct in isolation:

* `planner/mod.rs` emits a filter for `relationship.from.attrs` above the `CondTraverse`. Its comment says this is deliberate — the chain-reversal pass needs to see it there.
* `optimizer/select_scan_node.rs::make_scan_subtree` emits the same filter again when it builds that node's scan.

`optimizer/push_filters_down.rs` then merges the two stacked filters by flattening their conjuncts into a single `And` — with no deduplication.

### Impact

**Every row pays the predicate twice**, on what is close to the most common shape in Cypher.

**Index utilization is lost entirely.** Two conjuncts on one key become `IndexQuery::And`, which no index kind serves, so the pair is strictly worse than either conjunct alone and the query falls back to a full label scan. `MATCH (a:Person {id: 5}) RETURN a.name` uses the index; add a traversal and it does not.

### Reproducing

```
GRAPH.EXPLAIN g "MATCH (a:Person {id: 5})-[:KNOWS]-(b) RETURN count(b)"
```

The plan carries a `Filter` above the `Conditional Traverse` holding the same comparison already pushed into the scan below it.

### Scope

Affects the shipping engine, not only the `index-falkordb` build. It was found by running the benchmark suite against the native index, where an unserviceable `And` is a hard error rather than a silent fallback — 34 of that suite's 40 failures were this one shape.

### Fix

Deduplicate exact-duplicate conjuncts when merging stacked filters. The comparison must be conservative: a false negative costs one redundant evaluation, a false positive deletes a conjunct the query needs and silently returns extra rows. Non-deterministic functions must never compare equal even to themselves — `rand() < 0.5 AND rand() < 0.5` is two independent draws.

Unbounded recursion in expression evaluator: nested GRAPH.QUERY expression exhausts stack
issues.body:
Reported to `[email]` by `firewok137` / "JerryGW", who reports it against v4.20.1. Filing publicly with corrected severity.

**Maintainer note on the reported framing.** The report states no authentication is required. That is not accurate for any deployment with `requirepass` or ACLs configured — `GRAPH.QUERY` is subject to normal Redis authentication. Scored below as `PR:L`. PoC payload details are intentionally omitted here.

## Problem

`_AR_EXP_Evaluate` in `src/arithmetic/arithmetic_expression.c` (line 574) walks the arithmetic expression tree by recursion with no depth limit:

- `_AR_EXP_Evaluate` → `_AR_EXP_EvaluateFunctionCall` for `AR_EXP_OP` nodes
- `_AR_EXP_EvaluateFunctionCall` → `_AR_EXP_Evaluate` for each child (line 460)

Expression tree depth is a direct function of query text nesting, which the client controls. A query with deeply nested parenthesised arithmetic produces a correspondingly deep tree; the reporter reached `SIGSEGV` at ~50,000 levels against the default 8MB stack.

There is no depth counter, no configured maximum, and no stack headroom check anywhere on this path.

Because the stack is fully exhausted, the `SIGSEGV` handler cannot run and no `REDIS BUG REPORT` is emitted — the process simply disappears. That makes this materially harder to diagnose in production than a normal crash, and it is worth noting for triage that several of these reports share that property.

### Relationship to #2330

#2330 covers unbounded mutual recursion in `src/ast/param_parser.c` (`parse_array` ↔ `parse_value`). This is the same class of defect at a different stage: #2330 is reached while parsing parameters, this one while evaluating the expression tree. They are separate call graphs and need separate bounds, but a single shared "maximum nesting depth" configuration would sensibly govern both.

Worth checking as part of the same pass: the AST is also built and validated by recursive descent, so a nesting limit is probably best enforced once at parse time

issues.title: UDF hardening: graph.UDF missing write flag, fail-open ASSERT on RDB load, no JS interrupt handler
issues.body:
Reported to `[email]` by `firewok137` / "JerryGW", who reports it against v4.20.1. Filing publicly with substantially revised framing.

**Maintainer note on the reported framing.** The report is titled "unauthenticated JS execution" and presents JS execution itself as the vulnerability. Both parts need correcting:

- `GRAPH.UDF` is subject to normal Redis authentication. On any server with `requirepass`/ACLs it is not reachable unauthenticated.
- Executing user-supplied JavaScript **is the intended function of the UDF feature**, exactly as `EVAL` executes user-supplied Lua. An authorised user registering a script that runs is not a vulnerability on its own.

That said, the report does surface three real defects around the feature, which are the reason this is being filed rather than closed. PoC payload details are intentionally omitted here.

## Problem 1 — `graph.UDF` is not registered as a write command

`src/module.c` line 368:

```c
RedisModule_CreateCommand(ctx,
        "graph.UDF",
        Graph_UDF,
        "deny-script",     // no "write", no "deny-oom"
        0, 0, 0);
```

- Redis will not reject it on a read-only replica, so a replica can be given library state the primary does not have. That is a divergence source independent of the effects-replication path.
- It is not covered by `deny-oom`, so registration proceeds under memory pressure.
- With `0, 0, 0` the command declares no keys, so ACL key patterns cannot scope it. Operators can only allow or deny it wholesale via `-graph.UDF`. That is worth documenting explicitly, since a rule like `~graph:*` will not constrain UDF registration the way an operator would reasonably expect.

`src/serializers/decoders/current/v19/decode_udf.c`:

```c

for (uint64_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {

issues.title: Aggregates over an edge property fall off the vectorized path and cost 2.3x
issues.body:
## Symptom

Wrapping an edge property in an expression makes the query **cheaper**:

```
MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN sum(r.k)        2,864 instructions/edge
MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN sum(r.k * 2)    1,601 instructions/edge
```

Measured on `main` (`27edbd56`), 176,000 edges over 1,000 nodes, instructions from `proc_pid_rusage` on the server pid. Reproduces to 0.1% and is independent of query order. `max(r.k)` and `count(r.k)` sit with `sum(r.k)`; `sum(r.k + 0)` sits with `sum(r.k * 2)`. So it is not the aggregate function and not arithmetic — it is whether the argument is a *bare* property.

The C implementation does not have this shape: there, `sum(r.k)` (3,221) and `sum(r.k * 2)` (3,451) are ordered the way you would expect.

## Cause

`AggregateOp` classifies `sum(x.prop)` as `AggInputKind::Property` and serves it from a bulk materialiser. That materialiser is node-only:

- `Batch::extract_node_ids` returns `Some` only for `Column::NodeIds`, `None` otherwise
- `Runtime::materialize_node_property` has no relationship counterpart

Classification never consults the variable's type, so `sum(r.prop)` over a **relationship** takes that path too, fails `extract_node_ids` on every batch, and falls through to `consume_batch_per_row` — which calls `to_owned_row()`, allocating a `Vec` of every column for every row.

`sum(r.k * 2)` classifies as `AggInputKind::Computed` instead, stays on the vectorized path, and reads through a borrowed `BatchRow`. Hence the inversion: **the specialised path is slower than the general one because it is being abandoned.**

The code already documents this cost for the `Computed` case — "Falling back to `consume_input_per_row` … rebuilds a full owned `Row` per row, measured at ~1,320 instructions/row" — which matches the ~1,260/edge seen here. The relationship case simply was not considered when the classifier was written.

## Impact

Any aggregate over an edge property: `sum`, `count`, `max`, `min`, `collect`. Node aggregates are unaffected. It

rust: AOF replay crashes the server — cannot-block predicate is narrower than C's dispatcher
issues.body:
## Summary

The Rust engine decides "run inline vs block and hand off to the thread pool" on a narrower
predicate than the C reference. C's dispatcher treats five flags as "this context must not
block"; the Rust ports check only two.

`src/commands/cmd_dispatcher.c` on `master` (the C reference):

```c
bool main_thread = (is_replicated ||
    (flags & (REDISMODULE_CTX_FLAGS_MULTI       |
            REDISMODULE_CTX_FLAGS_LUA           |
            REDISMODULE_CTX_FLAGS_DENY_BLOCKING |
            REDISMODULE_CTX_FLAGS_LOADING))) ;
```

Every Rust guard site keeps `MULTI || REPLICATED` and drops `LUA`, `DENY_BLOCKING` and
`LOADING`:

* `src/graph_core.rs:861` — `GRAPH.QUERY` write path
* `src/graph_core.rs:1171` — `GRAPH.PROFILE`
* `src/commands/memory.rs:226` — `GRAPH.MEMORY`
* `src/commands/record.rs:247` — `GRAPH.RECORD`
* `src/commands/explain.rs:78` — `GRAPH.EXPLAIN`

AOF replay drives a fake client that carries `CLIENT_DENY_BLOCKING` but **not**
`CLIENT_MASTER` — so `REPLICATED` is not set for it and none of the remaining flags are
checked. The command therefore takes the blocking path and leaves the loading client
blocked, which Redis asserts against.

## Impact

**A server with `appendonly yes` crashes on restart.** Not a clean failure — `SIGSEGV`, and
the server never comes up:

```
# === ASSERTION FAILED ===
# ==> aof.c:1692 '(fakeClient->flags & CLIENT_BLOCKED) == 0' is not true
# Redis 255.255.255 crashed by signal: 11, si_code: 2
```

## Reproduction

Default configuration, **no index and no constraint anywhere**, two ordinary `CREATE`
statements. `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD` is raised only to make the verbatim-query branch
deterministic; see "Why this is not exotic" below.

```bash
MODULE=/path/to/libfalkordb.so
D=$(mktemp -d)
redis-server --port 7311 --daemonize yes --loadmodule "$MODULE" --dir "$D" \
  --appendonly yes --appendfsync always --logfile "$D/r.log"
sleep 2

redis-cli -p 7311 GRAPH.CONFIG SET EFFECTS_THRESHOLD 1000000
redis-cli -p 7311 GRAPH.QUERY

issues.title: ci(deps): consolidate the weekly dependabot bumps targeting `main` into a single PR
issues.body:
## Problem

Dependabot opened five separate PRs against `main` for this week's `github-actions` and `cargo` updates:

| PR | Bump |
| --- | --- |
| #2404 | `docker/login-action` 4.4.0 → 4.6.0 |
| #2405 | `Swatinem/rust-cache` 2.9.1 → 2.9.2 |
| #2406 | `actions/checkout` 7.0.0 → 7.0.1 |
| #2407 | `rquickjs` 0.12.1 → 0.12.2 |
| #2408 | `lru` 0.18.1 → 0.18.2 |

Each one runs the full CI matrix for what amounts to a handful of pinned-SHA and `Cargo.lock` line changes, so a single week of routine updates costs five complete CI runs and five separate reviews.

There is also a policy interaction worth naming: #2243 made "every PR closes an issue" a required check with **no exemptions for bots**, and explicitly recorded that dependabot PRs would each need an issue filed before they could merge. Consolidating turns that per-PR cost into one issue per batch.

## Proposal

Cherry-pick the five dependabot commits onto one branch and open a single PR against `main`, preserving dependabot's original authorship on each commit. Close the five superseded PRs pointing at the replacement.

## Requirements

- [ ] One commit per original dependabot PR, original author metadata preserved, so `git log` still attributes the bump correctly.
- [ ] The consolidated diff is exactly the union of the five source diffs — no drive-by edits, no logic changes.
- [ ] Verify containment before closing anything: every added line of each source PR must be present in the consolidated diff.
- [ ] Close #2404–#2408 with a comment naming the replacement PR.
- [ ] The consolidated PR closes this issue, satisfying the #2243 check.

## Notes

`main` is now the repository default branch, so a `Closes #N` body keyword does register a closing link here — unlike the `master` line, which still needs the Development sidebar (see #2243).

issues.title: rust: GRAPH.BULK declared node/edge counts are unbounded — one command aborts the server
issues.body:
## Summary

`GRAPH.BULK` trusts the client-declared `node_count` / `edge_count` and hands them straight
to `Vec::with_capacity`. A single command with a large count aborts the process.

`graph/src/graph/graph.rs`:

```rust
pub fn reserve_nodes(&mut self, count: usize) -> Vec<NodeId> {
    let count = count as u64;
    let mut ids = Vec::with_capacity(count as usize);   // <-- client-controlled
```

`reserve_relationships` has the identical shape, so both count fields are affected. Nothing
validates the declared counts against the token payload — the only existing check covers the
number of *tokens*:

```rust
if token_strings.len() != node_token_count + rel_token_count {
    return Err(... "token count mismatch" ...)
}
```

## Reproduction

One command. No binary payload, no CSV, no loader — `node_token_count` and `rel_token_count`
are both 0, so the token-count check passes and nothing is ever parsed.

```console
$ redis-cli GRAPH.BULK g BEGIN 9223372036854775807 0 0 0
Error: Server closed the connection

$ redis-cli ping
Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:6379: Connection refused
```

Log:

```

capacity overflow
Backtrace:

issues.title: Traversals resolve a representative edge id even when nothing reads the edge
issues.body:
## What

A chain-less `CondTraverse` binds its edge alias to a representative edge id for every row it emits, and finding one costs a tensor lookup per row: `Tensor::get` → `eff_get`, which reads through the `dp`/`dm`/`m` delta layers with up to three GraphBLAS `extractElement` calls.

That work is thrown away whenever the query never reads the edge:

```cypher
MATCH (a:N)-[:R]->(x:N) RETURN count(x)
```

## Why `emit_relationship` does not already cover it

`emit_relationship` answers a different question — row *multiplicity*. False means one row per `(src, dst)` pair instead of one per edge. An anonymous edge inside a named path gets `emit_relationship: false` (one row per pair is correct) and still has to be bound, because `PathBuilder` reads the alias to assemble the path. So "how many rows" and "does anything read the edge" need separate answers, and only the second licenses skipping the lookup.

The runtime comment at [`cond_traverse.rs`](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/blob/main/graph/src/runtime/ops/cond_traverse.rs) records exactly this: *"Required because downstream PathBuilder reads the edge alias even when emit_relationship is false."*

## Measured cost

1,000 nodes, 88,000 `(src, dst)` pairs, release build, instructions per pair (median of 5, macOS `proc_pid_rusage`):

| query | instr/pair |
|---|---:|
| `MATCH (a:N)-[:R]->(x:N) RETURN count(x)` | 1,467 |
| same, with the lookup destructively stubbed out | 796 |

So the lookup is ~46% of the operator's cost on a traversal that never uses its result. It is paid per pair regardless of multiplicity, so it is not a multi-edge-only problem — it shows up on ordinary single-edge graphs too.

## Fix

Give `CondTraverse` a `bind_relationship` flag, conservatively true, lowered by a `reduce_bound_edge` optimizer pass that walks ancestors for a reference to the edge alias — the same shape as the existing `emit_path` / `reduce_var_len_path` pair. When false, skip the lookup and leave the edge column unbound.

issues.title: Demoting multi-edge pairs is quadratic in the batch: 95x the C engine per transition
issues.body:
## What

Deleting an edge from a 2-edge pair — the *demote* transition that returns the surviving id to the inline slot — costs the Rust engine ~95x what it costs C, and the cost is **quadratic in how many pairs one query demotes**.

## Measured

macOS arm64, release, instructions from `proc_pid_rusage` on the server pid. Hub graph: one `:H` node, N `:N` nodes, two `:R` edges per pair, then `MATCH (h:H)-[r:R {k:1}]->(n:N) DELETE r`.

**Attribution — same query, same row count, with and without the transition:**

| engine | demote 2→1 | empty a 1-edge pair | the transition |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C | 10,712 | 8,390 | **2,322** instr/pair |
| Rust | 228,765 | 8,810 | **219,955** instr/pair (95x) |

Deleting an edge that merely empties a single-edge pair costs both engines the same (~8.4–8.8k), so the query, predicate and plan are not the difference. The transition is.

**Quadratic in batch size** (bystanders fixed, only the number of demoted pairs varies):

| pairs demoted | Rust total | Rust per-pair | C total | C per-pair |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 125 | 6,589,323 | 52,715 | 2,878,645 | 23,029 |
| 250 | 32,664,831 | 130,659 | 4,044,690 | 16,179 |
| 500 | 80,599,112 | 161,198 | 6,504,208 | 13,008 |
| 1000 | 228,783,748 | 228,784 | 10,773,052 | 10,773 |

Rust's per-pair cost *grows* 4.3x across an 8x batch; C's *falls* by half, which is what amortisation should look like.

**Flat in `|me|`** — 500 demotes while the overflow matrix grows 17x:

| `|me|` ids | Rust | C |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 | 162,919 | 25,739 |
| 5,000 | 164,691 | 31,233 |
| 17,000 | 166,353 | 47,867 |

So nothing is scanning `me`. (C is the one that scales with `|me|` here, from a far lower base.)

The per-edge slow path in `Tensor::remove_all` calls `eff_get(src, dst)` per edge, and `eff_get` opens with `wait_fwd()`. Demoting writes the survivor back through `dp` (`dp.insert` / `dp.erase`), so every iteration leaves `dp` pending and the next iteration's `wait_fwd()` mat

issues.title: Multi-edge point reads have two cost states, 1.27x apart, selected non-monotonically by graph size
issues.body:
## What

A bound multi-edge point read (`MATCH (a:N {id:0})-[r:R]->() RETURN count(r)`, 1,000 pairs from one source, 2 edges each) lands in one of two distinct cost states in the Rust engine — about 4.35k or about 5.5k instructions per pair — and which one it lands in depends on graph size, non-monotonically. The C engine is flat across the whole range.

Only the number of *other* populated adjacency rows varies. The read itself — same source, same 1,000 pairs, same k=2, same index, 20 reps — is identical in every row.

| populated pairs | Rust | C |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 | 4,432 | 4,235 |
| 11,000 | **5,443** | 4,271 |
| 41,000 | 4,347 | 4,293 |
| 88,000 | **5,507** | 4,283 |
| 121,000 | **5,513** | 4,288 |

Instructions per pair, `proc_pid_rusage` on the server pid, macOS arm64, release. The low state is at parity with C; the high state is 1.27–1.29x it.

Note this is not a single bump: low at 1k, high at 11k, low at 41k, high at 88k and 121k. Whatever selects the state crosses at least twice in this range, and both of the largest sizes measured are in the high state.

## Why this matters

The high state is what makes the Rust engine look 1.28–1.29x worse than C on single-pair lookup at µ=1.1 and µ=2 in the multiplicity sweep: that sweep's µ=2 graph has 88,000 populated pairs, which is measured above at 5,507 — the high state.

It is *not* a cost of the inline-first edge storage. In a controlled decomposition at equal k and equal graph size, a k=2 read is at parity (Rust 4,576 vs C 4,589), and Rust wins from k=3 up (0.92x at k=3, 0.75x at k=8) because its per-additional-id walk costs 448 instructions against C's 854. Its fixed charge for entering the sentinel path is 1,993 against C's 1,013, and those two cancel at k=2.

So a real and reproducible characteristic was being attributed to the design. Worth understanding before anyone optimises the wrong component.

## Hypotheses tested and refuted

1. **The sentinel path scales with `|me|`.** No — reading the same

issues.title: Document the relationship tensor's design, invariants and measured cost as a standalone paper
issues.body:
## Why

The relationship tensor — a UINT64 adjacency matrix holding a lone edge id inline, an overflow matrix `me` for multi-edge pairs, a reserved sentinel marking the transition, and three MVCC delta layers over all of it — is the least self-documenting part of the engine. Its correctness rests on invariants (`dp ∩ m = ∅`, `dm ⊆ m`, `dp ∩ dm = ∅`, cancel-to-clean, `multi_count` agreement) that are enforced across a dozen call sites and stated nowhere in one place. Several of the hazards in that code exist only because a delta cell can carry a *value* rather than mere presence, which no standard MVCC presentation covers.

Two things have since been produced that are worth capturing alongside it:

- **A Lean 4 mechanisation** of the state machine and the invariants (`proofs/tensor/`), which has already paid for itself twice — it identified two unreachable branches that were then removed, one of which fabricated edge id 0 on a backward read.
- **A measured evaluation** comparing the design against the C engine's container-per-cell design, at both the engine and the data-structure boundary, which corrected several things we believed from analytic reasoning alone.

## What

Land `docs/papers/tensor.tex` and the Lean development as repository documentation, so the design rationale, the invariant set, the proof strategies and the measurements live next to the code they describe rather than in commit messages and issue threads.

This is documentation and proofs only — no engine behaviour changes.

issues.title: GRAPH.INFO with no arguments returns an arity error on the Rust engine
issues.body:
On the Rust engine, `GRAPH.INFO` with no arguments returns an arity error. On the C engine it returns every section.

**Rust engine (`falkordb/falkordb:edge`, digest-shared with `:edge-rs`)**

```
127.0.0.1:6379> GRAPH.INFO
(error) ERR wrong number of arguments for 'graph.INFO' command
```

**C engine (`falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.1`)**

```
127.0.0.1:6379> GRAPH.INFO
# Running queries

# Waiting queries

Object Pool
Unique Objects in Pool
0
Average References per Object
0
```

Same result on `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-rs`, so it isn't specific to the Docker Hub tag.

Passing sections explicitly behaves the same on both engines, and `GRAPH.INFO runningqueries waitingqueries objectpool` returns byte-identical output to the old no-arg call.

### Impact

This breaks `db.info()` in the node client, which sends `GRAPH.INFO` with no section — 5 tests fail against `:edge`. Any client calling it bare hits the same thing.

### Not asking to change

An unknown section is now `ERR Unknown section: x` instead of the old `no section found` string. That looks like a deliberate improvement.

### Question

Is dropping the no-arg form intentional? If so it's worth flagging as a breaking change so clients can adapt; otherwise it looks like an arity check that got tightened by accident.

issues.title: OPTIONAL MATCH ignores a null-bound variable in a comma-separated pattern, inflating the result
issues.body:
**FalkorDB version**

FalkorDB v4.20.1 and the Rust rewrite `falkordb/falkordb:edge-rs` . Both versions reproduce the bug.

**Describe the bug**

FalkorDB returns the wrong row count when a variable null-bound by a failed `OPTIONAL MATCH` appears in a later comma-separated multi-part `OPTIONAL MATCH`. The null-bound element is silently dropped from the pattern, so the remaining part is matched against the whole graph (Cartesian product). Both the v4.20.1 (C engine) and the `edge-rs` Rust rewrite reproduce it identically.

On an empty database:

```cypher
CREATE (:A);
CREATE (:A);
MATCH (a) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)--(b) OPTIONAL MATCH (b),(c) RETURN count(*) AS n;
```

| | Result |
|---|---|
| FalkorDB v4.20.1 (`latest`) | **4** (wrong) |
| FalkorDB `edge-rs` (Rust) | **4** (wrong) |
| Neo4j 2026.06.0 | **2** (correct) |

Both `:A` nodes are isolated, so `OPTIONAL MATCH (a)--(b)` fails for each `a` and binds `b` to null. Under Cypher null propagation the multi-part pattern `(b),(c)` must fail as a whole, keeping the row with `b` and `c` null → 2 rows. FalkorDB instead matches `(c)` as if `(b)` were not part of the pattern. The returned rows make this visible (identical on both versions):

| FalkorDB (4 rows) | Neo4j (2 rows) |
|---|---|
| a = node1, b = **null**, c = node1 | a = node1, b = null, c = null |
| a = node1, b = **null**, c = node2 | a = node2, b = null, c = null |
| a = node2, b = **null**, c = node1 | |
| a = node2, b = **null**, c = node2 | |

In **every** FalkorDB row `b` is null yet `c` is bound to every node — exactly as if the `(b)` element did not exist.

**To reproduce**

On an empty graph, run:

```
GRAPH.QUERY demo "CREATE (:A)"
GRAPH.QUERY demo "CREATE (:A)"
GRAPH.QUERY demo "MATCH (a) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)--(b) OPTIONAL MATCH (b),(c) RETURN count(*) AS n"
```

The last one returns `4`, expected `2`.

issues.title: CondTraverse's bind_relationship duplicates emit_relationship and can be removed
issues.body:
## What

#2428 added a `bind_relationship` flag to `IR::CondTraverse`, plus a `reduce_bound_edge` optimizer pass to lower it, to decide whether the batched traversal path should resolve a representative edge id. That flag is redundant: it is equal to `emit_relationship` in every reachable case.

After the passes run:

- `emit_relationship` = `emit_rel_initial && referenced_by_ancestor`
- `bind_relationship` = `referenced_by_ancestor`

They can only differ when `referenced && !emit_rel_initial` — an anonymous edge that no named path mentions, yet which some ancestor references. `_anon…` aliases are synthesised by the binder and cannot be named in Cypher, and the only IR that references one is `PathBuilder`, which implies the edge *is* in a path's vars and therefore that `emit_rel` already returned true. So the case is unreachable.

Checked empirically as well: over 18 queries spanning named/anonymous edges, named paths, `relationships(p)`, `OPTIONAL MATCH`, `WITH` barriers, `DELETE`, `SET`, multi-hop, cartesian-plus-join and `DISTINCT`, the two flags agree on every `CondTraverse` — 0 disagreements.

## The stronger consequence

The flag needn't be replaced by a gate on `emit_relationship` either — the lookup it guards is unreachable. `batched_eligible` already requires `!emit_relationship`, so the batched path runs only when nothing above reads the edge alias. The representative-edge-id lookup in that path was therefore always dead work, for every query, and so was the `RelIds` column it filled.

The comment that justified it — "Required because downstream PathBuilder reads the edge alias even when emit_relationship is false" — is stale. `emit_rel` treats an anonymous edge appearing in a named path's vars as emitting, so a `PathBuilder` consumer forces `emit_relationship: true` and routes the query to the per-row path instead.

issues.title: multi_count is a cache of me's row structure and can be derived instead of maintained
issues.body:
## What

`Tensor::multi_count` tracks how many `(src, dst)` pairs are multi-edge. It exists only to make `Tensor::edge_count` — the cardinality identity `|m| + |dp| − |dm| − |dp ∩ m| − multi + |me|` — an O(1) computation.

It is not independent state. By promotion completeness, `ε(p) = MULTI_EDGE` exactly when row `κ(p)` of `me` is non-empty, so the quantity is a structural property of `me` and the field is a cache of it. That cache has to be maintained by hand: seven call sites add or remove a row of `me` and three of them touch the counter, so a future edit is the likely way it drifts, and the failure is quiet — a wrong edge count in some later query, or an underflow near `2^64` that reaches a `Vec` pre-allocation in one graph algorithm.

## Why it can simply go

Two things make removal cheaper than it looks:

- `has_multi_edge()` never used the counter — it is already `me.nvals() != 0`.
- `Decode` never read it from the blob; it derived it from the tensor-section counts. So the serialisation format is unaffected.

That leaves `edge_count()` as the only consumer, and it is called from planning, `db.*` procedures and two graph algorithms — never per row.

## Deriving it

- No multi-edge pair anywhere (the dominant case): `me.nvals() == 0`, answer 0.
- `me` assembled: its non-empty row count is metadata, since a hypersparse matrix stores its non-empty vectors and nothing else.
- `me` carrying live deltas: walk the effective rows, `O(multi)`, never `O(|E|)`.

The third case is the one worth worrying about, and measurement says it is not reached in practice: commit folds `me`, so by the time any query asks for a count the metadata path is taken.

## Measured

Full 317-query suite, instructions: **0.9961x** and **1.0018x** across two independent before/after pairs — no regression either way, and the write paths that promote and demote are flat (`write 1m` 1.002x, `create 10k` 1.000x, `multi-edge demote/promote` 0.995x).

issues.title: UNIQUE constraint silently not enforced for property values over 4096 bytes
issues.body:
**FalkorDB version**

FalkorDB v4.20.1 and v4.20.2. Both reproduce the bug, in different forms. The Rust rewrite `falkordb/falkordb:edge-rs` is **not** affected.

**Describe the bug**

A `UNIQUE` constraint is not honored for property values longer than **4096 bytes**: duplicate values above that size are silently accepted, with no error or warning, so the constraint gives no integrity guarantee. The same operation on v4.20.1 instead **crashes the server** (SIGSEGV in `EnforceUniqueEntity`, exit 139); v4.20.2 replaced the crash with silent non-enforcement. The 4096-byte boundary is identical in both.

On an empty graph with a single `Tag` node whose `Hash` = 4097 bytes, then a unique constraint, then a byte-identical second node:

| | Duplicate 4097-byte value under `UNIQUE` constraint |
|---|---|
| FalkorDB v4.20.1 | **server crashes** (SIGSEGV, exit 139) |
| FalkorDB v4.20.2 | **duplicate silently accepted** (2 nodes) |
| FalkorDB `edge-rs` | duplicate **rejected** (`unique constraint violation`) — correct |
| Neo4j 2026.06.0 | constraint creation **rejected** (`Property value is too large to index`) |

Values of exactly 4096 bytes are enforced correctly (duplicate rejected); 4097 bytes are not. The duplicate is byte-identical (`a.Hash = b.Hash` → true). The bypass is not a timing artifact: it persists >15 s after the constraint command returns, and pre-existing duplicates are likewise not detected when the constraint is created.

**To reproduce**

Using a string of 4097 `a` characters (4097 bytes):

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:Tag {Hash: '<4097 × ''a''>'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (t:Tag) ON (t.Hash)"
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g UNIQUE NODE Tag PROPERTIES 1 Hash    -- returns PENDING, no error
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:Tag {Hash: '<same 4097 × ''a''>'})"     -- expected: unique violation; actual: OK
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (t:Tag) RETURN count(t)"                   -- 2
```

- OS: Windows 11 with Docker Desktop
- Architecture: x86_64

issues.title: Parser: inlined CYPHER parameter payloads parse in quadratic time, and unbounded nesting aborts the server
issues.body:
## Summary

Queries that inline their parameters — `GRAPH.QUERY g "CYPHER batch=[{...},{...}] UNWIND \$batch AS row ..."` — spend time quadratic in the payload size **in the parser**, before any graph work happens. A 6.7 MB batch spends ~1.8 s parsing.

This is the shape bulk loaders (and LangChain/LlamaIndex-style graph writers) emit, so it shows up as a slow data-load with the server pinned at 100% CPU on a single thread.

## Reproduction

```python
import time, redis
r = redis.Redis(port=6379)

def run(nrows, vec_len):
    rows = ["{`id`:%d,`v`:[%s]}" % (i, ",".join("0.123456" for _ in range(vec_len)))
            for i in range(nrows)]
    q = "CYPHER `batch`=[%s] RETURN 1" % ",".join(rows)
    t = time.time()
    r.execute_command("GRAPH.QUERY", "repro", q, "--compact")
    print(f"rows={nrows:5d} payload={len(q)/1e6:.2f}MB  {(time.time()-t)*1000:8.1f} ms")

for n in (250, 500, 1000, 2000):
    run(n, 200)
```

Observed — 8x the input costs 77x the time:

```
rows=  250 payload=0.46MB      25.5 ms
rows=  500 payload=0.91MB      62.1 ms
rows= 1000 payload=1.82MB     176.1 ms
rows= 2000 payload=3.65MB    1969.6 ms
```

Holding the payload at a constant ~3.6 MB and varying only how many list literals it is split across isolates the trigger — it is the **count of `[`**, not the byte count:

| list literals | 1 | 100 | 1000 | 4000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| time | 154 ms | 165 ms | 616 ms | 3065 ms |

And the same 3.6 MB payload with no nested list literals at all parses in **19 ms** vs **3887 ms** with them — 185x, identical byte count.

Sampling `redis-server` mid-load shows 96% of the busy thread's samples in `alloc::fmt::format` → `_platform_memmove` under `parse_ident`, with no graph work in the profile at all:

```
execute_query → Graph::get_plan → Parser::parse_parameters
  → parse_expr → parse_primary_expr → parse_map        (nested)
    → parse_expr → parse_primary_expr → parse_ident
        → alloc::fmt::format  ...  _platform_memmove   ← 7,1

issues.title: Server crash: temporal constructor called with extra arguments takes the positional fast path
issues.body:
## What

A temporal constructor called with more than one argument kills the server.

```cypher
CREATE (:N {v:1});
WITH localdatetime({year: 1980, month: 12, day: 11, hour: 12, minute: 31, second: 14}) AS x,
     localdatetime({year: 1984, month: 10, day: 11, hour: 12, mid: true},
                   {list: [6], fd: 645876123}) AS d
RETURN x = d
```

The client sees `Connection closed by server`, then connection refused — the process is gone. Reproduced on a **release** build of `main` at `71c65bbd5`.

In a build with debug assertions it surfaces as:

```
graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:662
assertion `left == right` failed   left: 2   right: 10
```

which is `debug_assert_eq!(args.len(), 10)` in `localdatetime_struct_pure`.

## Cause

`rewrite_struct_constructor` (binder) rewrites a constructor call whose **single** argument is a constant-keyed Map into positional children — exactly one child per slot, absent keys becoming `Constant(Null)`. Anything else it leaves alone.

The evaluator then infers "the binder rewrote this" from arity alone:

```rust
if let Some(struct_fn) = func.struct_fn
    && node.num_children() > 1
```

`date`, `localtime` and `localdatetime` are declared **`var_arg`**, so arity validation accepts a two-argument call. It reaches `struct_fn`, which reads `args[3]` of a 2-element slice: a debug assertion in test builds, an out-of-bounds index that aborts the process in release.

`duration` escapes this only because it declares `args: [..]` (exactly one), so the extra argument is rejected before evaluation.

Found by the `fuzz` job. The crashing input is `crash-f59dcda13902eb54a39f325a408950c13598eae8`.

## Fix

Make the guard an equality against the slot count, since the rewrite always emits exactly `struct_slots.len()` children.

## Also worth fixing, separately

With the guard corrected, extra arguments are silently *ignored* rather than rejected:

```
RETURN localdatetime({year: 1984}, {x: 1})   -> 1984-10-11T00:00 (second argument dropp

On the C engine, `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... issues.title: [Rust] Fulltext index language is validated only when the RediSearch spec is created — bypassed when the label already has an index
issues.body:
## Summary

The Rust engine validates a fulltext index's `language` only inside `Index::create_rs_index` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1129-1138`), which `Indexer::create_index` **skips** when the label already has a RediSearch spec (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:300-328`). So an unsupported language is accepted and persisted whenever the label already carries any index (range or vector). The bad value then re-surfaces as an error on unrelated later operations, and the index is silently lost on reload.

No crash — Rust is not affected by the C segfault in #2448 (that path returns `Language is not supported: klingon` and the server stays up). This is the same missing-validation gap, with different consequences.

Found while analysing https://github.com/FalkorDB/private/issues/211 (a C-engine crash, see #2448) for Rust exposure.

## Reproduction

`falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-rs` (aarch64, Redis 8.6.3).

**1. Bypass — an unsupported language is accepted and stored**

```
GRAPH.QUERY b "CREATE (:Person {name:'hello world running quickly', age:30})"
GRAPH.QUERY b "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Person) ON (n.age)"                                    → Indices created: 1
GRAPH.QUERY b "CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX FOR (n:Person) ON (n.name) OPTIONS {language:'klingon'}"
                                                                                          → Indices created: 1   (should be rejected)
GRAPH.QUERY b "CALL db.indexes()"   → language: klingon, status: OPERATIONAL
```

Without the pre-existing range index the same statement is correctly rejected. A pre-existing **vector** index opens the same hole (verified).

**2. The label is now partly unusable — every op that rebuilds the spec re-validates and fails**

```
GRAPH.QUERY v "CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:P) ON (n.e) OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}"
                                                    → Language is not supported: klingon   (permanent)

GRAPH.QUERY b "DROP INDEX FOR (n:Person) ON (n.age)"

issues.title: Native index cannot serve numeric array elements or conjunction predicates
issues.body:
Under `--features index-falkordb` the native index is the only index, so a predicate it cannot
serve raises an error rather than falling back. Two shapes are unserved today, and both are
recorded in `tests/flow/nextgen_index_xfail.txt`.

## Array-valued properties

A property holding a list of numbers is not indexed at all — the encoder rejects lists, so no
element reaches the numeric column. `value IN n.samples` therefore cannot be served.

Sharing one key space with scalars is not an option: it would make `WHERE n.v = 1` match a node
whose `v` is `[1, 2]`, and the `Equal` plan carries no post-filter to catch it.

## Conjunctions

Three `AND` shapes are unserved:

- several bounds on one attribute (`n.x > 1 AND n.x < 9`) — `merge_range_queries` gives up
  whenever two conjuncts constrain the same side of the window, because at plan time the bounds
  may still be expressions it cannot compare
- bounds across two attributes (`n.x > 1 AND n.y < 9`)
- the same predicate appearing twice

## Scope

Numeric array elements and all three conjunction shapes. String elements inside arrays are out of
scope — they need a native text kind and belong with that work.

The master dies when the async constraint-enforcement thread replicates inside a replica-pause

issues.title: Parameter values are parsed into an expression tree and evaluated twice, making inlined payloads 13x slower than C
issues.body:
## Summary

A query that inlines its parameters — `GRAPH.QUERY g "CYPHER batch=[{...},{...}] UNWIND \$batch AS row ..."` — spends almost all of its time turning the parameter text into values. On a 6.7 MB batch that is **341 ms against the C module's 26 ms, 13.7x slower**, which misses the C-parity bar in CLAUDE.md.

This is what bulk loaders and LangChain/LlamaIndex-style graph writers emit, so it shows up as a slow data load.

(Measured on `main` at db4ac47a7, i.e. *after* #2442 removed the quadratic term from the same workload. #2442 took it from 2061 ms to 341 ms; the remaining 13.7x is a separate cause.)

## Reproduction

```python
import time, redis
r = redis.Redis(port=6379, socket_timeout=600)

rows = []
for i in range(1477):
    emb = ",".join("%.6f" % ((i % 200) / 100 - 1) for _ in range(384))
    rows.append('{`id`:"%d",`props`:{`document`:"%s",`embedding`:[%s]}}'
                % (i, "End_of_Sale_and_End_of_Life_Announcement_" * 20, emb))
q = "CYPHER `batch`=[%s] UNWIND $batch AS row RETURN count(row)" % ",".join(rows)

t = time.time()
r.execute_command("GRAPH.QUERY", "bulk", q, "--compact")
print(f"{(time.time()-t)*1000:.1f} ms")
```

| engine | min | median | p95 |
|---|---|---|---|
| C (reference) | 23.9 ms | **26.2 ms** | 34.9 ms |
| Rust (`main`) | 331.0 ms | **341.4 ms** | 351.3 ms |

## It is the parameters, not the query

Same 6.7 MB in each case:

| workload | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| params only (`RETURN 1`) | 20.6 ms | **302.3 ms** |
| params + `UNWIND` + count | 22.1 ms | 302.5 ms |
| **no params, same bytes** | 16.9 ms | **7.0 ms** |

Execution costs ~1.5 ms on both. On a 6.7 MB query with *no* parameters Rust is **2.4x faster than C** — lexing, I/O and the runtime are all fine.

## The cost is per literal

Holding the payload at 3.67 MB and varying only how many literals it contains:

| payload | C | Rust | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~400k numeric literals | 14.6 ms | 150.9 ms | 10.3x |
| ~4k string literals (same bytes) | 3.7 ms | 18.4

issues.title: ci: Dependabot does not cover Python, uv or Docker dependencies on main
issues.body:
## Problem

`.github/dependabot.yml` on `main` configures only two ecosystems, `github-actions` and `cargo` (plus a `target-branch: master` entry that keeps the C engine's Actions bumps alive after #2255).

Three dependency surfaces in the Rust tree are therefore not monitored at all. A published advisory affecting any of them would go unflagged indefinitely, because nothing else in CI watches these manifests:

| Surface | Manifest | Currently monitored |
|---|---|---|
| Test suite Python deps | `tests/requirements.txt` | ❌ |
| Benchmark harness | `bench/pyproject.toml` + `bench/uv.lock` | ❌ |
| Build / runtime / devcontainer base images | `build/Dockerfile`, `build/runtime/Dockerfile`, `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` | ❌ |

`tests/requirements.txt` is the most exposed of the three: it pulls `redis`, `falkordb`, `pytest`, `behave`, `RLTest` and `hypothesis` into every CI run.

## Proposal

Add one Dependabot entry per surface:

- `pip` at `/tests`
- `uv` at `/bench` — it is a separate uv project, and `pip` would not read `uv.lock`
- `docker` across `/build`, `/build/runtime` and `/.devcontainer`

Group each so they open one consolidated PR per week rather than one per dependency.

Two things should deliberately **not** happen:

- **`/bench` excluded from the docker entry** — `bench/Dockerfile` is `FROM ${C_IMAGE}`, an ARG-driven base Dependabot cannot resolve to a registry tag.
- **`gitsubmodule` not enabled** — `main` has no `.gitmodules`; submodules exist only on `master`, where `submodule-update.yml` already handles them. Enabling it would open duplicate PRs pinned to unreleased upstream commits.

## Context

Raised while auditing supply-chain controls for the trust centre. The published Vulnerability Management position commits to automated dependency monitoring; this closes the gap between that statement and what `main` actually watches.

issues.title: Extra or wrongly-typed arguments to date()/localtime()/localdatetime() crash the server
issues.body:
**FalkorDB version**

`main` (Rust engine), commit `db4ac47a7`.

**Describe the bug**

Calling `date()`, `localtime()` or `localdatetime()` with more arguments than they accept, or with an argument of the wrong type, terminates the server process. The connection is closed and the server does not come back:

```
127.0.0.1:6379> GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN date('2020-01-01','x')"
Error: Server closed the connection
127.0.0.1:6379> PING
Could not connect to Redis at 127.0.0.1:6379: Connection refused
```

This is reachable from any client that can run a query, so a single malformed query takes the database down.

**To Reproduce**

Each of these kills the server on its own:

```cypher
RETURN date('2020-01-01', 'x')
RETURN date({year: 2020}, 'x')
RETURN localtime(1, 2)
RETURN localdatetime(1, 2)
RETURN date(1)
RETURN localtime(1)
```

**Expected behavior**

A query error, as the fixed-arity constructors already produce:

```
127.0.0.1:6379> GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN point(1,2)"
(error) Received 2 arguments to function 'point', expected at most 1
```

The `fuzz` CI job on an unrelated PR, as a panic at `graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:635`:

```
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:635:5:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 2
 right: 7
==8307== ERROR: libFuzzer: deadly signal
```

Two independent defects, both rooted in the same thing: `date`, `localtime` and `localdatetime` are registered with a *var-length* signature, which is looser than what they actually accept. `GraphFn` documents why — the loose signature exists so the zero-argument "now" form binds:

> constructor functions are registered with a loose `var_arg` signature to accept zero-arg "now"-style invocations

**1. The struct-constructor fast path is entered by calls it was not meant to serve.**

The binder rewrites `date({year: 2020})` into one positional child per named slot, and `eval.rs` dispatches those through a stack `[Value; 10]

issues.title: Explicit two-hop pattern with an anonymous intermediate node collapses distinct paths (fused-hop traverse loses multiplicity)
issues.body:
### Summary

An explicit two-hop pattern returns **one row instead of two** when the intermediate node is **anonymous**. Naming the intermediate node, or binding a path variable, returns the correct result. All three forms describe the same set of paths, so they must return the same number of rows.

This is the same class of defect as #73 / #1450 (distinct paths collapsed into one), but it survives on a code path those issues do not cover: the planner's **fused-hop** optimization.

### Steps to reproduce

Two distinct length-2 paths from `a` to `c`:

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A{n:'0'}),(b1:B{n:'1'}),(b2:B{n:'2'}),(c:C{n:'3'}),
                      (a)-[:R]->(b1),(a)-[:R]->(b2),(b1)-[:R]->(c),(b2)-[:R]->(c)"
```

| # | query | rows | expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)` | **1** ❌ | 2 |
| 2 | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R]->(m)-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)` | 2 ✅ | 2 |
| 3 | `MATCH p=(a:A)-[:R]->()-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)` | 2 ✅ | 2 |
| 4 | `MATCH (a:A)-[:R*2]->(c) RETURN count(*)` | 2 ✅ | 2 |

Only query 1 is wrong. Merely *naming* the intermediate node (2) or binding a path variable (3) changes the result — the same surprising symptom reported in #354.

### Root cause

The two plans differ:

```
-- anonymous (wrong)
Project
    Conditional Traverse | (a)->(_anon_1) (+ 1 fused hop)
        Node By Label Scan | (a:A)

-- named (correct)
Project
    Conditional Traverse | (m)->(c)
        Conditional Traverse | (a)->(m)
            Node By Label Scan | (a:A)
```

When the intermediate node is anonymous and otherwise unreferenced, the planner fuses the two hops into a single `Conditional Traverse`. That fused traverse is evaluated as a boolean adjacency-matrix product, which records only *whether* `c` is reachable from `a` in two hops — not *how many* distinct paths reach it. This is exactly the mechanism @K-Jo described in #73: the multiplication "did not keep track of the actual paths that lead to it."

Binding a path variable (que

issues.title: Dependabot widens the deliberate redis<8.1 test pin
issues.body:
`tests/requirements.txt` pins `redis<8.1` with a documented reason:

```
# redis-py 8.1.0 adds `himport_registry` to ConnectionPool.connection_kwargs,
# which falkordb-py 1.6.2's async Is_Cluster forwards to the sync Redis()
# constructor, which rejects it. Every flow test that builds its own pool
# fails with a TypeError. Keep in sync with build/Dockerfile; drop both once
# falkordb-py releases a fix.
redis<8.1
```

When the `pip` ecosystem was added for `/tests` in #2464, no `ignore` rule accompanied it, on the incorrect assumption that Dependabot treats a `<` ceiling as a hard constraint. It does not — the pip ecosystem defaults to `versioning-strategy: auto`, which widens ranges.

Dependabot subsequently opened #2476, raising the ceiling to `redis<8.2`. That would:

1. **Re-admit the broken release.** `<8.2` permits redis-py 8.1.0 — precisely the version the comment says breaks every flow test that builds its own pool.
2. **Desync the two pins.** The same pin is duplicated at `build/Dockerfile:141` and the comment explicitly says to keep them in sync. #2476 changes only `tests/requirements.txt`.

### Why CI does not catch it

`tests/requirements.txt` is referenced by **no workflow**. The flow suites run inside `ghcr.io/falkordb/falkordb-build`, which bakes its own `'redis<8.1'` at `build/Dockerfile:141`. The changed file is therefore never installed in CI, and `flow-test-matrix` passes on #2476 without exercising it. The breakage would surface only for local or non-container test runs.

### Fix

Add an `ignore` rule for `redis` on the `/tests` pip entry so the ceiling can only be lifted deliberately, alongside `build/Dockerfile`, when falkordb-py ships a fix.

issues.title: Server panics on NUL byte in query parameter (remote DoS)
issues.body:
## Summary

A NUL byte inside a string query parameter crashes the server process a few
seconds after the query returns. The query itself succeeds and round-trips the
value correctly; the crash happens later, on a background thread, so it is not
attributable to the connection that caused it.

Found while reviewing falkordb-py. Reproduced against `falkordb/falkordb:edge`.

## Reproduction

```python
from falkordb import FalkorDB

db = FalkorDB(host="localhost", port=6379)
g = db.select_graph("crashme")
print(g.query("RETURN $p", {"p": "a\x00b"}).result_set)  # succeeds
# server dies a few seconds later
```

Equivalently, without a client:

```
GRAPH.QUERY crashme 'CYPHER `p`="a<NUL>b" RETURN $p'
```

## Observed behaviour

The query returns normally. Shortly afterwards the process aborts with a Rust
panic originating from an unchecked `CString::new(...).unwrap()`:

```
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at src/redismodule.rs:156:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: NulError(...)
```

The bytes in the `NulError` payload decode to the query header containing the
parameter, i.e. the NUL travels from the parameter into a string that is later
converted to a `CString` on a background (telemetry) thread.

## Impact

Any client able to run a query can terminate the server with a single
well-formed request. The crash is delayed and happens off-thread, which makes
it hard to attribute to the responsible query in production.

## Suggested fix

Validate or reject NUL bytes when parsing parameter values, and replace the
`CString::new(...).unwrap()` at `redismodule.rs:156` with error handling so a
malformed string cannot abort the process.

## Client-side mitigation

falkordb-py now rejects NUL bytes in string parameters
(FalkorDB/falkordb-py#273), but that only stops this one client from
triggering it; the server is still reachable via any other client or raw
`GRAPH.QUERY`.

issues.title: Reversed traversal chain puts the far hop at the bottom of the plan (82x on a 2-hop reverse pattern)
issues.body:
`MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:KNOWS]->(c:Person {id: 1}) RETURN count(a)` costs **34.4M instructions** against **419k** on the C engine — the worst Rust/C ratio in the 317-query benchmark set (134x on query work), and 20.6x on p99 latency (1.791 ms vs 0.087 ms).

## Cause

`select_scan_node` reverses a `CondTraverse` chain when the better scan endpoint is at the top. It reverses the hop list, then walks that list backwards again while rebuilding the plan — so the hop that lands directly on the new scan is the one *furthest* from it:

```
Aggregate
    Conditional Traverse | (c)<-(b)
        Conditional Traverse | (b)<-(a)     <- bottom hop: neither alias bound
            Node By Index Scan | (c:Person)
```

Nothing below that bottom traverse binds `a` or `b`, so the runtime cannot seek either matrix dimension and falls back to enumerating every edge of the type, once per input row. The C engine's plan for the same query starts from the anchor:

```
Aggregate
    Conditional Traverse | (c)->(a)
        Node By Index Scan | (c:Person)
```

Results are correct either way — brute force finds the same rows — so this only ever showed up as cost.

## Scope

Measured (300 executions each, M3 Pro):

| case | Rust | C | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| reverse 1 hop | 375,704 | 380,558 | 0.99 |
| reverse 2 hops | 34,354,035 | 418,834 | **82.0** |
| reverse 3 hops | 40,421,015 | 450,593 | **89.7** |
| forward 1/2/3 hops | 367,922 / 450,239 / 525,664 | 375,477 / 409,717 / 443,989 | ~1.0 |

One reverse hop is fine; two or more are not. Forward chains are unaffected.

## Expected

Every `Conditional Traverse` should name a source alias that an operator below it binds.

issues.title: bench: jemalloc MALLOC-STATS parse splits fixed-width rows on whitespace, producing petabyte alloc_bytes
issues.body:
`BenchClient.jemalloc_totals` splits the `bins:`/`large:` rows of `MEMORY MALLOC-STATS` on whitespace. Those tables are fixed-width and right-aligned, and the `(#/sec)` rate fields are 8 characters wide — so a rate ≥ 10,000,000/sec fills its field exactly and fuses with the `nmalloc` before it:

```text
nmalloc (#/sec)      ndalloc (#/sec)
    1379247  689623      1355704  677852     <- fine, 6-digit rates
21949879 10974939 21947904 10973952          <- fused, 8-digit rates
```

`line.split()` then reads `nmalloc` as one 16-digit number and shifts every later column left, so `ndalloc` picks up a fused value too. The parsed cumulative total jumps ~7e16 bytes when a hot size class crosses 10M allocs/sec and drops back when it cools — and since `measure` reports *deltas*, per-query allocation comes out in the petabytes, or negative when the fusion clears between snapshots.

## Observed

Three full 317-query runs on one host, each with exactly 8 physically impossible rows, consistently:

| query | rep 1 | rep 2 | rep 3 | correct value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `MSF nodes yield` | 351,207,481,011,826 | 351,207,097,013,232 | 351,210,249,012,702 | 10,649,197 |
| `write 1m` | −39,655,479,199,115,760 | −39,656,013,599,155,096 | −39,656,194,399,073,920 | — |
| `write 100k` | 320,185,648,034,151 | 320,142,448,020,056 | 320,139,888,012,900 | — |

It needs a full run to trigger; a handful of queries never gets a size class hot enough, which is why it survived.

## Why it matters

`alloc_bytes` is the column the `benchmark-cov` CI comment compares **against the C engine** — callgrind cannot measure that engine reliably — so this breaks the only vs-C reading CI has.

## Expected

Fields read by the character columns of their own table header, so overflow in a right-aligned field (which spills left, into a rate nothing uses) cannot corrupt them.

issues.title: CMD_INFO is registered and reported but never honoured; per-query telemetry costs ~83k instructions (1.48x query floor vs C)
issues.body:
`GRAPH.CONFIG GET CMD_INFO` reports the value and `CMD_INFO no` is accepted, but nothing reads it — every finished query is still logged to `telemetry{graph}`. There is no way to opt out of what that logging costs, and it costs more than the query.

## Measured

Stage ablation of `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1"` (M3 Pro, 2000 executions via redis-benchmark), instructions per query:

| | instr |
|---|---:|
| full path | 232,289 |
| without slow_log + telemetry | 149,316 |
| → slow_log alone | ~300 |
| → **telemetry** | **~83,000** |
| …channel send + flusher wakeup + formatting + GIL | 49,154 |
| …argument RedisString creation | 5,656 |
| …the XADD itself | 25,534 |
| …replicating the XADD | 2,395 |

C engine, same host, same command:

| | instr |
|---|---:|
| C default (`CMD_INFO yes`) | 159,343 |
| C `CMD_INFO no` | 148,324 |
| → **C's per-query logging** | **11,019** |

C appends a finished query to a per-graph circular buffer, and a cron task drains batches into the stream with `StreamAdd` and a preallocated field-name template. This port pays a channel send, a flusher wakeup, argument formatting, a GIL acquisition and an `RM_Call("XADD")` per query — 7.5x C's cost.

## Why it matters

This is the whole of the fixed per-query floor gap, and the floor is paid by every one of the 317 benchmark queries — it is what puts 84 of them in the 1.0–1.5x band on its own. With logging off, this port measures **150,283 against C's 148,324 (1.01x)**.

## Two parts

1. **`CMD_INFO no` should work** — small, and matches C.
2. **The enabled path should be as cheap as C's** — a per-graph buffer plus a batched `StreamAdd`. This needs a decision first: `StreamAdd` on an opened key does not replicate, while today's `RM_Call(..., replicate)` deliberately mirrors the stream to replicas.

issues.title: A label predicate (n:Label) materializes the node's label names per row (2.19x vs C on a filtered scan)
issues.body:
`n:Label` reaches the runtime as a `hasLabels` call, answered through `Runtime::get_node_labels`, which per row builds an `OrderSet<LabelId>` from the label matrix, applies pending label changes into it, then builds a **second** `OrderSet<Arc<String>>` of label *names* — after which the predicate compares strings. Two allocations and a name comparison per row, to read one bit of the label matrix.

## Measured

Benchmark graph (15k nodes), 100 executions each:

| query | Rust | C | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person RETURN count(n)` | 48,942,607 | 22,369,522 | **2.19** |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person AND n.id < 5 RETURN count(n)` | 55,573,511 | 24,897,885 | **2.23** |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n.id < 5 RETURN count(n)` | 1,987,320 | 8,981,777 | 0.22 |

3.3k instructions per row for the label test, against C's 1.5k — while the *property* filter over the same scan is 4.5x cheaper than C. p99 on the benchmark's `label predicate` row is 7.511 ms against C's 1.551 ms.

## Expected

A label test reads the label matrix by label id. It only needs the materialized label set when this query has added or removed labels on that node, or the node is pending-deleted.

## Related, still open

The aggregate family shows the mirror-image split, and is *not* this issue:

| | Rust | C | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `collect DISTINCT` | 36.3M | 16.8M | 2.16 |
| `percentileCont` | 26.7M | 12.9M | 2.07 |

issues.title: High Virtual vs. Physical Memory Discrepancy from Dense Entity Block Allocations for Attribute-Less Nodes/Edges
issues.body:
#### Description
When managing multi-tenant graphs with large numbers of nodes or edges that contain few or no attributes, FalkorDB exhibits a massive gap between allocator-tracked memory (`used_memory`) and actual physical host memory (`RSS`). 

For example, in a multi-tenant deployment, Redis `used_memory` reports **~12 GiB**, while container RSS hovers around **~6 GiB**. While this behavior is partially optimized by the Linux kernel's Virtual Memory Manager via system **Zero Page** mappings, it creates severe operational risks:
1. **Deceptive Telemetry:** Monitoring tools report low RSS, masking latent memory footprints, potentially reaching `maxmemory` when there's plenty of memory to handle data and queries.
2. **Page Fault Cascades / OOM Risks:** Broad database operations (e.g., sequential scans or `BGSAVE`) force the kernel to back these `NULL`-heavy allocations with physical hardware instantly, causing severe RSS spikes that trigger Kubernetes OOM kills.

---

#### Root Cause Analysis
FalkorDB uses fixed-stride block allocations (contiguous arrays) to store node and edge structures for cache-friendly access. Each entity slot reserves fixed pointer fields for label/type mappings, ID tracking, and property arrays.

When nodes or edges are created without attributes:
1. The property array pointers in these blocks are set to `NULL` (`0x0000000000000000`).
2. Jemalloc counts these contiguous block allocations toward `used_memory` (and enforces `maxmemory` against them).
3. The Linux kernel observes that large spans of these pre-allocated array pages contain nothing but `0x0` bytes, routing those virtual memory addresses to the system's shared, read-only 4 KB **Zero Page**.

While this saves physical RAM at rest, the underlying memory allocation model remains overcommitted at the database engine layer.

---

To eliminate the virtual overcommit bloat and ensure that `used_m

issues.title: Parallel edges collapse into one row when the edge variable is unreferenced
issues.body:
Two parallel relationships between the same pair of nodes are counted as one whenever the edge variable is not read downstream. This is a **single-hop** case, distinct from #2470 (which is the two-hop anonymous-intermediate fusion) though it shares the theme of the batched boolean path losing multiplicity.

## Reproduction

Tested against `main` (Rust engine).

```cypher
CREATE (a:X), (b:Y), (a)-[:R]->(b), (a)-[:R]->(b)
```
`Relationships created: 2` — both edges exist.

| Query | Result | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN count(r)` | 2 | 2 :white_check_mark: |
| `MATCH (a:X)-[r:R]->(b:Y) RETURN id(r)` | 2 rows (`0`, `1`) | 2 rows :white_check_mark: |
| `MATCH (a:X)-[r:R]->(b:Y) RETURN count(*)` | **1** | 2 :x: |
| `MATCH (a:X)-[:R]->(b:Y) RETURN count(*)` | **1** | 2 :x: |

Rows 2 and 3 are the same pattern; only the projection differs, yet they disagree on how many rows the `MATCH` produced.

## Analysis

The discriminator is `emit_relationship`. When the edge **is** read downstream (`id(r)`), the slow path enumerates the relationship tensor and correctly yields both edges. When it is not (`count(*)`), `batched_eligible` becomes true and execution takes the boolean matrix path in `graph/src/runtime/ops/cond_traverse.rs`, which yields one entry per reachable `(src, dst)` pair rather than one per relationship. The `bind_edge` branch calls `...get(mat_src, mat_dst).next()`, taking only the **first** edge between the pair.

Cypher relationship-isomorphism requires one row per distinct relationship, so both queries should return 2.

## Impact

Any aggregate over a pattern whose edge variable is unused silently under-counts in the presence of parallel edges — `count(*)`, `sum`, `avg`, `collect` sizes and `LIMIT`/`SKIP` cardinality are all affected.

issues.title: MATCH following a pattern-predicate WHERE is nested under Semi Apply, losing its cardinality
issues.body:
When a `MATCH ... WHERE <pattern predicate>` is followed by a second `MATCH`, the planner nests the second `MATCH` inside the `Semi Apply` **existence branch** instead of continuing the main stream. The second pattern then only contributes an existence test, so its rows never reach the result set and its cardinality is lost. The variables it binds also disappear from the plan.

This is distinct from #2470 and #2501 — it reproduces with a named intermediate, where no traversal fusion is involved at all.

## Reproduction

Tested against `main` (Rust engine).

```cypher
CREATE (a:A), (b1), (b2), (c:C), (z),
       (a)-[:Q]->(z),
       (a)-[:R]->(b1), (a)-[:R]->(b2), (b1)-[:R]->(c), (b2)-[:R]->(c)
```

```cypher
MATCH (a:A) WHERE (a)-[:Q]->() MATCH (a)-[:R]->(m)-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)
```

Returns **1**; expected **2** — there are two distinct 2-hop `:R` paths from `a`, and `a` satisfies the `:Q` predicate.

Splitting the predicate off with `WITH` gives the right answer, confirming the pattern itself matches twice:

```cypher
MATCH (a:A) WHERE (a)-[:Q]->() WITH a MATCH (a)-[:R]->(m)-[:R]->(c) RETURN count(*)
```

## Plan

```
Aggregate
    Semi Apply
        Node By Label Scan | (a:A)
        Conditional Traverse | (m)->(c)
            Conditional Traverse | (a)->(m)
                Conditional Traverse | (a)->(_anon_1)
                    Argument
```

The `(a)-[:R]->(m)-[:R]->(c)` traversals belong on the main stream above the `Semi Apply`, but they have been appended to the existence branch beneath the `(a)-[:Q]->(_anon_1)` traversal. Note also that `c` and `m` never appear as bindings usable by later clauses.

## Impact

Any query that combines a pattern-predicate `WHERE` with a subsequent `MATCH` in the same clause sequence silently under-reports rows, and variables bound by the later `MATCH` are unavailable. Aggregates, `LIMIT`/`SKIP` and `RETURN` of those variables are all affected.

issues.body:
docker 4.20.1
## Minimal reproduction

Run both queries on a fresh graph named `optional_empty_repro`.

### LEFT

```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n:X {id: 4})
WHERE 0 IN n.klist
WITH *
WHERE n IS NOT NULL
RETURN n;
```

### RIGHT

```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n:X {id: 4})
WHERE 0 IN n.klist
WITH {n: n} AS row
WITH collect(row) AS rows
UNWIND rows AS row
WITH row.n AS n
WITH *
WHERE n IS NOT NULL
RETURN n;
```

## Expected behavior

Both queries should return zero rows. The optional pattern has no match and
the `n IS NOT NULL` predicate must remove the all-NULL optional row.

## Actual behavior on FalkorDB 4.20.1

- LEFT returns one row with `n = NULL`.
- RIGHT returns zero rows.

issues.title: Support Leiden Algorithm
CI: PR Codecov drops service-mode flow coverage uploads
issues.body:
## Summary

PR coverage CI reports a large, false project-coverage regression because the
service-mode flow jobs upload no usable coverage reports.

Observed on #2509:

- base `a4860f6`: 119 Codecov sessions, 88.58% project coverage
- head `13db656`: 11 Codecov sessions, 65.39% project coverage
- Codecov reports: `HEAD has 108 uploads less than BASE`
- `codecov/patch` passes (`Coverage not affected`), while `codecov/project`
  fails because the apparent 23.19% drop exceeds the configured 2% threshold

## Root cause

The 108 `coverage-flow-svc` matrix jobs keep FalkorDB running as GitHub Actions
service containers. LLVM writes the module's `.profraw` profile when Redis exits,
but `.github/workflows/_flow-flavour.yml` scans for profiles while the services
are still running.

The original bind mount is also rooted under `github.workspace`. GitHub starts
service containers before workflow steps, then `actions/checkout` cleans the
repository. That cleanup removes the bind-mount source, so shutdown logs show:

```text
LLVM Profile Error: Failed to write file "/var/lib/falkordb/cov/...profraw": No such file or directory
```

The collection step previously treated missing profiles as a warning and exited
successfully. Codecov then auto-discovered only the instrumented shared library,
not a generated `codecov.txt`, so the job appeared green but contributed no
usable coverage session.

The 8 spawn-mode cells work because `tests/flow/common.py` stops their containers
before collection. Together with the general, unit-test, and fuzz reports, this
accounts for the 11 sessions received on the PR head.

## Proposed fix

- stop both service containers before export so LLVM flushes their profiles
- copy each service's isolated internal coverage directory into separate
  workspace directories after shutdown, avoiding both checkout cleanup and
  PID-1/module-hash filename collisions
- treat missing or empty `.profraw` files as an error
- upload `codecov.txt` explicitly instead of rely

issues.title: Upgrade GraphBLAS to 10.5.0-beta.1: stale FFI bindings, version-locked PreJIT kernels, and a build() iso-semantics change
issues.body:
## Summary

The pinned GraphBLAS is `v10.3.1` (`graphblas.sh`). Upgrading to `v10.5.0-beta.1`
is not a one-line version bump: three separate things are coupled to that pin,
two of which are currently wrong or would break silently.

## 1. The vendored PreJIT kernels are version-locked

All 218 kernels in `build/graphblas/PreJIT/` declare 10.3.1 in their `_query`
function:

```c
v [0] = 10 ; v [1] = 3 ; v [2] = 1 ;
```

GraphBLAS rejects a PreJIT kernel whose version does not match the running
library. Bumping the pin without re-harvesting therefore does not fail the build
or any test — it silently invalidates the entire vendored set and drops every
operation onto a generic kernel. That is exactly the regression PreJIT exists to
prevent, and nothing in CI would report it.

Re-harvesting must happen inside the Linux toolchain image, per the warning in
`gen_prejit.sh`.

## 2. The FFI bindings are stale by more than one release

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/mod.rs` reports:

```rust
pub const GxB_IMPLEMENTATION_DATE: &[u8; 13] = b"Mar 20, 2025\0";
pub const GxB_IMPLEMENTATION_MAJOR: u32 = 10;
pub const GxB_IMPLEMENTATION_MINOR: u32 = 0;
pub const GxB_IMPLEMENTATION_SUB: u32 = 2;
```

That is **10.0.2** — the bindings were never regenerated for 10.3.1 either. It
works only because the engine calls a subset of symbols that has not changed
shape. Regenerating exposes the 10.4/10.5 memory-arena API and the fork-safety
hooks.

Regeneration has a trap worth recording: bindgen renders `GB_Iterator_opaque` as
a one-byte `_address` placeholder while emitting a layout test asserting the
struct's real 224 bytes, so the output does not compile. This is not a
generator-version quirk — 0.71.1 and 0.72.0 behave identically, in both C and C++
parse modes, with and without the allowlist. The struct grew from 152 to 224
bytes in 10.4.0.

## 3. 10.5.0 changes `GrB_*_build` iso semantics

issues.title: Replicated GRAPH.EFFECT crash-loops a replica (AttributeSet_Update SIGSEGV) on v4.20.1 — #2459 fix is unreleased
issues.body:
## Summary

On **v4.20.1**, a read replica seeded by full sync entered a **continuous SIGSEGV crash-loop while applying a replicated `GRAPH.EFFECT`** — `AttributeSet_Update+0x25`, NULL dereference (`Accessing address: (nil)`). This is the **crashing** manifestation of the attribute-id-space mismatch fixed in #2459 (closes #2457), and it shares its crash site with #2235 (which reached it via AOF replay). The fix (#2459) **merged 2026-08-14, after the latest release v4.20.3 (2026-08-13)** — so there is no released version that contains it, and production on v4.20.1 is exposed.

We're filing because two things here go beyond what #2457/#2235 already document:

1. **#2457 presents as a hard crash, not only silent corruption.** #2457 describes the wrong-attribute write as "no error, no crash… fixes itself after a restart." In our case the mismatched id resolved to a NULL attribute slot and **segfaulted** instead — same root cause (a bare `u16` attribute id from a `GRAPH.EFFECT` interpreted against the replica's unified id space), different failure mode.
2. **Recovery is not automatic — partial resync poisons it into a multi-hour loop.** After each crash the replica restarted from its RDB, synthesised a cached master, and requested a **partial** resync at the same replid+offset — which re-delivered the same poisoned effect and crashed again (restart #43…). It only recovered ~2h later when the master's backlog had aged out (`repl_backlog_active:0`, replid changed) and the master was forced to **refuse the partial and full-sync** instead.

## Environment

- FalkorDB **v4.20.1** (both master and replica; no version skew), Redis 8.x, official image, default config (no `GRAPH.CONFIG` override).
- Master ↔ one read replica, replicated via `GRAPH.EFFECT`.

## Observed (production)

```

SIGSEGV (signal 11) — Accessing address: (nil)
  AttributeSet_Update+0x25
  ... Effects_Apply (replicated GRAPH.EFFECT apply path)

issues.title: Relationship isomorphism not enforced: converging pattern double-counts matches (Rust engine)
issues.body:
**FalkorDB version**
`falkordb/falkordb:edge` (module version 999999, Redis 8.6.3) — the current Rust rewrite on the `main` branch.

**Environment**
- Deployment: Docker (`docker run -p 3000:3000 -it --rm falkordb/falkordb:edge`)
- Connection method: RESP / `GRAPH.QUERY`

**Describe the bug**
Relationship isomorphism is not enforced: two single-hop relationship patterns within the same `MATCH` path are allowed to bind to the same physical edge, producing duplicated/over-counted rows for converging patterns.

This is the same defect originally reported in #1844 and fixed for the legacy C engine in PR #1926. That PR/issue were closed because the C codebase is no longer being maintained (development moved to the Rust engine), but reproducing the original repro against the current `edge` (Rust) image shows the bug is still present there.

**To Reproduce**
```cypher
CREATE (:Person {name:'Alice'})-[:FRIEND]->(:Person {name:'Bob'})<-[:FRIEND]-(:Person {name:'Charlie'});

MATCH (p1:Person)-[:FRIEND]->(p2:Person)<-[:FRIEND]-(p3:Person)
RETURN p2.name, count(p1);
```

**Expected behavior**
```
p2.name | count(p1)
Bob     | 2
```
(matches Neo4j and the fixed legacy-C engine behavior)

**Actual behavior** (verified against `falkordb/falkordb:edge`)
```
p2.name | count(p1)
Bob     | 4
```

**Root cause (from the prior C fix, PR #1926)**
Each `:FRIEND` traversal independently iterates over edges into `p2` with no check that the two pattern edges resolve to different physical edges, so the converging pattern double-counts. The Rust engine's planner/runtime needs an equivalent relationship-isomorphism (edge-uniqueness) check between distinct single-hop relationship variables that could resolve to the same edge within one MATCH/MERGE path.

**Related**
- Originally reported in #1844 (closed, C-engine fix landed in PR #1926, both closed as the C codebase is no longer maintained)

This is the same vulnerability class described in #2400 (unbounded recursion in the C engine's `_AR_EXP_Evaluate`) and #2330 (unbounded mutual recursion in `param_parser.c`), but reproduced independently against the Rust engine, which has no depth limit either.

issues.title: Rust engine enforces relationship uniqueness across separate MATCH clauses, silently dropping rows
issues.body:
## Summary

The Rust engine enforces relationship uniqueness (isomorphism) **across separate `MATCH` clauses**. openCypher scopes that rule to a *single* `MATCH` clause, so re-binding the same relationship in a later clause is legal. As a result the Rust engine silently returns **zero rows** for queries that the C engine (and Neo4j) answer correctly.

Found while verifying #2217.

## Minimal reproduction

```
docker run --rm -d -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb:edge

GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A {id:1})-[:R]->(:B {id:2})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a)-[r1:R]->(b) MATCH (a)-[r2:R]->(b) RETURN id(r1), id(r2)"
```

|---|---|
| C v4.18.11 | 1 — `[0, 0]` ✅ |
| C v4.20.3 (`latest`) | 1 — `[0, 0]` ✅ |

Expected: 1 row. `r1` and `r2` live in different `MATCH` clauses, so they are allowed to bind the same relationship.

Same one-edge graph. The correct answer is 1 row for every row except the first.

| `MATCH ()-[r1:R]->()-[r2:R]->()` — same clause, must be 0 | 0 ✅ | 0 ✅ |
| `MATCH ()-[r1:R]->() MATCH ()-[r2:R]->()` — no shared variable | 1 ✅ | 1 ✅ |
