issues.title: [Rust] Variable bound by a preceding CREATE clause is invisible to the next CREATE's property expressions ('a' not defined)
issues.body:
## Summary

On the Rust engine, a variable introduced by a `CREATE` clause is **not in scope** for expressions inside an immediately following `CREATE` clause. Valid Cypher that the C engine (and Neo4j) accept is rejected with `'a' not defined`.

Found while re-triaging #270, whose original C-engine symptom is fixed but which now fails differently on `main`.

**Environment**

| engine | image | digest |
|---|---|---|
| Rust (`main`) | `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge` | `sha256:3624c4b0…` |
| C (reference) | `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c` | `sha256:0fc0da0f…` |

## Reproduction

```cypher
CREATE (a) CREATE (b {x: id(a)}) RETURN b.x
```

| engine | result |
|---|---|
| C `edge-c` | `b.x` = `<id of a>` ✅ |
| Rust `main` | **`'a' not defined`** ❌ |

## Scope of the defect

The failure is narrow and specific — it only triggers when the reference is made from an **expression** (property map) in a `CREATE` that **directly follows** another `CREATE`.

| query | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (a) RETURN id(a)` | ok | ok ✅ |
| `CREATE (a) CREATE (b)-[:R]->(a) RETURN id(b)` | ok | ok ✅ (pattern reference is fine) |
| `CREATE (a) CREATE (b {x: id(a)}) RETURN b.x` | ok | **`'a' not defined`** ❌ |
| `CREATE (a {v:1}) CREATE (b {x: a.v}) RETURN b.x` | ok | **`'a' not defined`** ❌ |
| `MATCH (m) CREATE (a) CREATE (b {x: id(a)}) RETURN b.x` | ok | **`'a' not defined`** ❌ |
| `CREATE (a) WITH a CREATE (b {x: id(a)}) RETURN b.x` | ok | ok ✅ |
| `CREATE (a) SET a.z = 1 CREATE (b {x: id(a)}) RETURN b.x` | ok | ok ✅ |
| `CREATE (a) MERGE (b {x: id(a)}) RETURN b.x` | ok | ok ✅ |

So *any* intervening clause (`WITH`, `SET`, `MERGE`) fixes it, and referencing `a` from a **pattern** rather than an expression is fine.

## Analysis

Consecutive `CREATE` clauses are fused into a single `Create` operation, and the fused op resolves its property expressions against the scope as it existed *before* the first `CREATE` — so `a` has not been bound yet.

The Rust engine reports the `Labels added` query statistic as **the number of new label types registered in the schema**, whereas the C engine (and Neo4j) report **the number of label assignments made to nodes**. Found while re-triaging #270.

| engine | image | digest |
|---|---|---|
| Rust (`main`) | `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge` | `sha256:3624c4b0…` |
| C (reference) | `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c` | `sha256:0fc0da0f…` |

All on a freshly deleted graph unless noted.

| 1 | `CREATE (:Node),(:Node)` | `Labels added: 2` | **`Labels added: 1`** ❌ | 2 |
| 2 | `CREATE (:A:B)` | `Labels added: 2` | `Labels added: 2` ✅ | 2 |

issues.title: Scalar property writes on vector-indexed nodes cost up to 666x, scaling linearly with vector dimension
issues.body:
### Summary

Writing a **scalar property that carries no index**, on a node whose label has a vector index, costs up to ~666x more than the same write on a label without one. The vector property is never read or written by the query. The penalty scales linearly with vector dimension, which points at the whole vector being re-encoded and re-inserted into the HNSW index on any mutation of the node.

### Measurement

2,000 nodes. An `id` range index is present in every run, so the match is an index scan rather than a label scan. The `SET` touches `a` and `b`, neither of which is indexed, and never references `embedding`:

```cypher
UNWIND $ids AS i MATCH (k:K {id:i}) SET k.a = k.a + 1, k.b = 3.0
```

| vector dim | SET/node | vs no vector index |
|---:|---:|---:|
| none | 0.005 ms | baseline |
| 64 | 0.157 ms | 31x |
| 256 | 0.620 ms | 122x |
| 1024 | 3.382 ms | **666x** |

Two further observations:

- **Storing the vector is free; indexing it is what costs.** A label holding 1024-float `embedding` properties with *no* vector index measures the same as the baseline. The cost appears only once `CREATE VECTOR INDEX` exists.
- **It is per-node and flat, so batching does not amortise it.** 1 / 5 / 25 / 100 / 500 nodes in a single `SET` cost 6.56 / 4.94 / 4.78 / 4.85 / 4.47 ms per node respectively.

### Why it matters

Any workload that keeps mutable scalar state alongside an embedding pays this on every write. In our case (an agent-memory graph) each retrieval updates a few bookkeeping properties across the returned page, and a periodic sweep marks nodes dormant in bulk. Both are pure scalar writes, and both are dominated by vector-index maintenance that the query never asked for. A sweep touching 40,000 nodes takes ~3 minutes at dim 1024, during which nothing else on that graph proceeds.

Reproduced on graph module **4.14.10** (Redis 8.2.2) and on **4.20.4**, where it is worse — roughly 11 ms/node at dim 1024.

issues.title: perf: a computed GROUP BY key disables the vectorized aggregate path entirely
issues.body:
## Problem

`AggregateOp` has a columnar/vectorized path (`consume_input_vectorized`) and a per-row fallback (`consume_input_per_row`). `analyze()` picks between them once per operator.

Today the vectorized path is chosen only if **every** grouping key is a bare variable or a plain `n.prop`. Anything else — `n.id % 100`, `toUpper(n.name)`, `date(n.ts).year`, or a *relationship* property — makes `analyze()` return `None`.

Returning `None` disables vectorization for the **whole operator**, not just the key. The per-row path rebuilds an owned `Row` for every input row and re-walks every key *and every aggregate-input* expression tree per row, so one ordinary computed key also forfeits the bulk aggregate-input extraction that #2628 built.

This is asymmetric and stale: the *input* side was generalized to arbitrary trees via `AggInputKind::Computed` + `VectorEval` in #2628, and #2555 then deleted its hand-rolled property special case in favour of the single evaluator. The key side never got the same treatment.

## Impact

Two queries in the standard benchmark set hit this exact shape:

- `MATCH (p:Person) WITH p.id % 100 AS g, count(*) AS c ...` (`WITH pipeline`)
- `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.id % 5 AS k, count(*) ...` (`ORDER BY agg`)

Callgrind measures them at 3,170,892 and 2,905,861 instructions per execution respectively, roughly 1.6-1.7x what they cost once the operator stays vectorized.

Grouping by a bucketed or derived value (`x / 10`, `x % n`, a string function, a date part) is an extremely common analytics shape, so the cliff is easy to fall off unknowingly.

A second, smaller instance of the same bug: the property arm calls `batch.extract_node_ids(var.id)`, so grouping by a **relationship** property (`MATCH ()-[r:R]->() RETURN r.w, count(*)`) fails bulk extraction and falls back per batch, every batch.

issues.title: Devcontainer build fails: missing GraphBLAS patch and OpenSSL
issues.body:
## Environment

- FalkorDB: current `main` (Rust engine)
- Host: WSL2 / Dev Containers
- Reproduction: `docker build -f .devcontainer/Dockerfile .` (or Reopen in Container)
- Graph setup: not required
- Host prerequisite: `git submodule update --init --recursive`
  (`deps/RediSearch` must be checked out; `redisearch.sh` does not clone)

## Reproduction

Build the `.devcontainer` image from the repo root.

## Expected result

The image builds GraphBLAS + RediSearch the same way `build/Dockerfile` does, and the container is usable for local Rust/Python work.

## Actual result

Two hard failures, in order:

**1. `graphblas.sh`**

```
error: can't open patch '/data/build/graphblas/GB_control.patch': No such file or directory
```

`graphblas.sh` applies `SCRIPT_DIR/build/graphblas/GB_control.patch` and vendors PreJIT kernels from that tree. `build/Dockerfile` already copies `build/graphblas`; `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` only copied `graphblas.sh`.

**2. `redisearch.sh`** (after the patch is present)

```
CMake Error: Could NOT find OpenSSL
  (missing: OPENSSL_CRYPTO_LIBRARY OPENSSL_INCLUDE_DIR)
```

RediSearch 8.6 hiredis does `find_package(OpenSSL)`. `build/Dockerfile` installs `libssl-dev` for this; the devcontainer apt list does not.

## Problem

The devcontainer drifted from the production toolchain image. Two inputs that `graphblas.sh` / `redisearch.sh` now require were never added to `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`.

## Impact

"Reopen in Container" is broken on current `main`. Anyone following `.devcontainer/README.md` hits a failed image build.

## Proposed fix

Minimal Dockerfile updates only:

- `COPY build/graphblas /data/build/graphblas` (patch + PreJIT kernels)
- `apt install libssl-dev`

No script or layering changes. Nested RediSearch submodules stay a host checkout step, not a Dockerfile concern.

`redis-server --loadmodule target/debug/libfalkordb.so` dies immediately in the devcontainer with:

```
# Failed to configure LOCALE for invalid locale name.
```

The FalkorDB module never loads.

## Why

Redis 7.2+ (including 8.x) calls `setlocale(LC_COLLATE, …)` at startup and `exit(1)` if that locale is missing. The image is minimal Ubuntu: it has `C` / `C.UTF-8` / `POSIX`, not `en_US.UTF-8`.

Cursor / VS Code Dev Containers forward the host locale into the session. On WSL, macOS, and most Linux desktops that is `en_US.UTF-8`, so Redis exits before it finishes coming up.

`.devcontainer/Dockerfile` does not set a locale and does not generate one. CI / `build/Dockerfile` is unaffected: nothing there injects `en_US.UTF-8`.

## Workaround

```bash
export LANG=C.UTF-8 LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
redis-server --loadmodule target/debug/libfalkordb.so --protected-mode no
```

## Proposed fix

Add to `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
ENV LANG=C.UTF-8 LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
```

Alternative: `apt install locales` + `locale-gen en_US.UTF-8`. Either is enough; I personally prefer the `ENV` line.

issues.title: Deleting nodes builds a GraphBLAS iterator per node per relationship type, even for nodes with no edges
issues.body:
## Summary

`Graph::delete_implicit_edges` — the commit-time cascade that removes edges hanging off deleted nodes — constructs **two GraphBLAS iterators per (deleted node × relationship type)**. Deleting a million edgeless nodes across six relationship types builds roughly **twelve million iterators to yield nothing**.

`write 1m` in the benchmark ran at **2.58x** the C engine on this, the largest absolute gap remaining in the suite.

## Diagnosis

```rust
for type_idx in 0..self.relationship_matrices.len() {   // 6 types
    for node_id in deleted_nodes {                       // 1M
        ...matrices[type_idx].iter(node_id, node_id, false)   // outgoing
        ...matrices[type_idx].iter(node_id, node_id, true)    // incoming
```

Each construction allocates a `GxB_Iterator` per layer and, on the forward side, waits the tensor first. So the cost tracks the deleted set and the number of relationship types — neither of which has anything to do with how many edges those nodes actually carry.

A symbolicated profile puts `delete_implicit_edges` at **37.5% inclusive**, against a query thread that is 53% of the profile — about 71% of the query's real work. The leaves are pure iterator churn: `Iter::new`, `Iter::seek`, `GB_calloc_memory`, `GB_Context_data_arena`, `GxB_Iterator_free`.

## Reproduction

Delete 200k **isolated** nodes (no edges at all) and vary only the number of relationship types in the graph:

| relationship types | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ms | 145.4 | 197.8 | 266.4 | 417.6 |

Linear in type count, ~+39 ms per type, for nodes that have no edges. Nothing else would produce that shape.

## Suggested direction

`versioned_matrix::Iter` already has `seek` for exactly this reason — `CondTraverseOp` uses it to amortize iterator allocation across per-row scans. Giving `tensor::Iter` the same and hoisting the pair out of the node loop keeps the access pattern identical (a sparse deletion still visits only its own rows, rather than scanning the g

issues.title: bench: create 100 / create 10k measure recovery from write 1m, not create cost
issues.body:
## Summary

`create 100` and `create 10k` report **4.4x** and **3.0x** the C engine. On a fresh graph neither reproduces: Rust runs a 100-node create at **1.28x** and a 10k-node create at **0.74x** — ahead of C. The gap is measurement context, not engine code.

## Cause

The sized block groups the mixed `write N` rows first and the pure create/delete pairs after them:

```
321 write 1 … 327 write 1m … 328 create 100, 329 delete 100, 330 create 10k, 331 delete 10k
```

So `create 100` runs immediately after `write 1m`. A write costs more while the engine still carries a large deletion — every write query snapshots the graph, and that snapshot scales with the deleted-id set and the capacity a big delete leaves behind. Creating a **single** node:

| preceding delete | 10k | 100k | 500k | 1M |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first write | 0.51 ms | 0.70 ms | 1.45 ms | 2.56 ms |
| steady state | 0.05 ms | 0.13 ms | 0.37 ms | 0.69 ms |

13x for one node, and the steady state never recovers. Reads are unaffected (0.095 ms) — only writes pay.

`test_sized_write_queries_stay_last` keeps the sized block last, which protects the other 320 queries, but says nothing about ordering *within* the block.

## Suggested direction

Order the block by magnitude so no row is preceded by one an order larger. Measured, that alone takes `create 100` from 4.36x to **2.47x**, with every `write N` row within noise and the suite's total instruction ratio against C unchanged at 0.613x.

`create 10k` barely moves (3.03x → 2.95x) and that is expected: it follows `write 10k`, which churns 500k nodes at 50 reps under any ordering. What remains in both rows is the snapshot cost itself — tracked separately.

The existing grouping has a stated reason (keep the create/delete pairs after the mixed rows so those keep a stable context), but it trades one row's context for another's, and the rows it protects are the ones that churn most heavily anyway.

Worth a test rather than a comment: the module docstring alrea

issues.title: Writes after a mass delete cost far more than the work they do: all_nodes_matrix is maintained for a reader that no longer exists
issues.body:
## Summary

Every write pays GraphBLAS structural upkeep proportional to the size of the deleted-id set, not to what the write does. With node capacity held at 1M and only the deleted pool varying, creating a **single** node measures:

| pool | 0 | 10k | 100k | 500k |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rust | 0.053 | 0.190 | 0.654 | **1.879** ms |
| C | 0.037 | 0.038 | 0.015 | 0.022 ms |

C is completely flat. Rust is linear in the pool.

## How C avoids it

C has no matrix of live nodes at all:

```c
DataBlock *nodes;              // node storage, with uint64_t *deletedIdx free list
Delta_Matrix adjacency_matrix;
Delta_Matrix *labels;
Delta_Matrix node_labels;
```

Node existence lives in the `DataBlock`; `Graph_ScanNodes` returns `DataBlock_Scan(g->nodes)` and iterates storage directly, skipping deleted slots. Id reuse is a plain `uint64_t *deletedIdx` array. `Graph_CreateNode` allocates a slot and touches only the *label* matrices — O(1) bookkeeping, independent of how many ids are free.

## What Rust does instead

Rust additionally maintains `all_nodes_matrix`, a GraphBLAS diagonal `(id,id)=true` for every live node: `set_all` on create, `remove` on delete, plus dup into every write snapshot, fold, wait, resize.

A symbolicated profile of `CREATE (:Drain)` against a 500k pool puts essentially the entire query inside `Graph::create_nodes` (5.77% of a 5.82% query thread), and within it entirely in GraphBLAS structural work — `GB_hyper_prune` ~23%, `GB_cumsum` ~29%, `GB_memcpy` ~15%, `GB_select_positional` ~22%. A mass delete fragments that matrix and every later write pays to maintain it.

Worth noting what it is *not*: the MVCC snapshot's `deleted_nodes.clone()` never appears in the profile, and cloning that bitmap measures 0.0030 ms at 500k entries — 0.2% of the cost. Optimising the bitmap cannot help.

## Nothing reads it

The unfiltered `MATCH (n)` scan already ignores it, walking `0..=max_node_id` filtered by the roaring bitmap — its own comment says live ids are *"iden

issues.body:
## Environment

- FalkorDB: `falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.4`
- Redis: 8.6.3
- Engine: C 

## Reproduction

```cypher
CREATE (:A {k9: 'j'})-[:R]->(:X)-[:R]->(:B {k2: false, id: 117});
MATCH p0 = (:A {k9: "j"})-[:R*2]-(n0 {id: 117})
RETURN n0;
```
## Expected behavior
The query should return the node with id = 117.
## Actual behavior
FalkorDB returns:
Unable to resolve filtered alias 'n0'
The server remains alive, but a valid variable-length path query is rejected.
## Controls
Removing the endpoint property filter succeeds:
```cypher
MATCH p0 = (:A {k9: "j"})-[:R*2]-(n0)
RETURN n0;
```

Using an explicit two-hop path also succeeds:

issues.title: Exact-range variable-length pattern with WHERE on the terminal endpoint returns no rows
issues.body:
**Version**: falkordb/falkordb:latest docker image (module 4.20.x, Redis 8.6.3).

A variable-length pattern with an exact range (`*3..3`) combined with a `WHERE` filter on the **terminal** endpoint returns an empty result even when matching paths exist. The same filter on the anchor endpoint works, the same filter with an open range (`*1..3`) works, and the identical filter placed after `WITH *` answers correctly.

**Repro** (fresh graph):
```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:H {i:1, u:'u1'})-[:P]->(:H {i:2, u:'u1'})-[:P]->(:H {i:3, u:'u1'})-[:P]->(:H {i:4, u:'u1'})"

// returns [1,2,3] hops — correct
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH p=(a:H {i:1})-[:P*3..3]->(b:H) RETURN [r IN relationships(p) | r.hop] LIMIT 1"

// EMPTY — but b (i:4) has u='u1'
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH p=(a:H {i:1})-[:P*3..3]->(b:H) WHERE b.u='u1' RETURN b.i LIMIT 1"

// correct (anchor-side filter)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH p=(a:H {i:1})-[:P*3..3]->(b:H) WHERE a.u='u1' RETURN b.i LIMIT 1"

// correct (open range)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:H {i:1})-[:P*1..3]->(b:H) WHERE b.u='u1' RETURN count(b)"

// correct (same filter, post-WITH)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH p=(a:H {i:1})-[:P*3..3]->(b:H) WITH p, b WHERE b.u='u1' RETURN b.i LIMIT 1"
```

Looks like the endpoint-predicate pushdown interacts badly with min==max ranges specifically. Found while bringing a ~580-test Cypher application suite to green on FalkorDB; we work around it by respelling `MATCH … WHERE` as `MATCH … WITH * WHERE` when an exact range is present.

issues.title: RESULTSET_SIZE 0 means zero rows — worth a doc warning beside the -1 = unlimited convention
issues.body:
**Version**: falkordb/falkordb:latest docker image (module 4.20.x).

Small docs/DX report: `GRAPH.CONFIG SET RESULTSET_SIZE 0` is accepted and means "return zero rows" — every read thereafter comes back empty with no error — while `-1` means unlimited. Coming from conventions where `0` disables a cap (as it does for `TIMEOUT` in the same config surface, where `TIMEOUT 0` = no timeout), this is an easy foot-gun: we set `0` intending "no limit" while lifting the docker image's defaults (`TIMEOUT 1000`, `RESULTSET_SIZE 10000`) for a test rig, and spent a full CI cycle on a suite where every query silently returned nothing.

The inconsistency between the two knobs in the same config namespace (`TIMEOUT 0` = off, `RESULTSET_SIZE 0` = empty) is the sharp edge. Either rejecting `0`, treating it as unlimited for symmetry with TIMEOUT, or a prominent line in the GRAPH.CONFIG docs would prevent it.

issues.title: n:Label allocates a value per scanned row: hasLabels takes the generic function lane
issues.body:
## Summary

A label predicate over a scan allocates in proportion to the rows scanned. On the benchmark graph:

| query | allocated |
|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)` | 5,983 B |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE n.id < 5 RETURN count(n)` | 6,726 B |
| **`MATCH (n) WHERE n:Person RETURN count(n)`** | **976,643 B** |

~94 bytes per row, for a test that is one bit of a matrix. The benchmark row `label predicate` sits at **2.29x** the C engine on allocated bytes as a result.

## Cause

`n:Person` reaches the runtime as `hasLabels(n, ['Person'])`. `VectorEval::eval` sends any `FuncInvocation` to `eval_function`, which:

1. materializes each operand columnarly — for a node variable that is a `Vec<Value>`, 16 bytes a row
2. materializes the result as another `Vec<Value>`, 16 bytes a row
3. calls the function per row, and `hasLabels` then re-resolves every label **name** to its id on every row via `get_label_id`

None of that is needed for a label test. Note it is not the matrix read: `WHERE n:NoSuchLabel`, which returns from `node_has_label` before touching a matrix, costs 962,285 B — just as much.

It also scales with rows, not with the graph: `MATCH (n:Person) WHERE n:Person` over 10,000 nodes costs 941,053 B; `MATCH (n:Doc) WHERE n:Doc` over 100 nodes costs 6,254 B.

## Suggested direction

A column kernel for `hasLabels`, in the same spirit as the comparison kernels already in `vectorized.rs`: resolve the label names once for the batch, then write one matrix bit per row straight into an `ExprColumn::Bools`. Claim only the recognisable shape — a bound `NodeIds` column and a list of string constants — and leave everything else on the generic lane so three-valued logic and error messages stay defined in one place.

Two traps for whoever does it:

- `hasLabels` type-checks **every** element of the list even once an earlier one has settled the answer, so `hasLabels(n, ['NeverUsed', 1])` is a type error, not `false`. Resolve-and-short-circuit in a single pass swallows that; `test11

issues.title: Creating one edge copies the whole edge-endpoint index: O(E) allocation per edge-creating write
issues.body:
## Summary

Creating a **single** edge allocates in proportion to the number of edges **already in the graph**. Measured, one `CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b)` per query:

| existing edges | allocated for one edge |
|---|---|
| 0 | 63 KB |
| 50,000 | **667 KB** |
| 200,000 | **2,634 KB** |

4x the edges, 3.9x the allocation — linear, at roughly 13 bytes per existing edge.

It is specific to edges, not to writes. On the same graph:

| query | allocated |
|---|---|
| read-only `MATCH` | 5,643 B |
| `CREATE (:Throwaway)` | 7,400 B |
| `MATCH … SET a.tmp = 1` | 6,011 B |
| `CREATE (t) … DELETE t` | 6,678 B |
| **one edge create** | **244,088 B** |

## Cause

`Graph::create_relationships_bulk` maintains the graph-wide reverse index with

```rust
let endpoints = Arc::make_mut(&mut self.edge_endpoints);
```

`edge_endpoints` is an `Arc<EndpointIndex>`, and the MVCC snapshot taken for every write query clones that `Arc`. So the refcount is always ≥2 by the time the write runs, and `Arc::make_mut` deep-copies the **entire** index — one slot per edge id, 4/6/8/16 bytes wide depending on tier — to insert one entry.

Copy-on-write is working as designed; the granularity is the problem. The whole index is the unit of copying.

## Why it matters beyond the benchmark

On the benchmark graph (~20k edges) this shows up as the `delete indexed edge` (2.60x C) and `urel create delete` (1.54x C) allocation rows, which is easy to read as a rounding issue. The scaling is the real point: on a graph with 10M edges, every single-edge insert would copy on the order of 100 MB. The benchmark simply has no row large enough to show it.

Note what it is **not**: the index on the property is irrelevant — the unindexed variant (`TREL`, 705 KB) costs more than indexed `SIMILAR` (445 KB) or `UREL` (246 KB) — and the delete half is minor (`SIMILAR` create-only is 228 KB of the 447 KB round trip).

## Suggested directions

1. **Page the index** so copy-on-write copies only modified pages rather than the whole arra

issues.title: Value Hash Join always builds from the right side, retaining the larger input
issues.body:
## Summary

`id eq join` — `MATCH (p:Person {id: 5}) MATCH (q:Person) WHERE id(q) = id(p) RETURN count(q)` — allocates **3.34x** the C engine (1,590,154 B against 476,381 B).

Bisected on the benchmark graph:

| | allocated |
|---|---|
| single scan | 5,613 B |
| cartesian, no join predicate | 294,917 B |
| **full query (Value Hash Join)** | **1,613,036 B** |

So the join adds ~1.3 MB over a plain cartesian, about 130 bytes per row for 10k rows.

## Cause

`ValueHashJoinOp::build_hash_table` always builds from the **right** sub-plan and retains every right batch:

```rust
for result in self.right.by_ref() {
    ...
    self.right_batches.push(batch);
}
```

The plan for this query is

```
Value Hash Join
    Node By Index Scan | (p:Person)     <- 1 row
    Node By Label Scan | (q:Person)     <- 10,000 rows
```

so it retains 10,000 rows of batch data plus a hash entry each, to find at most one match, while the other side is a single row. Building from the left would retain one row.

The operator's own doc notes the build side "allocates nothing per row" — true of the hash entries, which store `RightRowRef` positions rather than owned rows, but the retained batches are the cost.

## Suggested direction

Choose the build side by size rather than by position. Equality is symmetric so an inner equi-join is free to swap, but two things need care:

- **Cardinality.** Neither side's size is known before consuming it. The planner already has the information that matters here — an index scan or id seek yields few rows, a full label scan yields many — so the decision probably belongs there rather than in the operator.
- **Row order.** Swapping build and probe changes the order rows are emitted. Cypher guarantees nothing without `ORDER BY`, but existing tests may depend on the current order, so this wants checking before it is called safe.

A cheaper interim option, if swapping proves disruptive: bail out of retention when the build side exceeds some size and fall back to a ne

perf: collect DISTINCT — an aggregate that is not at the root of its tree still falls back to per-row
issues.body:
Split out of #2693, which fixed the other members of this cluster.

`AggregateOp::analyze_agg_tree` requires the aggregate to be the **root** of the projection's expression tree:

```rust
let ExprIR::FuncInvocation(func) = root.data() else {
    // Root is not an aggregate function (e.g., Map, Add, etc.)
    // — fall back to per-row which can recurse to find all aggregates.
    return None;
};
```

So `RETURN size(collect(DISTINCT p.age))` — the aggregate wrapped in `size(...)` — sends the whole operator down `consume_input_per_row`. The planner does not split the wrapper into a separate Project:

```
Aggregate
    Node By Label Scan | (p:Person)
```

## Measured

The wrapper alone, over 10,000 rows:

| query | instructions |
|---|---|
| `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN collect(DISTINCT p.age)` | 6,775,416 |
| `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN size(collect(DISTINCT p.age))` | 35,906,300 |

**5.3×**, from nothing but the `size(...)`. Both replies are small, so this is not serialisation.

Benchmark row `collect DISTINCT`: 35.79 M instructions against C's 16.79 M — **2.13×**, the largest remaining aggregate gap and the largest single absolute gap in the cluster (19.0 M).

## Why it was not fixed in #2693

The other three gates there — computed keys, `DISTINCT` over an expression, multi-argument aggregations — all reduce to "materialise this input as a column", which the existing `AggInputKind::Computed` already does. This one does not. The aggregate has to be found by recursion (as `run_agg_expr` and `set_agg_expr_zero` already do), accumulated under its own accumulator variable, and then the *enclosing* expression applied per group at finalize time. That is a change to how the operator finalizes, not to how it extracts, so it wants its own PR and its own tests.

## Suggested shape

`analyze_agg_tree` returns one `VectorizableAgg` per tree today. Recursing to collect the aggregates inside a tree — each already carrying its own `acc_var` — would let the existing finalize step evaluate

issues.title: Implement effects wire format v3
issues.body:
Umbrella issue. Tracks both engines; neither ships alone.

## Why

Engine migration — upgrading a C deployment to Rust, and downgrading back, without a dump and reload. #2459 made RDBs mutually loadable, so a replica of one engine can full-sync from a master of the other. **Effects are the remaining gap.** After the sync the master keeps streaming `GRAPH.EFFECT`, and neither engine can read the other's buffers.

Measured, not assumed:

- Rust → C segfaults C in `AttributeSet_Update` on the first property `SET`
- C → Rust rejects with `unknown effect type: 0`

## Why a new version rather than cloning v2

Cloning C's v2 byte-for-byte would interoperate with shipped C, but it means adopting two decisions that are hostile to a second implementation:

1. **`CREATE_NODE` carries no entity id.** The replica infers it from creation order, so any disagreement corrupts the replica silently and the record carries nothing to check against.
2. **`SET_LABELS`/`REMOVE_LABELS` carry a `GxB_Vector_serialize` blob** — a GraphBLAS-internal encoding embedded in the replication stream. It couples the wire to a library's serialization version, and it is large: 10,000 nodes gaining one label is 23,314 bytes against 46 for the explicit form.

This is not fighting C's design, it *is* C's design: C's reader accepts any version `<=` its own and already branches per version. The v1→v2 bump existed to change the label records; v3 changes them again.

## The rollout constraint

`EFFECTS_VERSION` picks what a node **emits**. Reads are dispatched on the version byte that arrived, so a node reads every version it understands regardless. That asymmetry is the rollout, and it is the same one C uses: **upgrade readers, then flip writers.**

The default therefore cannot move to 3 until the C engine reads v3. A master emitting v3 at a peer that cannot read it is silent data loss, not a degraded mode. A test asserts the default rather than leaving it to review.

## Scope

- Rust side — see sub-issue
- C

issues.title: Implement effects v3 in Rust
issues.body:
Parent: #2696

The Rust half of the v3 wire format: the codec, the emitter, the replica-side apply path, and the config that selects between v2 and v3. Lands behind `EFFECTS_VERSION`, which stays at 2 — see the parent for why the default cannot move until C reads v3.

## Shape of the format

    u8  version = 3
    u8  flags                   bit 0 = compressed
    u32 uncompressed_length     only when compressed
    u32 crc32                   only when compressed
    records… | zstd frame

The header is never compressed, so a reader knows what it holds before committing to decode anything. The flags byte is reserved whether or not compression is on: adding a byte later would cost another version bump for one byte.

A reader meeting a flag bit outside the mask it understands **rejects the buffer** rather than ignoring it. Decoding anyway would apply a prefix of something whose shape it does not know.

Every batchable record is `u32 opcode · u32 count · blocks…`. There is no separate "batch" record type — `count == 1` and `count == 10_000` are the same record, so nothing is left un-batchable and the decoder has one shape per opcode.

| Record | Partition key | Per row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CREATE_NODE` | `LabelSet` + `AttrIds` | id, values |
| `CREATE_EDGE` | `RelType` + `AttrIds` | id, src, dst, values |
| `UPDATE_NODE` / `UPDATE_EDGE` | `LabelSet` + `AttrIds` | id, values |
| `SET_LABELS` / `REMOVE_LABELS` | `LabelSet` | id |
| `DELETE_NODE` / `DELETE_EDGE` | `LabelSet` / `RelType` | id (+ src, dst) |
| `ADD_SCHEMA`, `ADD_ATTRIBUTE`, index, constraint | singular — no count | — |

**`ADD_SCHEMA` and `ADD_ATTRIBUTE` carry their id.** v2 sent the name alone and let the replica infer the id from its own append order — the assumption every other record's bare ids rest on, and the only one that could not be checked. issues.title: Implement effects v3 in C
issues.body:
Parent: #2696

The C half of the v3 wire format. **No plan yet** — this issue exists to hold the scope and to make the dependency visible; sub-issues come once the work is broken down.

## Why this gates everything

`EFFECTS_VERSION` cannot default to 3 until C reads v3. A master emitting v3 at a peer that cannot read it is silent data loss. The Rust side ships first and stays behind the flag, so nothing changes for anyone until this lands.

## What it has to cover

- **Read v3.** C's reader already accepts any version `<=` its own and branches per version, so the dispatch point exists.
- **Write v3**, selected the same way — read every version understood, emit one.
- **The cross-engine harness**, which is the real gate for both halves and cannot run until this exists. Byte-level unit tests on either side are necessary and not sufficient: a wrong width does not fail on the far side, it makes C read misaligned bytes as a type and write through the resulting pointer.

## Known differences the C side will meet

Recorded from reading `origin/master` while building the Rust side, so they are decisions rather than surprises:

- **Constraint effects carry a status in v3.** `EffectsBuffer_AddCreateConstraintEffect` and `...DropConstraint...` declare identical formats today and neither writes one. v3 adds it to the *create* record only — a replica does not validate, so it is the only way it can learn whether a constraint is enforcing, and it is what makes the second announcement after async validation converge rather than duplicate. The drop record carries none, matching C.
- **Index DDL carries its `OPTIONS` map.** v2 could not encode it and forced those statements to replicate as verbatim queries.
- **Divergence handling.** C's `DivergenceGuard_OnFailure` forces a full resync; the Rust side now mirrors it, with one deliberate difference — it keys off the command being replayed, because `GRAPH.EFFECT` is a payload any client can send and answering a malformed one with a for

issues.title: effects v3: the codec, the emitter and the apply path
issues.body:
Parent: #2697 · **PR 1 of the stack** — reuses #2570.

Everything under `graph/src/` and `src/`. Tests, benches and the spec follow in their own PRs so this one is reviewable as behaviour.

## Contents

- **The codec** — `graph/src/effects/v3/`: the five blocks, all fourteen records, encode and decode, and the `IdList` encoding ladder (`Range`, `Sorted`, `Dictionary`, `Plain`).
- **The emitter** — grouping `Pending` into records by partition key.
- **The apply path** — decode to `Record`, apply to `Graph`, with the divergence checks v2 could not make.
- **Config** — `EFFECTS_VERSION`, `EFFECTS_COMPRESSION`, `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD`, all living with the code that reads them.
- **Index and constraint DDL as effects**, including the `OPTIONS` map v2 had to replicate verbatim.
- **The divergence guard** — a replica that refuses an effect now forces a full resync instead of serving data it has proved wrong.

## Divergence checks this adds

v3 detects thirteen distinct conditions where v2 detected almost none. Several were found by review while building it and are worth calling out because each is a silent-corruption path in v2:

- an `AttrSet` that is not strictly ascending — the stores merge it as a span, so wire order is load-bearing, and only a `debug_assert` stood behind it
- `ADD_ATTRIBUTE` judged against the id the name actually holds, not the dictionary's length, which false-accepted a buffer whose id belonged to a different attribute
- one buffer holding one wire version, so a mid-query `GRAPH.CONFIG SET EFFECTS_VERSION` cannot mix v2 records behind a v3 header
- bounded allocations: a 15-byte payload could otherwise force a ~34 GB `Vec`, and a ~100-byte zstd frame could inflate to gigabytes before its declared length was checked
- a depth limit on nested values — ~350 KB of nested array tags was a stack overflow, not a `DecodeError`

Payload for `UNWIND range(0,9999) AS i CREATE (:Person {name, age})`: **260,001 → 120,051 bytes**. By how much the shapes

From review comment #04 on #2570.

## What this was expected to be

A hundred-site refactor: roughly 68 references in `graph/src/runtime/pending.rs` and 35 in `graph/src/graph/graph.rs`, threading index-document bookkeeping through the mutation paths as loose parallel collections. Big enough to want its own PR, placed between the functional work and the tests so it would not be reviewed alongside replication behaviour, and so tests written before it would not be rewritten by it.

## What it actually was

**+137 / −131 across four files.**

The type already existed. `DeferredIndexes` had exactly the four fields — node adds, node removes, edge adds, edge removes — and a `merge` doing exactly what `Pending`'s four hand-written fold loops did. It just was not used for storage, so `Pending` kept eight loose fields and converted them into the struct at the end.

So the work was *use the type we have*:

- `Pending` holds `index_docs` and `deferred_docs`; the four fold loops become `deferred_docs.absorb(&mut index_docs)`
- `take_deferred_indexes` becomes `mem::take`, where it used to rebuild the struct field by field
- the v3 applier's `IndexOps` and the v2 applier's four locals both hold one `IndexDocs`, so all three collection sites are the same shape
- `EdgeDocRemovals` names `FxHashMap<u64, FxHashMap<u64, (u64, u64)>>` once instead of at six sites

The reference count was real but misleading: it was mostly the same four names repeated, not a hundred places each needing a decision.

`graph.rs`'s signatures are deliberately unchanged. Each of those functions touches exactly one of the four maps, and taking `&mut IndexDocs` would hand every one of them access to all four — the duplication was in the storage and the folding, never in the parameters.

## Why it is not its own PR

At that size it does not earn one, and keeping it separate costs more in stack maintenance than it buys in reviewability. The stack is now fo

issues.body:
Parent: #2697 · **PR 3 of the stack.**

`tests/flow/test_effects_v3.py` — 35 tests, seven classes, every one asserting on *both* sides of a real master/replica pair. `test_effects.py` covers the shapes a mutation can take and runs at whatever `EFFECTS_VERSION` defaults to; this file is about v3 specifically, and about the replica-side apply path.

## What the classes pin

| class | what it catches |
| --- | --- |
| `NullIsRemove` | `SET x = NULL` removes on both sides — the property is *absent*, not null |
| `ConstraintAsEffect` | v3 sends one `GRAPH.EFFECT` and zero `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT`; v2 sends the legacy pair |
| `ConstraintConvergence` | a large label is announced exactly twice and the replica ends with **one** constraint at OPERATIONAL |
| `Shapes` | record partitioning, 100k nodes + 20k edges, deletes interleaved with creates, whole-graph `graph_eq` |
| `IndexDDLMechanism` | index DDL rides a `GRAPH.EFFECT` under v3 and stays verbatim under v2 — the same statement, opposite counts |

| `DivergenceForcesResync` | a refused effect forces a full resync; a client-sent malformed one does not |
| `PromotedReplica` | a promoted replica settles a constraint it inherited UNDER CONSTRUCTION |

issues.title: effects v3: benchmarks for the codec and the encoding ladder
issues.body:
Parent: #2697 · **PR 4 of the stack.**

`graph/benches/effects_blocks.rs` and `graph/benches/effects_versions.rs` — v2 against v3 on the same staged writes, and the `IdList` ladder against the shapes that pick each rung.

## What they measure

- **encode / decode**, v2 vs v3 vs v3+zstd, across five orders of magnitude
- **the ladder** — which encoding wins for which shape, and what each costs to choose
- **construction** — what `push` costs and what it allocates, which no other group could see because they all start from a finished `IdList`

## Why construction mattered

It settled a design question that reasoning could not. The `IdList` representation degrades `Range → Ascending → Spilled`, and whether the middle rung was worth having came down to numbers:

| shape, 1M ids | two rungs | three rungs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| consecutive | 1.181 ms | 1.179 ms |
| shuffled | 2.982 ms | 3.003 ms |
| gapped | 2.029 ms | 7.639 ms |

Consecutive — what every allocator hands out — pays nothing. Gapped pays ~3.8x, and that part is inherent: a per-id roaring `insert` is a `BTreeMap` lookup plus a container insert, against a bounds check and a store for `Vec::push`.

The first run of that comparison showed consecutive paying 20% as well, which turned out to be a mistake in the *implementation* rather than the design — building the bitmap inside `push` bloated a function that runs once per id. Moving it behind `#[inline(never)]` returned it to baseline exactly. Worth recording because the benchmark is what caught it.

## Caveat to carry forward

These are criterion wall-clock numbers. The `gapped` figure in particular is noisy between runs — 613 µs, 780 µs and 550 µs at 100k on the same binary — so the ~3-4x magnitude is trustworthy and the exact multiplier is not. Deterministic instruction counts need callgrind, which means the Linux toolchain image; worth doing before any of these numbers are quoted as a target.

## Requires

The `test-util` feature, which exposes `IdList::wri

issues.title: effects v3: the spec
issues.body:
Parent: #2697 · **PR 5 of the stack.**

`docs/effects-v3.md` — the wire format written down for whoever implements the other side, which is the point: this is the document the C work in #2698 is built against.

## What it has to state

- the header, the record shapes, the five blocks, and the four `IdList` encodings
- which decisions are **normative** and which are an encoder's free choice. The decoder supports every encoding, so the encoder's choice never has to match across engines — but `optimize()` on a roaring bitmap *is* normative, because an unoptimized bitmap serializes to different bytes and two engines that disagree about calling it produce different buffers for the same set.
- the sizing arithmetic behind each choice, so a second implementation can check it rather than take it

## One thing the spec had wrong

`T_NULL` in a value slot was documented as meaning "absent" while the applier treats it as "remove this attribute" — and the removal reading is the load-bearing one, because it is how `SET n.x = NULL` replicates at all.

The two only coexist because the partition key is the entity's *exact* attribute set, so no row is ever padded. That makes shape-exactness a rule rather than an accident, and it is worth stating plainly: widening the key to group different-but-overlapping shapes is the obvious next optimisation, and under this encoding it is unsound — the pad it inserts is byte-identical to a removal, so the replica would delete a property the master still holds. A C emitter written to the spec as previously published would have done it immediately.

## Also

The deck, which is ~20 commits behind the code and needs re-syncing against what actually shipped.

issues.title: perf(aggregate): grouping allocates a key Vec per input row, not per group
issues.body:
## Problem

`AggregateOp`'s vectorized grouping loop allocates a `Vec<Value>` for **every input row** purely to probe the group map, and drops it again as soon as the group turns out to already exist.

`graph/src/runtime/ops/aggregate.rs`:

```rust
for row_idx in 0..num_active {
    let key_values: Vec<Value> =                            // one malloc per row
        key_columns.iter().map(|col| col[row_idx].clone()).collect();
    let group_key = GroupKey(key_values);

    let entry = groups.entry(group_key).or_insert_with(|| { // ...freed right here on a hit
```

Only the first row of each group ever retains its key. Grouping 10,000 rows into 100 groups therefore pays 10,000 malloc/free pairs to keep 100 — the allocator traffic scales with the *input* cardinality while the useful work scales with the *group* cardinality.

The same pattern is in the per-row fallback (`consume_batch_per_row`).

## Impact

Every grouped aggregation is affected — `WITH … count(*)`, `RETURN expr, count(*)`, `GROUP BY`-shaped queries. Measured with the repo's own callgrind harness (`bench callgrind`, `THREAD_COUNT 1`), the allocation accounts for ~7.6% of total instructions on the benchmark set's two grouping queries, both of which group 10k rows:

| query | instructions |
|---|---:|
| `WITH pipeline` — `MATCH (p:Person) WITH p.id % 100 AS g, count(*) AS c WHERE c > 50 …` | 3,175,918 |
| `ORDER BY agg` — `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.id % 5 AS k, count(*) …` | 2,906,770 |

## Suggested fix

Back `GroupKey` with an inline-capacity vector so single-key grouping — the shape that carries the allocations — can probe the map without touching the allocator. `smallvec` is already a direct dependency of the `graph` crate.

The inline capacity must be **one** slot, not two: `Value` is 16 bytes, so the key measures 32 bytes at one inline slot and 48 at two, versus `Vec`'s 24, and that width is carried by every group of every shape — including the empty key held by keyless aggregation (`count(*)`, `su

issues.title: BGREWRITEAOF segfaults its child under aof-use-rdb-preamble no, so the AOF can never be compacted
issues.body:
Affects **both engines**. Not a regression from the Rust migration — I checked C too, see below.

## Reproduction

```bash
redis-server --port 7801 --loadmodule <falkordb.so> \
  --appendonly yes --aof-use-rdb-preamble no
redis-cli -p 7801 graph.query g "CREATE (:P {v:1})"
redis-cli -p 7801 bgrewriteaof
```

One graph key with one node is enough.

```
# Background AOF rewrite terminated by signal 11
aof_last_bgrewrite_status:err
```

The parent survives — it still answers `PING` — so nothing fails loudly. The child crash report lands in the log and the rewrite never completes.

**Control:** the same server with `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes`, which is the Redis default, reports `aof_last_bgrewrite_status:ok`. The no-preamble path is the trigger.

## Both engines

| engine | result |
| --- | --- |
| Rust (`target/release/libfalkordb.dylib`, `feat/effects-v3`) | signal 11, `status:err` |
| C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`, built 2026-07-13) | signal 11, `status:err` |

Same repro, same outcome. `git log -S "aof_rewrite: None"` points at #2279 (the Rust migration), but that is only when the Rust *line* was written — C has the same gap, so the migration inherited it rather than caused it.

## Cause

Neither module type registers an `aof_rewrite` callback:

- Rust — `src/redis_type.rs`: `aof_rewrite: None` on the graph type, and again on the meta type
- C — `src/serializers/graphcontext_type.c`: `RedisModuleTypeMethods tm = { 0 };` and `aof_rewrite` is never assigned; same in `graphmeta_type.c`

With `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes` Redis writes an RDB preamble and reaches `rdb_save`, which both engines do implement. With it `no`, Redis rewrites every key as commands and calls `mt->aof_rewrite(...)` for a module key — unconditionally, on a NULL pointer.

## Impact

Confined to deployments that turn the preamble off, but unpleasant there:

- **the AOF can never be compacted.** Every rewrite dies, so the file grows without bound.
- **it retries on its own.** `auto-aof-rewr

issues.title: perf: a scalar function with all-constant arguments is evaluated once per row
issues.body:
`split+trim+replace` is the worst instruction ratio in the benchmark suite: **2.83× C** (871,972 against 308,153).

## The cause

`VectorEval::eval_function` evaluates a scalar function once per row even when every argument column is an `ExprColumn::Scalar` — one value already shared by the whole batch:

```rust
let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(len);
let mut args = Vec::with_capacity(columns.len());
for i in 0..len {
    args.clear();
    args.extend(columns.iter().map(|c| c.get(i)));
    func.validate_args_type(&args)?;
    out.push(func.func.call(self.runtime, &args)?);
}
Ok(ExprColumn::Values(out))
```

So a constant subexpression costs exactly as much as a row-dependent one, and materialises a `Vec<Value>` of identical results on the way out.

The benchmark row is nothing but constants:

```cypher
UNWIND range(0, 99) AS i
RETURN count(split(replace(trim('  a,b,c  '), ',', ';'), ';'))
```

## Measured

Marginal cost per row, each function measured against the same query with `count(1)` as the floor:

| function | instructions/row |
|---|---|
| `trim` | 813 |
| `toUpper` | 833 |
| `replace` | 1,107 |
| **`split`** | **3,578** |

`split` alone costs more than C's entire query (3,081/row). The implementation is not the problem — five allocations for three parts is reasonable — it is being called 100 times to produce one answer.

## Why the existing constant-folding pass does not catch it

The optimizer already folds constants, but through `GraphFn::pure_fn` — a `Runtime`-free form only the temporal and map constructors provide. `trim`/`replace`/`split` have none, so the pass cannot reach them.

## Suggested fix

Fold in the evaluator: when every argument column is a `Scalar`, call the function once and return a `Scalar`. This needs no new per-function plumbing and **composes** — the literal is a `Scalar`, so `trim` returns one, so `replace` sees one, so `split` does too, and the chain collapses to three calls per batch from three per row. It also catches arguments t

issues.title: perf: four algo procedures duplicate the adjacency matrix they just built
issues.body:
`algo.WCC`, `algo.labelPropagation` and two neighbours build an owned adjacency matrix and then immediately `GrB_Matrix_dup` it, dropping the original one line later. The copy exists purely to satisfy ownership: `Matrix::inner` documents that its caller must not free the handle while LAGraph frees every matrix it is given.

## The fix already exists in the file

`create_lagraph_graph_borrowed` / `delete_lagraph_graph_borrowed` detach `G->A` before deleting, so LAGraph does not free a caller-owned handle. `algo.BFS` has used them since they were added, with a comment saying why. The other four should keep the `Matrix` wrapper alive for the call and lend its handle instead of copying it.

Each of these procedures has two paths that differ in ownership — the unfiltered path lends a matrix it built, the compact path hands over a raw matrix nothing else owns — so the teardown has to match the construction per path or the handle is freed twice.

## Measured

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `algo.WCC({})` | 2,945,862 | 2,818,862 |
| `algo.WCC({relationshipTypes:[…]})` | 2,936,717 | 2,774,328 |
| `algo.labelPropagation` | 2,860,348 | 2,698,694 |

About 5%.

## The larger finding, which this does not fix

While measuring the above: these procedures allocate in proportion to the node **id space** rather than to live nodes, and **both engines do**.

| graph with 10,463 live nodes | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| fresh | 2.77 MB | 2.76 MB |
| after 500k nodes created + deleted | **67.4 MB** | **42.6 MB** |

24× on Rust and 15× on C for the same 10,463 live nodes, because `n = node_count + deleted_nodes_count` sizes the matrix by every id slot ever used. The benchmark runs `WCC all types` after its write rows, which is why that row reads 1.57× C — and 67.4 / 42.6 is 1.58×, the same number.

So the row's ratio is not the dup, and it is not the "all types" path either: `WCC all types` 2.95 MB ≈ `WCC typed` 2.94 MB ≈ `WCC null` 2.96 MB, while `WCC labeled` is *higher* at 3.72 MB.

issues.title: perf: one computed grouping key or DISTINCT argument drops the whole aggregate to per-row
issues.body:
`AggregateOp::analyze` whitelists a few expression shapes and returns `None` — sending the **whole operator** to `consume_input_per_row` — when anything falls outside one. The fallback is per-operator, not per-expression, so a single arithmetic grouping key also costs the *aggregate inputs* their bulk extraction.

Aggregate inputs already have an `AggInputKind::Computed` variant that keeps the columnar path (#2555). Keys, `DISTINCT` arguments and multi-argument aggregations never got one.

## Isolated

A control that changes nothing but the shape — same data, same groups, same output, one `+ 0` between them:

| grouping key | instructions (10,000 rows) |
|---|---|
| `p.age` | 15,964,859 |
| `p.age + 0` | 28,289,118 |

`ORDER BY` contributes nothing to that (15,967,319 with it, 15,964,859 without) — the gap is entirely the key expression. Per row it is ~1,230 instructions, and the reported gaps against C land on the same figure: `ORDER BY agg` 1,201/row, `WITH pipeline` 1,223/row, `percentileDisc` 1,375/row. That is what makes these one cause rather than five.

## The gates

- a key that is not a bare variable or property — `p.id % 5 AS k`
- `DISTINCT` over anything but a variable or property — `DISTINCT p.id % 100`
- a multi-argument aggregation — `percentileDisc(p.score, 0.5)`

## Affected rows

| query | vs C |
|---|---|
| `count distinct` | 1.93× |
| `percentileCont` / `percentileDisc` | 2.05× |
| `WITH pipeline` | 1.74× |
| `ORDER BY agg` | 1.72× |
| `distinct aggs` | 1.71× |

## Two hazards on the way

Both are latent in code that a fix newly routes traffic through, and both were found by measurement rather than reading:

- The general accumulate loop validates argument *types* but not their *domain*, which is harmless while every aggregation reaching it is single-argument and unconstrained. `percentileDisc(x, 1.2)` is neither, and its kernel indexes by the percentile — out of range it **crashes the server** rather than raising.

issues.title: Unbounded value nesting crashes the server: reduce() with ~20k levels kills the process
issues.body:
## Impact

Any client with write access can take the process down with a single ~70-byte
query. No replication involved, no special command — one `RETURN`.

## Repro

```
redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN size(reduce(acc = [], x IN range(1, 20000) | [acc]))"
```

Measured against a release build:

| depth  | result                              |
|--------|-------------------------------------|
| 5,000  | ok                                  |
| 10,000 | ok                                  |
| 20,000 | **server gone**, connection refused  |

The process dies without a Redis-level log line, consistent with a stack
overflow rather than a panic.

A deeply nested value can also be *stored*: `CREATE (:Deep {v: reduce(acc = [],
x IN range(1, 300) | [acc])})` succeeds and reads back, so the value reaches the
attribute store and the RDB as well as the query result.

## Cause

`Value` is recursive — `Value::List(Arc<ThinVec<Value>>)` — so every operation
on a deeply nested one recurses once per level. `Drop` is the unavoidable one:

```
drop(Value::List(Arc<ThinVec<Value>>))
  -> drop(Arc)               refcount reaches 0
    -> drop(ThinVec<Value>)  drops each element
      -> drop(Value::List)   the same shape again
```

There is no hand-written `Drop` impl; this is compiler-generated glue, which is
why it does not appear in the source. `PartialEq`, `Debug` and the encoders walk
the same way.

Isolated with `std::mem::forget`: a 50,000-level value **decodes** without
touching the stack and only aborts when it is dropped. Forget it and nothing
crashes — so the recursion is in the drop, not in any one consumer.

## Likely not specific to the Rust engine

`src/datatypes/array.c` on `master` frees arrays recursively as well —
`SIArray_Free` → `SIValue_Free` → `SIArray_Free` — with no depth guard, so the
same shape exists in C.

**This has not been executed against the C module**, only read. Worth confirming
against `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-c` before treating it as engine-spe

issues.title: Rust engine rejects `startNode(null)` and `endNode(null)` from `OPTIONAL MATCH`
issues.body:
Environment
- C image: falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.4
- Rust image: falkordb/falkordb:edge-rs 

## Description

The Rust engine returns:

```text
Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null
```
when startNode() or endNode() receives a nullable relationship produced by OPTIONAL MATCH.
The C engine accepts the same query and returns null.
According to the FalkorDB function documentation, startNode(null) and endNode(null) should return null:
https://docs.falkordb.com/cypher/functions
## Reproduction
Create a graph:
```cypher
CREATE (:A)-[:R]->(:B);
```
Then execute:
```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r:R]->()
WHERE false
RETURN startNode(r) AS s, endNode(r) AS e;
```
## Observed behavior
C engine
FalkorDB v4.20.4 returns one nullable row:
```text
s     e
null  null
```
Rust engine
FalkorDB edge-rs fails without returning a result:
```text
Type mismatch: expected Edge but was Null
```
The same error occurs with either of these queries:
```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r:R]->()
WHERE false
RETURN startNode(r) AS s;
```
```cypher
OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r:R]->()
WHERE false
RETURN endNode(r) AS e;
```
## Expected behavior
Both Rust and C engines should return a row containing null values:
```text
s     e
null  null
```
No type error should be raised because the relationship binding is legitimately null after OPTIONAL MATCH.

issues.title: FalkorDB edge-rs: identity `CALL` barriers change cardinality and writes
effects v3: apply cannot decide node-id liveness, so a divergent buffer is applied silently
issues.body:
### Summary

Applying an effects buffer cannot decide whether a node id is live, so it
approximates the question with two buffer-scoped stand-ins. A buffer that leaves
the replica's id space in a state no master could have been in is applied
silently.

### Why the question cannot be asked

`Graph` holds `node_count` and `deleted_nodes` and no live set, so the only
boundary it can offer is `node_count + deleted_nodes.len()`. That is the boundary
*if the id space is dense*, and every accessor derived from it carries the same
assumption — `first_unallocated_node_id`, `max_node_id`. An assertion written in
terms of them therefore checks one derivation of the state against another
derivation of the same state, and passes on a graph that is already wrong.

Density is a property of buffer boundaries, not of the records inside one. v3
emits records grouped by shape, so a `CREATE_NODE` of 500..600 may precede one of
0..500. Between them the graph holds 100 live nodes whose highest id is 599 and
reports its boundary as 100 — claiming 0..99 are live, that 500..599 were never
handed out, and that 100 is the next fresh id.

### What stands in for it today

Two approximations in `graph/src/effects/v3/apply.rs`:

- `entry_unallocated`, the boundary frozen at buffer entry, passed to
  `Graph::create_nodes` because the graph's own boundary is wrong mid-buffer.
- `created_here`, a running set of the ids the buffer has created so far,
  maintained only so that a create-then-delete-then-recreate inside one buffer is
  not misread as a double claim.

Neither can say anything about the ids that *no* record creates, which is the
case that matters: a buffer whose creates skip an id leaves that id allocated on
the master and unaccounted for on the replica, and nothing notices.

### Impact

A replica that applies such a buffer holds an id space its master does not have,
and the next id it allocates after promotion collides with a live node. That
specific corruption is fixed separately, on th

issues.title: test_ldbc.py self-loop header rewrite uses macOS-only sed -i, breaks on GNU/Linux
issues.body:
Sub-task of #2560 (Linux breakage bullet).

`tests/test_ldbc.py:392` rewrites the header of self-loop edge CSVs with:

```python
subprocess.run(["sed", "-i", "", f"1s/.*/{line}/", f"data/{base_path}/{file['file']}"], check=True)
```

`sed -i ""` is the BSD/macOS form. On GNU sed the separate `""` is parsed as the script, so the `1s/.../` argument is treated as an input file and sed exits 2 with `can't read 1s/.../` — the exact failure quoted in #2560. Any Linux run of the LDBC loader dies here for every self-loop edge file (all same-label files take this branch).

Additionally, interpolating the header into a sed `s///` script is fragile: a header containing `/` or `&` would corrupt the replacement.

Proposed fix: do the one-line header replacement in pure Python (read lines, replace index 0, write back) — portable across macOS/Linux/Windows and immune to sed metacharacters.

issues.title: Constraint on an unregistered label or property is lost or silently rewritten by RDB save/load
issues.body:
## Summary

A constraint whose label or property has not been registered in the graph's schema is **not persisted correctly**. Depending on which one is missing, an RDB save/load either silently drops the constraint or silently rewrites it to enforce a **different property**.

This is pre-existing on `main` (verified on merge-base `17692da9f`) and is unrelated to effects replication.

## Symptom 1 — the constraint disappears

Label never registered:

```
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CREATE (:Other {aaa: 1})"
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT create g MANDATORY NODE Zed PROPERTIES 1 zzz
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CALL db.constraints()"   ->  Zed [zzz] OPERATIONAL
DEBUG RELOAD
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CALL db.constraints()"   ->  (empty array)
```

## Symptom 2 — the constraint enforces a different property

Label registered, property not. `aaa` is registered first, so it owns attribute id 0:

```
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CREATE (:Filler {aaa: 1})"
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Reg) ON (n.aaa)"
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT create g MANDATORY NODE Reg PROPERTIES 1 neverseen
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CALL db.constraints()"   ->  Reg [neverseen] OPERATIONAL
DEBUG RELOAD
GRAPH.QUERY      g "CALL db.constraints()"   ->  Reg [aaa]       OPERATIONAL
```

The constraint now enforces `aaa` instead of `neverseen`, with no error and no log line. This is the more serious of the two: the graph goes on enforcing a rule nobody asked for, and stops enforcing the one that was asked for.

## Cause

`Graph::create_constraint` stores the label and property **names** without registering either in the schema. The RDB encoder then needs ids for both and has no way to get them:

- **Symptom 1** — `src/serializers/mod.rs:246-270` writes constraints nested inside the loop over registered labels. A constraint on a label that is not in `node_labels` is never visited, so it is never written.
- **Symptom 2** — `encode_constraint_block` (`src/serializers/mod.rs:433-436`) resolves each property name with `position(..).unwrap_or(0)`. An unregistered

issues.title: effects v3: the wire codec
issues.body:
The wire half of #2699, split out so it can be reviewed on its own.

#2699 covered "the codec, the emitter and the apply path" as one unit, and at 15k lines that was not reviewable. The codec is separable: it turns bytes into records and back, and knows nothing about a graph. That makes it reviewable against `docs/effects-v3.md` by someone who has never read this engine's runtime — and it is the only part the C implementation needs, since C has to match these bytes and nothing else.

## Scope

    graph/src/effects/reader.rs      a bounds-checked cursor
    graph/src/effects/writer.rs      the EffectWrite sink
    graph/src/effects/error.rs       DecodeError
    graph/src/effects/mod.rs         EffectEncode<V> / EffectDecode<V> / EffectDecodeSized<V>
    graph/src/effects/v3/value.rs    the SIValue codec
    graph/src/effects/v3/blocks.rs   RelType, LabelSet, AttrIds, AttrValues
    graph/src/effects/v3/id_list.rs  the id block and its encoding ladder
    graph/src/effects/v3/records.rs  the records, and reading a whole payload
    graph/src/effects/v3/fixtures.rs the cross-engine conformance corpus

The wire types travel with it, because they are wire types: `si_type` and `index_field_type` become `u32`, which is what C declares, and `T_MAP` is added — v3 can carry a map where the RDB stream cannot.

## Done when

- `grep -E '\bGraph\b|\bPending\b'` over `graph/src/effects/` returns doc comments only
- the committed conformance corpus regenerates byte-identical on every run, so a change that moves one byte fails with the case that moved
- hostile input is refused before it is allocated for: a count the buffer cannot satisfy must not reach a `Vec::with_capacity`
- the id-list width helpers assert their own byte order, since a round trip cannot detect a byte swap

The emitter and the apply path remain #2699, and land on top of this as #2570.

issues.title: perf(aggregate): a computed GROUP BY key forces the whole aggregate onto the per-row path
issues.body:
## Problem

`AggregateOp` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/aggregate.rs`) has two execution paths: a columnar one (`consume_input_vectorized`) and a per-row fallback (`consume_batch_per_row`). `analyze()` decides between them, and returning `None` selects the fallback **for the whole operator**.

Grouping keys were only accepted in two shapes:

- a bare variable — `WITH n AS x, count(*)`
- a one-level property access on a variable — `WITH n.age, count(*)`

Any other key expression returned `None`. That is much more costly than it sounds: it doesn't merely deoptimize the key, it abandons the entire vectorized path — the bulk aggregate-input extraction and the columnar accumulate loop go down with it. The operator then rebuilds a full owned `Row` for every input row (`BatchRow::to_owned_row`) and re-walks every key tree *and* every aggregate tree scalar-wise.

The queries this penalizes are ordinary Cypher, not exotic:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person) WITH n.id % 100 AS bucket, count(*) AS c RETURN bucket, c
MATCH (n:Person) RETURN toUpper(n.name) AS k, avg(n.age)
MATCH (n:Person) RETURN CASE WHEN n.age < 30 THEN 'young' ELSE 'old' END AS band, count(*)
```

Bucketing, normalizing, and binning a value are among the most common reasons to group at all, so the common shape was the one paying the slowest path.

## Why this is a gap rather than a design decision

Aggregate **inputs** already solved exactly this. `AggInputKind::Computed` evaluates an arbitrary input tree a column at a time through `VectorEval`, and its doc comment already lays out the rationale. Grouping keys simply never received the same treatment. `VectorEval` is also already the sole evaluator for every `RETURN` projection (`project.rs`) and every `WHERE` predicate (`filter.rs`), so the machinery needed is present and heavily exercised — keys were the odd one out.

## Impact

Measured on the `WITH pipeline` benchmark query with callgrind: **3,167,610 instructions/exec**, of which the per-row fallback is the dominant

## Summary

When both endpoints of an edge are deleted in the same operation, `Graph::delete_implicit_edges` deliberately skips clearing the combined adjacency matrix, and `Graph::delete_nodes` never touches it either. issues.body:
## Summary

`Apply` (the operator behind per-row `CALL {}` subqueries) resets DISTINCT deduplication state by clearing the **entire runtime-wide** deduper map, not just the entries belonging to its own sub-plan. Any `DISTINCT` aggregation in an enclosing scope loses its accumulated state every time a subquery invocation finishes, so duplicates that span a batch boundary are counted/collected more than once.

## Affected code

`graph/src/runtime/ops/apply.rs:279-284`

```rust
st.current = None;
// Clear DISTINCT deduplication state between per-row
// subquery invocations so that each CALL {} execution
// starts with a fresh deduper.
self.runtime.value_dedupers.borrow_mut().clear();
```

The map is shared by every `DISTINCT` in the plan — `graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:145`, populated in `graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:827-828` keyed by `(node.idx(), group_id)`, i.e. plan-node index plus aggregation group. Nothing restricts the key space to the sub-plan, and `graph/src/runtime/ops/aggregate.rs:553` reads the same map. `clear()` drops all of it.

## Trigger

Two conditions:

1. The `CALL {}` body forces per-row mode. `Apply::new` (`apply.rs:119-133`) sets `can_batch = false` when the sub-plan contains `Aggregate`, `Sort`, `Limit`, `Distinct`, `Union`, `Merge`, `Optional`, `Apply`, or `CartesianProduct`.
2. An enclosing `count(DISTINCT …)` / `collect(DISTINCT …)` accumulates across more than one batch.

Because `Apply` fills a whole batch (`BATCH_SIZE = 1024`, `graph/src/runtime/batch.rs:81`) before handing it to the aggregation, within-batch dedup still works; the loss is at batch boundaries. So the repro needs more than 1024 driving rows:

```cypher
UNWIND range(1, 3000) AS i
WITH i % 5 AS x
CALL { WITH x MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) AS c }
RETURN count(DISTINCT x)
```

## Expected vs actual

- **Expected:** `5`.
- **Actual:** roughly one count of each distinct value per 1024-row batch — about `15`. The number is a function of batch alignment, which also makes it non-determini

perf: a leaf scan packs a full 1024-row batch regardless of a downstream LIMIT
issues.body:
`... LIMIT 10` over a label scan does roughly 100x the work it needs and throws the rest away: the scan packs a full `BATCH_SIZE` (1024) batch before anything downstream can stop it.

The tell is a step function at the batch boundary rather than a curve in the limit. 10k `:Person` plus a 10k `:KNOWS` ring, instructions per query:

| query | instructions |
|---|---:|
| `scan LIMIT 10` | 702,890 |
| `scan LIMIT 1000` | 1,178,868 |
| `scan LIMIT 1024` | 1,188,376 |
| `scan LIMIT 2048` | 2,245,072 |

1.7x more work for 100x the rows, then exactly 2x the moment the limit crosses 1024. That is the batch size showing through, not the query getting harder.

## Most of the machinery already exists

- `BatchedResultEmitter::set_pack_ceiling` / `apply_record_cap` are already there, and the doc comment already describes this exact case — "an operator fed by a downstream `Skip`/`Limit` lowers it ... so a capped query produces a small first batch". Only `UNWIND` ever called it.
- `Runtime::record_cap` already walks `Project` / `Skip` / `CondTraverse` / `ExpandInto` to find the budget, and already stops at row-reducing barriers such as `Filter`.

The scan simply never asked.

## The budget is a hint, not a bound

At a leaf scan the budget cannot be treated as a bound on the operator's own output, because something between the scan and the `Limit` may discard rows — `effective_limit` deliberately walks *through* `CondTraverse`, which passes rows 1:0 as readily as 1:N. A ceiling pinned at the limit is then a losing bet, and an unbounded one.

Measured on 100,000 nodes where only the last 200 have an outgoing edge, `MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN id(b) LIMIT n`:

| | ceiling pinned | ceiling grows |
|---|---:|---:|
| `LIMIT 1` | 8,433,461,433 | 91,466,726 |
| `LIMIT 10` | 998,926,139 | 91,442,059 |
| no `LIMIT` | 90,826,764 | 90,793,233 |

Pinning is a **92x regression** on `LIMIT 1`. Doubling the ceiling back to `BATCH_SIZE` after each emitted batch bounds the downside to `O(log BAT

issues.title: Constraint properties are order-sensitive in Rust and sorted in C: (a,b) and (b,a) are two constraints here, one in C
issues.body:
## Summary

A constraint's properties are compared **positionally** in Rust and **as a sorted set** in C, and neither engine's `create_constraint` agrees with the other about what counts as the same constraint. Two consequences:

- `ON (n.a, n.b)` and `ON (n.b, n.a)` are **two** constraints here and **one** in C.
- `ON (n.a, n.a)` is accepted here and refused in C with `Properties cannot contain duplicates`.

This is pre-existing on `main` — `Constraint::matches` is byte-identical between `main` and the effects-v3 branch, and neither `create_constraint` has a duplicate check. Filing it separately because it is not an effects change.

## Reproduced

Live server, module built from the effects-v3 branch (the comparison code is unchanged from `main`):

```
GRAPH.QUERY ord "CREATE (:P {a:1,b:2})"
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE ord MANDATORY NODE P PROPERTIES 2 a b   -> PENDING
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE ord MANDATORY NODE P PROPERTIES 2 b a   -> PENDING

CALL db.constraints()
  MANDATORY  P  [a, b]  NODE  OPERATIONAL
  MANDATORY  P  ...           (a second row)
```

C rejects the second create as a duplicate.

MANDATORY is the reachable path: UNIQUE requires a supporting range index first.

## Where the two engines differ

**Rust** — `graph/src/graph/constraint.rs:79` (`Constraint::matches`) compares with `zip(...).all(...)`, so order is significant. Nothing sorts or de-duplicates: not `Graph::create_constraint`, not the command layer.

**C** — `GraphHub_AddConstraint` (`src/graph/graph_hub.c`, master `9bc012c14`):

| line | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| 643 | `GraphHub_FindOrAddAttribute` — names to ids |
| 657 | `qsort (attr_ids, ...)` — canonical order |
| 667 | refuses `Properties cannot contain duplicates` |
| 682 | rebuilds the **names** array aligned to the sorted ids |
| 700 | `Schema_GetConstraint (s, ct, attr_ids, n)` — duplicate check on sorted ids |

So C canonicalises to attribute-id order before it decides whether the constraint already exists, and stores the names

issues.title: Consider a row-major Pending so commit and emit share one attribute shape
issues.body:
## Summary

The master builds the same attribute shape twice, from one source, in two layouts — once to commit and once to replicate. `Pending` stores node attributes per entity, so both consumers have to convert, and each pays a `Value` copy doing it.

Consider having `Pending` hold the row-major shape itself, so commit and emit read one structure.

Raised from @AviAvni's review comment on #2570 (`gather_rows` "clones the Value which can be very heavy"). The clone is real; it is a symptom of the layout rather than the thing itself.

## What exists today

`Pending::new_nodes_attrs` is `FxHashMap<u64, Vec<(u16, Value)>>` — one `Vec` per entity, attribute ids repeated for every entity of the same shape.

For **N entities of width W** in one shape:

| | commit — `import_attrs` | apply (replica) — `insert_attrs_rows` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| input | per-entity map | row-major `(ids, attr_ids, rows)` |
| storage | N `Vec` allocations, N×W ids | one block, W ids shared |
| per entity | `scratch.extend(…cloned())` — **N×W clones** | none; the row is a slice |
| store call | `set_span` (drains) | `merge_span` (borrows) |
| nulls | filtered out | passed through = remove |

And `emit::gather_rows` is the adapter between them: it re-groups the same map by `(labels, attr_ids)` and rebuilds the row-major layout the apply side wants — **another N×W clones**, plus a `find` per cell.

So the grouping happens twice and the values are copied twice, because `Pending` holds them in the one layout neither consumer wants. `insert_attrs_rows`' own comment says the row-major form exists precisely to avoid this:

> Building `(id, value)` pairs from them cloned every `Value` in the record — `count x width` clones to say what the two slices already said, since `merge_span` clones again at the point it stores.

That optimisation was applied to the apply path and never to commit.

## What a shape-keyed `Pending` would buy

- the grouping runs **once** instead of twice
- N per-entity `Vec` alloca

issues.body:
## Summary

`index::falkordb::data_structures::cow_btree::tests::snapshot_is_isolated_from_a_concurrent_writer` fails intermittently. The failure is in the test's own liveness assumption, not in the COW B-tree: the isolation assertion never fires, only the "did the reader run at all" check does.

## Reproduction

The flake is scheduling-sensitive, so it needs contention to show up. At the default test-thread count it passed 12/12 for me; under `--test-threads=16` it failed **3 out of 40** runs (~7.5%):

```bash
cargo test -p graph --lib            # builds the test binary
BIN=$(ls -t target/debug/deps/graph-* | grep -v '\.d$' | head -1)
for i in $(seq 1 40); do "$BIN" --test-threads=16 2>&1 | grep -E "^test result:"; done
```

```
test index::falkordb::data_structures::cow_btree::tests::snapshot_is_isolated_from_a_concurrent_writer ... FAILED
thread '...' panicked at graph/src/index/falkordb/data_structures/cow_btree/tests.rs:229:5
test result: FAILED. 296 passed; 1 failed; 16 ignored
```

## Root cause

`graph/src/index/falkordb/data_structures/cow_btree/tests.rs:229` is:

```rust
let reads = reader.join().unwrap();
assert!(reads > 0, "reader thread never completed a read");
```

The test spawns a reader that loops `while !done_reader.load(Ordering::Relaxed)`, then the main thread churns the writer and sets `done = true`. Nothing forces the reader to complete an iteration before that happens. When the machine is saturated, the spawned thread can fail to be scheduled until after the writer has finished and set `done`, so the `while` body never runs, `reads == 0`, and the assert fires.

So the assertion encodes a scheduling assumption rather than a property of the data structure. Note the real isolation check inside the loop —

```rust
assert_eq!(..., expected, "snapshot observed a concurrent writer's mutation");
```

— did **not** fire in any failing run, so there is no evidence of a COW correctness problem here.

Make the reader's first read happe

issues.title: Id allocator can hand out a live id after a cancelled reservation, fusing two entities
issues.body:
### Summary

After a `CREATE` in the same query is cancelled by a `DELETE`, the id allocator
can hand out an id that is already live. Two nodes — or two relationships — end
up sharing one id, so the query silently creates fewer entities than it was
asked for. No error is raised and the `Nodes created` statistic under-reports to
match.

### Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a), (b), (c) DELETE b CREATE (d), (e)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) RETURN id(n) ORDER BY id(n)"
```

Four nodes should survive — `a`, `c`, `d`, `e`; `b` was created and deleted
inside the one query.

| | `Nodes created` | surviving ids |
|---|---|---|
| observed | 3 | `0, 2, 3` |
| expected | 4 | four distinct ids |

`c` and `d` are the same node: the second `CREATE` was handed id 2, which the
first clause had already given to `c`, and wrote over it.

The relationship allocator has the same defect. Cascading a delete through a
pending node returns an edge id, and the two surviving edges then come back
under one id:

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b), (c)-[:R]->(d) DELETE a CREATE (x)-[:R]->(y)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN id(r) ORDER BY id(r)"
```

observed `1, 1` — the same relationship returned twice — against an expected two
distinct ids. Note that deleting a relationship *directly* does not reproduce
this; only a node delete cascading through `remove_pending_relationships_for_node`
returns a relationship id.

### How often

Not a corner case. Seeded sequences of ordinary creates, pending
create-then-deletes and committed deletes — checking after every step that no
two live entities share an id — collide in **23 of 25 trials within eight
steps**. Over 2,880 steps across four seeds, two seeds of `origin/main` produced
30 and 27 collisions.

Most are on **relationships** rather than nodes: two edges returned under one id
(`[1, 1]`), and shapes like `[0, 2, 2]` and `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 6]`.

The recycle bin's own maintenance is sound — self-loops, edges with both
endpoints dele

Part of #2698.

Everything above this PR reads or writes the same bytes. This is the contract
they code against, and it is separate so that the decoder and the encoder could
be built from the spec without either reading the other's source — the split
that let the conformance corpus arbitrate between them instead of one
implementation defining correctness for the other.

**What this does NOT do**
