issues.title: [Flaky] test17_sp_duplicate_edges: algo.SPpaths/SSpaths return duplicate paths when relTypes repeats a type
issues.body:
## Summary

When `relTypes` lists the same type more than once, `algo.SPpaths` and `algo.SSpaths` return the same path several times. This happens every time on current trunk. It also explains why `test_path_algorithms:testAllShortestPaths.test17_sp_duplicate_edges` is flaky: the test only notices the duplicates on some random graphs.

## Reproduction

Run against `falkordb/falkordb-server:edge-rs` (built 2026-09-24 from `main`):

```cypher
CREATE (a:L {v: 1}), (b:L {v: 2}), (c:L {v: 3}), (d:L {v: 4}),
       (a)-[:E {weight: 1}]->(b), (b)-[:E {weight: 1}]->(d),
       (a)-[:E {weight: 2}]->(c), (c)-[:E {weight: 2}]->(d)

MATCH (n:L {v: 1}), (m:L {v: 4})
CALL algo.SPpaths({sourceNode: n, targetNode: m, relTypes: ['E', 'E'],
                   weightProp: 'weight', maxLen: 3, pathCount: 3})
YIELD path RETURN [x IN nodes(path) | x.v]
```

| Call | `relTypes: ['E']` | `relTypes: ['E', 'E']` |
|---|---|---|
| SPpaths `pathCount: 3` (graph above, 2 paths) | `[1,2,4]`, `[1,3,4]` | `[1,2,4]` ×3 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 3`, plus `(a)-[:E {weight: 5}]->(d)` (3 paths) | `[1,2,4]`, `[1,3,4]`, `[1,4]` | `[1,2,4]` ×3 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 3`, only `(a)-[:E]->(d)` (1 path, 1 hop) | `[1,4]` | `[1,4]` ×2 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 0` (all minimal) | `[1,2,4]` | `[1,2,4]` ×4 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 1` | `[1,2,4]` | `[1,2,4]` (correct) |
| SSpaths from `a`, `maxLen: 2`, `pathCount: 10` | 4 paths | 10 rows: each path ×2 (1 hop) or ×4 (2 hops), cut off by `pathCount` |

## Root cause

`relTypes` is never deduplicated:
- `parse_common_path_config` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs`) copies the list as given.
- `Graph::get_node_relationships_by_type` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs`) collects one matrix per listed type, so it scans `E` twice.

As a result, `node_successors` yields every edge once per repeat. `enumerate_paths` then explores each subtree once per copy, so every path is found 2^hops times. `record_found_path` doesn't drop identical paths, so the copies take up the k

issues.title: [Flaky] test_udf_cluster: spawn-mode cluster bootstrap doesn't wait for announced hostnames, so the client connects to "?:6379"
issues.body:
## Summary

`test_udf_cluster:testUDFCluster.test_udf_delete_propagation` sometimes errors on its first `udf_load` (test line 93):

```
  File "/__w/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/tests/flow/test_udf_cluster.py", line 93, in test_udf_delete_propagation
    res = self.db.udf_load(lib, script)
  File ".../falkordb/falkordb.py", line 288, in udf_load
    resp = client.execute_command(*args)
  ...
redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error -2 connecting to ?:6379. Name or service not known.
```

It's rare: 2 failures in ~290 `release-flow` runs this week, one of them in the merge queue. It's a race in the test harness rather than a product bug, and it can hit any spawn-mode `oss-cluster` test.

## Evidence (Sep 17–24; PRs to `main`/`6.0` plus the merge queue)

| PR | Lane | Job |
|---|---|---|
| #2846 | `release-flow` amd64 | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35915227485/job/107367542497 |
| merge queue (#2533) | `release-flow` arm64 | https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB/actions/runs/35983587637/job/107582756419 |

| Lane | Failed / passed |
|---|---|
| `release-flow` amd64 | 1 / 145 |
| `release-flow` arm64 | 1 / 142 |
| `a-sanitizer-flow` | 0 / 134 |
| `coverage-flow` | 0 / 147 |

## Root cause

1. `_spawn_falkordb_cluster` (`tests/flow/common.py`) starts each shard with `--cluster-announce-hostname <alias> --cluster-preferred-endpoint-type hostname`. With that setting, a node whose hostname isn't known yet is reported as **`?`** in `CLUSTER SLOTS` and MOVED replies (documented in `redis.conf`: "If the preferred endpoint type is set to hostname, but no announced hostname is set, a '?' will be returned instead").
2. `_bootstrap_cluster` returns as soon as every shard reports `cluster_state:ok` and `cluster_known_nodes == n`. A peer that was learned through gossip counts as known before its hostname has arrived, so this check doesn't guarantee the hostnames have spread to every shard.
3. `Env()` builds the `FalkorDB` client right away. `RedisCluster` loads its slot map

issues.title: [Rust] A list literal of aggregates collapses to one aggregate: [min(x), max(x)] returns 2
issues.body:
### Summary

A list literal whose elements include an aggregate collapses to the value of that one aggregate. `[min(x), max(x)]` returns `2`, not `[1, 2]`, and `size([count(x)])` fails with a type error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x RETURN [min(x), max(x)] AS a, [count(x), 5] AS b"
Rust: 2, 2
C:    [1, 2], [2, 5]

GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x RETURN size([count(x)])"
Rust: Type mismatch: expected List, String, or Null but was Integer
C:    1
```

### Mechanism

`ExprEval::eval_compound` (`graph/src/runtime/eval.rs:525`) evaluates `ExprIR::List` on an explicit stack: it pushes a re-enter frame for the list, then one frame per element. When an element is a finished aggregate, the `FuncInvocation` arm (`eval.rs:864-880`) reads the accumulator and finalizes it with `return match finalize { .. }`. That `return` leaves the whole stack machine, so the list frame and the other elements are thrown away and the aggregate's value becomes the value of the whole expression. `[count(x)+0]`, maps and function arguments go through `eval_node` recursion and are not affected.

### Expected (C behaviour)

`[1, 2]`, `[2, 5]` and `1`.

### Suggested fix

Push the finalized value onto the result stack and `continue`, like every other arm.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the aggregate operators (`proofs/ops_aggregate`), theorem `stackEval_return_drops_frame`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_aggregate.rs` (`bug_list_literal_of_aggregates_collapses`).

issues.title: [Rust] A write that only registers schema or only cancels entities replicates nothing: next payload refused (full resync), AOF load exits, or silent dictionary divergence
issues.body:
### Summary

A write that only registers a name, or whose every entity is created and deleted in the same query, puts **nothing** on the replication stream or in the AOF. It still changes the primary: the label/attribute dictionary grows and the id space moves (the cancelled ids sit in the recycle bin). The replica never hears about it, so:

* the **next** payload's `ADD_SCHEMA` is refused ("assigns label 'B' id 2, but this replica would assign 0") and the replica is forced into a **full resync**;
* during **AOF load** the same refusal **shuts the server down** ("A full resync cannot repair already-loaded state, shutting down");
* for a cancelled edge attribute (`CREATE (a)-[:T1 {p4:1}]->(b) DELETE a, b`) the replica **silently** ends up with a shorter attribute dictionary than its primary, with no error.

Examples: `CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a`, `OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6`, `MERGE (a:M1 {p5:1}) DELETE a`, `CREATE (a)-[:T1 {p4:1}]->(b) DELETE a, b`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac, primary + replica)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {p:1}) DELETE a"
GRAPH.QUERY g "OPTIONAL MATCH (n:Nope) SET n:L6"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MERGE (a:M1 {p5:1}) DELETE a"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a)-[:T1 {p4:1}]->(b) DELETE a, b"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:B {q:2})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:K4)-[:T2]->()"
```

issues.title: Port algo.AStar (and #2630's algo.SPpaths routing) from the C engine to Rust
issues.body:
## Gap
`algo.AStar` exists only on the C engine's `master` branch. It isn't in the Rust engine (`main`, 6.0) or in any C release: `CALL dbms.procedures()` on v4.20.7 and on the 6.0 RC lists the same 24 procedures, with no A\*. Since 6.0 replaces the C engine, A\* reaches users only if it is ported.

## What C has
- **#2630** (merged to `master` 2026-08-26) adds `algo.AStar`: an A\* search that uses great-circle (haversine) distance over user-supplied `latitudeProperty` / `longitudeProperty` as its heuristic. It supports relationship-type and direction filters and parallel edges, and has a k-shortest variant built on Yen's algorithm and driven by the same A\* engine. Code: `src/algorithms/AStar.{c,h}`, `src/algorithms/yen.{c,h}`, `src/procedures/proc_astar_paths.c`.
- **#2720** (merged 2026-09-04) adds a goal-directed spur to Yen, for #2730, which is still open.
- **Also in #2630:** `algo.SPpaths` no longer enumerates paths with a DFS in the unconstrained case (`src != dst`, no `maxCost`, no `maxLen`):
  - `pathCount: 1` uses Dijkstra;
  - `pathCount: 0` uses bidirectional Dijkstra plus shortest-path DAG enumeration;
  - `pathCount > 1` uses Yen's k-shortest loopless paths.

  The Rust `algo.SPpaths` takes its own approach (#2276), so compare the two when porting rather than assuming parity.

## Port
- `algo.AStar` with the same signature, outputs and error messages as C.
- Its flow tests: `tests/flow/test_astar.py` (24 `algo.AStar` calls), plus the A\* cases in `test_path_algorithms.py` and `test_procedures.py` from #2630.
- Whether Rust's `algo.SPpaths` should adopt #2630's algorithm routing, measured against C.

Open C follow-ups: #2656 (A\* optimality, `pathCost` hop count) and #2732 (k-shortest-paths landmark mode). Port those as well if they merge.

issues.title: [Rust] toInteger('-9223372036854775809') returns i64::MIN instead of null (f64 fallback rounds to -2^63)
issues.body:
### Summary

`toInteger()` of an integer string just below `i64::MIN` returns `i64::MIN` instead of `null`. `toIntegerList` inherits the bug. C returns `null`, and the positive side is already `null` in both engines.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toInteger('-9223372036854775809'), toInteger('-9223372036854776832'), toIntegerList(['-9223372036854775809'])"
-- Rust: -9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808, [-9223372036854775808]
-- C:    null, null, [NULL]

GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toInteger('9223372036854775808')"
-- Rust and C: null
```

### Mechanism

`value_to_integer` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/conversion.rs:53-64`): `s.parse::<i64>()` fails with overflow, so the code falls back to `s.parse::<f64>()`. Every value in `[-2^63-1024, -2^63-1]` rounds to exactly `-2^63`, and the guard `floored < i64::MIN as f64` is strict, so the rounded value passes as `i64::MIN`.

### Expected

Match C: a plain integer string (optional sign, digits only) that doesn't fit in i64 is `null`. Only strings with a fraction or exponent go through the float path (where C also gives `toInteger('-9223372036854775807.5') = -9223372036854775808`).

### Found by

Lean 4 model of `conversion.rs` (`proofs/value_math`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_value_math.rs::bug_to_integer_negative_overflow_clamps_to_min`.

issues.title: [Rust] coalesce() with zero arguments is accepted (C: expected at least 1)
issues.body:
### Summary

`coalesce()` with no arguments is accepted and returns `null`. C rejects it at compile time.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN coalesce()"
-- Rust: null
-- C:    Received 0 arguments to function 'coalesce', expected at least 1
```

### Mechanism

`coalesce` is registered as `var_arg` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/math.rs:314`). `GraphFn::validate` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/mod.rs:787`) does no arity check for `FnArguments::VarLength`. The other built-in variadics, `indegree`/`outdegree`, check `args.is_empty()` themselves at runtime (`entity.rs:310`).

### Expected

Every built-in variadic function needs at least one argument (true of `coalesce`, `indegree` and `outdegree` in C). Reject zero arguments in `validate` for non-UDF `VarLength` functions, using C's message. UDFs stay unconstrained.

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/value_math`, theorem `coalesce_zero_args_accepted`, TypeCheck.lean); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_value_math.rs::bug_coalesce_accepts_zero_arguments`.

issues.title: [Rust] LIMIT/SKIP budget is a hard stop through traverses and counts one SKIP: two-hop, ExpandInto, stacked-SKIP and ORDER BY+MATCH queries drop rows
issues.body:
### Summary

A `LIMIT` (optionally with `SKIP`) above two traverses, above a traverse fed by a stacked `SKIP`, or above a `Sort` feeding a traverse silently drops rows: Rust returns `[]` where C returns the answer. The runtime pushes the `Limit`/`Skip` row budget down the plan as a *hard* stop for `CondTraverse`, `ExpandInto` and Sort's top-k, but computes it with a walk that crosses operators which can discard rows, and counts only the first `Skip`.

| `CREATE (:A {id:1}), (:A {id:2})-[:R]->(:B {id:20})` | `MATCH (a:A) WITH a ORDER BY a.id MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b) RETURN b.id LIMIT 1` | `[]` | `[]` (openCypher: `[20]`) |

issues.title: [Rust] Range index returns every node of the label, or drops rows, when the value is one it can't look up (date(), point(), computed ints >= 2^52, IN [date(), ..])
issues.body:
### Summary

When a range index serves a predicate whose value the index can't look up exactly, the Rust engine returns wrong rows. The scan either falls back to *every* node of the label with the filter already removed, or looks the value up and silently finds nothing. All of these give the right answer without the index, and on C with the index.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:5, k:'int'}), (:L {v:date('2020-01-01'), k:'date'})"
```

| Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = date('2020-01-01') RETURN n.k` | `date` | **`date`, `int`** | `date` |
| `MATCH (n:L {v: date('2020-01-01')}) RETURN n.k` | `date` | **`date`, `int`** | `date` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > date('2019-01-01') RETURN n.k` | `date` | **`date`, `int`** | `date` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v IN [date('2020-01-01'), 5] RETURN n.k` | `date`, `int` | **`int`** | `date`, `int` |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = 4503599627370495 + 4503599627370495 + 3 RETURN n.k` | — | **`date`, `int`** (every node) | — |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 4503599627370495 * 2 RETURN n.k` | — | **every node** | — |

and with `CREATE (:L {v: point({latitude:1.0, longitude:2.0}), k:'p'})`:

| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v = point({latitude:1.0, longitude:2.0}) RETURN n.k` | `p` | **—** | `p` |
|---|---|---|---|

1. **Filter dropped for values the runtime then refuses.** `is_non_indexable_subexpr` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/utilize_index.rs:910-928`) is a deny-list: it flags variables, parameters, lists, maps, function calls and lossy *literal* ints. issues.title: [Rust] Range index stores temporals as plain numbers, so n.v > 0 returns dates
issues.body:
### Summary

A range index stores Date / DateTime / LocalTime / Duration values as their raw number in the same numeric field as Int and Float. A numeric range query then matches them: `n.v > 0` returns dates. Without the index, and on C, it does not.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:5, k:'int'}), (:L {v:date('2020-01-01'), k:'date'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 0 RETURN n.k"
-- Rust + index: 'date', 'int'     no index: 'int'     C + index: 'int'
```

`n.v < 0` with a date before 1970, and `n.v = <seconds of the date>` behave the same way.

### Mechanism

`Document::set` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:785-792`) adds temporals with `RediSearch_DocumentAddFieldNumber` to the property's numeric field, the one Int/Float queries use. No query ever looks temporals up in the index: the scan op's `can_utilize_index` rejects every temporal value and falls back to a label scan. So indexing them buys nothing and only produces false positives for numeric queries.

### Expected

`n.v > 0` returns only numbers, like C (C indexes each type under its own field name).

### Suggested fix

Don't add temporals to the numeric field. (Indexing them under a separate sub-field, as C does, is a later feature: the Rust planner can't serve temporal predicates from the index today anyway.)

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_temporal_in_numeric_range`), also `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C2). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] Multi-label (n:A:B): conditions on B's indexed property are pushed into A's index (AND returns nothing, OR loses rows)
issues.body:
### Summary

For a multi-label pattern `(n:A:B)` where `A` has a range index on `x` and `B` one on `y`, the Rust engine merges the condition on `B`'s property into a query on `A`'s index, which has no such field. `AND` returns nothing and `OR` loses rows. C returns the right rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:A) ON (n.x)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:B) ON (n.y)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A:B {x:1, y:2, k:'ab'}), (:A:B {x:1, y:3, k:'ab2'})"
```

| Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:A:B) WHERE n.x = 1 AND n.y = 2 RETURN n.k` | `ab` | **—** | `ab` |
| `MATCH (n:B:A) WHERE n.y = 2 AND n.x = 1 RETURN n.k` | `ab` | **—** | `ab` |
| `MATCH (n:A:B) WHERE n.y = 2 OR n.x = 1 RETURN n.k` | `ab`, `ab2` | **`ab`** | `ab`, `ab2` |
| `MATCH (n:A:B {x:1, y:2}) RETURN n.k` | `ab` | **—** | `ab` |

### Mechanism

`try_single_filter_scan` picks, per conjunct, the first label that indexes the property. `try_filter_pushdown` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/utilize_index.rs:770-826`) then merges every pushable conjunct (AND) or branch (OR) into one `IndexQuery` and keeps only the *first* label. At runtime `build_query_node` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1547`, `:1564`) can't find `y` in `A`'s index and returns a null node: a null `AND` child nulls the whole intersection (no rows), a null `OR` child is skipped (its rows are lost).

### Expected

Same rows as without the index (C).

### Suggested fix

In `try_filter_pushdown`, merge only conjuncts served by the same label as the first one and leave the rest in the post-filter; for `OR`, give up on the index when branches need different labels.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_multilabel_and`, `bug_multilabel_or`), also `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C5, C6). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a' returns 'a' through a range index (equal-bounds shortcut ignores exclusivity)
issues.body:
### Summary

`n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a'` (or `>= 'a' AND < 'a'`) returns the node with `v = 'a'` when `v` has a range index. The range is empty; without the index, and on C, the query returns nothing.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {v:'a', k:'a'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v > 'a' AND n.v < 'a' RETURN n.k"
-- Rust + index: 'a'      no index: (empty)     C + index: (empty)
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.v >= 'a' AND n.v < 'a' RETURN n.k"
-- Rust + index: 'a'      no index: (empty)     C + index: (empty)
```

### Mechanism

The two conjuncts are merged into one `Range { min: 'a', max: 'a', include_min: false, include_max: false }`. `build_string_range_node` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1403-1449`, shortcut at `:1418`) turns any string range with equal bounds into an exact-token match, ignoring both include flags.

### Expected

Empty result, like C and the full scan.

### Suggested fix

Take the exact-token shortcut only when both bounds are inclusive; otherwise return an empty node.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the index layer, `proofs/index_layer` (`bug_exclusive_equal_bounds`; `strRange_exact` needs equal bounds to be inclusive), also `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C11). Live repro `proofs/index_layer/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] IN with a computed indexed side is pushed as n.a IN [..]; 2 IN [n.a, n.b] becomes array-contains on n.a
issues.body:
### Summary

An `IN` predicate whose indexed side is an expression that merely *contains* the indexed property is pushed into the range index as if it were the bare property. `abs(n.a) IN [1]` becomes `n.a IN [1]`, and `2 IN [n.a, n.b]` becomes an array-contains lookup on `n.a`. Both return different rows than the same query without the index. C returns the right rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.a)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {k:1, a:1}), (:L {k:2, a:-1}), (:L {k:3, a:2, b:7})"
```

| Query | no index | Rust + index | C + index |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE abs(n.a) IN [1] RETURN n.k` | 1, 2 | **1** | 1, 2 |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE toString(n.a) IN ['1'] RETURN n.k` | 1 | **—** | 1 |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.a + 1 IN [2] RETURN n.k` | 1 | **—** | error |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE 2 IN [n.a, n.b] RETURN n.k` | 3 | **—** | 3 |
| `MATCH (n:L) WHERE -1 IN [n.a] RETURN n.k` | 2 | **—** | error |

### Mechanism

`try_in_filter_scan` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/utilize_index.rs:612-665`) only checks that one side *contains* a property of the scanned alias (`subtree_has_property_of`), then takes the first property it finds in that subtree (`extract_attribute_from_subtree`) and builds `InList { key: a, .. }` or `ArrayContains { key: a, .. }` from it. The filter is then dropped (or, for array-contains, kept but the index has already returned the wrong candidates). The comparison path (`try_single_filter_scan`) already requires the side to be `ExprIR::Property`.

### Expected

Same rows as without the index (C).

### Suggested fix

Push an `IN` only when the indexed side *is* `Property(scanned alias)`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the scan-selection passes, `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IndexCex` C7, C7', C8). Live repro `proofs/optimizer_scan/repro.py`.

issues.title: [Rust] Id seek on a graph that never held a node returns a phantom node 0; SET on it leaks into the next CREATE
issues.body:
### Summary

On a graph that has never held a node, an id seek returns a phantom node 0. Writes to it survive: `SET` on the phantom lands on the next node `CREATE` makes, and `DELETE` errors. C returns no rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac, fresh graph each block)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 0 RETURN id(n)"
-- Rust: [[0]]      C: []
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) >= 0 RETURN count(n)"
-- Rust: [[1]]      C: [[0]]
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 0 SET n.x = 1, n:Z RETURN id(n)"
-- Rust: [[0]], Labels added: 1, Properties set: 1      C: [] and no stats
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (m:Q) RETURN id(m)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) RETURN labels(n), properties(n)"
-- Rust: [[Z, Q], {x: 1}]      C: [[Q], {}]
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 0 DELETE n"
-- Rust: error "0 was never allocated here"      C: no-op
```

### Mechanism

`Runtime::evaluate_id_filter` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:1316`) takes the upper bound from `Graph::max_node_id` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:1495`), which returns a `0` *sentinel* when `node_count == 0`. That is indistinguishable from "the highest id is 0", so the inclusive range is `{0}`. `NodeByIdSeekOp` (`node_by_id_seek.rs:67`) only subtracts the recycle bin, which is empty on a graph that never held a node, so id 0 survives. (Once any node has been deleted, the bin contains 0 and hides the bug.) `NodeByLabelAndIdScan` uses the same range but intersects it with the label matrix, so it is not affected.

### Expected (C)

No rows, no writes, no error.

### Suggested fix

Bound the range by `Graph::node_id_bound()` (exclusive; `node_count + deleted_nodes.len()`, which is exactly what `IdSpace` already uses and has no sentinel), and return no range when it is 0.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/optimizer_scan` (`IdSeek.gEmpty` examples: `seek gEmpty [(.int 0, .eq)] 0 = true` vs `reference … = false`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_optimizer_scan.rs::bug_id_seek_phantom_node_*`.

An entity created and deleted inside the same commit segment vanishes from the write statistics: neither its create, nor its delete, nor its properties are counted. C counts all three. A pending edge deleted *directly* is counted, so Rust is inconsistent with itself too.

| `CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b) DELETE a` | `Nodes created: 1` | `Nodes created: 2, Relationships created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |

| after `CREATE (:A)`: `MATCH (a:A) CREATE (a)-[:R {x:1}]->(b) DELETE a` | `Nodes created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1` | `Nodes created: 1, Properties set: 1, Relationships created: 1, Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 1` |

issues.body:

A `SET`/`REMOVE` on a relationship that the same query has already deleted is applied and counted. For nodes the same write is skipped (C behaviour). Two holes:

- `REMOVE r.v` after `DELETE r`: `ops/remove.rs` has no deletion check for relationships at all (nodes have one).

issues.title: [Rust] Grouped count(DISTINCT) shares state between groups whose key rows collide in a 64-bit hash
issues.body:
### Summary

Grouped `count(DISTINCT ..)` / `collect(DISTINCT ..)` / `sum(DISTINCT ..)` keep each group's seen-set in a side table keyed by a 64-bit FxHash of the group's key row. Two different groups whose key rows hash the same share one seen-set, so a value seen in one group is skipped in the other. FxHash is unseeded and fast to invert, so a client can pick such keys on purpose.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [[[0,0],1],[[1,-1452335207727870361],1]] AS p
               WITH p[0] AS k, p[1] AS v RETURN k, count(*) AS n, count(DISTINCT v) AS c"
Rust: [0, 0]|1|1 ; [1, -1452335207727870361]|1|0
C:    [0, 0]|1|1 ; [1, -1452335207727870361]|1|1
```

The grouping is correct (`count(*)` is 1 in each group) but the second group's `count(DISTINCT v)` is 0.

### Mechanism

- The groups themselves are collision-free: `GroupMap` is keyed by `GroupKey`, which resolves collisions with `Value::eq` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/aggregate.rs:59`, `:83`).
- The DISTINCT state is not. It lives in `Runtime::value_dedupers`, keyed by `(Distinct node, group_id)`, where `group_id = entry.0.hash_u64()`, an FxHash of the group's key row. That is `aggregate.rs:715` on the vectorized path and `:959` on the per-row path, which feeds `eval.rs:835`. Colliding groups therefore land on the same `ValuesDeduper`.

### How this differs from #2780 (closed, not planned)

#2780 is about the DISTINCT *values* (and `DistinctOp` rows) being remembered by their 64-bit hash with no equality check. Fixing that means storing every distinct value, which costs memory, and it was declined for that reason. This issue is a different site. Here it is two *groups* whose state gets merged, and the exact group key is already stored in `GroupMap`. Only the lookup into the side table throws it away and uses its hash. Fixing it costs nothing: give each group an id when it is inserted into `GroupMap`, and key the dedupers by that id. That also saves hashing the whole key row o

[Rust] MATCH … WHERE followed by a MATCH that traverses from it: the WHERE (and the clauses below it) is dropped — DELETE removes unmatched data
issues.body:
### Summary

When a `MATCH … WHERE` clause is followed by another `MATCH` that traverses from (or merely follows) it, the Rust optimizer throws away the earlier clause's plan and replaces it with a fresh scan. The earlier `WHERE` is lost, and so are any clauses planned below it and any variable it binds. The rows then flow into writes: `DETACH DELETE` deletes a node that the `WHERE` should have excluded. **Data-loss severity.** C is correct.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5}), (a)-[:R {w:3}]->(b), (b)-[:S {w:1}]->(:C {v:7})"
```

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 99 MATCH (a)-[r:R]->(b) RETURN count(r)` | 2 | 0 |
| `MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 99 MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b) DETACH DELETE b` | Nodes deleted: 1, Relationships deleted: 3 | nothing |
| `MATCH (a:A) WHERE a.v = 2 MATCH (a)-[r:R]->(b:B) RETURN count(r)` | 2 | 0 |
| `MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 0 MATCH (x)-[:S]->(a) RETURN count(x)` | 1 | 0 |
| `UNWIND [1,2] AS i MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 1 MATCH (a)-[r:R]->(b) RETURN count(r)` | 2 (UNWIND lost) | 4 |

issues.title: [Rust] A UDF can forge node/edge references: server crash and dangling edges
issues.body:
### Summary

A JS UDF can forge a reference to a graph entity: any object it returns with `__falkor_type: 'edge'` / `'node'` and a `__falkor_*_id` is converted into a `Relationship` / `Node` with that id. issues.title: [Rust] GRAPH.EFFECT UPDATE_NODE/UPDATE_EDGE/SET_LABELS/REMOVE_LABELS on a dead id, and DELETE_NODE of a node with edges, are applied: next entity inherits the write/edge
issues.body:
### Summary

This is the same root cause as #2924: `apply_effects` never checks that the entity a record acts on is **live**. #2924 covers `CREATE_EDGE` endpoints. The same gap exists in five more records:

* `UPDATE_NODE`, `UPDATE_EDGE`, `SET_LABELS` and `REMOVE_LABELS` accept an id that is in the recycle bin or was never allocated. The write lands in the store or label matrix, and **the next entity that reclaims the id is born with it**.
* `DELETE_NODE` accepts a node that **still has relationships**. The delete does not cascade (the primary always ships the `DELETE_EDGE`s first), so the edge is left hanging off a recycled id, and the next created node inherits it.

`src/divergence_guard.rs` treats a client `GRAPH.EFFECT` as a malformed command to refuse. `CREATE_NODE`/`DELETE_NODE`/`DELETE_EDGE` already refuse non-live ids through `IdSpace` (`AlreadyLive`, `NotLive`). These records are the ones that skip it.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

The replica is seeded with nodes 0 `(:A {x:1})`, 1 `(:A)`, 2, edge 0 `0-[:R]->1`, and node 3 deleted (in the bin). The hostile payloads are built with the v3 encoder, and each is applied as `GRAPH.EFFECT` does it:

| `UPDATE_NODE ids=[3] x=666` | `Ok` | `CREATE (:Fresh)` gets id 3 and `{x: 666}` |
| `UPDATE_NODE ids=[50] x=777` | `Ok` | (never-allocated id accepted) |
| `SET_LABELS ids=[3] [A]` | `Ok` | `CREATE (:Fresh)` → `labels = ['A','Fresh']` |
| `UPDATE_EDGE ids=[5] R x=888` | `Ok` | the 6th new `:R` edge is born with `{x: 888}` |
| `REMOVE_LABELS ids=[3, 2^40]` | `Ok` in release, GraphBLAS `debug_assert` (`matrix.rs:1109`) in debug | |
| `SET_LABELS ids=[2^40]` | `Ok` in release, `debug_assert` (`matrix.rs:1339`) in debug | |
| `DELETE_NODE ids=[1]` (endpoint of edge 0) | `Ok` | edge 0 now has a dead endpoint; `CREATE (:Fresh)` reuses id 1 and inherits the incoming edge |

issues.title: [Rust] percentileDisc/percentileCont with a row-dependent percentile use the last row's value (C: first)
issues.body:
### Summary

When the percentile argument of `percentileDisc`/`percentileCont` changes from row to row, Rust uses the **last** row's value. C uses the **first**.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1,10) AS x RETURN percentileDisc(x, x/10.0) AS p, percentileCont(x, 1.0 - x/10.0) AS q"
Rust: 10, 1        (p = 1.0 and p = 0.0, from the last row)
C:    1, 9.1       (p = 0.1 and p = 0.9, from the first row)
```

### Mechanism

The accumulator is `[percentile, values]`. Both the scalar body (`graph/src/runtime/functions/aggregation.rs:253`) and `percentile_batch` (`:539`) do `*stored_percentile = <this row's percentile>` on every row, so the last row wins.

### Expected (C behaviour)

The first row's percentile is used. openCypher expects the argument to be constant, so this only matters for non-constant arguments. The result still should not depend on which row happens to come last.

### Suggested fix

Store the percentile only while the collected-values list is empty, i.e. on the first non-null row.

Note: C also takes the percentile from a leading row whose *value* is null. Rust's aggregate operator skips null inputs before calling the function, so Rust takes it from the first non-null row. Matching that corner exactly would need a change in the aggregate operator.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the aggregate operators (`proofs/ops_aggregate`), theorem `pct_last_wins`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_aggregate.rs` (`bug_percentile_row_dependent_argument_last_wins`).

issues.title: [Rust] Consecutive MATCH/CREATE clauses (and a WHERE pattern predicate plus the next MATCH) are parsed into one pattern: per-clause semantics lost
issues.body:
### Summary

The parser folds consecutive clauses with the same keyword into **one** pattern: `MATCH p MATCH q` is parsed as `MATCH p, q`, `CREATE p CREATE q` as `CREATE p, q`, and `OPTIONAL MATCH p MATCH q` as `OPTIONAL MATCH p, q`. A WHERE pattern predicate is parsed with the same routine, so `WHERE (n)-->() MATCH (x)` also swallows the next MATCH into the predicate.

In openCypher each clause has its own scope for pattern semantics (relationship uniqueness, optionality) and sees the variables of the clauses before it. Several open bugs are symptoms of this one fold. This issue tracks the root cause and a design decision for it.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Graph: `CREATE (:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5})`

| query | C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`) | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE (a {v:1}) CREATE (b {v: a.v}) RETURN b.v` | `[[1]]` | **`'a' not defined`** (#2654) |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) MATCH (a)-[s]->(b) RETURN count(*)` | `[[1]]` | **`[[0]]`**: uniqueness is enforced across the two clauses (#2534) |
| `MATCH (n:A) WHERE (n)-->() MATCH (:B) RETURN count(*)` | `[[2]]` | **`[[1]]`**: `MATCH (:B)` becomes part of the predicate (#2502) |
| `MATCH (n:A) WHERE (n)-->() MATCH (x:B) RETURN x.v` | `[[0],[5]]` | **`'x' not defined`** |
| `MATCH (x:A) OPTIONAL MATCH (x)-[:NOPE]->(n) MATCH (n)-->(m) RETURN n` | error: a WITH is required | **one row, `n = null`**: the mandatory MATCH became optional. openCypher gives no rows. |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) MATCH (c:B {v: id(r)*0}) RETURN c.v` | `[[0]]` | **`'r' not defined`** (#2923, fixed without un-folding by PR #2981) |

* `graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:1551-1556` (`parse_pattern`): after a pattern part, the loop continues on `,` and also on `token == *clause`, so a following `MATCH`/`CREATE` keyword is consumed and parsed into the same `QueryGraph`.

issues.title: [Rust] MATCH … WHERE followed by a multi-component MATCH is cross-joined instead of correlated (extra rows)
issues.body:
### Summary

When `MATCH … WHERE` is followed by a MATCH with several comma-separated components, and one of those components uses a variable of the first clause, the two clauses are cross-joined instead of correlated. The component that uses the earlier variable binds it again from scratch, so rows come back that the first clause's WHERE excluded. C returns the correlated result.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5}), (a)-[:R {w:3}]->(b), (b)-[:S {w:1}]->(:C {v:7})"
```

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 0 MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b), (c:C) RETURN a.v, b.v, c.v` | `[1, 0, 7]` | `[]` |
| `MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 0 MATCH (x)-[:S]->(a), (b:B) RETURN a.v, b.v, x.v` | `[7,0,0]`, `[7,5,0]` (a.v = 7!) | `[]` |
| `MATCH (a {v:5}) WHERE true MATCH (x:C), (a)-[:R]->(b) RETURN count(*)` | 1 | 0 |

```
GRAPH.EXPLAIN g "MATCH (a) WHERE a.v = 0 MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b), (c:C) RETURN a.v, b.v, c.v"

    Cartesian Product
```

- The next MATCH has two components, so it becomes a `CartesianProduct`. Its component `(a)-[:R]->(b)` is planned with `a` already visited, i.e. as a leaf traversal from a bound `a`.

So nothing feeds `a` to the traversal: the branch scans `a` again, and the CartesianProduct merge overwrites the earlier binding.

issues.title: [Rust] MERGE with a named path as the last clause (query, CALL {} or FOREACH body) fails: "Variable _anon_0 not found"
issues.body:
### Summary

A `MERGE` with a named path fails with `Variable … not found` when it is the **last** clause of a query, of a `CALL {}` body, or of a `FOREACH` body. Adding any clause after it (e.g. `RETURN …`) makes it work. C creates the pattern.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5}), (a)-[:R {w:3}]->(b), (b)-[:S {w:1}]->(:C {v:7})"
```

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:A) MERGE p=(a)-[:T]->(x:X)` | `Variable _anon_0 not found` | Nodes created: 1, Relationships created: 1 |
| `UNWIND [1,2] AS i MERGE p=(x:X {v:i})` | `Variable x not found` | Nodes created: 2 |
| `MATCH (a:A) CALL { WITH a MERGE p=(a)-[:T]->(:X) }` | `Variable _anon_0 not found` | Nodes created: 1, Relationships created: 1 |
| `FOREACH (i IN [1] \| CREATE (y:Y) MERGE p=(y)-[:T]->(:X))` | `Variable _anon_0 not found` | Nodes created: 2, Relationships created: 1 |
| `MATCH (a:A) MERGE p=(a)-[:T]->(x:X) RETURN length(p)` | works | works |

### Mechanism

- The MERGE arm plans a named path as `PathBuilder(Merge(match_branch))` (`graph/src/planner/mod.rs:3013-3027`).
- `plan_query`'s stitching loop steps over `PathBuilder` when it looks for the next insertion point (`mod.rs:2725`). Its first walk, the one for the last clause's plan (`mod.rs:2638-2644`), does not. So the preceding clause is stitched as a new child 0 of the `PathBuilder`, next to the Merge: `PathBuilder(prev, Merge(..))`. The runtime only builds child 0 of a `PathBuilder`, so the Merge never runs, and the path is built from variables nothing bound.
- The FOREACH body stitching (`mod.rs:3335`) has the same gap.

### Expected

As in C, the preceding clause feeds the Merge, as it already does when a clause follows the MERGE.

### Suggested fix

Add `IR::PathBuilder(_)` to the first walk in `plan_query`, and step over a `PathBuilder` in the FOREACH body walk.

issues.title: [Rust] UNIQUE constraint enforcement rescans the whole label per affected entity: bulk writes are quadratic (19 s vs C 0.24 s at 8000 rows)
issues.body:
## Summary
UNIQUE constraint enforcement rescans the entire label (or relationship type) once for every entity a write query touches. A single write query that creates or updates `a` entities in a label of `N` members therefore costs Θ(a·N) key builds. Bulk loads under a UNIQUE constraint are quadratic, 40-80x slower than C at a few thousand rows.

## Reproduction
```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)"
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g UNIQUE NODE L PROPERTIES 1 v
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1, n) AS x CREATE (:L {v: x})"
```
Release builds, same machine, runs alternating between Rust and C (C = `bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`). The machine is shared (load average 25-60).

| n | Rust main | C | Rust, no constraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 | 1.03 s | 0.024 s | 0.006 s |
| 8000 | 19.3 s | 0.24 s | 0.022 s |
| 20000 | ~99 s | — | — |

The same happens for relationship constraints (`UNWIND … CREATE (a)-[:T {v:x}]->(z)`: ~101 s at 20000).

## Mechanism
`graph/src/runtime/pending.rs:1437-1462` (`check_node_constraint`) and `:1510-1535` (`check_edge_constraint`) are called at commit. For **each** affected entity they iterate the whole label matrix or relationship tensor, rebuild a `seen` map of every member's key, and look for any duplicate.

## Expected
Enforcement should be linear in the entities touched. C's `EnforceUniqueEntity` does one exact-match query on the supporting range index per entity.

## Suggested fix
Per commit and per constraint, key the affected members once into a set; a collision in that set is a violation. Then do one pass over the rest of the label, checking each key against the set. That is O(N + a) per commit instead of O(a·N).

A later step could probe the supporting range index the way C does, which would make a small write into a huge label O(a·log N) instead of O(N). That is harder, because index documents are deferred until the query succeeds and the index may still be populating, so it is not part of this fix.

`Co

issues.title: [Rust] Write queries ignore the per-query TIMEOUT when TIMEOUT_MAX/TIMEOUT_DEFAULT is set (C times out and rolls back)
issues.body:
### Summary

With `TIMEOUT_MAX` (or `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`) configured, a write query ignores its per-query `TIMEOUT` argument and runs to completion. C applies the per-query timeout to writes in that mode, times the query out and rolls it back.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.CONFIG SET TIMEOUT_MAX 100000
GRAPH.QUERY t "UNWIND range(1,300000) AS x CREATE (:T)" TIMEOUT 1
GRAPH.QUERY t "MATCH (n) RETURN count(n)"
```

| | Rust | C (`master`) |
|---|---|---|
| write with `TIMEOUT 1` | `Labels added: 1, Nodes created: 300000` | `ERR Query timed out` |
| `count(n)` afterwards | 300000 | 0 |

### Mechanism

`compute_effective_timeout` (`src/graph_core.rs:896-931`) only takes the per-query value when `!is_write`; for a write it falls through to `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` / `TIMEOUT_MAX`, so `TIMEOUT 1` is replaced by 100000 ms.

C's `_read_flags` (`src/commands/cmd_dispatcher.c`) sets `timeout_rw = true` as soon as `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` or `TIMEOUT_MAX` is set, and `Graph_Query` enforces the (per-query or default) timeout for `readonly || timeout_rw`. Only under the deprecated `TIMEOUT` config alone are writes exempt.

### Expected

Match C: once `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` or `TIMEOUT_MAX` is set, the per-query `TIMEOUT` applies to writes too, and a write that times out is rolled back (Rust already rolls back writes that hit `TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`, via `abandon_write`).

### Suggested fix

In `compute_effective_timeout`, accept the per-query value for writes when `TIMEOUT_MAX > 0 || TIMEOUT_DEFAULT > 0`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the Redis layer (`proofs/redis_layer`, theorem `rustTimeout_write_ignores_pq` / `write_timeout_divergence`); live repro `proofs/redis_layer/repro_live.py` (T1).

issues.title: [Rust] A self-loop hop after other hops drops them when its node is reached by a var-length hop: MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b)-[:S*]->(c)-[:L]->(c) returns a = null
issues.body:
### Summary

In a pattern where a fixed-length self-loop hop `(c)-[:L]->(c)` comes after other hops, and `c` is only reached through a variable-length hop, the hops planned before the self-loop are silently dropped. Their variables come back `null`, and rows are no longer constrained by them. C is correct.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {v:1})-[:R]->(b:B {v:2})-[:S]->(c:C {v:3}), (c)-[:L]->(c)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a)-[:R]->(b)-[:S*]->(c)-[:L]->(c) RETURN a.v, b.v, c.v"
```

- Rust: `[null, 2, 3]`
- C: `[1, 2, 3]`

`[:S*1..1]` also gives `[1, 2, 3]` on Rust (that plan has a different hop order), and so does a pattern without the var-length hop.

```
GRAPH.EXPLAIN (Rust)
Project
    Conditional Variable Length Traverse (Expand Into) | (b)-[_anon_1:S*1..INF]->(c)
        Expand Into | (c)->(c)
            All Node Scan | (c)
            Conditional Traverse | (a)->(b)      <- second child: never built
                All Node Scan | (a)

GRAPH.EXPLAIN (C)
Project
    Expand Into | (c)->(c)
        Conditional Variable Length Traverse | (b)-[@anon_1:S*1..INF]->(c)
            Conditional Traverse | (a)->(b)
                All Node Scan | (a)
```

- `plan_match` sorts var-length hops after fixed ones (`graph/src/planner/mod.rs:1752-1784`). So the self-loop `(c)-[:L]->(c)` is planned right after `(a)-[:R]->(b)`, while `c` is still unbound.
- For an unbound self-loop past the first hop, the chaining loop builds `ExpandInto(scan c, res)` (`mod.rs:2129-2153`): the scan and the hops planned so far become two children.
- The runtime only builds child 0 of `ExpandInto`, so `res` (every earlier hop) is lost. The later var-length hop then runs in expand-into mode between an unbound `b` and `c`.

### Expected

As in C, the self-loop checks `c` after the var-length hop has bound it, and `a` stays bound: `[1, 2, 3]`.

### Suggested fix

- After sorting, move such an unbound fixed-length self-loop to just after

issues.title: [Rust] Merging stacked filters runs the pushed-down conjunct before its guard (spurious Division by zero)
issues.body:
## Summary

When `push_filters_down` merges two stacked `Filter`s, it puts the parent's (outer) conjuncts before the child's. `And` stops at the first false conjunct, so the conjunct that used to guard the pushed-down one now runs after it. A query that succeeds on C fails with `Division by zero`.

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1, 5) AS i CREATE (:N {v: i})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:N) WHERE n.v <> 1 MATCH (m:N) WHERE 1 / (n.v - 1) = 0 RETURN count(*)"
```

| | result |
|---|---|
| Rust `main` (2363723ac) | `Division by zero` |
| C (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`) | `15` |

## Mechanism

`graph/src/planner/optimizer/push_filters_down.rs:122`:

```rust
for f in [&filter, &child_filter] {
```

The second `WHERE` (`1 / (n.v - 1) = 0`, which reads only `n`) is pushed down onto the first `Filter(n.v <> 1)`. The two are merged as `And(1/(n.v-1) = 0, n.v <> 1)`, so the division runs for `n.v = 1` before the guard can drop the row. Both the per-row `And` (`eval.rs:674`) and the columnar `eval_and_or` (`vector_expr.rs:392`) short-circuit left to right.

## Expected

`15`, as C returns. Merging must keep the order in which the two filters ran.

## Suggested fix

Merge child-first: `for f in [&child_filter, &filter]`. The Lean model proves the merge exact when the inner conjunct comes first (`merge_child_first_row`).

Residual note: the `And` short-circuits on `false` but not on `null`, so a guard that evaluates to null still lets the pushed conjunct run. Within one `WHERE`, that order is implementation-defined anyway.

## Found by

Lean theorem `merge_order_rust_errors` (and `merge_child_first_row` for the fix), `proofs/optimizer_rewrites` (W2-rewrites-1).

issues.title: [Rust] SHUTDOWN crashes (signal 6) after a UDF ran on the main thread: QuickJS runtime freed before cached functions
issues.body:
### Summary

After a UDF has run on the Redis main thread (e.g. `GRAPH.QUERY` inside `MULTI`), `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE` crashes the server with signal 6 (QuickJS assertion in `JS_FreeRuntime`), followed by a signal 11 in the crash handler.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.UDF LOAD sd "falkor.register('f', function(x){ return x; });"
MULTI
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN sd.f(1)"
EXEC
SHUTDOWN NOSAVE
```
Server log:
```
Redis 8.6.2 crashed by signal: 6, si_code: 0
...  JS_FreeRuntime + 1972
Redis 8.6.2 crashed by signal: 11, si_code: 2
```
Any thread that ran a UDF aborts the same way when it exits (the thread-local destructor runs).

### Mechanism

`ThreadJsState` (`graph/src/udf/js_context.rs:129-136`) declares `runtime`, then `context`, then `functions` (`Persistent<Function>`). Rust drops fields in declaration order, so when the thread-local is destroyed the QuickJS runtime is freed while the persistent functions still hold objects, and QuickJS asserts `list_empty(&rt->gc_obj_list)`. `rebuild_context` drops the fields in the right order by hand (`:193-197`), but the thread-local destructor does not.

### Expected

Clean exit (exit code 0), as in C.

### Suggested fix

Declare the fields in drop order (`functions`, `context`, `runtime`) or implement `Drop` for `ThreadJsState`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the UDF layer (`proofs/algo_udf`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_algo_udf.rs::bug_udf_thread_exit_aborts` (ignored by default: aborts the test process).

issues.title: [Rust] Unterminated edge filter in shortestPath hangs a worker thread forever (C: syntax error)
issues.body:
### Summary

An unterminated relationship filter inside `shortestPath` / `allShortestPaths` sends the parser into an infinite loop. The query never returns and the worker thread spins at 100% CPU forever. Each such query takes one worker, so a handful of them (11 on a default thread pool) stop every graph query on the server. C returns a syntax error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
$ timeout 6 redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN shortestPath((a)-[{"
$ echo $?
124            # never answers; redis-server stays at ~100% CPU afterwards
```

Other inputs that hang the same way:

```
RETURN shortestPath((a)-[$p
RETURN shortestPath((a)-[{x: [1, {y: 2
MATCH (a), (b) RETURN shortestPath((a)-[* {x: 1
MATCH (a), (b) RETURN allShortestPaths((a)-[:R {x: 1
```

C (`edge-c` module):

```
errMsg: Invalid input at end of input: expected a property name or '}' line: 1, column: 27, offset: 26 errCtx: RETURN shortestPath((a)-[{ errCtxOffset: 26
```

### Mechanism

`parse_shortest_path_expr` does not parse an edge filter; it skips it token by token (`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:1819-1845`), counting `{`/`}` and stopping only at `]` or at the `}` that closes it. At end of input the loop hits the `_ => self.lexer.next()` arm, and `next()` at `EndOfFile` stays at `EndOfFile`, so the loop goes on forever.

### Expected

A syntax error, as C gives. A complete filter should still get the existing `filters on relationships in shortestPath are not allowed` error.

### Suggested fix

Parse the filter with `parse_map` (or take the parameter token), then drop it. A malformed or unterminated filter then fails the way it would anywhere else, and the caller still rejects a well-formed one.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the parser (`proofs/parser_grammar`, theorem `skipFilter_eof_diverges`). Rust repro: `graph/tests/lean_parser_grammar.rs::bug_shortest_path_filter_skip_loops_forever_at_eof`.

issues.title: [Rust] Binder removes scope-table entries whose ids are still used: WHERE/SKIP/LIMIT copies and pattern-comprehension locals get their slots reused (wrong rows, 'Invalid node id')
issues.body:
### Summary

The binder mints a variable id as the **current size of the scope table** (`fresh_var`, `graph/src/planner/binder.rs:2214`; the parent copy in `resolve_name`, `:2195`). The planner then mints its own ids from `scope_vars[scope].len()` (`planner/mod.rs:721-735`). In two places, entries are **removed** from a scope table while the bound IR still uses their ids. After that, `len()` is below a live id, and the next variable of that scope, from either the binder or the planner, gets the same id and shares its record slot. The result is wrong rows, missing rows, or a runtime error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Graph: `CREATE (:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5})`

| `MATCH (n) WITH n.v AS k WHERE n.v >= 0 RETURN k, [(x)-->(y) \| y.v] AS l` | `[[0,[0]],[1,[0]],[5,[0]]]` | **`[[0,[]],[1,[0]],[5,[]]]`** |
| `MATCH (n:A) WHERE size([(n)-[r]->(m) \| m]) > 0 MATCH (x)-[s]->(y) WHERE size([(x)-[r2]->(m2) \| m2]) > 0 RETURN n.v, x.v, s.w, y.v` | error (C can't resolve the second comprehension) | **`Invalid node id for 'to' in relationship pattern`**; openCypher gives `[[1,1,2,0]]` |

2. The pattern-comprehension and pattern-predicate cleanup (`binder.rs:1893`, `:2068`) `retain`s only the outer names and `_anon*`. That removes the pattern-local aliases, plus any `_lc_`/`_quant_` reservations made w

issues.title: [Rust] ORDER BY variables cross WITH/RETURN: 'WITH n.v AS k ORDER BY n.v RETURN n' accepted, RETURN * adds columns, CALL {} fails with 'already declared'
issues.body:
### Summary

A variable that `ORDER BY` reads from before a `WITH`/`RETURN` projection stays visible **after** the projection. openCypher and C only let the projected columns cross. As a result, Rust accepts queries that should fail, `RETURN *` returns extra columns, and a CALL {} body that sorts by an imported variable fails with "already declared".

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Graph: `CREATE (:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5})`

| query | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) WITH n.v AS k ORDER BY n.v RETURN n` | `'n' not defined` | **returns the 3 nodes** |
| `MATCH (n) WITH n.v AS k ORDER BY n.v RETURN *` | columns `[k]` | **columns `[k, n]`** |
| `MATCH (n) CALL { WITH n RETURN n.v AS k ORDER BY n.v } RETURN k` | `[[0],[1],[5]]` | **`Variable `n` already declared in outer scope`** |

### Mechanism

`bind_projection` (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs`) hides the parent copies that only the filter needs, by snapshotting the scope's keys and removing the keys added afterwards (`:1216`, `:1231-1239`). The snapshot is taken **after** ORDER BY is bound (`:1183`), so ORDER BY's copies count as projected and stay in scope. In a CALL {} body, `bind_call_subquery` then treats the copied `n` as a returned column that clashes with the outer `n`.

### Expected

Match C and openCypher: only the projected aliases are visible after `WITH`/`RETURN`.

### Suggested fix

Take the snapshot before ORDER BY is bound. The copies must then be hidden **without** being removed, or their ids get reused (see the companion issue on removed scope-table entries). The two are fixed together.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/binder` (W2-binder-5): `orderBy_leaks`. Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_binder.rs` (`bug_order_by_variable_crosses_with`, `bug_order_by_variable_returned_from_call`).

issues.title: [Rust] id() seek errors on a non-integer bound (id(n) = null / 1.0 / > 1.5) where the filter it replaces returns rows
issues.body:
## Summary

When the optimizer turns `WHERE id(n) <op> x` into a `NodeByIdSeek` or a `Node By Label and ID Scan`, it raises `Node ID must be an integer` for any bound that is not an `Int` at runtime. Examples are `id(n) = null`, `id(n) = 1.0`, `id(n) > 1.5` and `id(n) = '1'`. The `Filter` it replaced returns rows for these (or none, for null and non-numeric bounds). So a valid query fails only because it was optimized. This is a regression of the fixed #1878 (`WHERE id(n) >= 0.0`), which now errors instead of returning no rows.

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1, 5) AS i CREATE (:N {v: i})"
```

| query | Rust `main` (2363723ac) | same predicate unoptimized: `WHERE (id(n) <op> x) = true` | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = null RETURN count(n)` | `Node ID must be an integer` | 0 | 0 |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = '1' RETURN count(n)` | error | 0 | 0 |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) = 1.0 RETURN count(n)` | error | **1** | 0 |
| `MATCH (n) WHERE id(n) > 1.5 RETURN count(n)` | error | **3** | 0 |
| `MATCH (n:N) WHERE id(n) >= 3.0 RETURN count(n)` | error | **2** | 0 |

## Mechanism

`Runtime::evaluate_id_filter` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:1324`) matches only `Value::Int(id) => id as u64` and returns `Err("Node ID must be an integer")` for everything else. The same `as u64` cast is also the negative-bound bug of #2266 / #2648: `id(n) > -1` gives 0 rows and `id(n) <= -1` gives every node.

## Expected

The seek returns what the filter would return:
- A null, NaN or non-numeric bound never compares true, so no rows (as C does).
- A float compares numerically, so `id(n) = 1.0` is node 1 and `id(n) > 1.5` is ids 2 and up. This is openCypher's `1 = 1.0`, and it is what Rust's own unoptimized filter returns. Here C is the odd one out: it returns 0 rows for every float bound, which is the inconsistency reported against C in #515.

## Suggested fix

Turn each bound into an integer bound before narrowing the range: `ceil`/`floor` for floats, and satu

issues.title: [Rust] Query command flag parsing diverges from C: non-UTF-8 arg ends parsing, TIMEOUT/version accept +10/010/-5, RO_QUERY/PROFILE/EXPLAIN ignore bad flags, no arity cap
issues.body:
### Summary

`GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.RO_QUERY`, `GRAPH.PROFILE` and `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` each parse their trailing flags with their own ad-hoc loop, and all of them diverge from C's single dispatcher (`_validate_command_arity` + `_read_flags`, `cmd_dispatcher.c`).

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b; C = `master`)

| command | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" "\xff" --compact` | verbose reply (`--compact` dropped) | compact reply |
| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" TIMEOUT -5` / `+10` / `010` | runs | `Failed to parse query timeout value` |
| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" TIMEOUT abc` | `invalid digit found in string` | `Failed to parse query timeout value` |
| `GRAPH.RO_QUERY g "RETURN 1" TIMEOUT abc` (or missing value) | runs, timeout silently dropped | `Failed to parse query timeout value` |
| `GRAPH.PROFILE g "RETURN 1" TIMEOUT abc` | runs | `Failed to parse query timeout value` |
| `GRAPH.EXPLAIN g "RETURN 1" TIMEOUT abc` | runs (flags never read) | `Failed to parse query timeout value` |
| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" version 4294967296` | accepted, then version mismatch | `Failed to parse graph version value` |
| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" version x` | `invalid digit found in string` | `Failed to parse graph version value` |
| `GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN 1" a b c d e f` (9 args) | runs | `wrong number of arguments for 'graph.QUERY' command` |

### Mechanism

- `src/commands/query.rs:61` (`while let Ok(arg) = args.next_str()`) — the first non-UTF-8 argument ends the loop, so later flags are ignored. Same in `ro_query.rs`/`profile.rs`.
- Values are parsed with `str::parse::<i64/u64>`, which accepts `+10`, `010` and negatives and reports the raw `ParseIntError` text; C uses Redis `string2ll` (canonical decimal only) and rejects negative timeouts and versions outside `0..=UINT_MAX`.
- `ro_query.rs:49-53` and `profile.rs:29-33` swallow a bad or missing timeout (`.ok()`); `explain.rs` never looks at the flags.
- No arity cap (C: `3 <= argc <= 8`).

issues.title: [Rust] Value Hash Join inside a batched Apply/Optional joins rows of different outer rows (16 where C gives 8)
issues.body:
### Summary

A Value Hash Join inside a batched correlated sub-plan (Apply, or Optional under OPTIONAL MATCH) joins rows that came from **different** outer rows. Results are multiplied or duplicated.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS i CREATE (:A {v:1, w:i}), (:B {v:1, w:i})"

GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x MATCH (a:A),(b:B) WHERE a.v = b.v RETURN count(*)"
Rust: 16
C:    8

GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x OPTIONAL MATCH (a:A),(b:B) WHERE a.v = b.v AND a.w = x AND b.w = x RETURN x, a.w, b.w"
Rust: 1|1|1, 2|2|2, 1|1|1, 2|2|2
C:    1|1|1, 2|2|2
```

Plan (both engines): `Aggregate <- Apply(Unwind, Value Hash Join(NodeByLabelScan(a) <- Argument, NodeByLabelScan(b) <- Argument))`.

### Mechanism

In batched mode, `ApplyOp` and `OptionalOp` hand their sub-plan one argument batch that holds all the outer rows. Each row is tagged with its `origin_row` (`Batch::clone_active_rows_seq_origin`). Every operator allowed in a batched sub-plan must keep the rows of different origins apart. `can_batch` enforces that with a blacklist (`apply.rs:119-133`, `optional.rs:104-106`). `IR::ValueHashJoin` is missing from it. `ValueHashJoinOp` (`value_hash_join.rs:366-446`) builds one table over the right side's rows for *all* origins and probes it with every left row without comparing `origin_row`. So a left row of outer row 1 matches right rows of outer rows 1 and 2.

### Expected (C behaviour)

The join only pairs rows of the same outer row: `8`, and each OPTIONAL row once.

### Suggested fix

Either add `IR::ValueHashJoin` to both blacklists, which forces per-row mode, or make the join origin-aware: when it receives a multi-row argument batch, build one table per origin and probe the table of the left row's origin. The second keeps batching.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the correlated operators (`proofs/ops_apply`), theorems `vhj_not_separable`, `canBatchApply_admits_vhj`, `vhj_batched_16_vs_8`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops

issues.title: [Rust] Server hangs forever when more than ~1024 queries are queued (bounded pool/write queues block under the GIL)
issues.body:
### Summary

Flooding the server with more queued queries than a fixed queue holds hangs it **permanently**: 0% CPU, `PING` never answers, only a restart recovers. Two independent lock cycles, both caused by blocking sends into bounded (1024-slot) channels. C completes the same load.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b, default `THREAD_COUNT`)

3000 concurrent writes over 16 graphs (each graph < 1024 writes), one connection per write (`proofs/search_concurrency/repro/flood2.py`):

```
python flood2.py <port> 3000 16 "UNWIND range(1,3000) AS x CREATE (:N)" 45
t=3s  done=21/3000 ping=TimeoutError()
...
t=43s done=21/3000 ping=TimeoutError()      <- forever
```

3000 concurrent `CREATE (:N)` on **one** graph hangs the same way (`flood2.py <port> 3000 1 "CREATE (:N)" 30`: `done=0/3000 ping=TimeoutError()`).

C (`falkordb.so`, same machine): the 16-graph flood completes 3000/3000 in 12 s. (C itself crashes on the single-graph flood — a separate C bug.)

### Mechanism

**Cycle 1 — pool queue vs GIL** (`sample` of the hung process: main thread in `crossfire…blocking_tx…send` under `query_mut`, all 11 workers in `QuerySession::upgrade_to_write` → `RM_ThreadSafeContextLock`):

- `spawn` is called from `query_mut` (`src/graph_core.rs:1015`) on the Redis main thread, which holds the GIL.
- Every running worker executing a write escalates at its first mutation and waits for the GIL. No worker drains the queue, the main thread never releases the GIL.

issues.title: [Rust] Hash join drops Int/Float key pairs above 2^53 that = matches (optimizer changes the result)
issues.body:
## Summary

`replace_cartesian_with_hash_join` turns `MATCH (a),(b) WHERE a.x = b.x` into a `ValueHashJoin`. The join's keys use exact integer equality, but Cypher `=` between an `Int` and a `Float` compares `i as f64`. Above 2^53 the two disagree, so the optimized query drops rows that the same predicate keeps when it is not rewritten.

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {x: 9007199254740993}), (:L {x: 9007199254740992.0})"
```

| query | Rust `main` (2363723ac) | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a:L), (b:L) WHERE a.x = b.x RETURN count(*)` (Value Hash Join) | **2** | 4 |
| `MATCH (a:L), (b:L) WHERE (a.x = b.x) = true RETURN count(*)` (Filter) | 4 | 4 |

`9007199254740993 = 9007199254740992.0` is `true` in Rust, C and in the `Filter`.

## Mechanism

- `value_hash_join.rs:153` `key_as_i64` maps `Int(n)` to `n` and a whole `Float(f)` to `f as i64`. `2^53 + 1` and `2^53.0` get different keys. The all-`Column::Ints` build path (`:290`) keys every integer exactly too.
- `Value`'s `Hash` (`value.rs:835`) hashes `Int(n)` as `n` and a whole `Float` as `f as i64`, so on the general path the two also land in different buckets. That is also a violation of the `Hash`/`Eq` contract, since `PartialEq` says they are equal.
- `=` is not transitive across the types above 2^53: `2^53 = 2^53.0 = 2^53 + 1`, but `2^53 <> 2^53 + 1`. So grouping build keys under one entry with `keys_match` (`insert_value`) is not sound either.

## Expected

The join returns what the `Filter` returns, which is what `=` does (compare `i as f64`). C returns 4. #2891 / PR #2912 introduced an *exact* Int/Float comparison, but only for sort order. `=` and grouping keep `as f64`, and the join has to agree with `=`.

## Suggested fix

- Keep the integer fast path for keys below 2^53 only, where Int/Float equality is exact and transitive. A larger build key moves the table to the general path, and a larger probe key cannot match anything in the integer table.
- Hash an `Int` above 2^53 as its `f64` image,

issues.title: [Rust] GRAPH.CONFIG accepts values/arity C rejects (VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT -5, CMD_INFO 1, JS_HEAP_SIZE 5, GET x extra, Unicode name folding); ASYNC_DELETE reports 0
issues.body:
### Summary

`GRAPH.CONFIG` accepts several requests that C rejects, and reports `ASYNC_DELETE` differently.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b; C = `master`)

| command | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `GRAPH.CONFIG SET VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT -5` | `OK` (then read back as `-5`, used `as u64`) | `Failed to set config value VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT to -5` |
| `GRAPH.CONFIG SET CMD_INFO 1` (also `true`, `0`, `false`; same for `ASYNC_DELETE`, `DELAY_INDEXING`) | `OK` | `Failed to set config value CMD_INFO to 1` |
| `GRAPH.CONFIG SET JS_HEAP_SIZE 5` (also `0`; same for `JS_STACK_SIZE`) | `OK` | `JS_HEAP_SIZE must be at least 1MB (1048576)` |
| `GRAPH.CONFIG GET TIMEOUT extra` | `[TIMEOUT, 0]` | wrong number of arguments |
| `GRAPH.CONFIG SET TIMEOUT` | `Missing value for configuration parameter` | wrong number of arguments |
| `GRAPH.CONFIG GET tımeout` (dotless `ı`) | `[TIMEOUT, 0]` | `Unknown configuration field` |
| `GRAPH.CONFIG GET ASYNC_DELETE` (default) | `0` | `1` |

### Mechanism (`src/commands/config_cmd.rs`)

- `validate_config_set`: `VKEY_MAX_ENTITY_COUNT` has no lower bound; booleans accept `1/0/true/false` besides `yes/no` (C `_Config_ParseYesNo` takes only `yes`/`no`); `JS_HEAP_SIZE`/`JS_STACK_SIZE` only require `>= 0` (C: positive and `>= 1048576`).
- `graph_config`: no arity check (C: `GET` needs exactly 3 args, `SET` an even count `>= 4`); names are folded with `str::to_uppercase`, which is Unicode-aware (`ı` → `I`), where C uses ASCII `strcasecmp`.
- `config.rs`: `ASYNC_DELETE` starts at 0, but this engine always frees graphs off-thread (`graph_core::graph_free`), and C's default is `yes`.
- Unknown field error is `Unknown configuration field 'X'`; C's is `Unknown configuration field`.

### Expected

Match C for all of the above.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the Redis layer (`proofs/redis_layer`, `Config.validate` / `Config.rustSet` vs `Config.cSet`); live repro `proofs/redis_layer/repro_live.py` (C1-C6).

issues.title: [Rust] A refused GRAPH.EFFECT buffer keeps its CREATE_INDEX/DROP_INDEX: Indexer is shared across MVCC versions, rollback cannot undo it
issues.body:
### Summary

When `GRAPH.EFFECT` refuses a buffer, the buffer is supposed to have no effect: `MvccGraph::rollback` drops the private version. Index DDL is the exception. A `CREATE_INDEX` (or `DROP_INDEX`) that ran before the refusing record **stays applied**. The reason is that `Indexer` is shared by `Arc` across MVCC versions: `Graph::new_version` clones the handle (`graph.rs:960`), and `create_index` mutates the shared `ArcSwap` map. Dropping the version does not undo it. Constraints are per-version, and they roll back correctly.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Payload `[ADD_ATTRIBUTE 1 "zz", CREATE_INDEX A(zz) range, CREATE_NODE [0]]` on a graph where node 0 is live:

```
GRAPH.EFFECT g <payload>   -> ERR effect apply failed: effects buffer creates node 0, which is already live ... the buffer was not applied.
CALL db.indexes()          -> A [zz]          <- index from the refused buffer
CALL db.propertyKeys()     -> (no 'zz')       <- the attribute *was* rolled back
```

The index now names an attribute that the dictionary does not hold.

In-process, `refused_buffer_leaves_its_index_behind` in `graph/tests/lean_effects_emit_apply.rs` shows the same thing. It is `#[ignore]` because it needs RediSearch.

### Impact

* **Replica**: a refusal already forces a full resync, and the RDB reload rebuilds the indexes, so the stale index is transient.
* **Client-sent `GRAPH.EFFECT`**: the index persists, and so does its population job.
* **AOF load**: a refusal shuts the server down anyway (see #2946 for one way to reach that).

Severity is low, but "the buffer was not applied" is untrue for this record.

### Mechanism

* `apply_effects` (`graph/src/effects/v3/apply.rs:72`) applies records in order. `Record::CreateIndex` / `Record::DropIndex` (`apply.rs:419`, `:468`) call `Graph::create_index` / `drop_index` right away.
* `Graph::create_index` (`graph.rs:3243`) mutates `self.node_indexer`, an `Indexer` whose map is `Arc<ArcSwap<…>>` shared with the co

issues.title: [Rust] GRAPH.BULK header naming a property twice stores duplicate attribute entries (properties(n) = {p: 1, p: 3, q: 2}; n.p reads last, C reads first)
issues.body:
### Summary

A `GRAPH.BULK` token header that names the same property twice (e.g. `p,q,p`) leaves two entries for one attribute on the entity. `properties(n)` then shows a duplicate key, and `n.p` / `{p: …}` read the *last* value, where C reads the first.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

Node token: label `L`, header `p,q,p`, one record `(1, 2, 3)` (all `BI_LONG`):

```
GRAPH.BULK d BEGIN 1 0 1 0 <token>
GRAPH.QUERY d "MATCH (n) RETURN n.p, properties(n)"
GRAPH.QUERY d "MATCH (n {p:3}) RETURN count(n)"
```

| | Rust | C (`master`) |
|---|---|---|
| `n.p, properties(n)` | `3, {p: 1, p: 3, q: 2}` | `1, {q: 2, p: 3}` |
| `count(n {p:3})` | 1 | 0 |

Edges behave the same way (header `p,p`, values `5,6`: Rust `e.p = 6`, C `e.p = 5`).

### Mechanism

`process_node_token` / `process_edge_token` (`src/commands/bulk_insert.rs:386-410`, `:470-495`) resolve each header column to an attribute id and push `(attr_id, value)` for every non-null column, so a repeated column pushes the same id twice into the entity's attribute slot (`attribute_store.rs:224-238`).

### Expected

One entry per attribute. C's loader appends both but every lookup returns the first non-null one, so keep the first non-null value per attribute (C's own `properties()` is inconsistent with its `n.p` here; the fix follows `n.p`).

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the bulk reader (`proofs/redis_layer`, `Bulk.go/attach`, `Bulk.getOrCreate`); live repro `proofs/redis_layer/repro_live.py` (B1).

issues.title: [Rust] UNION branches inside CALL {} reuse the outer query's scope 0: branch variables read outer slots (wrong/missing/duplicated rows)
issues.body:
### Summary

A `UNION` inside `CALL {}` binds each branch with a fresh binder whose scopes start at **0**, and scope 0 is the outer query's scope. A branch variable gets the same `(scope, id)` as an outer variable, so it reads and writes the outer variable's record slot. That gives wrong values, missing rows, or duplicated rows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Graph: `CREATE (:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5})`

| query | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n:A) CALL { MATCH (q:B) RETURN q UNION MATCH (q:B) RETURN q } RETURN n.v, q.v` | `[[1,0],[1,5]]` | **`[[1,1]]`**: `q` reads `n`'s slot |
| same with `UNION ALL` | `[[1,0],[1,0],[1,5],[1,5]]` | **`[[1,1],[1,1]]`** |
| `MATCH (n) CALL { MATCH (q:B) RETURN q.v AS qv UNION ALL MATCH (q:A) RETURN q.v AS qv } RETURN n.v, qv` | 9 rows | **18 rows** (each row twice) |
| `MATCH (n:A) CALL { MATCH (q:B) RETURN q.v AS x UNION MATCH (q:A) RETURN q.v AS x } WITH n, x MATCH (m:B) RETURN n.v, x, m.v` | 6 rows | **2 rows** |

A plain (non-UNION) CALL body gives the correct answer.

### Mechanism

`bind_call_body`, UNION arm (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs:868-876`), builds each branch binder with `env_stack: vec![HashMap::new()]`, so the branch's first scope is 0. The Query arm pushes a new scope at `env_stack.len()` (`:817`), so its variables never share a scope id with the live outer scopes (Lean: `callBody_query_disjoint`).

### Expected

Match C: branch variables are independent of the outer query's variables.

### Suggested fix

Start each branch binder's scopes at `self.env_stack.len()`, the way a plain CALL body does, with empty placeholder tables below that.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/binder` (W2-binder-4): `callBody_union_aliases`, `callBody_query_disjoint`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_binder.rs::bug_call_union_branch_scopes_alias_outer`.

issues.title: [Rust] question/decision: count property statistics net at commit (Rust) or per clause (C)?
issues.body:
### Question / decision needed

Rust and C count property statistics differently, and neither is obviously a bug. This issue is to pick one; no code change until then.

- **C counts per clause**: every `SET`/`REMOVE` that writes a property counts, even if a later clause of the same query overwrites or reverts it.
- **Rust counts net at commit**: `Pending` keeps the last staged value per (entity, attribute), and `Pending::commit` counts what it actually changes in the store (`import_*_attrs`, `set_*_attributes` → `insert_attrs`).

### Examples (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac vs C, fresh graph)

| setup ; query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| — ; `CREATE (n {v:1}) SET n.v = 2` | `Properties set: 1` | `Properties set: 2, Properties removed: 1` |
| `CREATE ({v:1})` ; `MATCH (n) SET n.v = 2 SET n.v = 1` | `Properties set: 1, Properties removed: 1` | none |
| `CREATE ({v:0})` ; `MATCH (n) UNWIND range(1,3) AS i SET n.v = i` | `Properties set: 1, Properties removed: 1` | `Properties set: 3, Properties removed: 3` |
| `CREATE (:A)` ; `MATCH (n) REMOVE n:A SET n:A` | none | `Labels added: 1, Labels removed: 1` |
| `CREATE (:A {v:1})` ; `MATCH (n) DELETE n WITH count(*) AS c CREATE (m {v:2}) SET m.v = 3` | `Properties set: 1` | `Properties set: 2, Properties removed: 1` |

(Rows from the Lean investigation in `proofs/pending_commit`; `c_eq_rust_plus_cancelled` in `Stats.lean` models the create/delete counters, not these.)

### Options

1. **Match C (per clause)**: count at staging time in `set.rs`/`remove.rs`, against the value visible at that point. Pros: C/TCK-style parity; tools written against C's stats keep working. Cons: counts writes that do not reach the store; staging has to compute old-vs-new per write (it already reads the old value for the no-op check).
2. **Keep net (Rust today)**: counts describe the change the query made to the graph. Pros: cheaper, arguably more useful. Cons: diverges from C in every multi-write query; needs documenting.

Not changed by the st

issues.title: [Rust] algo.WCC / algo.labelPropagation with nodeLabels return compact indices instead of node ids
issues.body:
### Summary

With `nodeLabels`, `algo.WCC` and `algo.labelPropagation` report `componentId` / `communityId` as an index into the filtered node set instead of a node id. The ids can name nodes outside the result (here node 1, a `:B` node) and differ from the unfiltered run and from C.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A {id:0}), (:B {id:1}), (:A {id:2}), (:A {id:3})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:2}),(b {id:3}) CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}),(b {id:1}) CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CALL algo.WCC({nodeLabels:['A']}) YIELD node, componentId RETURN id(node), componentId ORDER BY id(node)"
-- Rust: [0,0] [2,1] [3,1]      C: [0,0] [2,2] [3,2]
GRAPH.QUERY g "CALL algo.labelPropagation({nodeLabels:['A']}) YIELD node, communityId RETURN id(node), communityId ORDER BY id(node)"
-- Rust: [0,0] [2,1] [3,2]      C: [0,0] [2,2] [3,3]
```

### Mechanism

On the compact path LAGraph runs on a matrix indexed by compact index, and both the vector index and the value (the representative vertex) are compact indices. `graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:888-896` (WCC) and `:1295-1304` (CDLP) map the index through `compact_to_id` but push the value unmapped.

### Expected

Match C (and the unfiltered run): the id is the original id of the representative node.

### Suggested fix

Map the value through `compact_to_id` too.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the algo procedures (`proofs/algo_udf`, theorem `Compact.wcc_compact_component_id_not_member`); Rust repros `graph/tests/lean_algo_udf.rs::bug_wcc_label_filter_component_ids_are_compact_indices`, `bug_cdlp_label_filter_community_ids_are_compact_indices`.

issues.title: [Rust] Tensor::decode accepts multi-edge ids for a pair that is not multi-edge: phantom edges, edge_count panics, graph can't be saved
issues.body:
### Summary

`Tensor::decode` trusts the tensor section of an RDB / `GRAPH.RESTORE` payload. An entry for a `(src, dst)` pair whose forward value is not a multi-edge marker (absent, or a single edge) still gets an `me` row. That breaks the invariant `edge_count` relies on (a pair has `me` ids exactly when its inline value is `MULTI_EDGE`): iteration yields a phantom edge, `edge_count` panics, and since `Tensor::encode` calls `edge_count`, the restored graph can no longer be saved (the next SAVE / BGSAVE / GRAPH.COPY panics). The converse (a pair marked multi-edge whose ids never arrive) is accepted too and gives a wrong edge count.

### Reproduction (`main` @ 55204c94b)

Encode an empty 16x16 tensor, then append a tensor section with one entry `(7, 9)` → id blob `{3}`, and decode:

```
Tensor::decode -> Ok
iter_edges()   -> [(7, 9, 3)]          // phantom edge, no forward entry
edge_count()   -> panic: Tensor::edge_count: multi exceeds the effective pattern
```

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/tensor.rs:1575-1611` — for every tensor-section entry the ids are written into `me` at `compound_key(src, dst)` without looking at the forward value of `(src, dst)`; nothing checks that every `MULTI_EDGE` marker got ids. `edge_count` (`tensor.rs:1221`) then panics on the broken identity (intentionally, since #2563).

The load is refused with an error; a payload the encoder could have written (every multi-edge marker has its ids, no ids elsewhere) still loads. (C is not comparable: different in-memory layout.)
