issues.title: [Rust] A list slice bound that fails to parse is silently read as 0 / end of list ([1,2,3][abs()..2] returns [1, 2])
issues.body:
### Summary

A list slice bound that fails to parse is silently replaced by `0` (for `from`) or `i64::MAX` (for `to`), so an invalid slice runs and returns a wrong result instead of an error. C reports the error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

| Query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN [1,2,3][abs()..2]` | `[1, 2]` | `Received 0 arguments to function 'abs', expected at least 1` |
| `RETURN [1,2,3][1..abs()]` | `[2, 3]` | same arity error |
| `RETURN [1,2,3][1+..2]` | `[1, 2]` | `Invalid input '.': expected NOT, '+', '-', …` |
| `RETURN [1,2,3][(1..2]` | `[1, 2]` | `Invalid input '.': expected a property name` |

Leaving out a bound on purpose (`[..2]`, `[1..]`, `[..]`) works on both engines and must keep working.

### Mechanism

`parse_list_operator_expression` (`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:2123-2131`) calls `parse_expr` for each bound and keeps the `Result`. Then `from.unwrap_or_else(|_| 0)` / `to.unwrap_or_else(|_| i64::MAX)` treats *any* parse error as "bound left out". The error is dropped, and the lexer resumes from wherever the failed parse left it.

### Expected

A bound is missing only when `..` or `]` comes where the bound would start. Otherwise the bound is parsed and its error is returned, as in C.

### Suggested fix

Check the current token (`DotDot` before `from`, `RBrace` before `to`) to decide whether the bound is present, and propagate `parse_expr`'s error with `?`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the parser (`proofs/parser_grammar`, theorem `slice_bound_error_swallowed`). Rust repro: `graph/tests/lean_parser_grammar.rs::bug_slice_bound_error_is_swallowed`.

issues.title: [Rust] select_scan_node treats the best endpoint as bound when it keeps an outer child, so an inline filter runs before its variable is bound (0 rows)
issues.body:
## Summary

When the bottom `CondTraverse` of a chain keeps an outer-context child (`WITH b LIMIT 1`, `WITH DISTINCT b`, `ORDER BY`, `SKIP`, ...), `select_scan_node` still treats the endpoint it scored best as bound, even though no scan is built for it. The hops are then ordered, and the inline-attribute filter placed, as if that variable were bound. In the plan below, `c`'s filter `{v: 1}` runs before `c` is bound, and every row is dropped.

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (b:A), (d:D), (c {v:1}), (z:Z), (d)-[:X]->(b), (d)-[:R]->(c), (c)-[:R]->(z)"
```

| query | Rust `main` (2363723ac) | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (b:A) WITH b LIMIT 1 MATCH (b)<-[]-(d)-[:R]->(c {v:1})-[:R]->(z) RETURN count(*)` | **0** | 1 |
| same with `WITH DISTINCT b` | **0** | 1 |
| same with plain `WITH b` | 1 | 1 |

```
GRAPH.EXPLAIN g "MATCH (b:A) WITH b LIMIT 1 MATCH (b)<-[]-(d)-[:R]->(c {v:1})-[:R]->(z) RETURN count(*)"
Aggregate
    Conditional Traverse | (c)->(z)
        Conditional Traverse | (d)->(c)
            Filter                          <- c.v = 1, but c is bound only by the hop above
```

```rust

        b.extend(collect_subtree_variables(&child.root()));
    }
    b
};
```

With `existing_child` kept, `make_scan_subtree(&best_node, ..)` is never built (`:1080`), yet `placed_bound` starts with `c`, so the inline filter on `c` is placed right after the first hop. issues.title: [Rust] MERGE's created-pattern cache is shared by all MERGE clauses: 'Variable b not found' / UNION branch aliases the other branch's node
issues.body:
### Summary

The MERGE "already created in this query" cache is shared by **every** MERGE clause of a query. A later MERGE whose pattern hashes the same as an earlier clause's (same labels and property map) reuses the earlier clause's cached bindings. Its own variable is then left unbound and the query is rolled back. In a UNION branch it silently aliases the other branch's node instead of creating its own.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "MERGE (a:M {v:1}) ON CREATE SET a.v = 2 MERGE (b:M {v:1}) RETURN a.v, b.v"
Rust: Variable b not found        (query rolled back, 0 nodes)
C:    2|1                         (2 nodes)

GRAPH.QUERY g "MERGE (a:U {v:1}) ON CREATE SET a.v = 2 RETURN a.v AS v UNION ALL MERGE (b:U {v:1}) RETURN b.v AS v"
Rust: 2, 2                        (1 node)
C:    2, 1                        (2 nodes)
```

### Mechanism

`Runtime::merge_pattern_cache` (`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs:163`) is keyed only by the pattern hash from `compute_merge_pattern_hash`. That hash covers labels, property values and bound endpoints, but not which MERGE it came from. In `MergeOp::do_create_fallback` (`merge.rs:118-135`), the second clause finds no match in the graph (the first node now has `v = 2`), gets a cache hit on the first clause's entry, and inserts the cached `(variable id, value)` pairs. Those are the **first** clause's variable ids: `b` stays unbound ("Variable b not found"). In a UNION branch, where variable ids start again, `b` gets the first branch's node.

### Expected (C behaviour)

The dedup of created patterns is per MERGE operator (C keeps `unique_entities` per op). The second clause creates its own node: `2|1`, 2 nodes.

### Suggested fix

Key the cache by `(MergeOp plan idx, pattern hash)`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of MERGE (`proofs/ops_apply`), theorems `cross_clause_unbound`, `per_clause_cache_fixes`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_apply.rs` (`bug_merge_cache_shared_across_clauses`, `bug_merge_cache_

issues.title: [Rust] MERGE result depends on BATCH_SIZE: matching runs per input batch and sees earlier batches' creations
issues.body:
### Summary

The result of a MERGE depends on where the 1024-row batch boundaries fall. MERGE matches its pattern once per input **batch**. Rows in later batches therefore see what earlier batches created (after `ON CREATE SET`), while rows in the same batch do not. The same two rows create 2 nodes when they are adjacent and 1 node when they are 1024 rows apart.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(1,2) AS x WITH x WHERE x = 1 OR x = 2
               MERGE (n:L {v: CASE x WHEN 1 THEN 1 ELSE 2 END}) ON CREATE SET n.v = 2"
Rust: Nodes created: 2       C: Nodes created: 2

GRAPH.QUERY g2 "UNWIND range(1,1025) AS x WITH x WHERE x = 1 OR x = 1025
                MERGE (n:L {v: CASE x WHEN 1 THEN 1 ELSE 2 END}) ON CREATE SET n.v = 2"
Rust: Nodes created: 1       C: Nodes created: 2
```

In the second query the first row creates `(:L {v:1})`, and `ON CREATE SET` turns it into `v:2`. The last row is in the next batch, so its match sub-plan runs afterwards and finds that node.

### Mechanism

`MergeOp::next` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/merge.rs:313-343`) pulls one input batch, runs the match sub-plan for that batch, then creates or updates row by row. Only then does it pull the next batch. Within a batch, only `merge_pattern_cache` stands in for earlier rows' creations. Across batches, the match sub-plan sees them directly, including their `ON CREATE`/`ON MATCH` updates.

### Expected (C behaviour)

C's `op_merge.c` is eager and batch-independent. It consumes the whole input, matches every row against the graph as it was before this MERGE created anything, and only then creates the rows that did not match. Rows that would create a duplicate are postponed and matched after the commit. Both queries create 2 nodes.

### Suggested fix

Make `MergeOp` eager like C: pull all input batches and run the match sub-plan for each of them before any create or `SET`, then create/update and emit. Batching of the match sub-plan stays. Only the i

issues.title: [Rust] MERGE p=(a)-[:R]->(b) with a, b bound returns only the first of several parallel matches
issues.body:
### Summary

`MATCH (a:A),(b:B) MERGE p=(a)-[:R]->(b)` with two parallel `:R` edges returns one row, not two. When every node and every *named* relationship of the pattern is already bound, MERGE keeps only the first match. A path variable over an anonymous relationship still tells the matches apart.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A),(b:B),(a)-[:R {k:1}]->(b),(a)-[:R {k:2}]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:A),(b:B) MERGE p=(a)-[:R]->(b) RETURN count(p)"
Rust: 1
C:    2
```

### Mechanism

`MergeOp::next` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/merge.rs:368-400`) computes `all_vars_bound`: all nodes bound, and every relationship alias not starting with `_anon_` bound. In that case it emits only `matches[0]`. That is right when the output cannot tell the matches apart. A path variable (`p = ...`) binds the anonymous relationship, though, so every parallel edge is a distinct result row.

### Expected (C behaviour)

One row per match: `2`.

### Suggested fix

Don't take the shortcut when the MERGE pattern binds a path variable.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of MERGE (`proofs/ops_apply`), theorem `allBound_first_only`; Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_apply.rs` (`bug_merge_all_bound_drops_path_matches`).

issues.title: [Rust] Verbose reply text differs from C: top-level point has 'latitude: ' spacing, NaN in list/map/vector prints NaN instead of nan
issues.body:
### Summary

Two verbose-reply texts differ from C byte for byte: a top-level point has a space after each colon, and NaN inside a list / map / vector is spelled `NaN` instead of C's `nan`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN point({latitude: 1, longitude: 2}), [0.0/0.0, 1.0/0.0], {a: 0.0/0.0}, vecf32([0.0/0.0])"
```

| column | Rust | C (`master`) |
|---|---|---|
| top-level point | `point({latitude: 1.000000, longitude: 2.000000})` | `point({latitude:1.000000, longitude:2.000000})` |
| list | `[NaN, inf]` | `[nan, inf]` |
| map | `{a: NaN}` | `{a: nan}` |
| vector | `<NaN>` | `<nan>` |

(A point *inside* a list/map is already identical: `point({latitude: 1.000000, …})` on both.)

### Mechanism

- `reply_verbose_value`, `Value::Point` arm (`src/reply.rs:520-526`) uses the nested `SIValue_ToString` format; C's top-level verbose point reply is `"point({latitude:%f, longitude:%f})"`.
- `format_value_to_string` (`src/reply.rs:46-48`, `:88`) formats floats with Rust's `{:.6}`, which matches C's `%f` on every finite value and on `inf`/`-inf`, but prints NaN as `NaN`.

### Expected

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the Redis layer (`proofs/redis_layer`, header "Confirmed divergences" 6); live repro `proofs/redis_layer/repro_live.py` (V1, V2).

issues.title: [Rust] algo.HarmonicCentrality skips the highest node ids after a delete (vector sized by node_count)
issues.body:
### Summary

After a node is deleted, unfiltered `algo.HarmonicCentrality` drops the node with the highest id from its results, and every score and `reachable` count that should include that node is too small.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND range(0, 4) AS i CREATE (:A {id: i})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:A), (b:A) WHERE b.id = a.id + 1 AND a.id > 0 CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n:A {id: 0}) DELETE n"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CALL algo.HarmonicCentrality() YIELD node, reachable, score RETURN node.id, reachable, score ORDER BY node.id"
-- Rust: 1|3|1.5027  2|2|1.0015  3|1|0            (node 4 missing)
-- C:    1|4|1.8372  2|3|1.5027  3|2|1.0015  4|1|0
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2777-2779` sizes the source vector with `g.node_count()`, while the unfiltered matrix has `node_count + deleted_nodes_count` rows (`:2755`). With `k` deleted nodes the top `k` ids are never sources.

A sweep of the other `algo.*` procedures in the file found no other place that sizes by `node_count()` alone: pageRank, WCC, betweenness and CDLP use `node_count + deleted_nodes_count`, BFS and MSF use the matrix or the collected ids, maxFlow uses `max_node_id() + 1`.

### Expected

Match C: every live node is a source and is reported.

### Suggested fix

Size the vector with `node_count + deleted_nodes_count` (the id bound), as the matrix is.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the algo procedures (`proofs/algo_udf`, theorem `Harmonic.unfiltered_drops_high_ids`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_algo_udf.rs::bug_harmonic_centrality_with_deleted_node`.

issues.title: [Rust] Collapsed (unread) named edge still takes part in relationship uniqueness, so the count depends on which parallel edge was picked
issues.body:
## Summary

`reduce_expand_into` collapses a named-but-unread edge to one row per (src, dst) pair and binds one representative edge. A sibling traverse in the same pattern still checks relationship uniqueness against that representative (`edge_already_used`). So the row count depends on *which* parallel edge was picked, and it matches neither C nor openCypher.

## Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:N {id:1}), (b:N {id:2}), (c:N {id:3}), (a)-[:R {w:1}]->(b), (a)-[:R {w:2}]->(b), (b)-[:R {w:3}]->(c)"
```

| query | Rust `main` (2363723ac) | C |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(x)<-[s]-(c) RETURN count(*)` | **1** | 2 |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(x)<-[s]-(c) RETURN a.id, c.id` | **`1,1`** | `1,1` / `2,2` |
| `MATCH (a)-[r]->(x)<-[s]-(c) RETURN r.w, s.w` | `1,2` / `2,1` | 4 rows (C checks no uniqueness here) |

The `(b)->(c)` pair has one edge, `e3`. With `r` collapsed to `e3`, the traverse for `s` rejects `e3` as "already used", so the `(2,2)` row disappears. For `(a,b)`, one of the two parallel edges survives, whichever the representative isn't.

## Mechanism

- `planner/optimizer/reduce_expand_into.rs:118-143` sets `emit_relationship = false` for `r` and `s`, because no ancestor reads them.
- Both traverses keep each other in `sibling_edges` (`planner/mod.rs:1888`). The runtime check `ops/mod.rs:155 edge_already_used` compares against whatever edge the collapsed sibling bound.

PR #2918 (#2896) does not change this. Its `variable_read_outside` / `ir_references_variable` still ignore `sibling_edges`, so the same collapse happens on that branch.

## Expected

A collapsed edge stands for all of its parallel edges, so the uniqueness check cannot use its arbitrary representative. C semantics for unread edges is one row per endpoint pair with no uniqueness check against them. That gives 2 here, and `(1,1), (2,2)`.

## Suggested fix

When `reduce_expand_into` collapses an edge, drop it from every sibling list in the same scope. Only edges that are emitted per edge take part

issues.title: [Rust] Labels from CREATE and from pattern comprehensions tighten the earlier MATCH scan (0/1 rows where C returns 3)
issues.body:
### Summary

The binder merges every label written on a node variable, across the whole query, into one set per `(scope, id)`, and writes that set back into **every** occurrence of the node (`update_all_node_labels`). Only OPTIONAL MATCH and pattern predicates save and restore this set. CREATE and pattern comprehensions do not, so their labels tighten the scan of the MATCH that bound the node.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Graph: `CREATE (:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5})`

| query | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (a) CREATE (a:Z)-[:T]->(:C) RETURN count(*)` | `[[3]]` (3 edges created) | **`[[0]]`**: the MATCH became `MATCH (a:Z)` |
| `MATCH (a) RETURN a.v, [(a:A)-->(b) \| b.v] AS l` | `[[0,[]],[1,[0]],[5,[]]]` | **`[[1,[0]]]`**: the MATCH became `MATCH (a:A)` |

### Mechanism

* `bind_graph` extends `node_labels[(scope, id)]` with the labels of every occurrence (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs:1327-1331`).
* `update_all_node_labels` (`:122-154`) then replaces the labels of every MATCH node with that set.
* OPTIONAL MATCH (`:338`) and pattern predicates (`:2061`) clone `node_labels` before `bind_graph` and restore it after. CREATE (`bind_graph_create` → `bind_graph`, `:1645`) and pattern comprehensions (`:1847-1904`) do not.

### Expected

Match C: a label in CREATE is a label to create, and a label inside a pattern comprehension filters only the comprehension. Neither constrains the earlier MATCH.

### Suggested fix

Save and restore `node_labels` around the CREATE bind and around a pattern comprehension's `bind_graph`, as OPTIONAL MATCH and pattern predicates already do.

### Found by

Lean model `proofs/binder` (W2-binder-6): `labels_leak`. Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_binder.rs` (`bug_create_labels_leak_into_match`, `bug_pattern_comprehension_labels_leak_into_match`).

issues.title: [Rust] GRAPH.MEMORY rejects SAMPLES 0; GRAPH.CONSTRAINT accepts LABEL/EDGE and +1/01 property counts (C rejects)
issues.body:
### Summary

Two small argument-parsing divergences from C in admin commands.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b; C = `master`)

| command | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE g SAMPLES 0` | `ERR SAMPLES count must be a positive integer` | report (0 is clamped to 1 sample) |
| `GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE g SAMPLES -20` | `ERR SAMPLES count must be a positive integer` | `SAMPLES must be a non-negative integer` |
| `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g MANDATORY NODE L PROPERTIES +1 q` (also `01`) | `PENDING` (constraint created) | `Number of properties must be an integer between 1 and 255` |
| `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE g MANDATORY LABEL L PROPERTIES 1 z` (also `EDGE`) | `PENDING` (constraint created) | `Invalid constraint entity type` |

The property count is read with `str::parse` (accepts `+1`, `01`); C uses `RedisModule_StringToLongLong` (`string2ll`). Keywords are folded with Unicode `to_uppercase` rather than ASCII (`strcasecmp`).

issues.title: [Rust] Parser accepts invalid syntax (NOT NOT x → x, SET [n).x, f(1,), MATCH MATCH, LOAD CSV WITH FROM) and rejects x IS NULL IN [..]
issues.body:
### Summary

The hand-written parser accepts several inputs outside the openCypher grammar, some of which then run with a changed meaning. It also rejects one input the grammar allows. Each case is a small local slip in `graph/src/parser/cypher.rs`. C matches the grammar in every case below.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

| # | Query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `RETURN NOT NOT 1` | `1` | `Type mismatch: expected Boolean or Null but was Integer` |
| 2 | `MATCH (n:N) SET [n).x = 5 RETURN n.x` | `5` (runs as `SET n.x = 5`) | `Invalid input ')' …` |
| 2 | `MATCH (n) REMOVE [n).x` | runs as `REMOVE n.x` | syntax error |
| 3 | `RETURN 1 IS NULL IN [false]` | `Unexpected clause following RETURN … pos 16` | `true` |
| 3 | `RETURN 'a' IS NULL STARTS WITH 'a'` | same syntax error | parses (then a type error) |
| 4 | `RETURN abs(-1,)` | `1` | `Invalid input ')' …` |
| 5 | `MATCH MATCH (n) RETURN n` | `[]` | `Invalid input '(': expected '='` |
| 6 | `LOAD CSV WITH FROM 'x' AS r RETURN r` | parses (fails later on the file path) | `Invalid input 'F': expected WITH HEADERS` |

### Mechanism

1. **`NOT NOT x` → `x`** (`cypher.rs:2193`): the NOT prefix keeps only the parity of the count, so an even run disappears. NOT type-checks its operand, so the check is lost with it.
2. **`SET`/`REMOVE` target** (`3225-3229`, `3291-3295`): `parse_primary_expr` returns `recurse = true` for both `(` and an open list `[`. The target code treats both as `(`: it drops the list node, parses `n`, and expects `)`.
3. **Predicate after `IS NULL`** (`2405`): after the `IS [NOT] NULL` loop, level 5 returns instead of going back for more predicates. The grammar is `AddOrSubtract ( StringPredicate | ListPredicate | NullPredicate )*`.

issues.title: [Rust] Pattern predicate in WITH ... WHERE rebinds a pre-projection variable as a fresh node (WHERE (n)-->() tests any node)
issues.body:
### Summary

In `WITH … WHERE`, a scalar predicate can read a variable from before the projection: `WITH n.v AS k WHERE n.v > 0` refers to the matched `n`, in both C and Rust. A **pattern predicate** naming that variable does not refer to it in Rust. Its `n` is bound as a fresh, unconstrained node, so the predicate tests "does any node have an out-edge" instead of "does this `n`".

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

Graph: `CREATE (:A {v:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(:B {v:0}), (:B {v:5})`

| query | C | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| `MATCH (n) WITH n.v AS k WHERE (n)-->() RETURN k` | `[[1]]` | **`[[0],[1],[5]]`** |
| `MATCH (n) WITH n.v AS k WHERE NOT (n)-->() RETURN k` | `[[0],[5]]` | **`[]`** |
| `MATCH (n) WITH n.v AS k WHERE (n)<--() RETURN k` | `[[0]]` | **`[[0],[1],[5]]`** |
| `MATCH (n) WITH n AS m WHERE (n)-->(:B) RETURN m.v` | `[[1]]` | **`[[0],[1],[5]]`** |
| `MATCH (n) WITH n AS m WHERE size([(n)-->(x) \| x]) > 0 RETURN m.v` | error (C can't resolve the comprehension) | **`[[0],[1],[5]]`** (expected `[[1]]`) |

### Mechanism

`bind_graph` resolves pattern aliases through `define_name_in_scope` (`graph/src/planner/binder.rs:2114-2121`), which only looks in the current scope table. The parent-scope lookup that scalar references get lives in `resolve_name` (`:2182`). Pattern comprehensions copy parent names in first (`:1853`), but pattern predicates do not. And when the projection renamed the variable (`WITH n AS m`), `resolve_name` finds it through `parent_to_child_scope`, but under `m`, so even the comprehension pre-copy leaves `n` undefined for `bind_graph`.

### Expected

Match C: in `WITH … WHERE` (and ORDER BY), a pattern's name that matches a pre-projection variable refers to that variable, as it does in a scalar predicate.

### Suggested fix

Share the pattern comprehension's pre-copy with pattern predicates. When the resolved variable lives under another name (the rename case), enter it under the pattern's name for the duration of the pattern bind.

issues.title: [Rust] UDF libraries: qualified-name collisions accepted (silent shadowing) and function names case-folded
issues.body:
### Summary

UDF library loading accepts qualified-name collisions between libraries, and UDF function names are case-folded, so one library can silently shadow another's function and `f` / `F` in one library run the same body. C rejects the colliding library and keeps names case-sensitive.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.UDF LOAD Coll "falkor.register('f', function(){ return 1; });"
GRAPH.UDF LOAD coll "falkor.register('f', function(){ return 2; });"
-- Rust: OK                C: Failed to evaluate UDF library 'coll', Exception: TypeError: function: 'coll.f' already registered
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN Coll.f()"
-- Rust: 2 (shadowed)      C: 1
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN COLL.f()"
-- Rust: 2                 C: Unknown function 'COLL.f'

GRAPH.UDF LOAD a "falkor.register('b.c', function(){ return 1; });"
GRAPH.UDF LOAD a.b "falkor.register('c', function(){ return 2; });"
-- Rust: OK                C: ... function: 'a.b.c' already registered

GRAPH.UDF LOAD cased "falkor.register('f', function(){ return 1; }); falkor.register('F', function(){ return 2; });"
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN cased.f(), cased.F()"
-- Rust: 2, 2              C: 1, 2
```

Deleting the shadowing library also unregisters the other library's function while `GRAPH.UDF LIST` still shows it.

### Mechanism

- `graph/src/udf/repository.rs:98-140` (`UdfRepo::load`) only checks the library name, not the qualified function names other libraries hold.
- The UDF registry is keyed by the lowercased qualified name (`graph/src/runtime/functions/mod.rs:1121` `register_udf`, `unregister_udf`, `Functions::get`), and so is the per-thread JS function cache (`graph/src/udf/js_context.rs:228`, `call_udf_bridge`).

### Expected

Match C: reject a library whose qualified name is already held by another library (C compares ignoring case), and resolve UDF calls case-sensitively.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the UDF repository (`proofs/algo_udf`, theorems `Repo.collision_accepted`, `Repo.delete_breaks

issues.title: [Rust] Index created on a label while another is populating is never populated, yet reports OPERATIONAL
issues.body:
### Summary

If a second index is created on a label while the first one is still being populated, the new field is often **never populated**. The index still turns `OPERATIONAL`, and the planner uses it, so queries through it silently return 0 rows. C returns the full count.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY ti "UNWIND range(0,29999) AS x CREATE (:L {a:x, b:x})"
GRAPH.QUERY ti "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.a)"
GRAPH.QUERY ti "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.b)"       -- sent right after, while (n.a) is populating
-- wait until CALL db.indexes() reports OPERATIONAL
GRAPH.QUERY ti "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.a >= 0 RETURN count(n)"   -- 30000
GRAPH.QUERY ti "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.b >= 0 RETURN count(n)"   -- 0      (plan: Node By Index Scan)
```

Out of 10 back-to-back rounds, 7 were wrong at 30k nodes and 8 at 100k (`b` = 0 each time). C: 0 of 5. With 300k nodes and a delay between the two `CREATE INDEX` (`proofs/search_concurrency/repro/twoidx.py`), it depends on timing.

### Mechanism

- `Indexer::create_index` (`graph/src/index/indexer.rs:319-331`) bumps the index generation (`bump_id`) only when it adds a vector field (`recreate_index`). For a range or fulltext field, the new population job gets a ticket in the **same** generation as the one still running.
- `populate_index_batch` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:510`) bails when `ticket_pending_changes(&ticket) > 1`. The new job (field snapshot `{a,b}`) is queued while the old job's batch holds the indexer lock. When the lock is released, it usually sees 2 pending tickets and bails first. The old job (snapshot `{a}`) then continues to the end and releases its ticket, `pending` reaches 0, and the index goes OPERATIONAL without `b`.

### Expected

Matches C: every field that is indexed covers all existing entities by the time the index is OPERATIONAL.

### Suggested fix

Bump the generation whenever a field is added to an existing entry, not only for vector fields. The stale job then fails `is_

issues.title: [Rust] Batched OPTIONAL MATCH emits NULL-fallback rows after matched rows (order differs from input and from C; low)
issues.body:
### Summary

Low severity. A batched `OPTIONAL MATCH` emits all of a batch's unmatched (NULL) rows **after** all of its matched rows, so the output order differs from the input order. openCypher leaves this order unspecified, but it shows through `collect()` and in results without `ORDER BY`, and C keeps input order.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:A {w:1}), (:A {w:2})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [3,1,2] AS x OPTIONAL MATCH (a:A {w:x}) RETURN collect(x)"
Rust: [1, 2, 3]
C:    [3, 1, 2]
```

### Mechanism

`OptionalOp::next_batched` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/optional.rs:172-186`), and the optional arm of `ApplyOp::next_batched` (`apply.rs:210-229`), emit each sub-plan output batch as soon as it is produced. Only after the sub-plan is exhausted do they gather the origins that never matched into one NULL-fallback batch. Per-row mode keeps input order.

### Expected (C behaviour)

Rows in input order: `[3, 1, 2]`.

### Why no fix yet

Interleaving the fallback rows means buffering all of the sub-plan's output for an input batch and re-gathering it by origin. That adds a copy and a gather to every batched OPTIONAL MATCH, which is a hot path, only to reproduce an order the language does not guarantee. A cheap special case would be: when the sub-plan produced exactly one output batch, merge it with the fallback rows by origin. That still costs a gather per batch. Filed so the divergence is on record. It is worth doing only if a zero-cost way appears, or if matching C's order becomes a requirement.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the correlated operators (`proofs/ops_apply`), theorems `optionalBatched_order_differs` (and `optionalBatched_perm_ref`: the output is only a permutation); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_apply.rs` (`bug_optional_fallback_rows_reordered`).

issues.title: [Rust] UDF result conversion alters values C round-trips: -0.0, maps with a constructor key, vecf32 with inf
issues.body:
### Summary

Three values that C passes through an identity UDF unchanged are altered or rejected by the Rust UDF result conversion (`js_to_value`):

| query (`rt.id = function(x){ return x; }`) | Rust | C |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RETURN rt.id(-0.0) AS z, 1/rt.id(-0.0)` | `Division by zero` (z is Int 0) | `-0`, `-inf` |
| `RETURN rt.id({constructor: {name: 'Date'}})` | `Date getTime error: Error converting from js 'undefined' into type 'function'` | the map |
| `RETURN rt.id({constructor: {name: 'RegExp'}})` | `'[object Object]'` (a string) | the map |
| `RETURN rt.id(vecf32([1e39]))` | `VecF32 element at index 0 is not finite` | `[inf]` |

(`main` @ 2363723ac, release build, compared with the C module on live servers.)

### Mechanism (`graph/src/udf/type_convert.rs`)

1. `:170-175`: every integral number with `|f| < 2^53` becomes `Value::Int`, and `-0.0 == floor(-0.0)`, so the sign is lost.
2. `:314-350`: Date / RegExp are detected by reading the object's `constructor.name` property, which a plain object (a Cypher map converted to JS) can carry as an own key.
3. `:239-241`: VecF32 elements must be finite, although `vecf32()` accepts inf and `value_to_js` produces them.

### Expected

Match C: -0.0 stays a Float; only real Date / RegExp objects (by internal class) convert to temporal / string values; any f32 round-trips in a VecF32.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the UDF marshalling (`proofs/algo_udf`, theorems `Marshal.neg_zero_not_preserved`, `Marshal.constructor_key_breaks_roundtrip`, `Marshal.vecf32_inf_not_roundtrip`); Rust repros `graph/tests/lean_algo_udf.rs::bug_udf_negative_zero_becomes_integer_zero`, `bug_udf_constructor_key_mistaken_for_date`, `bug_udf_vecf32_inf_rejected`.

issues.title: [Rust] A vector of the wrong dimension removes the entity from all indexes on its label
issues.body:
### Summary

When an entity's vector has a different dimension from the label's vector index, the entity drops out of **every** index on that label, including unrelated range and fulltext indexes. Index scans then miss it. C skips only the vector field and keeps the entity in the other indexes.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY vd "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.name)"
GRAPH.QUERY vd "CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v) OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}"
GRAPH.QUERY vd "CREATE (:L {name:'a', v:vecf32([1,2,3])})"
GRAPH.QUERY vd "MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.name='a' RETURN n.name"
Rust: (empty)       C: a
```

The same happens when the entity is indexed by background population, and when a later `SET` writes a wrong-dimension vector.

### Mechanism

`Document::set` (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:720-731`) adds every `VecF32` value to the vector field without checking the index's dimension. RediSearch rejects the whole document (all fields of the label share one spec and one document), so the entity is removed from every index on the label. C checks the dimension first and skips the vector field (`src/index/index.c:470-476`, "vector dimension mis-match, can't index this vector").

### Expected

Same as C: a vector of the wrong dimension is not added to the vector index, and the entity stays in the other indexes.

### Suggested fix

In `Document::set`, skip the vector field when `vec.len() != vector_options.dimension`.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Search.vector_dim_mismatch_drops_range_entry`, fix: `Search.fixed_doc_always_accepted`).

issues.title: [Rust] GRAPH.UDF LOAD rejects libraries that reference the graph global at top level
issues.body:
### Summary

`GRAPH.UDF LOAD` rejects a library that references the `graph` global at top level, although the runtime context defines `graph` and C loads it.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.UDF LOAD gg "var G = graph; falkor.register('f', function() { return typeof G.traverse; });"
-- Rust: ReferenceError: 'graph' is not defined
-- C:    OK, and RETURN gg.f() -> 'function'
```

### Mechanism

`setup_validate_globals` (`graph/src/udf/js_globals.rs:48-96`), used by `validate_script` at LOAD, defines only `falkor`; `setup_runtime_globals` also defines `graph` (traverse, getNodeById, iterateNodes, iterateEdges).

### Expected

Match C: the validation context defines the same `graph` global as the runtime.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the UDF layer (`proofs/algo_udf`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_algo_udf.rs::bug_udf_validation_context_lacks_graph`.

issues.title: [Rust] Matrix::decode leaks the container's five component vectors on every RDB load / RESTORE
issues.body:
### Summary

Every matrix loaded from an RDB / `GRAPH.RESTORE` / full sync leaks the five empty component vectors its `GxB_Container` was created with. On a 200k-node / 900k-edge graph plus 40 small graphs, `used_memory` grows by ~810 KB on every `DEBUG RELOAD`, without bound (80 reloads: 62.7 MB → 127.5 MB used_memory, RSS +66 MB).

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
# graph: 200k :A nodes, 9 relationship types (100k multi-edge pairs), plus 40 small graphs
# 2 warm-up DEBUG RELOADs, then 80 more:
reloads=80  RSS 282128KB -> 348400KB (+828.4 KB/reload)  used_memory 62692264 -> 127526856 (+810432 B/reload)
```

A small graph (`UNWIND range(1,100) AS i CREATE (a:A:B {v:i})-[:R]->(b:C {v:i}), (a)-[:R]->(b), (a)-[:S]->(b), (b)-[:T]->(a)`) grows ~30 KB per reload.

Loading a graph repeatedly keeps memory flat (C does not leak here), and a rejected container is a load error.

issues.title: [Rust] Filter after an aggregating WITH is pushed into one Cartesian branch (variable-id collision): 0 rows where C returns 2
issues.body:
### Summary

A MATCH that follows an aggregating `WITH` can lose all its rows. When the WHERE is an equality between two of its pattern parts, filter push-down puts the whole predicate into one branch of the Cartesian Product, where the other variable is unbound. Every row is then filtered out. This happens whenever an earlier clause bound enough variables for their ids to collide with the new ones. No write is needed: the CREATE in the original report only supplies the two colliding variables. It is not a pending-visibility problem.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:B {v:0}),(:B {v:5}) WITH count(*) AS s MATCH (b:B),(c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v RETURN count(*)"
-- Rust: 0        C: 2

GRAPH.RO_QUERY g "MATCH (x:B),(y:B) WITH count(*) AS s MATCH (b:B),(c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v RETURN count(*)"
-- Rust: 0        C: 2
```

The plan shows the predicate pushed under the `c` scan instead of becoming a Value Hash Join:

```
Aggregate
    Apply
        Aggregate
            Commit
                Create | (_anon_0:B), (_anon_1:B),
        Cartesian Product
            Node By Label Scan | (b:B)
                Argument
            Filter                      <- c.v = b.v, but b is not bound here
                Node By Label Scan | (c:B)
                    Argument
```

With a single pre-WITH variable (`MATCH (x) WITH count(*) ...`) or a non-aggregating `WITH 1 AS s`, the same query is planned as a Value Hash Join and returns the right count. The following also return 0 on main: `... WHERE c.v=b.v AND s > 0`, `WITH collect(x) AS s ... WHERE c.v >= b.v`, and `MATCH (b:B) MATCH (c:B) WHERE c.v=b.v` after the same WITH.

### Mechanism

A `Variable::id` is an index into its own scope's env, so ids start again at every `WITH`, and `x`/`y` (scope 0) share ids with `b`/`c` (scope 1). The optimizer's variable sets are keyed on `id` alone:

- `collect_subtree_variables` (`graph/src/planner/optimizer/mod.rs:102`) walks the entire subtree through `G

issues.title: [Rust] UDF getNeighbors / graph.traverse with returnType 'edges' return a self-loop twice
issues.body:
### Summary

In a JS UDF, `node.getNeighbors({returnType: 'edges'})` and `graph.traverse(..., {returnType: 'edges'})` return a self-loop twice.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.UDF LOAD nbr "falkor.register('e', function(x, d) { return x.getNeighbors({direction: d, returnType:'edges'}).map(function(y){ return y.id; }); });"
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {id:0})-[:R]->(b:A {id:1})-[:R]->(c:A {id:2}), (a)-[:R]->(a), (c)-[:S]->(a), (a)-[:R]->(b)"
-- edges: e0 a->b, e1 b->c, e2 a->a, e3 c->a, e4 a->b
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (n {id:0}) RETURN nbr.e(n, 'outgoing'), nbr.e(n, 'incoming'), nbr.e(n, 'both')"
-- Rust: [2, 0, 4, 2]   [3, 2, 2]   [3, 2, 0, 4, 2]
-- C:    [2, 0, 4]      [2, 3]      (C's 'both' returns only outgoing edges, [2, 0, 4])
```
`graph.traverse([n], {direction: d, returnType: 'edges'})` gives the same duplicates for 'outgoing' / 'incoming'.

### Mechanism

`collect_edges` (`graph/src/udf/js_classes.rs:97-127`) filters `Graph::get_node_relationships`, which yields a self-loop once as outgoing and once as incoming, by `src == node` / `dst == node` only, so both copies pass.

### Expected

Each self-loop reported once, as in C.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the UDF graph API (`proofs/algo_udf`, theorem `Neighbors.self_loop_twice`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_algo_udf.rs::bug_udf_get_neighbors_self_loop_twice`.

issues.title: [Rust] Huge k in db.idx.vector.queryNodes crashes the server (Vec::with_capacity(k))
issues.body:
### Summary

A very large `k` in `db.idx.vector.queryNodes` / `queryRelationships` crashes the server. A `k` near `i64::MAX` returns no rows. C returns all matching rows in both cases.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```
GRAPH.QUERY hk "CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v) OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'euclidean'}"
GRAPH.QUERY hk "CREATE (:L {v:vecf32([1,2])})"
GRAPH.QUERY hk "CALL db.idx.vector.queryNodes('L','v',1000000000000000,vecf32([1,2])) YIELD node RETURN count(node)"
Rust: Error: Server closed the connection        C: 1
```

After fixing the allocation, `k = 9223372036854775807` returns `0` rows (C: `1`).

### Mechanism

- `Graph::vector_query_nodes` / `vector_query_edges` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:3744,3799`) call `Vec::with_capacity(k)` with the user's `k`. That aborts on allocation failure, which kills the server.
- The unclamped `k` also goes to `RediSearch_CreateVecSimNode`. For `k` near `i64::MAX` the KNN iterator yields nothing.

### Expected

Same as C: the call returns every indexed entity when `k` is at least the index size.

### Suggested fix

Size the output by the number of results rather than by `k`, and clamp `k` to the entity count, which is an upper bound on the index size, before building the KNN query.

### Found by

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concurrency` (`Search.huge_k_kills_server`, fix: `Search.capped_capacity_ok`).

issues.title: [Rust] Concurrent drop of two Matrix clones (or a clone and an Iter) leaks the GrB_Matrix
issues.body:
### Summary

Two clones of a `Matrix` (or a clone and an `Iter` over it) dropped at the same time on different threads can both skip freeing the shared `GrB_Matrix`, which then leaks. MVCC snapshots and read queries on the thread pool clone matrices constantly, so this can happen in normal operation. No interleaving double-frees; it is a leak only.

### Reproduction (`main` @ 55204c94b)

100,000 `Matrix::<bool>::new(4, 4)` clone pairs (a third of them an `Iter` + the matrix), each pair dropped simultaneously on two threads, with a counting allocator installed into GraphBLAS:

```
assertion `left == right` failed: 9918 GraphBLAS blocks never freed
assertion `left == right` failed: 3678 GraphBLAS blocks never freed
assertion `left == right` failed: 5895 GraphBLAS blocks never freed      (3 runs)
```

(`graph/tests/lean_graphblas_wrappers.rs::bug_matrix_concurrent_drop_leaks`: 19–65 of 200,000 pairs leaked per run.)

### Mechanism

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/matrix.rs:388` (`Matrix::drop`) and `:1588` (`Iter::drop`):

```rust
if let Some(m) = Arc::get_mut(&mut self.m) { GrB_Matrix_free(m); }
// ... then the Arc field is dropped (decrement)
```

`Arc::get_mut` and the later decrement are two separate steps. With two owners: both check `get_mut` while the count is 2 (both `None`), then both decrement to 0; nobody frees the handle.

### Expected

Exactly one free when the last owner goes, whatever the thread interleaving.

### Suggested fix

Put the `GrB_Matrix_free` in the `Drop` of an owned handle type stored *inside* the `Arc` (`Arc<Handle>`), so the `Arc`'s own atomic count decides who frees.

### Found by

Lean 4 model of the ownership protocol (`proofs/graphblas_wrappers`, `Own.lean`: `race_leaks` witness, `never_double_free`, `sequential_frees_once`); Rust repro named above.

issues.title: [Rust] Index OPTIONS validation diverges from C (missing vector dimension/similarityFunction accepted, 'Euclidean' rejected, unknown fulltext keys ignored)
issues.body:
### Summary

Index `OPTIONS` validation differs from C in several ways. All come from one cause: `map_to_index_options` treats required vector options as optional and does not check fulltext option keys.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

| Query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE VECTOR INDEX FOR (n:A) ON (n.v)` (no OPTIONS) | `field type 0x0010 and the options block disagree about the vector half` | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {}` | accepted (dimension 0) | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {similarityFunction:'euclidean'}` (no dimension) | accepted (dimension 0: no vector can ever be indexed) | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {dimension:2}` (no similarityFunction) | accepted | `Invalid vector index configuration` |
| `... OPTIONS {dimension:2, similarityFunction:'Euclidean'}` / `'COSINE'` | `Unknown similarity function 'Euclidean'` | accepted (`strcasecmp`) |
| `CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... OPTIONS {foo:1}` | accepted, `foo` silently ignored | `invlaid index configuration` |

`graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs` `map_to_index_options`:

- `similarityFunction` is compared case-sensitively later on (`graph/src/index/mod.rs:1265`). C uses `strcasecmp`.
- The fulltext branch reads only the keys it knows and ignores the rest. C's `_validateOptions` rejects unknown keys.
- `index_ddl::create_index` passes `None` options for a vector index straight through.

### Expected / suggested fix

Match C: require `dimension` and `similarityFunction` for vector indexes (error prefix `Invalid vector index configuration`), match the similarity function case-insensitively and store it lowercase, and reject unknown fulltext option keys.

issues.title: [Rust] Write inside MULTI/EXEC fails with 'another write is in progress' while a queued write is still matching
issues.body:
### Summary

An inline write (inside `MULTI/EXEC`, and likewise Lua or any other path that must run on the main thread) fails with `another write is in progress, retry the query` whenever a queued write on the same graph is still in its read/match phase. The inline write is lost, even though nothing is actually writing yet. C executes it.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

A queued write with a slow match phase on one connection; 0.3 s later, `MULTI; GRAPH.QUERY mr "CREATE (:M)"; EXEC` on another (`proofs/search_concurrency/repro/multi_race.py`, with the UNWIND raised to 40M so the match phase lasts about 0.5 s):

```
Rust: multi = ['another write is in progress, retry the query']   count: N=1, Seed=1   (M missing)   2/2 runs
C:    multi = ['Labels added: 1', 'Nodes created: 1', ...]        count: M=1, N=1, Seed=1
```

(C sometimes crashes on this repro. That is a separate C bug.)

### Mechanism

`execute_query_write` (`src/graph_core.rs:748`) claims the MVCC write slot (`MvccGraph::write`, a CAS) at the **start** of the queued write, while the query is still a reader: no GIL, graph read lock only. It escalates to GIL + write lock lazily at its first mutation. The inline writer runs on the main thread holding the GIL (`QuerySession::begin_writer`) and takes the write lock once the queued query drops its read lock to escalate. Its own `graph.write()` CAS then fails because the slot belongs to the queued writer. That writer cannot make progress until the inline writer releases the GIL, so waiting is impossible and the only option today is the error.

### Design options

The fix changes the MVCC write-slot protocol, so here are the options for review before implementing.

**A. Claim the slot at escalation (optimistic, recommended).** The queued writer builds its private COW version without claiming the slot. When it escalates (GIL + write lock held), it claims the slot and checks that the committed version is still the base of its private version. I

issues.title: [Rust] Writes racing index population leave stale or resurrected index entries
issues.body:
### Summary

When writes run on a label while one of its indexes is being populated, the index can end up permanently inconsistent with the data: stale values stay indexed, and deleted entities can be resurrected in it. Index scans then return wrong counts until the entity is written again. C stays consistent.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

`proofs/search_concurrency/repro/poprace.py`: 200k `(:L {k, v:0})` nodes, a writer loop running `MATCH (n:L) WHERE n.k % 50 = $m SET n.v = n.v + 1`, and `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:L) ON (n.v)` while it runs. After quiescence it compares the index count per value with a label scan:

```
round 0: mismatches=[(0, 132000, 132400), (1, 64000, 63600)]      # (v, scan count, index count)
round 1: mismatches=[(0, 72000, 72200), (1, 88000, 87800)]
...
BAD ROUNDS 4 (of 4)       C: BAD ROUNDS 0 (of 3)
```

### Mechanism

- `populate_index_batch` (`graph/src/graph/graph.rs:~469`) builds documents from the **committed** graph (`indexer.get_graph()`).
- A writer publishes its index documents during the query (`Graph::commit_index*`, under the indexer lock), **before** its MVCC commit swaps in the new graph.
- A batch that runs between those two steps reads the pre-write value from the committed graph and overwrites the writer's newer document. The same happens for a deleted entity, which the batch re-adds. Nothing corrects it afterwards.

This is a different root cause from #3069 (the missing generation bump), though it hits the same population code.

### Expected

Same as C: once population finishes, the index matches the data, whatever writes ran during it.

### Suggested fix

While a generation is populating, record the ids whose documents a writer set or removed (under the indexer lock the batches already take). Batches skip those ids, because the writer's document comes from newer state. Clear the set when the generation's population completes or the generation is bumped.

Lean 4 model `proofs/search_concur

issues.title: [Rust] Serialized matrix headers (RDB, DUMP, GRAPH.COPY payloads) contain live heap addresses
issues.body:
### Summary

Every serialized matrix header contains live heap addresses of the writing process. `Matrix::encode` writes the whole 608-byte `GxB_Container` struct, including its `p`, `h`, `b`, `i`, `x` `GrB_Vector` pointers, into RDB files, `DUMP` payloads and the `GRAPH.RESTORE` payloads `GRAPH.COPY` replicates. Whoever can read one of these learns part of the server's heap layout. No reader uses the values: the decoder nulls them and rebuilds every component from the data that follows.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

`GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A)-[:R]->(b:B), (a)-[:R]->(b)"`, then `GRAPH.COPY g g2`, take the `GRAPH.RESTORE` payload from the AOF, and read the pointer words of each 608-byte container record (offsets 192..232):

```
15 container structs in payload; first p,h,b,i,x words:
  ['0x10277e000', '0x1091fe000', '0x1091fdf00', '0x1091fde00', '0x109c88700'], ...
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/graph/graphblas/matrix.rs:527-530` (`Encode<19> for Matrix<T>`): `w.write_buffer(slice::from_raw_parts(container, CONTAINER_STRUCT_SIZE))` after `GxB_unload_Matrix_into_Container`, so the struct's pointer fields hold the addresses of the unloaded component vectors. The C encoder does the same (`src/serializers/encoder/v19/encode_matrix.c`, `SerializerIO_WriteBuffer(rdb, container, sizeof(struct GxB_Container_struct))`).

### Expected

Serialized payloads carry no process addresses. Both decoders (Rust `Matrix::decode`, C `decode_matrix.c`) already null the component pointers before loading, so writing them as zero keeps every reader and the on-disk format compatible.

### Suggested fix

Copy the header and zero its pointer fields (`p h b i x`, `vector_future`, `Y`, `matrix_future`, `void_future`) before writing it. The C encoder could get the same change.

### Found by

Review of the Lean model of the GraphBLAS wrappers (`proofs/graphblas_wrappers`, "Suspicions / notes"), confirmed on a live payload.

issues.title: [Rust] Exponential backtracking on nested [(x {k: [...]})] lists: a 251-byte query spends 20 s in the parser
issues.body:
### Summary

The parser backtracks exponentially on nested `[(...)]` lists. A 251-byte query keeps a worker busy for 20 s in the parser alone, and every extra level of nesting doubles that. No graph data or valid query is needed: the time is spent before the query is rejected (or planned), so this is a cheap DoS. C is exponential on the same shape too (8 levels > 500 s), so this is not a regression; it is a hole in both engines.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 55204c94b)

```python
e = "1"
for _ in range(22):
    e = "[(x {k: " + e + "})]"
q = "RETURN " + e            # 251 bytes
```

```
$ time redis-cli GRAPH.QUERY g "$q"
'x' not defined
real 20.50
```

Parse time alone, in process (best of 5):

| levels | bytes | parse time |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 96 | 2.7 ms |
| 12 | 140 | 25 ms |
| 16 | 184 | 393 ms |
| 20 | 228 | 6.4 s |

The same happens with `[p = (x {k: …})]`, `[(x {k: …}) - 1]`, and in `WHERE (x {k: [ … ]})`.

### Mechanism

`parse_list_literal_or_comprehension` (`graph/src/parser/cypher.rs:2784-2803`) tries each `[` as a named, then an unnamed, pattern comprehension first. The attempt parses the node pattern `(x {k: …})` in full, including its property map. Only then does it find that no relationship follows, restore the position, and parse the same text again as a list literal. The map value holds the next `[(…)]`, which does the same thing inside both passes, so level *n* is parsed 2ⁿ times.

### Expected

Parse time proportional to what an equally nested list literal costs (`[{k: [{k: …}]}]`: 0.2 ms at 20 levels).

### Suggested fix

- Try the pattern comprehension only where it can succeed. A pattern comprehension has a `|` before the closing `]`, outside any nested bracket and before any top-level `,`. A list literal never has that `|`. A bracket-counting token scan can check this without parsing.
- Never repeat an attempt that already failed at the same position in the same context (`allow_pattern_predicate`, the forbidden-comprehension con

issues.title: [Rust] Decision: operator precedence where Rust follows openCypher and C does not (2^3^2, chained comparisons, STARTS WITH / IS NULL after +, SKIP (1))
issues.body:
### Decision needed: operator precedence where Rust follows openCypher and C does not

The Rust engine treats C as the reference, but in the cases below the Rust parser follows the openCypher grammar (`graph/src/Cypher.g4`) and C does not. Nothing here crashes. Each is a user-visible result difference between the engines, so each needs a decision: **keep the grammar behaviour (and document the C difference), or copy C.** This issue is for that decision; no PR is attached.

Results: Rust = release build of `main` @ 55204c94b. C = local `master` build of the C module (`bin/macos-arm64v8-release/falkordb.so`).

| # | Query | Rust | C | openCypher grammar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `RETURN 2^3^2` | `64` | `512` | `PowerOfExpression = Unary ( '^' Unary )*`, left-associative → `(2^3)^2 = 64` |
| 2a | `RETURN 1 = 1 = 1` | `true` | `false` | Comparisons chain: `a op1 b op2 c` = `a op1 b AND b op2 c` → `true` |
| 2b | `RETURN 1 < 2 < 3 < 0` | `false` | **`true`** | chained → `false` |
| 2c | `CREATE (:N {x:0})` then `MATCH (n:N) WHERE n.x = 0 = true RETURN count(n)` | `0` | `1` | chained: `n.x = 0 AND 0 = true` → `0` rows |
| 3a | `RETURN 'a' + 'b' STARTS WITH 'ab'` | `true` | `'afalse'` | `StringListNullPredicate` sits *below* `+`: `('a' + 'b') STARTS WITH 'ab'` → `true` |
| 3b | `RETURN 1 + 2 IS NULL` | `false` | `1` | `(1 + 2) IS NULL` → `false` |
| 3c | `RETURN - 1 IS NULL` | `false` | `Type mismatch: expected Integer, Float, or Null but was Boolean` | `(-1) IS NULL` → `false` |
| 3d | `RETURN 5.0 / 0 IS NULL` | `false` | same type mismatch | `(5.0 / 0) IS NULL` → `false` |
| 4 | `UNWIND [1,2,3] AS x RETURN x SKIP (1)` | `SKIP specified value of invalid type, must be a positive integer` | `[[2], [3]]` | `SKIP Expression` → accepted, `[[2], [3]]` |

### Notes per item

1. **`^` associativity.** Most languages make `^` right-associative, and C does. The openCypher grammar is explicitly left-associative. Neo4j is believed to follow it (64), but that was not checked here.

issues.title: [Rust] Chained anonymous undirected hops drop or duplicate rows: bidirectional dedup keys on the wrong tuple
issues.body:
### Summary

Two or more chained anonymous undirected hops (`(a)-[]-()-[]-(b)`) go through a cross-row `(source, destination)` dedup in `CondTraverse`. It is meant to reproduce C's matrix-multiply semantics: one row per *input record* and destination. The key it uses is wrong in three ways, so rows are silently dropped or duplicated:

1. It keys on the source **node**, not the input record, so rows that differ only in another column (`UNWIND [1,2] AS x ...`) are collapsed, and so are two equal input records.
2. At 3+ hops the source is the child traverse's `from` alias, which is an **intermediate** node, so rows from different start nodes collide.
3. The seen-set is **cleared per child batch**. When one start node's first hop spans more than one batch (> 1024 rows), its destinations are emitted once per batch.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:N {id:1})-[:R]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R]->(c:N {id:3})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,2] AS x MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-(b) RETURN x, a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 5 rows (all x=1).   C: 10 rows (5 per x)
GRAPH.QUERY g "UNWIND [1,1] AS x MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-(b) RETURN x, a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 5 rows.             C: 10 rows (one set per input record)
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:N {id:1})-[:R]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R]->(c:N {id:3})-[:R]->(d:N {id:4}), (b)-[:R]->(e:N {id:5})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a)-[]-()-[]-()-[]-(b) RETURN a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 7 rows (4|1, 4|3, 4|5, 5|2, 5|4 missing).   C: 12 rows
```

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (u:U {id:1}), (v:U {id:2}) WITH u, v UNWIND range(1,3000) AS i CREATE (u)-[:R]->(:L {id:i})<-[:R]-(v)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:U)-[]-()-[]-(b:U) RETURN a.id, b.id, count(*)"
-- Rust: 1|1|3, 1|2|3, 2|1|4, 2|2|4.   C: every count is 1
```

### Mechanism

`graph/src/runtime/ops/cond_traverse.rs`:
* `CondTraverseOp::new` (`:273-299`) picks `child_ct.relationship_pattern.from.alias` as the dedup source. For the third hop that is the first intermediate node, not the scan source.
* `expand_

issues.title: [Rust] Anonymous undirected hop returns each node pair twice when edges exist in both directions (CondTraverse and ExpandInto)
issues.body:
### Summary

An anonymous undirected single hop `(a)-[]-(b)` collapses parallel edges to one row per `(a, b)` pair (C semantics), but it does so separately for each stored direction. When edges exist in both directions between the same two nodes, every pair is returned twice. `ExpandInto` (both endpoints already bound) has the same bug.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (a:A {id:1})-[:R]->(b:B {id:2}), (b)-[:R]->(a), (a)-[:R]->(b)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a)-[]-(b) RETURN a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 1|2, 1|2, 2|1, 2|1     C: 1|2, 2|1
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a:A), (b:B) WITH a, b MATCH (a)-[]-(b) RETURN a.id, b.id"
-- Rust: 1|2, 1|2               C: 1|2
```

### Mechanism

* `CondTraverseOp::expand_row` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/cond_traverse.rs:876-942`) runs the forward and the reverse scan, and `process_pairs` (`:1063-1081`) keeps one representative edge per *matrix* pair in each. `a→b` and `b→a` are different matrix pairs that map to the same pattern pair.
* `ExpandIntoOp::expand_row` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/expand_into.rs:182-221`) probes `(src,dst)` and `(dst,src)` and keeps a representative from each.

### Expected

C: one row per pattern pair (the traversal matrix is `A + Aᵀ` over the boolean semiring), so 2 rows and 1 row above.

### Suggested fix

In collapse mode (anonymous edge, no edge filter), drop reverse-scan results whose pattern pair the forward scan already produced; in `ExpandInto`, stop after the first direction that yields an edge.

### Found by

Lean 4 model (`proofs/ops_traverse`, `CondTraverse.bidir_collapse_duplicates_pair`, `expandInto_bidir_collapse_two_rows`); Rust repro `graph/tests/lean_ops_traverse.rs::bug_undirected_anonymous_collapse_duplicates_pairs`.

issues.title: [Rust] allShortestPaths returns a directed cycle in reverse (relationships last-to-first)
issues.body:
### Summary

`allShortestPaths` whose source and destination are the same node (a cycle) returns the path in backtrack order for a directed pattern. Relationships come out last-to-first, so the path is not a walk in the pattern's direction: for `(a)-[*]->(a)` Rust walks the cycle against the arrows, and for `(a)<-[*]-(a)` along them.

C is also wrong here, in a different way: for both patterns it returns nodes `[0,2,1,0]` with relationships `[1,2,3]`, which is inconsistent for `->`.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (s:N {id:0})-[:R {w:1}]->(a:N {id:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R {w:3}]->(s)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}), (b {id:0}) WITH a, b MATCH p=allShortestPaths((a)-[*]->(b)) RETURN [n in nodes(p) | n.id], [r in relationships(p) | r.w]"
-- Rust: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [3, 2, 1]    C: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [1, 2, 3]    correct: [0, 1, 2, 0] | [1, 2, 3]
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}), (b {id:0}) WITH a, b MATCH p=allShortestPaths((a)<-[*]-(b)) RETURN [n in nodes(p) | n.id], [r in relationships(p) | r.w]"
-- Rust: [0, 1, 2, 0] | [1, 2, 3]    C: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [1, 2, 3]    correct: [0, 2, 1, 0] | [3, 2, 1]
```

Undirected cycles are palindromes today and are unaffected.

### Mechanism

`AllShortestPathsOp::expand_row` (`graph/src/runtime/ops/all_shortest_paths.rs:284-288`) backtracks from `dst` to `src`, so edges are collected last-to-first, and reverses them into `src→dst` order only when `src != dst` ("Cycles keep the DFS predecessor-chain order"). `PathBuilder` then walks the edge list from `a`, which for a cycle gives the reversed walk.

The flow test `test_all_shortest_paths.py::test06_all_shortest_cycle` encodes the wrong order for `->` and asserts that `->` and `<-` give the same node lists, which cannot both be walks.

### Expected

openCypher: a path matched by `(a)-[*]->(a)` is a walk along the relationships, so `nodes(p)` = `[0,1,2,0]` and `relationships(p)` = `[1,2,3]`; for `<-` the mirror image. This deliberately d

issues.title: [Rust] algo.SPpaths/SSpaths charge 0 per relationship without costProp, so maxCost limits nothing (C charges 1)
issues.body:
### Summary

`algo.SPpaths` / `algo.SSpaths` charge a cost of **0** per relationship when no `costProp` is given, so `maxCost` without `costProp` limits nothing and `pathCost` is always 0. C charges 1 per relationship (`GraphEntity_GetNumericPropertyOrDefault(..., SI_LongVal(1))`), so `maxCost` bounds the number of hops.

### Reproduction (release build, `main` @ 2363723ac)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (s:N {id:0})-[:R {w:1}]->(a:N {id:1})-[:R {w:2}]->(b:N {id:2})-[:R {w:3}]->(s), (b)-[:R {w:4}]->(c:N {id:3}), (s)-[:R {w:10}]->(c), (a)-[:R {w:1}]->(c), (c)-[:R {w:1}]->(c)"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (a {id:0}), (b {id:3}) CALL algo.SPpaths({sourceNode: a, targetNode: b, relTypes: ['R'], weightProp: 'w', maxCost: 1, pathCount: 0}) YIELD path, pathWeight, pathCost RETURN [n in nodes(path) | n.id], pathWeight, pathCost"
-- Rust: [0, 1, 3] | 2 | 0      C: [0, 3] | 10 | 1
```

| config (no `costProp`) | Rust | C |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SPpaths `maxCost: 1, pathCount: 0` | `[0,1,3]`, cost 0 | `[0,3]`, cost 1 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 0` | cost 0 | cost 2 |
| SPpaths `maxCost: 2, pathCount: 1` | cost 0 | cost 2 |
| SSpaths `maxCost: 1` / `pathCount: 1` | cost 0 | cost 1 |
| SPpaths `pathCount: 1` (Dijkstra fast path) | cost 0 | cost 0 |

`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2397` (`bfs_find_bound`) and `:2518` (the DFS enumeration shared by SPpaths/SSpaths) call `edge_numeric_attr(g, edge_id, config.cost_prop.as_ref(), 0.0)`: the `0.0` default applies both when `costProp` is not configured and when an edge lacks the property. C defaults both to 1.

C: 1 per relationship without `costProp` (or when the edge lacks it). C's Dijkstra fast path (`pathCount: 1`, no `maxCost`, no `maxLen`) reports `pathCost` 0 when no `costProp` is given (`_sum_path_cost`); Rust already matches that at `:2308`.

### Suggested fix

Default the cost to `1.0` at `:2397` and `:2518`, leaving the reporting-only Dijkstra sum at `:2308` as is.

issues.title: [Rust] duration() drops a trailing number that has no unit: duration('P5') returns PT0S
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`duration('P5')` and `duration('P-')` are accepted and return a zero-length duration (`PT0S`). A number with no unit after it is not a valid ISO 8601 duration, and the digits that follow the last unit are dropped without any error.

### Reproduction (release build, `main`)

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN duration('P5')"
-- Rust: PT0S
-- C:    null
-- Neo4j: error
```

The same happens for every spelling whose last component has no unit:

| query | Rust | C |
|---|---|---|
| `RETURN duration('P5')` | `PT0S` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P-')` | `PT0S` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1Y5')` | `P1Y` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('P1M2')` | `P1M` | `null` |
| `RETURN duration('PT4H5')` | `PT4H` | `null` |

Note the second half of the table: the trailing component is not merely a syntax error, it is **discarded**, so `duration('P1Y5')` silently means `P1Y`. A caller that builds the string by concatenation gets a different duration than it asked for, with no signal.

### Mechanism

`parse_duration_string` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/temporal.rs:347`) accumulates digits into `num_buf` and only converts them when a unit character (`Y`/`M`/`W`/`D`/`H`/`S`) closes them:

```rust
for ch in date_part.chars() {
    if ch.is_ascii_digit() || ch == '-' {
        num_buf.push(ch);
    } else {
        let n: i64 = num_buf.parse()...;
        num_buf.clear();
        match ch { 'Y' => years = n, ... }
    }
}
```

Neither loop inspects `num_buf` after it finishes, so whatever is left over is dropped.

### Expected

Reject the string, the way C and Neo4j both do. Checking `num_buf` for emptiness once, after the time part, is enough: the two loops share the buffer, and a non-empty buffer at that point can only mean "a number with no unit".

### Notes

`duration('P1DT')` (a trailing `T` with an empty time part) and `duration('PT1.5S')` (fractional seconds, truncated because durations have one-second resolution) are left alone - they are separate questions, tracked in #2595

issues.title: [Rust] algo.SPpaths/SSpaths: a costProp an edge does not have contributes 0, not 1 (C parity; pathCost under-reported and maxCost prunes differently)
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`algo.SPpaths` / `algo.SSpaths` under-report `pathCost` when `costProp` names a property that a relationship on the path does not have. C contributes `1` for such an edge; Rust contributes `0`.

Split out of #343, which asks for two things at once. This is the half that is a C-parity bug and can be fixed without a policy decision. The other half of #343 - replacing a *negative or zero* weight or cost with 1 - is not a parity bug: C does not clamp either (`Dijkstra.h:21-31` states non-negative weights as an unguarded precondition), so that half is a Rust-vs-C policy choice for a maintainer and is deliberately not addressed here.

### Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "CREATE (:L {id:'A'})-[:E {weight:1, cost:2}]->(:L {id:'B'})-[:E2 {weight:1}]->(:L {id:'C'})"
GRAPH.QUERY g "MATCH (s:L {id:'A'}), (t:L {id:'C'})
              CALL algo.SPpaths({sourceNode: s, targetNode: t,
                                 weightProp: 'weight', costProp: 'cost'})
              YIELD pathWeight, pathCost RETURN pathWeight, pathCost"
```

`costProp: 'cost'` is configured, and `:E2` does not have a `cost` property.

| engine | pathWeight | pathCost |

| Rust `main` | 2 | **1** |

`edge_numeric_attr` (`graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs:2104`) takes a single `default` and uses it for two different C cases:

```rust
        Some(Value::Int(i)) => i as f64,
        _ => default,
```

issues.title: [Rust] date()/localtime() drop every non-digit from a compact string: date('2o15o7o21') silently returns 2015-07-21
issues.body:
﻿### Summary

`date()` and `localtime()` accept arbitrary junk embedded in a compact (separator-less) string. Every non-digit character is silently dropped before the string is interpreted, so a malformed input returns a valid-looking value with no error.

### Reproduction

```
GRAPH.QUERY g "RETURN toString(date('2o15o7o21'))"
-- Rust: '2015-07-21'
-- C:    error
```

The `o`s vanish and the result is indistinguishable from the correct answer. Same for:

| query | Rust | expected |

FalkorDB 4.16.7 can persist a staged UPDATE_EDGE after deletion
issues.body:
### Summary

In a disposable test using FalkorDB 4.16.7, I reproduced a conditional ordering where an edge update is staged, a main-thread execution path deletes the edge before the updater commits, and the already-staged UPDATE_EDGE is persisted after the deletion.

This reports the reproduced behavior; it does not establish that this mechanism caused any particular production incident.

### Observed behavior

I paused an updater after it staged an edge-property update and before commit, then compared two cleanup paths:

- **Normal writer path:** a normal GRAPH.QUERY cleanup remained queued behind the updater. The update effect persisted before the deletion effect.
- **Main-thread bypass path:** a MULTI/EXEC cleanup deleted the edge while the updater was paused. The cleanup persisted first. When the updater resumed, the graph mutation was skipped because the edge had been deleted, but its previously staged UPDATE_EDGE effect was still persisted afterward.

The second schedule produced this synthetic AOF order:

```text
create GRAPH.EFFECT
cleanup GRAPH.QUERY
stale UPDATE_EDGE in GRAPH.EFFECT
```

The synthetic edge ID was 0. The test used disposable generated data and did not use production AOF/RDB inputs.

### Reproduction notes

The test used a controlled pause at `QueryCtx_LockForCommit` after update evaluation/effect staging:

1. Start an updater that stages an edge-property update.
2. Pause it before commit.
3. Submit deletion through the normal writer path (control), then repeat with the MULTI/EXEC main-thread path.
4. Resume the updater and inspect persisted command order.

Environment: FalkorDB 4.16.7, image `falkordb/falkordb:v4.16.7`; Redis 8.2.3.

The attached ZIP contains the synthetic AOF result fixtures for both cases and per-file SHA-256 checksums. They are captured outputs, not a standalone driver for reproducing the scheduling race. The two cases use separately generated base RDB files with logically equivalent initial state; the bases are not byte

Bug: `--requirepass` (and other CLI args) silently ignored on `falkordb/falkordb-server` image
issues.body:
### Summary

Passing Redis CLI arguments to the `falkordb/falkordb-server` container — e.g. the standard Redis-image convention `docker run falkordb/falkordb-server --requirepass <password>` — silently has no effect. The server starts with no authentication configured, with no error or warning printed anywhere.

### Affected version

`v4.20.7` (also reproduced on current `master`).

### Root cause

The image's `ENTRYPOINT` is `build/docker/run.sh`. That script execs `redis-server` itself and only splices in the `${REDIS_ARGS}` and `${FALKORDB_ARGS}` **environment variables** — it never forwards its own positional arguments (`"$@"`) into the command it runs:

```sh
# build/docker/run.sh
else
    exec redis-server ${REDIS_ARGS} --protected-mode no \
        --dir "${FALKORDB_DATA_PATH}" \
        --loadmodule "${FALKORDB_BIN_PATH}/falkordb.so" ${FALKORDB_ARGS}
fi
```

Any arguments appended after the image name on `docker run` (e.g. `--requirepass foo`) become positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …) to `run.sh` via `ENTRYPOINT`, but the script never references `$1`/`$2`/`"$@"` anywhere, so they are silently dropped before `redis-server` is invoked.

This appears to date back to #1027 (switching the image from `CMD`-only to `ENTRYPOINT` + `CMD`) — the script was never updated to forward its arguments after that change.

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
docker run -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb-server:v4.20.7 --requirepass mysecret
# in another shell:
redis-cli -p 6379 PING
# expected: (error) NOAUTH Authentication required.
# actual:   PONG   (no password required at all)
```

### Expected behavior

`--requirepass mysecret` (or any other redis-server CLI flag passed after the image name) should be honored, matching the behavior of the upstream `redis` image and standard Docker `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` conventions.

### Actual behavior

The flag is accepted by Docker but never reaches the `redis-server` process. No error, warning, or log line indicates it was dropped.

issues.title: Exit with a distinct code when a data load fails
issues.body:
When Redis fails to load an RDB or AOF it exits with a hard-coded status: `exit(1)`, or `exit(0)` when the `redis-check-rdb` pass it runs in-process after a failed load from a file finds the file structurally sound (for example when FalkorDB rejects a graph whose checksum is valid). Whatever restarts the server (Kubernetes, systemd, an entrypoint script) therefore can't tell a failed load from a clean shutdown or any other startup error, and can't react to it, e.g. by moving a bad local `dump.rdb` aside so a replica resyncs instead of crash-looping on it.

The module API has no way to set the exit code. FalkorDB can still do it: track whether a load is in progress with the `Loading` and `CronLoop` server events, and replace the exit status with a dedicated code (`EX_DATAERR`, 65) from an `atexit()` handler when the process exits mid-load.

Builds on #3141.

issues.title: Path finding issues - A* suboptimal paths, SPpaths pathCost, Yen cost prop
issues.body:
three post-merge review findings on the Yen/A*/all-shortest work:

    A* returned suboptimal paths when only some nodes have lat/lon: the haversine heuristic is admissible but inconsistent across coordinate / coordinate-less nodes, and AStarCtx_Run never reopened finalized nodes. Now a strictly shorter g to an already-finalized node reopens and re-expands it, restoring optimality; all-coords graphs stay consistent so no reopening occurs.

    algo.SPpaths pathCost regressed to 0 without costProp for the accelerated pathCount:0 / pathCount>1 paths (the DFS reported hop count). _sum_path_cost now sums a default of 1 per edge, so pathCost is the hop count without costProp -- matching the DFS -- across all pathCount values.

    The Yen fast path selected k paths by (weight, length), ignoring costProp, diverging from the DFS among equal-weight ties. Thread cost_prop (may be ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE) into Yen_KShortestPaths / AStar_KShortestPaths and select by (weight, cost, length) -- matching path_cmp so selection and reported order agree. Without costProp, cost == hop count == length, so weight-only queries are unaffected.

Schema-mutating commands bypass the single-writer election → schema/matrix corruption (crash or duplicate-label-id RDB)
issues.body:
GRAPH.CONSTRAINT (async worker thread) and GRAPH.EFFECT (main thread) acquire the graph write lock directly, outside the write_in_progress/pending_write_queue election that serializes GRAPH.QUERY writes. Because the GraphContext.writelocked reentrancy flag isn't thread-aware, a concurrent worker-thread query write and one of these commands can each skip the other's lock and mutate the shared schema/attribute arrays + label/relation matrices at the same time.

Result: a torn realloc → SIGSEGV, or a silently-corrupt graph where the schema block carries a duplicate label/relationship-type id (or schema-count ≠ matrix-count) that gets serialized into the RDB and then crashes any server that loads it — the customer-reported symptom.

A pattern such as `()-[r:T1|T2|…|Tk]->()` with more than 255 relationship types returns wrong results. The server returns no error.
`EdgeTraverseCtx.n_rels` is a `uint8_t`, so the type count wraps modulo 256. The edge collection then uses only the first `k mod 256` types.

The source history shows the bug in the C engine from v4.18.3 and v4.20.0, and in the C `master` branch. We tested v4.18.11, v4.20.7 and v4.22.0, and all three have the bug. v4.18.2 and the Rust engine (6.0.1) give correct results.

issues.title: CI: coverage jobs fail since Rust 1.99 (raw profile v11 vs llvm-profdata-22)
issues.body:
Since `rustup default stable` started resolving to **Rust 1.99.0** (released 2026-09-28), every coverage job in the Rust PR workflow fails at the merge step. That's the `coverage` job and every `coverage-flow` cell, 78–88 failed jobs per run. The tests themselves pass.

```
raw profile version mismatch: Profile uses raw profile format version = 11; expected version = 10
error: no profile can be merged
```

**Cause:** Rust 1.99 is built on LLVM 23, which writes raw coverage profiles in format v11. The workflows merge them with `llvm-profdata-22` / `llvm-cov-22` from the LLVM 22 toolchain image, and those only read v10.

| run | rustc | coverage |
|---|---|---|
| merge queue for #3153 (2026-10-01) | 1.98.1 | ✅ |
| #3161 and today's dependabot PRs (2026-10-04) | 1.99.0 | ❌ |

Affected: `_flow-artifact.yml`, `_flow-flavour.yml`, `rust-pr.yml`, `rust-push.yml`. It hits every PR regardless of content.

**Fix:** move the toolchain (and everything that references LLVM 22) to LLVM 23. Doing so also needs `build/libomp.sh` updated, because LLVM 23 removed OpenMP's standalone CMake build.

issues.title: `point({x, y})` rejects Cartesian coordinates and incorrectly requires latitude/longitude
issues.body:
### FalkorDB version

```text
FalkorDB v4.20.7
Docker image: falkordb/falkordb:v4.20.7
```

### Description

FalkorDB rejects Cartesian point construction using `x` and `y` coordinates:

```cypher
RETURN point({x: 2.3, y: 4.5}) AS p;
```

with the error:

```text
Did not find 'latitude' value in point map
```

The same query succeeds on Neo4j, Memgraph, and ArcadeDB.

This appears to be a Cypher compatibility issue in `point()` handling: FalkorDB treats every point map as a geographic latitude/longitude point and does not recognize the Cartesian `{x, y}` form.

### Minimal reproduction

No graph data is required.

Run:

```cypher
RETURN point({x: 2.3, y: 4.5}) AS p;
```

### Actual behavior

FalkorDB returns an error:

```text
Did not find 'latitude' value in point map
```

The query is therefore rejected before a Cartesian point can be constructed.

### Expected behavior

The `{x, y}` map should be accepted as a Cartesian point.

For example, the equivalent result on comparison engines represents a point with:

```text
x = 2.3
y = 4.5
CRS = cartesian
```

### Cross-engine comparison

| Engine | Result |
| --- | --- |
| FalkorDB v4.20.7 | ERROR: `Did not find 'latitude' value in point map` |
| Neo4j | SUCCESS: Cartesian point `(2.3, 4.5)` |
| Memgraph | SUCCESS: Cartesian point `(2.3, 4.5)` |
| ArcadeDB | SUCCESS: `{crs: "cartesian", x: 2.3, y: 4.5}` |

The behavior was reproduced consistently in two independent runs.

### Control query

Geographic point construction uses latitude and longitude:

```cypher
RETURN point({latitude: 2.3, longitude: 4.5}) AS p;
```

The failing case is specifically the Cartesian coordinate representation:

```cypher
RETURN point({x: 2.3, y: 4.5}) AS p;
```

### Why this looks like a bug

The error indicates that FalkorDB unconditionally expects a `latitude` field when evaluating a point map.

However, `{x, y}` represents a different point coordinate system rather than a malformed latitude/longitude point.
